For many categories (monoids, modules, rings, ...) the set-theoretic image of a morphism  is
a subobject of the codomain. When this is the case, it is useful to define the range of a morphism
in such a way that the underlying carrier set of the range subobject is definitionally
. In particular this means that the types  and  are
interchangeable without proof obligations.

A convenient candidate definition for range which is mathematically correct is , just as
 could have been defined as . However, this lacks the desired definitional
convenience, in that it both does not match , and that it introduces a redundant
term which clutters proofs. In such a case one may resort to the
pattern. A  function converts the definitional problem for the carrier set of a subobject
into a one-off propositional proof obligation which one discharges while writing the definition of
the definitionally convenient range (the parameter  in the example below).

A good example is the case of a morphism of monoids. A convenient definition for
 would be . However since this lacks the required
definitional convenience, we first define  as follows:
and then finally define:

### Implementation details

When adding new definitions that transfer type-classes across an equivalence, please use
. See note [reducible non-instances].

For many type classes, we have a definition that lets us transfer instances from one type to another
using an equivalence, such as  for .
Constructing data instances in this way is discouraged because the resulting data is inefficient
to unfold. To somewhat mitigate this problem, in these definitions we don't write the
projections on  in the usual way using  and , and instead use
 and  directly. As a result, unification has to do less unfolding.

Note also that when constructing data instances in this way, it usually helps to use
 to get a faster instance.

See note [instance transfer via equivalence]

# Unique products and related notions

A group  has *unique products* if for any two non-empty finite subsets , there is an
element  that can be written uniquely as a product of an element of  and an element
of .  We call the formalization this property .  Since the condition requires no
property of the group operation, we define it for a Type simply satisfying .  We also
introduce the analogous "additive" companion, , and link the two so that
converts  into .

A common way of *proving* that a group satisfies the  property is by assuming
the existence of some kind of ordering on the group that is well-behaved with respect to the
group operation and showing that minima/maxima are the "unique products/sums".
However, the order is just a convenience and is not part of the  setup.

  maximal ideal is again contained in the unique maximal ideal. This
  is developed earlier, and in the generality of monoids, as it allows

# Groups with an adjoined zero element

This file describes structures that are not usually studied on their own right in mathematics,
namely a special sort of monoid: apart from a distinguished “zero element” they form a group,
or in other words, they are groups with an adjoined zero element.

Examples are:

* division rings;
* the value monoid of a multiplicative valuation;
* in particular, the non-negative real numbers.

## Main definitions

Various lemmas about  and .
To reduce import dependencies, the type-classes themselves are in
.

## Implementation details

As is usual in mathlib, we extend the inverse function to the zero element,
and require .

To match .

To match .

In a monoid with zero, if zero equals one, then zero is the only element.

In a monoid with zero, if zero equals one, then zero is the unique element.

Somewhat arbitrarily, we define the default element to be .
All other elements will be provably equal to it, but not necessarily definitionally equal.

# Documentation of the algebraic hierarchy

A library note giving advice on modifying the algebraic hierarchy.
(It is not intended as a "tour".) This is ported directly from the Lean3 version, so may
refer to files/types that currently only exist in mathlib3.

## TODO

Add sections about algebra-order and algebra-topology mixins and interactions with
normed typeclasses.

# The algebraic hierarchy

In any theorem proving environment,
there are difficult decisions surrounding the design of the "algebraic hierarchy".

There is a danger of exponential explosion in the number of gadgets,
especially once interactions between algebraic and order/topological/etc. structures are considered.

In mathlib, we try to avoid this by only introducing new algebraic typeclasses either
1. when there is "real mathematics" to be done with them, or
2. when there is a meaningful gain in simplicity by factoring out a common substructure.

(As examples, at this point we don't have , or ,
but we do have ,  and !
We also have , as an exemplar of point 2.)

Generally in mathlib we use the extension mechanism (so  extends )
rather than mixins (e.g. with separate  and  classes),
in part because of the potential blow-up in term sizes described at

However there is tension here, as it results in considerable duplication in the API,
particularly in the interaction with normed structures.

This library note is not intended as a design document
justifying and explaining the history of mathlib's algebraic hierarchy!
Instead it is intended as a developer's guide, for contributors wanting to extend
(either new leaves, or new intermediate classes) the algebraic hierarchy as it exists.

(Ideally we would have both a tour guide to the existing hierarchy,
and an account of the design choices.
See  for an overview of mathlib as a whole,
with some attention to the algebraic hierarchy and

for a summary of what is in mathlib today.)

## Instances

When adding a new typeclass  to the algebraic hierarchy
one should attempt to add the following constructions and results,
when applicable:

* Instances transferred elementwise to products, like .
  See  for more examples.
* Instances transferred elementwise to pi types, like .
  See  for more examples.
* Instances transferred to , like .
  See  for more examples.
* Instances transferred to , like .
  See  for more examples.
* Definitions for transferring the proof fields of instances along
  injective or surjective functions that agree on the data fields,
  like  and .
  We make these definitions , see note [reducible non-instances].
  See  for more examples.
* Instances transferred elementwise to s, like .
  See  for more examples.
* Instances transferred elementwise to s, like .
  See  for more examples.
* Definitions for transferring the entire structure across an equivalence, like .
  See  for more examples. See also the
  tactic.

## Subobjects

When a new typeclass  adds new data fields,
you should also create a new   with a  field.

This can be a lot of work; for now try to closely follow the existing examples
(e.g. , , ).
We would very much like to provide some automation here, but a prerequisite will be making
all the existing APIs more uniform.

If  extends , then  should usually extend .

When  adds only new proof fields to an existing structure ,
you should provide instances transferring

Typically this is done using the  definition mentioned above.

## Morphisms and equivalences

## Category theory

For many algebraic structures, particularly ones used in representation theory, algebraic geometry,
etc., we also define "bundled" versions, which carry  instances.

These bundled versions are usually named by appending ,
so for example we have  as a bundled , and
(which bundles together , , and ).

These bundled versions have many appealing features:
* a uniform notation for morphisms
* a uniform notation (and definition) for isomorphisms
* a uniform API for subobjects, via the partial order
* interoperability with unbundled structures, via coercions to
  (so if , you can treat  as a type,
  and it automatically has an  instance)
  and lifting maps , when  is a type with an  instance.

If, for example you do the work of proving that a typeclass  has a good notion of tensor product,
you are strongly encouraged to provide the corresponding  instance
on a bundled version.
This ensures that the API for tensor products is complete, and enables use of general machinery.
Similarly if you prove universal properties, or adjunctions, you are encouraged to state these
using categorical language!

One disadvantage of the bundled approach is that we can only speak of morphisms between
objects living in the same type-theoretic universe.
In practice this is rarely a problem.

# Making a pull request

With so many moving parts, how do you actually go about changing the algebraic hierarchy?

We're still evolving how to handle this, but the current suggestion is:

* If you're adding a new "leaf" class, the requirements are lower,
  and an initial PR can just add whatever is immediately needed.
* A new "intermediate" class, especially low down in the hierarchy,
  needs to be careful about leaving gaps.

In a perfect world, there would be a group of simultaneous PRs that basically cover everything!
(Or at least an expectation that PRs may not be merged immediately while waiting on other
PRs that fill out the API.)

However "perfect is the enemy of good", and it would also be completely reasonable
to add a TODO list in the main module doc-string for the new class,
briefly listing the parts of the API which still need to be provided.
Hopefully this document makes it easy to assemble this list.

Another alternative to a TODO list in the doc-strings is adding Github issues.

Some definitions that define objects of a class cannot be instances, because they have an
explicit argument that does not occur in the conclusion. An example is  that has a
function  as an explicit argument to lift a preorder on  to a preorder on .

If these definitions are used to define instances of this class *and* this class is an argument to
some other type-class so that type-class inference will have to unfold these instances to check
for definitional equality, then these definitions should be marked .

For example,  is used to define  and  is used
to define . In some cases it is important that type-class inference can
recognize that  and  give rise to the same  instance.
For example, you might have another class that takes  as an argument, and this argument
sometimes comes from  and sometimes from .
Therefore,  and  are marked .

There are places where typeclass arguments are specified with implicit  brackets instead of
the usual  brackets. This is done when the instances can be inferred because they are implicit
arguments to the type of one of the other arguments. There are several reasons for doing so.

When they can be inferred from these other arguments,
it is faster to use this method than to use type class inference.
For example, when writing lemmas about , it is faster to specify the fact that
and  are s as  rather than the usual
.

When handling non-canonical instances, it is necessary that the relevant declarations take these
instance arguments implicitly, otherwise Lean will refuse to apply them.
For example, in measure theory a space  will often come equipped with a canonical base
sigma-algebra  along with many sub-sigma algebras, also of type
. In homological algebra,  appears regularly as the category of
abelian groups, but terms  come with two (propeq)  instances:
one from being -modules, and one from being abelian groups.

Certain instances always apply during type-class resolution. For example, the instance
 applies to all type-class
resolution problems of the form , and type-class inference will then do an
exhaustive search to find a commutative group. These instances take a long time to fail.
Other instances will only apply if the goal has a certain shape. For example
 or
. Usually these instances
will fail quickly, and when they apply, they are almost always the desired instance.
For this reason, we want the instances of the second type (that only apply in specific cases) to
always have higher priority than the instances of the first type (that always apply).
See also mathlib#1561.

Therefore, if we create an instance that always applies, we set the priority of these instances to
100 (or something similar, which is below the default value of 1000).

Certain instances only apply if the goal has a certain shape. For example
 or .
Usually these instances will fail quickly, and when they apply, they are almost always
the desired instance. For performance reasons it is sometimes useful to increase the
priority of these instances, especially if they are defined very early on in mathlib
(which would mean that they would be tried very late if they had the default priority).

Therefore, if we create an instance that only applies in specific circumstances, and that
is essentially always the right answer when it does apply, we may want to set the
priority of these instances to 1100 (or something similar, which is above the default
value of 1000).

When type class inference applies an instance, it attempts to solve the sub-goals from left to
right (it used to be from right to left in lean 3). For example in
we make sure to write  on the left of  to avoid an expensive
search for  when there is no instance for .

This helps to speed up failing type class searches, for example those triggered by  lemmas.

In some situations, we can't reorder type class assumptions because one depends on the other,
for example in
where the  instance appears in . Future work may be done to improve the
type class synthesis order in this situation.

The algebraic hierarchy is designed so that commutativity (e.g., of multiplication) is bundled
into the type class, so that we have, for example  and ,  and ,
etc.

It is often the case that one may desire to work with a commutative subobject inside an
ambient noncommutative type. In cases like  or , the subobject is
*always* commutative, and in these cases one should simply imbue those subobjects (coerced to
) with the appropriate  instance. However, in other cases, the commutativity of the
subobject may be conditional on commutativity of some other object. For example,
 is not always commutative, but it is when  is a commutative subset.
Likewise, if  is a commutative subgroup, then  is also
commutative.

For such scenarios, users should prefer to use the unbundled  typeclass, and to
provide theorems such as:
or even *instances* such as
and
Note that we prefer to name these instances manually because they are occasionally useful as
theorems. For example, the proof of the topological closure instance for subgroups above is proved
immediately from the one for monoids via: .

In practice, we wish to be able to use the library of theorems about (bundled) commutativity for
subobjects as well, and so we also provide instances which take as input the unbundled

deleterious effects to type class synthesis for bundled commutativity (by forcing Lean to search
the entirery of both the bundled and unbundled hierarchies), these instances are only
available inside the  scope and are simultaneously given the very low priority

# Morphisms to K-injective complexes in the derived category

In this file, we show that if  is K-injective,
then for any , the functor
induces a bijection from the type of morphisms
(i.e. homotopy classes of morphisms of cochain complexes) to the type of
morphisms in the derived category.
We obtain that a morphism between -injective cochain complexes is a quasi-isomorphism
iff it is a homotopy equivalence. In particular, a morphism between cochain complexes
indexed by  which consist of injective objects is a quasi-isomorphism iff
it is a homotopy equivalence.

When  is a K-injective cochain complex, cohomology classes
in  identify to elements in a type  relatively
to quasi-isomorphisms.

# Euler characteristic of homological complexes

The Euler characteristic is defined using the  typeclass,
which provides the alternating signs for each index. This allows the definition to work
uniformly for chain complexes, cochain complexes, and complexes with other index types.

The definitions work on graded objects, with the homological complex versions
defined as abbreviations that apply the graded object versions to  and .

 (0 for modules not free of finite rank).

quasi-isomorphisms and the fibrations are those morphisms
that are degreewise epimorphisms with an injective kernel.

# Exact functors

In this file, it is shown that additive functors which preserves homology
also preserves finite limits and finite colimits.

## Main results

Let  be an additive functor:

- : if  preserves homology,
  then  preserves finite limits.
- : if  preserves homology, then
  preserves finite colimits.

If we further assume that  and  are abelian categories, then we have:

- : the following are equivalent:
  1. for every short exact sequence ,
      is exact.
  2. for every exact sequence  where  is mono,
      is exact and  is mono.
  3.  preserves kernels.
  4.  preserves finite limits.

- : the following are equivalent:
  1. for every short exact sequence ,
      is exact.
  2. for every exact sequence  where  is epi,
      is exact and  is epi.
  3.  preserves cokernels.
  4.  preserves finite colimits.

- : the following are equivalent:
  1. for every short exact sequence ,
      is exact.
  2. for every exact sequence ,  is exact.
  3.  preserves homology.
  4.  preserves both finite limits and finite colimits.

An additive functor which preserves homology preserves finite limits.

An additive which preserves homology preserves finite colimits.

if  is exact then  is exact)
then it preserves monomorphism.

  then  is exact.

  is mono, then  is exact and  is mono as well.

If a functor  preserves exact sequences on the right-hand side (i.e.
if  is exact then  is exact),
then it preserves epimorphisms.

For an additive functor  between abelian categories, the following are equivalent:

-  preserves exact sequences on the right-hand side, i.e. if  is exact where
  is epi, then  is exact and  is epi as well.

# The snake lemma

The snake lemma is a standard tool in homological algebra. The basic situation
is when we have a diagram as follows in an abelian category , with exact rows:

    L₁.X₁ ⟶ L₁.X₂ ⟶ L₁.X₃ ⟶ 0
      |       |       |
      |v₁₂.τ₁ |v₁₂.τ₂ |v₁₂.τ₃
      v       v       v
0 ⟶ L₂.X₁ ⟶ L₂.X₂ ⟶ L₂.X₃

We shall think of this diagram as the datum of a morphism  in the
category  such that both  and  are exact, and  is epi
and  is a mono (which is equivalent to saying that  is the cokernel
of  and  is the kernel of ). Then, we may introduce the kernels
and cokernels of the vertical maps. In other words, we may introduce short complexes
 and  that are respectively the kernel and the cokernel of . All these
data constitute a .

Given such a , we define a connecting homomorphism
 and show that it is part of an exact sequence
. Each of the four exactness
statement is first stated separately as lemmas , ,
 and  and the full 6-term exact sequence is stated
as . This sequence can even be extended with an extra
on the left (see ) if  is a mono (i.e.  is short exact),
and similarly an extra  can be added on the right ()
if  is an epi (i.e.  is short exact).

These results were also obtained in the Liquid Tensor Experiment. The code and the proof
here are slightly easier because of the use of the category ,
the use of duality (which allows to construct only half of the sequence, and deducing
the other half by arguing in the opposite category), and the use of "refinements"
(see ) instead of a weak form of pseudo-elements.

A snake input in an abelian category  consists of morphisms
of short complexes  (which should be visualized vertically) such
that  and  are respectively the kernel and the cokernel of ,
 and  are exact,  is epi and  is mono.

# Jordan rings

Let  be a non-unital, non-associative ring. Then  is said to be a (commutative, linear) Jordan
ring if the multiplication is commutative and satisfies a weak associativity law known as the
Jordan Identity: for all  and  in ,
i.e. the operators of multiplication by  and  commute.

A more general concept of a (non-commutative) Jordan ring can also be defined, as a
(non-commutative, non-associative) ring  where, for each  in , the operators of left and
right multiplication by  and  commute.

Every associative algebra can be equipped with a symmetrized multiplication (characterized by
) making it into a commutative Jordan algebra ().
Jordan algebras arising this way are said to be special.

A real Jordan algebra  can be introduced by

## Main results

-  : Linearisation of the commutative Jordan axiom

## Implementation notes

We shall primarily be interested in linear Jordan algebras (i.e. over rings of characteristic not
two) leaving quadratic algebras to those better versed in that theory.

The conventional way to linearise the Jordan axiom is to equate coefficients (more formally, assume
that the axiom holds in all field extensions). For simplicity we use brute force algebraic expansion
and substitution instead.

## Motivation

Every Jordan algebra  has a triple product defined, for   and  in  by
$$
{a\,b\,c} = (a * b) * c - (a * c) * b + a * (b * c).
$$
Via this triple product Jordan algebras are related to a number of other mathematical structures:
Jordan triples, partial Jordan triples, Jordan pairs and quadratic Jordan algebras. In addition to
their considerable algebraic interest ([mccrimmon2004]) these structures have been shown to have
deep connections to mathematical physics, functional analysis and differential geometry. For more
information about these connections the interested reader is referred to [alfsenshultz2003],
[chu2012], [friedmanscarr2005], [iordanescu2003] and [upmeier1987].

There are also exceptional Jordan algebras which can be shown not to be the symmetrization of any
associative algebra. The 3x3 matrices of octonions is the canonical example.

Non-commutative Jordan algebras have connections to the Vidav-Palmer theorem
[cabreragarciarodriguezpalacios2014].

## References

* [Cabrera García and Rodríguez Palacios, Non-associative normed algebras. Volume 1]
  [cabreragarciarodriguezpalacios2014]
* Hanche-Olsen and Størmer, Jordan Operator Algebras
* McCrimmon, A taste of Jordan algebras

A (non-commutative) Jordan multiplication.

A commutative Jordan multiplication

see Note [lower instance priority]
A (commutative) Jordan multiplication is also a Jordan multiplication

see Note [lower instance priority]
Semigroup multiplication satisfies the (non-commutative) Jordan axioms

see Note [lower instance priority]

The Jordan axioms can be expressed in terms of commuting multiplication operators.

with a Lie Bracket via .

Lie algebras over fields of characteristic zero in terms of the Killing form: solvability
via its vanishing on , semisimplicity via its non-degeneracy.

  is contained in the solvable radical.
* : **Cartan's criterion for semisimplicity**: if a
  finite-dimensional Lie algebra has trivial solvable radical, then its Killing form is
  non-degenerate.

## Implementation notes

### Matrices or endomorphisms

Given a finite type and a commutative ring, the corresponding square matrices are equivalent to the
endomorphisms of the corresponding finite-rank free module as Lie algebras, see .
We can thus define the classical Lie algebras as Lie subalgebras either of matrices or of
endomorphisms. We have opted for the former. At the time of writing (August 2020) it is unclear
which approach should be preferred so the choice should be assumed to be somewhat arbitrary.

### Diagonal quadratic form or diagonal Cartan subalgebra

For the algebras of type  and , there are two natural definitions. For example since the
 matrix:
$$
  J = \left[\begin{array}{cc}
              0_l & 1_l\\
              1_l & 0_l
            \end{array}\right]
$$
defines a symmetric bilinear form equivalent to that defined by the identity matrix , we can
define the algebras of type  to be the Lie subalgebra of skew-adjoint matrices either for  or
for . Both definitions have their advantages (in particular the -skew-adjoint matrices define
a Lie algebra for which the diagonal matrices form a Cartan subalgebra) and so we provide both.
We thus also provide equivalences ,  which show the two
definitions are equivalent. Similarly for the algebras of type .

# Engel's theorem

This file contains a proof of Engel's theorem providing necessary and sufficient conditions for Lie
algebras and Lie modules to be nilpotent.

The key result  says that if  is a Lie module of a
Noetherian Lie algebra , then  is nilpotent iff the image of  consists of
nilpotent elements. In the special case that we have the adjoint representation , this says
that a Lie algebra is nilpotent iff  is nilpotent for all .

Engel's theorem is true for any coefficients (i.e., it is really a theorem about Lie rings) and so
we work with coefficients in any commutative ring  throughout.

On the other hand, Engel's theorem is not true for infinite-dimensional Lie algebras and so a
finite-dimensionality assumption is required. We prove the theorem subject to the assumption
that the Lie algebra is Noetherian as an -module, though actually we only need the slightly
weaker property that the relation  is well-founded on the complete lattice of Lie subalgebras.

## Remarks about the proof

Engel's theorem is usually proved in the special case that the coefficients are a field, and uses
an inductive argument on the dimension of the Lie algebra. One begins by choosing either a maximal
proper Lie subalgebra (in some proofs) or a maximal nilpotent Lie subalgebra (in other proofs, at
the cost of obtaining a weaker end result).

Since we work with general coefficients, we cannot induct on dimension and an alternate approach
must be taken. The key ingredient is the concept of nilpotency, not just for Lie algebras, but for
Lie modules. Using this concept, we define an _Engelian Lie algebra_  to
be one for which a Lie module is nilpotent whenever the action consists of nilpotent endomorphisms.
The argument then proceeds by selecting a maximal Engelian Lie subalgebra and showing that it cannot
be proper.

The first part of the traditional statement of Engel's theorem consists of the statement that if
is a non-trivial -module and  is a finite-dimensional Lie subalgebra of nilpotent
elements, then there exists a non-zero element  that is annihilated by every element of .
This follows trivially from the result established here , that
 is a nilpotent Lie module over , since the last non-zero term in the lower central series
will consist of such elements  (see: ). It seems
that this result has not previously been established at this level of generality.

The second part of the traditional statement of Engel's theorem concerns nilpotency of the Lie
algebra and a proof of this for general coefficients appeared in the literature as long ago
as 1937. This also follows trivially from  simply by
taking .

It is pleasing that the two parts of the traditional statements of Engel's theorem are thus unified
into a single statement about nilpotency of Lie modules. This is not usually emphasised.

## Main definitions

  *
  *
  *
  *

A Lie algebra  is said to be Engelian if a sufficient condition for any -Lie module  to
be nilpotent is that the image of the map  consists of nilpotent elements.

Engel's theorem  states that any Noetherian Lie algebra is
Engelian.

*Engel's theorem*.

Note that this implies all traditional forms of Engel's theorem via

# Lie algebras with non-degenerate Killing forms.

In characteristic zero, the following three conditions are equivalent:
1. The solvable radical of a Lie algebra is trivial
2. A Lie algebra is a direct sum of its simple ideals
3. A Lie algebra has non-degenerate Killing form

In positive characteristic, it is still true that 3 implies 2, and that 2 implies 1, but there are
counterexamples to the remaining implications. Thus condition 3 is the strongest assumption.
Furthermore, much of the Cartan-Killing classification of semisimple Lie algebras in characteristic
zero, continues to hold in positive characteristic (over a perfect field) if the Lie algebra has a
non-degenerate Killing form.

This file contains basic definitions and results for such Lie algebras.

## Main declarations

* : a typeclass encoding the fact that a Lie algebra has a non-singular
  Killing form.
* : if a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field
  has non-singular Killing form then it is semisimple.
* : if a Lie algebra over a PID
  has non-singular Killing form then it has trivial radical.
* : if a Lie algebra has non-singular Killing form then for all
  ideals, an ideal and its Killing orthogonal complement are complements.

We say a Lie algebra is Killing if its Killing form is non-singular.

NB: This is not standard terminology (the literature does not seem to name Lie algebras with this
property).

We say a Lie algebra is Killing if its Killing form is non-singular.

The converse of this is true in characteristic zero; it is
. There are counterexamples
over fields with positive characteristic.

Note that when the coefficients are a field this instance is redundant since we have

# Loop Lie algebras and their central extensions

Given a Lie algebra , the loop algebra is the Lie algebra of maps from a circle into . This
can mean many different things, e.g., continuous maps, smooth maps, polynomial maps. In this file,
we consider the simplest case of polynomial maps, meaning we take a base change with the ring of
Laurent polynomials.

Loop Lie algebras admit central extensions attached to invariant inner products on the base Lie
algebra. When the base Lie algebra is finite dimensional and simple, the corresponding central
extension (with an outer derivation attached) admits an infinite root system with affine Weyl group.
These extended Lie algebras are called untwisted affine Kac-Moody Lie algebras.

We implement the basic theory using  instead of  for
flexibility. The classical loop algebra is then written .

## Main definitions
* : The tensor product of a Lie algebra with an .
* : A linear equivalence from the loop algebra to the space of
  finitely supported functions.
* : The 2-cochain for a loop algebra with trivial
  coefficients attached to a symmetric bilinear form on the base Lie algebra.
* : The 2-cocycle for a loop algebra with trivial
  coefficients attached to a symmetric invariant bilinear form on the base Lie algebra.

## Main declarations

A nontrivial Lie module is *irreducible* if its only Lie submodules are  and .

A Lie algebra *has trivial radical* if its radical is trivial.
This is equivalent to having no non-trivial solvable ideals,
and further equivalent to having no non-trivial abelian ideals.

In characteristic zero, it is also equivalent to .

Note that the label 'semisimple' is apparently not universally agreed
upon
for general coefficients.

For example Seligman, page 15 uses the label for ,
whereas we reserve it for Lie algebras that are a direct sum of simple Lie algebras.

A Lie algebra *has central radical* if its radical coincides with its center. Such Lie algebras
are called *reductive*, if the coefficients are a field of characteristic zero.

Note that there is absolutely no agreement on what
the label 'reductive' should mean when the coefficients are not a field of characteristic zero.

A Lie algebra is simple if it is irreducible as a Lie module over itself via the adjoint
action, and it is non-Abelian.

A *semisimple* Lie algebra is one that is a direct sum of non-abelian atomic ideals.
These ideals are simple Lie algebras, by .

Note that the label 'semisimple' is apparently not universally agreed
upon
for general coefficients.

For example Seligman, page 15 uses the label for ,
the weakest of the various properties which are all equivalent over a field of characteristic zero.

In a semisimple Lie algebra, the supremum of the atoms is the whole Lie algebra.

In a semisimple Lie algebra, the atoms are independent.

In a semisimple Lie algebra, the atoms are non-abelian.

# Serre construction of Lie algebras from Cartan matrices

This file provides the Serre construction of Lie algebras from Cartan matrices.
Given a Cartan matrix , we construct a Lie algebra as a quotient of the free Lie algebra
on generators  by the Serre relations:
$$
\begin{align}
  [H_i, H_j] &= 0\\
  [E_i, F_i] &= H_i\\
  [E_i, F_j] &= 0 \quad\text{if $i \ne j$}\\
  [H_i, E_j] &= A_{ij}E_j\\
  [H_i, F_j] &= -A_{ij}F_j\\
  ad(E_i)^{1 - A_{ij}}(E_j) &= 0 \quad\text{if $i \ne j$}\\
  ad(F_i)^{1 - A_{ij}}(F_j) &= 0 \quad\text{if $i \ne j$}\\
\end{align}
$$

## Main definitions

*  : The Lie algebra constructed from a Cartan matrix via Serre relations

### Classical Lie algebras
* , , ,

## Alternative construction

This construction is sometimes performed within the free unital associative algebra
, rather than within the free Lie algebra , as we do here.
However the difference is illusory since the construction stays inside the Lie subalgebra of
 generated by , and this is naturally isomorphic to
(though the proof of this seems to require Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt).

# Lie algebras of skew-adjoint endomorphisms of a bilinear form

When a module carries a bilinear form, the Lie algebra of endomorphisms of the module contains a
distinguished Lie subalgebra: the skew-adjoint endomorphisms. Such subalgebras are important
because they provide a simple, explicit construction of the so-called classical Lie algebras.

This file defines the Lie subalgebra of skew-adjoint endomorphisms cut out by a bilinear form on
a module and proves some basic related results. It also provides the corresponding definitions and
results for the Lie algebra of square matrices.

## Main definitions

  *
  *
  *
  *

## Tags

lie algebra, skew-adjoint, bilinear form

Given an -module , equipped with a bilinear form, the skew-adjoint endomorphisms form a
Lie subalgebra of the Lie algebra of endomorphisms.

An equivalence of modules with bilinear forms gives equivalence of Lie algebras of skew-adjoint
endomorphisms.

The Lie subalgebra of skew-adjoint square matrices corresponding to a square matrix .

An invertible matrix  gives a Lie algebra equivalence between those endomorphisms that are
skew-adjoint with respect to a square matrix  and those with respect to .

An equivalence of matrix algebras commuting with the transpose endomorphisms restricts to an
equivalence of Lie algebras of skew-adjoint matrices.

* : the field with two elements (or indeed any perfect field of characteristic two),

# Lie-Rinehart algebras

This file defines Lie-Rinehart algebras and their morphisms. It also shows that the derivations of
a commutative algebra over a commutative Ring form such a Lie-Rinehart algebra.
Lie-Rinehart algebras appear in differential geometry as section spaces of Lie algebroids and
singular foliations. The typical Cartan calculus of differential geometry can be restated fully in
terms of the Chevalley-Eilenberg algebra of a Lie-Rinehart algebra.

## References

* Rinehart, G. S., Differential forms on general commutative algebras. Zbl 0113.26204
  Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 108, 195-222 (1963).

A Lie-Rinehart ring is a pair consisting of a commutative ring  and a Lie ring  such that
and  are each a module over the other, satisfying compatibility conditions.

A Lie-Rinehart algebra with coefficients in a commutative ring , is a pair consisting of a
commutative -algebra  and a Lie algebra  with coefficients in , such that  and
are each a module over the other, satisfying compatibility conditions.

As shown below, this data determines a linear map  satisfying a Leibniz-like
compatibility condition. This could even be taken as a definition, however the definition here has
the advantage of being -valued, thus mitigating potential diamonds.

The derivations of a commutative Algebra themselves form a LieRinehart-Algebra.

to use a canonical  typeclass throughout.

# Characteristic polynomials of linear families of endomorphisms

The coefficients of the characteristic polynomials of a linear family of endomorphisms
are homogeneous polynomials in the parameters.
This result is used in Lie theory
to establish the existence of regular elements and Cartan subalgebras,
and ultimately a well-defined notion of rank for Lie algebras.

In this file we prove this result about characteristic polynomials.

# Structure of finitely generated modules over a PID

## Main statements

*  : A finitely generated torsion module over a PID is
  isomorphic to a direct sum of some  where the  are prime powers.
*  : A finitely generated module over a PID is isomorphic to the
  product of a free module (its torsion free part) and a direct sum of the form above (its torsion
  submodule).

## Notation

*  is a PID and  is a (finitely generated for main statements) -module, with additional
  torsion hypotheses in the intermediate lemmas.
*  is an irreducible element of  or a tuple of these.

## Implementation details

We first prove () that a finitely generated
torsion module is the internal direct sum of its -torsion submodules for some
(finitely many) prime powers . This is proved in more generality for a Dedekind domain
at .

Then we treat the case of a -torsion module (that is, a module where all elements are
cancelled by scalar multiplication by some power of ) and apply it to the -torsion
submodules (that are -torsion) to get the result for torsion modules.

Then we get the general result using that a torsion free module is free (which has been proved at
 at .)

# Projective modules

This file contains a definition of a projective module, the proof that
our definition is equivalent to a lifting property, and the
proof that all free modules are projective.

## Main definitions

Let  be a ring (or a semiring) and let  be an -module.

*  : the proposition saying that  is a projective -module.

## Main theorems

*  : a map from a projective module can be lifted along
  a surjection.

*  : If for all R-module surjections , all
  maps  lift to , then  is projective.

*  : Free modules are projective

## Implementation notes

The actual definition of projective we use is that the natural R-module map
from the free R-module on the type M down to M splits. This is more convenient
than certain other definitions which involve quantifying over universes,
and also universe-polymorphic (the ring and module can be in different universes).

We require that the module sits in at least as high a universe as the ring:
without this, free modules don't even exist,
and it's unclear if projective modules are even a useful notion.

## References



## Tags

from the free -module on  to  splits.
An R-module is projective if it is a direct summand of a free module, or equivalently
if maps from the module lift along surjections. There are several other equivalent
definitions.

A projective R-module has the property that maps from it lift along surjections.

# Monoid algebras

When the domain of a  has a multiplicative or additive structure, we can define
a convolution product. To mathematicians this structure is known as the "monoid algebra",
i.e. the finite formal linear combinations over a given semiring of elements of a monoid .
The "group ring"  or the "group algebra"  are typical uses.

In fact the construction of the "monoid algebra" makes sense when  is not even a monoid, but
merely a magma, i.e., when  carries a multiplication which is not required to satisfy any
conditions at all. In this case the construction yields a not-necessarily-unital,
not-necessarily-associative algebra but it is still adjoint to the forgetful functor from such
algebras to magmas, and we prove this as .

In this file we define  and  as one-field structures around
, and then define the convolution product on these.

When the domain is additive, this is used to define polynomials:

When the domain is multiplicative, e.g. a group, this will be used to define the group ring.

## Notation

We introduce the notation  for both  and .
The notations are scoped to their respective namespaces, and which one  resolves to therefore
depends on which of the two namespaces is open.

## sup-degree and inf-degree of an

Let  be a semiring and let  be a .
For an element , this file defines
* : the sup-degree taking values in ,
* : the inf-degree taking values in .

If the grading type  is a linearly ordered additive monoid, then these two notions of degree
coincide with the standard one:
* the sup-degree is the maximum of the exponents of the monomials that appear with non-zero
  coefficient in , or , if ;
* the inf-degree is the minimum of the exponents of the monomials that appear with non-zero
  coefficient in , or , if .

The main results are
* :
  the sup-degree of a product is at most the sum of the sup-degrees,
* :
  the inf-degree of a product is at least the sum of the inf-degrees,
* :
  the sup-degree of a sum is at most the sup of the sup-degrees,
* :
  the inf-degree of a sum is at least the inf of the inf-degrees.

# The Schwartz-Zippel lemma

This file contains a proof of the
Schwartz-Zippel lemma.

This lemma tells us that the probability that a nonzero multivariable polynomial over an integral
domain evaluates to zero at a random point is bounded by the degree of the polynomial over the size
of the field, or more generally, that a nonzero multivariable polynomial over any integral domain
has a low probability of being zero when evaluated at points drawn at random from some finite subset
of the field. This lemma is useful as a probabilistic polynomial identity test.

  the supremum of  ranging over monomials  of the polynomial.

  with the RHS being the sum of .

In mathematics, an indicator function or a characteristic function is a function
used to indicate membership of an element in a set ,
having the value  for all elements of  and the value  otherwise.
But since it is usually used to restrict a function to a certain set ,
we let the indicator function take the value  for some function , instead of .
If the usual indicator function is needed, just set  to be the constant function .

The indicator function is implemented non-computably, to avoid having to pass around
arguments. This is in contrast with the design of  or .

# Ordered algebras

An ordered algebra is an ordered semiring, which is an algebra over an ordered commutative semiring,
for which scalar multiplication is "compatible" with the two orders.

The prototypical example is 2x2 matrices over the reals or complexes (or indeed any C^* algebra)
where the ordering the one determined by the positive cone of positive operators,
i.e.  iff  for some .
(We don't yet have this example in mathlib.)

## Implementation

Because the axioms for an ordered algebra are exactly the same as those for the underlying
module being ordered, we don't actually introduce a new class, but just use the
and  mixins.

## Implementation notes

Archimedean classes are equipped with a linear order, where elements with smaller absolute value
are placed in a *higher* classes by convention. Ordering backwards this way simplifies
formalization of theorems such as the Hahn embedding theorem.

To naturally derive this order, we first define it on the underlying group via the type
synonym (-), and define (-) as  of
the order.

conditionally complete.

# Chebyshev's sum inequality

This file proves the Chebyshev sum inequality.

Chebyshev's inequality states
when  monovary, and the reverse inequality when  and  antivary.


## Main declarations

* : Chebyshev's inequality.
* : Chebyshev's inequality, dual version.
* : Special case of Chebyshev's inequality when .

## Implementation notes

In fact, we don't need much compatibility between the addition and multiplication of , so we can
actually decouple them by replacing multiplication with scalar multiplication and making  and
land in different types.
As a bonus, this makes the dual statement trivial. The multiplication versions are provided for
convenience.

The case for / pairs of functions over a  is not deduced in this
file because it is easily deducible from the  API.

### Scalar multiplication versions

**Chebyshev's Sum Inequality**: When  and  monovary together (e.g. they are both
monotone/antitone), the scalar product of their sum is less than the size of the set times their
scalar product.

**Chebyshev's Sum Inequality**: When  and  antivary together (e.g. one is monotone, the
other is antitone), the scalar product of their sum is less than the size of the set times their
scalar product.

**Chebyshev's Sum Inequality**: When  and  monovary together (e.g. they are both
monotone/antitone), the scalar product of their sum is less than the size of the set times their
scalar product.

**Chebyshev's Sum Inequality**: When  and  antivary together (e.g. one is monotone, the
other is antitone), the scalar product of their sum is less than the size of the set times their
scalar product.

### Multiplication versions

other is antitone), the product of their sum is greater than the size of the set times their scalar
product.

# Lattice ordered groups

Lattice ordered groups were introduced by Birkhoff. They form the algebraic
underpinnings of vector lattices, Banach lattices, AL-space, AM-space etc.

A lattice ordered group is a type  satisfying:
*
*
*
*

This file establishes basic properties of lattice ordered groups. It is shown that when the group is
commutative, the lattice is distributive. This also holds in the non-commutative case
(Birkhoff,Fuchs) but we do not yet have the machinery to establish this
in mathlib.

## References

* Birkhoff, Lattice-ordered Groups
* Bourbaki, Algebra II
* Fuchs, Partially Ordered Algebraic Systems
* Zaanen, Lectures on "Riesz Spaces"
* Banasiak, Banach Lattices in Applications

# Order homomorphisms for products of linearly ordered groups with zero

This file defines order homomorphisms for products of linearly ordered groups with zero,
which is identified with the  of the lexicographic product of the units of the groups.

The product of linearly ordered groups with zero  is a
linearly ordered group with zero itself with natural inclusions but only one projection.
One has to work with the lexicographic product of the units  since otherwise,
the plain product  would not be linearly ordered.

Diamond inheritance cannot depend on s in the following circumstances:
* there are three classes , ,
* all of these classes have a parameter
* all of these classes have an instance parameter  that depends on this
* the  class has two child classes:  and , these are siblings in the hierarchy
* the instance  takes a  parameter
* the instance  takes a  parameter
* there is a  class that inherits from both  and .

In that case, given instances  and , Lean cannot synthesize a  instance,
even though the hypotheses of the instances  and  are satisfied.

There are two workarounds:
* You could replace the bundled inheritance implemented by the instance  with
  unbundled inheritance implemented by adding a  parameter to the  class. This is
  the preferred option since it is also more compatible with Lean 4, at the cost of being more work
  to implement and more verbose to use.
* You could weaken the  instance by making it depend on a subclass of
  's parameter, in this example replacing  with .

# Monotonicity of scalar multiplication by positive elements

This file defines typeclasses to reason about monotonicity of the operations
* , "left scalar multiplication"
* , "right scalar multiplication"

We use eight typeclasses to encode the various properties we care about for those two operations.
These typeclasses are meant to be mostly internal to this file, to set up each lemma in the
appropriate generality.

Less granular typeclasses like  and  should be enough for most
purposes, and the system is set up so that they imply the correct granular typeclasses here.
If those are enough for you, you may stop reading here! Else, beware that what
follows is a bit technical.


In all that follows,  and  are orders which have a  and such that  acts on  by scalar
multiplication. Note however that we do not use lawfulness of this action in most of the file. Hence
 should be considered here as a mostly arbitrary function .

not covered by the current implications, please bring it up on Zulip!

## Implementation notes

This file uses custom typeclasses instead of abbreviations of /
because:
* They get displayed as classes in the docs. In particular, one can see their list of instances,
  instead of their instances being invariably dumped to the /
  list.
* They don't pollute other typeclass searches. Having many abbreviations of the same typeclass for
  different purposes always felt like a performance issue (more instances with the same key, for no
  added benefit), and indeed making the classes here abbreviation previous creates timeouts due to
  the higher number of / instances.
* / do not fit in the framework since they relate  on two
  different types. So we would have to generalise / to three
  types and two relations.
* Very minor, but the constructors let you work with ,  instead of
  . This actually makes some instances surprisingly cleaner to prove.
* The / framework is only useful to automate very simple logic
  anyway. It is easily copied over.

In the future, it would be good to make the corresponding typeclasses in
 custom typeclasses too.

# Canonically ordered monoids

An ordered additive monoid is
if the ordering coincides with the subtractibility relation,
which is to say,  iff there exists  with .
This is satisfied by the natural numbers, for example, but not
the integers or other nontrivial ordered groups.

We have  and  as separate fields. In the commutative case the second field
is redundant, but in the noncommutative case (satisfied most relevantly by the ordinals), this
extra field allows us to prove more things without the extra commutativity assumption.

For any  and ,

An ordered monoid is
 if the ordering coincides with the divisibility relation,
 which is to say,  iff there exists  with .
 Examples seem rare; it seems more likely that the
 of a naturally-occurring lattice satisfies this than the lattice
 itself (for example, dual of the lattice of ideals of a PID or
 Dedekind domain satisfy this; collections of all things ≤ 1 seem to
 be more natural that collections of all things ≥ 1).

# Ordered monoids

This file provides the definitions of ordered monoids.

TODO: assume weaker typeclasses

An ordered (additive) monoid is a monoid with a preorder such that addition is monotone.

An ordered monoid is a monoid with a preorder such that multiplication is monotone.

An ordered cancellative additive monoid is an ordered additive
monoid in which addition is cancellative and monotone.

An ordered cancellative monoid is an ordered monoid in which
multiplication is cancellative and monotone.

# Order homomorphisms for products of ordered monoids

This file defines order homomorphisms for products of ordered monoids, for both the plain product
and the lexicographic product.

The product of ordered monoids  is an ordered monoid itself with both natural inclusions
and projections, making it the coproduct as well.

# Covariants and contravariants

This file contains general lemmas and instances to work with the interactions between a relation and
an action on a Type.

The intended application is the splitting of the ordering from the algebraic assumptions on the
operations in the  hierarchy.

The strategy is to introduce two more flexible typeclasses,  and
:

*  models the implication  (multiplication is monotone),
*  models the implication .

Since  takes as input the operation (typically  or ) and the order
relation (typically  or ), these are the only two typeclasses that I have used.

The general approach is to formulate the lemma that you are interested in and prove it, with the
 typeclass of your liking.  After that, you convert the typeclass,
say , into whichever typeclasses, e.g.

and have a go at seeing if the proof still works!

Note that it is possible to combine several  assumptions together.
Indeed, the usual ordered typeclasses arise from assuming the pair

on top of order/algebraic assumptions.

A formal remark is that normally  uses the -relation, while
 uses the -relation. This need not be the case in general, but seems to be
the most common usage. In the opposite direction, the implication
holds -- note the  assumption on the -relation.

## Formalization notes

We stick to the convention of using  (or ), for the
typeclass assumptions, since  is slightly better behaved than .
However, sometimes as a **non-typeclass** assumption, we prefer  (or ),
as it is easier to use.

instance orderedAddCommMonoid [OrderedAddCommMonoid α] : OrderedAddCommMonoid (WithTop α) where
add_le_add_left _ _ := add_le_add_left

instance linearOrderedAddCommMonoidWithTop [LinearOrderedAddCommMonoid α] :
LinearOrderedAddCommMonoidWithTop (WithTop α) :=
{ WithTop.orderTop, WithTop.linearOrder, WithTop.orderedAddCommMonoid with
top_add' := WithTop.top_add }

instance canonicallyOrderedAddCommMonoid [CanonicallyOrderedAddCommMonoid α] :
CanonicallyOrderedAddCommMonoid (WithTop α) :=
{ WithTop.orderBot, WithTop.orderedAddCommMonoid, WithTop.existsAddOfLE with
le_self_add := fun a b =>
match a, b with
| ⊤, ⊤ => le_rfl
| (a : α), ⊤ => le_top
| (a : α), (b : α) => WithTop.coe_le_coe.2 le_self_add
| ⊤, (b : α) => le_rfl }

instance [CanonicallyLinearOrderedAddCommMonoid α] :
CanonicallyLinearOrderedAddCommMonoid (WithTop α) :=
{ WithTop.canonicallyOrderedAddCommMonoid, WithTop.linearOrder with }

## Implementation Notes

Instead of  we could also use , which is definitionally equal.
However, using the explicit subtype has a big advantage: when writing an element explicitly
with a proof of nonnegativity as , the  is expected to have type . If we would
use , then the type is expected to be . Although these types are definitionally
equal, this often confuses the elaborator. Similar problems arise when doing cases on an element.

The disadvantage is that we have to duplicate some instances about  to this subtype.

use , then the type is expected to be . Although these types are definitionally
equal, this often confuses the elaborator. Similar problems arise when doing cases on an element.

The disadvantage is that we have to duplicate some instances about  to this subtype.

# Theory of quantales

Quantales are the non-commutative generalization of locales/frames and as such are linked
to point-free topology and order theory. Applications are found throughout logic,
quantum mechanics, and computer science (see e.g. [Vickers1989] and [Mulvey1986]).

The most general definition of quantale occurring in literature, is that a quantale is a semigroup
distributing over a complete sup-semilattice. In our definition below, we use the fact that
every complete sup-semilattice is in fact a complete lattice, and make constructs defined for
those immediately available. Another view could be to define a quantale as a complete idempotent
semiring, i.e. a complete semiring in which + and sup coincide. However, we will often encounter
additive quantales, i.e. quantales in which the semigroup operator is thought of as addition, in
which case the link with semirings will lead to confusion notationally.

In this file, we follow the basic definition set out on the wikipedia page on quantales,
using a mixin typeclass to make the special cases of unital, commutative, idempotent,
integral, and involutive quantales easier to add on later.

## Main definitions

*  and  : Typeclass mixin for a (additive) semigroup distributing
  over a complete lattice, i.e satisfying  and
  ;

*  and  : Structures serving as a typeclass alias, so one can write
   instead of ,
  and similarly for the additive variant.

* , , ,  :
  Defining the left- and right- residuations of the semigroup (see notation below).

* Finally, we provide basic distributivity laws for sSup into iSup and sup, monotonicity of
  the semigroup operator, and basic equivalences for left- and right-residuation.

Each typeclass here comprises
* an algebraic class (, , , )
* an order class (, )

* " respects " means "monotonicity of addition"
* " respects " means "strict monotonicity of addition"
* " respects " means "monotonicity of multiplication by a nonnegative number".
* " respects " means "strict monotonicity of multiplication by a positive number".

# Ring orderings

Let  be a commutative ring. A preordering on  is a subset closed under
addition and multiplication that contains all squares, but not .

The support of a preordering  is the set of elements  such that both  and  lie in .

An ordering  on  is a preordering such that
1.  contains either  or  for each  in  and
2. the support of  is a prime ideal.

We define preorderings, supports and orderings.

A ring preordering can intuitively be viewed as a set of "non-negative" ring elements.
Indeed, an ordering  with support  induces a linear order on  making it
into an ordered ring, and vice versa.

## References

- *An introduction to real algebra*, T.Y. Lam

but not containing .

the set of elements  in  such that both  and  lie in .

# Standard part function

Given a finite element in a non-archimedean field, the standard part function rounds it to the
unique closest real number. That is, it chops off any infinitesimals.

Let  be a linearly ordered field. The subset of finite elements (i.e. those bounded by a natural
number) is a , which means we can construct its residue field
, roughly corresponding to the finite elements quotiented by infinitesimals.
This field inherits a  instance, which makes it into an Archimedean linearly ordered
field, meaning we can uniquely embed it in the reals.

Given a finite element of the field, the  function returns the real number
corresponding to this unique embedding. This function generalizes, among other things, the standard
part function on .

# Commutative star-ordered rings are ordered rings

A noncommutative star-ordered ring is generally not an ordered ring. Indeed, in a star-ordered
ring, nonnegative elements are self-adjoint, but the product of self-adjoint elements is
self-adjoint if and only if they commute. Therefore, a necessary condition for a star-ordered ring
to be an ordered ring is that all nonnegative elements commute.  Consequently, if a star-ordered
ring is spanned by it nonnegative elements (as is the case for C⋆-algebras) and it is also an
ordered ring, then it is commutative.

In this file we prove the converse: a *commutative* star-ordered ring is an ordered ring.

This example shows that nonnegative elements in an ordered semiring which is also star-ordered
must commute. We provide this only as an example as opposed to a lemma because we never expect the
type class assumptions to be satisfied without a  instance already in scope; not that
it is impossible, only that it shouldn't occur in practice.

A commutative star-ordered semiring is an ordered semiring.

# Laurent polynomials

We introduce Laurent polynomials over a semiring .  Mathematically, they are expressions of the
form
$$
\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} a_i T ^ i
$$
where the sum extends over a finite subset of .  Thus, negative exponents are allowed.  The
coefficients come from the semiring  and the variable  commutes with everything.

Since we are going to convert back and forth between polynomials and Laurent polynomials, we
decided to maintain some distinction by using the symbol , rather than , as the variable for
Laurent polynomials.

## Notation
The symbol  stands for .  We also define

*  the inclusion of constant polynomials, analogous to the one for ;
*  the sequence of powers of the variable .

## Implementation notes

We define Laurent polynomials as .
Thus, they are essentially s .
This choice differs from the current irreducible design of , that instead shields away
the implementation via s.  It is closer to the original definition of polynomials.

As a consequence,  plays well with polynomials, but there is a little roughness
in establishing the API, since the  implementation of  is well-shielded.

Unlike the case of polynomials, I felt that the exponent notation was not too easy to use, as only
natural exponents would be allowed.  Moreover, in the end, it seems likely that we should aim to
perform computations on exponents in  anyway and separating this via the symbol  seems
convenient.

I made a *heavy* use of  lemmas, aiming to bring Laurent polynomials to the form .
Any comments or suggestions for improvements is greatly appreciated!

# Descartes' Rule of Signs

We define the "sign changes" in the coefficients of a polynomial, and prove Descartes'
Rule of Signs: a real polynomial has at most as many positive roots as there are sign
changes. A sign change is when there is a positive coefficient followed by a negative
coefficient, or vice versa, with any number of zero coefficients in between.

## Main Definitions

- : The number of sign changes in a polynomial's coefficients,
  where  coefficients are ignored.

## Main theorem

- . States that
  , so that positive roots are counted with multiplicity.
  It's currently proved for any  with . There is likely some correct
  statement in terms of a (noncommutative) , but  is only defined for
  commutative rings.

## Reference

Wikipedia: Descartes' Rule of Signs

Counts the number of times that the coefficients in a polynomial change sign, with
the convention that 0 can count as either sign.

Sign variations of a monomial are always zero.

If the first two signs are the same, then  is unchanged by

If we drop the leading coefficient, the sign changes drop by 0 or 1 depending on whether
the first two nonzero coefficients match.

We can only lose, not gain, sign changes if we drop the leading coefficient.

We can only lose at most one sign changes if we drop the leading coefficient.

The number of sign changes does not change if we negate.

The number of sign changes does not change if we multiply by any nonzero scalar.

# Racks and Quandles

This file defines racks and quandles, algebraic structures for sets
that bijectively act on themselves with a self-distributivity
property.  If  is a rack and  is the self-action,
then the self-distributivity is, equivalently, that
where multiplication is composition in  as a group.
Quandles are racks such that  for all .

One example of a quandle (not yet in mathlib) is the action of a Lie
algebra on itself, defined by .

Quandles and racks were independently developed by multiple
mathematicians.  David Joyce introduced quandles in his thesis
[Joyce1982] to define an algebraic invariant of knot and link
complements that is analogous to the fundamental group of the
exterior, and he showed that the quandle associated to an oriented
knot is invariant up to orientation-reversed mirror image.  Racks were
used by Fenn and Rourke for framed codimension-2 knots and
links in [FennRourke1992]. Unital shelves are discussed in [crans2017].

The name "rack" came from wordplay by Conway and Wraith for the "wrack
and ruin" of forgetting everything but the conjugation operation for a
group.

## Main definitions

*  is a type with a self-distributive action
*  is a shelf with a left and right unit
*  is a shelf whose action for each element is invertible
*  is a rack whose action for an element fixes that element
*  defines a quandle of a group acting on itself by conjugation.
*  is homomorphisms of shelves, racks, and quandles.
*  gives the universal group the rack maps to as a conjugation quandle.
*  gives the rack with the action replaced by its inverse.

## Main statements

### Universal enveloping group of a rack

The universal enveloping group  of a rack  is the
universal group such that every rack homomorphism  is
induced by a unique group homomorphism .
For quandles, Joyce called this group .

The  functor is left adjoint to the  forgetful
functor, and the way we construct the enveloping group is via a
technique that should work for left adjoints of forgetful functors in
general.  It involves thinking a little about 2-categories, but the
payoff is that the map  has a nice description.

Let's think of a group as being a one-object category.  The first step
is to define , which gives formal expressions for all
the 1-morphisms and includes the unit element, elements of ,
multiplication, and inverses.  To introduce relations, the second step
is to define , which gives formal expressions
for all 2-morphisms between the 1-morphisms.  The 2-morphisms include
associativity, multiplication by the unit, multiplication by inverses,
compatibility with multiplication and inverses ( and
), the axioms for an equivalence relation, and,
importantly, the relationship between conjugation and the rack action
(see ).

None of this forms a 2-category yet, for example due to lack of
associativity of .  The  relation is a
-valued version of , and making it
-valued essentially introduces enough 3-isomorphisms so that
every pair of compatible 2-morphisms is isomorphic.  Now, while
composition in  does not strictly satisfy the category
axioms,  and  do form a weak
2-category.

Since we just want a 1-category, the last step is to quotient
 by , and the result is the
group .

For a homomorphism , how does
 work?  Let's think of  as
being a 2-category with one object, a 1-morphism per element of ,
and a single 2-morphism called  for each 1-morphism.  We
define the map using a "higher " -- not only do we
evaluate elements of  as expressions in  (this is
), but we evaluate elements of
 as expressions of 2-morphisms of  (this is
).  That is to say,
 recursively evaluates formal
expressions of 2-morphisms as equality proofs in .  Now that all
morphisms are accounted for, the map descends to a homomorphism
.

Note: -valued relations are not common.  The fact it is
-valued is what makes  have
well-founded recursion.

Since it assumes that the ring is a cancellative  it applies also,
for instance, to .

only if the  is trivial.  This is useful when figuring out stopping conditions for
regular sequences: if  is ever an element of a regular sequence, then we can extend the sequence
by adding one further .

The final goal is to develop part of the API to prove, eventually, results about non-zero-divisors.

algebras.

# Centroid homomorphisms

Let  be a (nonunital, non-associative) algebra. The centroid of  is the set of linear maps
 on  such that  commutes with left and right multiplication, that is to say, for all
and  in ,
$$
T(ab) = (Ta)b, T(ab) = a(Tb).
$$
In mathlib we call elements of the centroid "centroid homomorphisms" () in keeping
with  etc.

We use the  design, so each type of morphisms has a companion typeclass which is meant to
be satisfied by itself and all stricter types.

# Extensionality lemmas for rings and similar structures

In this file we prove extensionality lemmas for the ring-like structures defined in
, ranging from  to . These
extensionality lemmas take the form of asserting that two algebraic structures on a type are equal
whenever the addition and multiplication defined by them are both the same.

refer to the multiplication specified by a typeclass instance  on a type  (and similarly for
addition). We abbreviate these using some local notations.

sometimes we don't need them to prove extensionality.

are not in this file, and they will ultimately be deprecated.

 (pull back) them along ring homomorphisms.

# Skew Monoid Algebras

Given a monoid  acting on a ring , the skew monoid algebra of  over  is the set
of finitely supported functions  for which addition is defined pointwise and
multiplication of two elements  and  is given by the finitely supported function whose
value at  is the sum of  over all pairs  such that ,
where  denotes the action of  on . When this action is trivial, this product is
the usual convolution product.

In fact the construction of the skew monoid algebra makes sense when  is not even a monoid, but
merely a magma, i.e., when  carries a multiplication which is not required to satisfy any
conditions at all, and  is a not-necessarily-associative semiring. In this case the construction
yields a not-necessarily-unital, not-necessarily-associative algebra.

# Univariate skew polynomials

Given a ring  and an endomorphism  on  the skew polynomials over
are polynomials
$$\sum_{i= 0}^n a_iX^n, n\geq 0, a_i\in R$$
where the addition is the usual addition of polynomials
$$\sum_{i= 0}^n a_iX^n + \sum_{i= 0}^n b_iX^n= \sum_{i= 0}^n (a_i + b_i)X^n.$$
The multiplication, however, is determined by
$$Xa = \varphi (a)X$$
by extending it to all polynomials in the obvious way.

Skew polynomials are represented as ,
where  is usually at least a Semiring. In this file, we define
and provide basic instances.

The implementation uses  instead of , since Mathlib does not contain an

the action needs to respect for associativity. There is no version of this in Mathlib that

# The Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt inequality and Tsirelson's inequality.

We establish a version of the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality
(which is a generalization of Bell's inequality).
This is a foundational result which implies that
quantum mechanics is not a local hidden variable theory.

As usually stated the CHSH inequality requires substantial language from physics and probability,
but it is possible to give a statement that is purely about ordered \*-algebras.
We do that here, to avoid as many practical and logical dependencies as possible.
Since the algebra of observables of any quantum system is an ordered \*-algebra
(in particular a von Neumann algebra) this is a strict generalization of the usual statement.

Let  be a \*-ring.

A CHSH tuple in  consists of
* four elements , such that
* each  and  is a self-adjoint involution, and
* the  commute with the .

The physical interpretation is that the four elements are observables (hence self-adjoint)
that take values ±1 (hence involutions), and that the  are spacelike separated from the
(and hence commute).

The CHSH inequality says that when  is an ordered \*-ring
(that is, a \*-ring which is ordered, and for every , ),
which is moreover *commutative*, we have


On the other hand, Tsirelson's inequality says that for any ordered \*-ring we have


(A caveat: in the commutative case we need 2⁻¹ in the ring,
and in the noncommutative case we need √2 and √2⁻¹.
To keep things simple we just assume our rings are ℝ-algebras.)

The proofs I've seen in the literature either
assume a significant framework for quantum mechanics,
or assume the ring is a C⋆-algebra.
In the C⋆-algebra case,
the order structure is completely determined by the \*-algebra structure:
 iff there exists some  so .
There's a nice proof of both bounds in this setting at

The proof given here is purely algebraic.

## Future work

One can show that Tsirelson's inequality is tight.

then every eigenvalue has absolute value at most .
There is a CHSH tuple in 4-by-4 matrices such that

is not required to have a star operation, nor do we need  or  structures on

As with , in the non-unital case the multiplications are not assumed to be
associative or unital, or even to be compatible with the scalar actions. In a typical application,
the operations will satisfy compatibility conditions making them into algebras (albeit possibly
non-associative and/or non-unital) but such conditions are not required here for the definitions.

The primary impetus for defining these types is that they constitute the morphisms in the categories
of unital C⋆-algebras (with s) and of C⋆-algebras (with s).

# Torsors of group actions

This file defines torsors of additive and multiplicative group actions.

## Notation

The group elements are referred to as acting on points.  This file
uses the notation  for adding a group element to a point and
 for subtracting two points to produce a group element, as well as  and  for the
corresponding operations in multiplicative torsors.

## Implementation notes

Affine spaces are a motivating example of additive torsors. Additional simply transitive
actions which give rise to torsors include the action of the Weyl group on Weyl chambers, the
action of non-zero scalars on the non-vanishing elements of the top exterior power of a
finite-dimensional vector space, the action of the general linear group of a vector space on the
bases of that space, and the monodromy action of the fundamental group of a space on a fibre of its
universal cover. Both the additive and multiplicative notation will be useful to formalise
such examples.

*  is a notation for , the left action of a multiplicative monoid;
*  is a notation for , the quotient of two points in a multiplicative
  torsor as an element of the corresponding multiplicative group;

### Multiplicative structure

In the general non-commutative case, the power operator is

$$\begin{align}
(r + m)^n &= r^n + r^{n-1}m + r^{n-2}mr + \cdots + rmr^{n-2} + mr^{n-1} \\
          & =r^n + \sum_{i = 0}^{n - 1} r^{(n - 1) - i} m r^{i}
\end{align}$$

In the commutative case this becomes the simpler $(r + m)^n = r^n + nr^{n-1}m$.

The second element of a product $\prod_{i=0}^n (r_i + m_i)$ is a sum of terms of the form
$r_0\cdots r_{i-1}m_ir_{i+1}\cdots r_n$.

# Quasi-compact covers

A cover of a scheme is quasi-compact if every affine open of the base can be covered
by a finite union of images of quasi-compact opens of the components.

This is used to define the fpqc (faithfully flat, quasi-compact) topology, where covers are given by
flat covers that are quasi-compact.

A cover of a scheme is quasi-compact if every affine open of the base can be covered
by a finite union of images of quasi-compact opens of the components.

If the component maps of  are open,  is quasi-compact. This in particular
applies if  is the fppf topology (i.e., flat and of finite presentation) and hence in
particular for étale and Zariski covers.

Any open cover is quasi-compact.

If  is a refinement of  such that  is quasicompact, also  is quasicompact.

Lift a quasi-compact cover of a -scheme in an arbitrary universe to . The indexing
type is constructed by choosing finitely many compact opens above every affine open.
This cover is again quasi-compact.

The refinement morphism of the lifted cover.

The object property on the category of pre--hypercovers of a scheme given
by quasi-compact covers.

in .

ideal class group of the *affine coordinate ring* . This is given by

the invertible ideal . Proving that this is well-defined and preserves addition
reduces to equalities of ideals checked in

## Implementation notes

Analogously to , the bivariate polynomials

ring division, but more crucially to allow the definition of  and  as univariate
polynomials without needing to work under the coordinate ring, and to allow the computation of their

hence also avoiding the need to work in the coordinate ring.

# Negation and addition formulae for nonsingular points in Jacobian coordinates

Let  be a Weierstrass curve over a field . The nonsingular Jacobian points on  can be given
negation and addition operations defined by an analogue of the secant-and-tangent process in
, but the polynomials involved are
-homogeneous, so any instances of division become multiplication in the -coordinate.
Most computational proofs are immediate from their analogous proofs for affine coordinates.

# Reduction of Weierstrass curves over local fields

This file defines reduction of Weierstrass curves over local fields, or more generally,
fraction fields of discrete valuation rings.

## Main definitions

* : a predicate expressing that a given Weierstrass equation
  has integral coefficients.
* : a predicate expressing that a given Weierstrass equation
  has minimal valuation of discriminant among all isomorphic integral Weierstrass equations.
* : the reduction of a Weierstrass curve given by a minimal Weierstrass equation,
  which is a Weierstrass curve over the residue field.
* : a predicate expressing that a given minimal Weierstrass equation
  has valuation of its discriminant equal to zero.

## Main statements

* : any Weierstrass curve is isomorphic to one given by
  an integral Weierstrass equation.
* : any Weierstrass curve is isomorphic to one given by
  a minimal Weierstrass equation.

## References

* J Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*

## Tags

elliptic curve, weierstrass equation, minimal weierstrass equation, reduction

A Weierstrass equation over the fraction field  is integral if
it has coefficients in the ring .

An integral model of an integral Weierstrass curve.

The valuation of the discriminant of a Weierstrass curve ,
which is at most 1 if  is integral. Zero otherwise.

A Weierstrass equation over the fraction field  is minimal if the (multiplicative) valuation
of its discriminant is maximal among all isomorphic integral Weierstrass equations.
We still use 'minimal' for the naming, so as to standardize the naming with Silverman's book.

A minimal Weierstrass equation for a given Weierstrass curve over .

The reduction of a Weierstrass curve over  given by a minimal Weierstrass equation,
which is a Weierstrass curve over the residue field of .

A minimal Weierstrass equation has good reduction if and only if
the valuation of its discriminant is 1.

A minimal Weierstrass equation has multiplicative reduction if and only if
the valuation of its discriminant is less than 1 and the valuation of  equals 1.

A minimal Weierstrass equation has additive reduction if and only if
the valuation of its discriminant is less than 1 and the valuation of  is less than 1.
