# Weierstrass equations of elliptic curves

This file defines the structure of an elliptic curve as a nonsingular Weierstrass curve given by a
Weierstrass equation, which is mathematically accurate in many cases but also good for computation.

## Mathematical background

Let  be a scheme. The actual category of elliptic curves over  is a large category, whose
objects are schemes  equipped with a map , a section , and some axioms (the map is
smooth and proper and the fibres are geometrically-connected one-dimensional group varieties). In
the special case where  is the spectrum of some commutative ring  whose Picard group is zero
(this includes all fields, all PIDs, and many other commutative rings) it can be shown (using a lot
of algebro-geometric machinery) that every elliptic curve  is a projective plane cubic isomorphic
to a Weierstrass curve given by the equation  for some
in , and such that a certain quantity called the discriminant of  is a unit in . If  is
a field, this quantity divides the discriminant of a cubic polynomial whose roots over a splitting
field of  are precisely the -coordinates of the non-zero 2-torsion points of .

## Main definitions

* : a Weierstrass curve over a commutative ring.
* : the discriminant of a Weierstrass curve.
* : the Weierstrass curve mapped over a ring homomorphism.
* : the 2-torsion polynomial of a Weierstrass curve.
* : typeclass asserting that a Weierstrass curve is an elliptic curve.
* : the j-invariant of an elliptic curve.

## Main statements

* : the discriminant of a Weierstrass curve is a
  constant factor of the cubic discriminant of its 2-torsion polynomial.

## Implementation notes

The definition of elliptic curves in this file makes sense for all commutative rings , but it
only gives a type which can be beefed up to a category which is equivalent to the category of
elliptic curves over the spectrum  of  in the case that  has trivial Picard group
 or, slightly more generally, when its 12-torsion is trivial. The issue is that for a
general ring , there might be elliptic curves over  in the sense of algebraic geometry
which are not globally defined by a cubic equation valid over the entire base.

## References

* N Katz and B Mazur, *Arithmetic Moduli of Elliptic Curves*
* P Deligne, *Courbes Elliptiques: Formulaire (d'après J. Tate)*
* J Silverman, *The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves*

# Subscheme structure on an irreducible component

We define the subscheme structure on an irreducible component of a Noetherian scheme. Typically,
one takes the reduced induced subscheme structure, but this will throw away information if the
irreducible component is not already reduced. Instead, we take the closed subscheme defined by
the kernel of the restriction to the complement of the union of the other irreducible components.

# Immersions of schemes

A morphism of schemes  is an immersion if the underlying map of topological spaces
is a locally closed embedding, and the induced morphisms of stalks are all surjective. This is true
if and only if it can be factored into a closed immersion followed by an open immersion.

## Main results
- :
  A morphism is a (locally-closed) immersion if and only if it can be factored into
  a closed immersion followed by a (dominant) open immersion.
- :
  A quasicompact morphism is a (locally-closed) immersion if and only if it can be factored into
  an open immersion followed by a closed immersion.

A morphism of schemes  is an immersion if
1. the underlying map of topological spaces is an embedding
2. the range of the map is locally closed
3. the induced morphisms of stalks are all surjective.

Given an immersion , this is the biggest open set  containing the image of
such that  is closed in .

The first part of the factorization of an immersion  to a closed immersion
 and a dominant open immersion .

Any (locally-closed) immersion can be factored into
a closed immersion followed by a (dominant) open immersion.

A morphism is a (locally-closed) immersion if and only if it can be factored into
a closed immersion followed by an open immersion.

The diagonal morphism is always an immersion.

The map  induced by any  is always an immersion.

If  is a quasi-compact immersion, then  is the pullback of the
closed immersion  and an open immersion .

A quasi-compact morphism is a (locally-closed) immersion if and only if it can be factored into
an open immersion followed by a closed immersion.

# Preimmersions of schemes

A morphism of schemes  is a preimmersion if the underlying map of topological spaces
is an embedding and the induced morphisms of stalks are all surjective. This is not a concept seen
in the literature but it is useful for generalizing results on immersions to other maps including
 and inclusions of fibers .

A morphism of schemes  is a preimmersion if the underlying map of
topological spaces is an embedding and the induced morphisms of stalks are all surjective.

# Universally injective morphism

A morphism of schemes  is universally injective if  is injective
for all base changes . This is equivalent to the diagonal morphism being surjective
().

We show that being universally injective is local at the target, and is stable under
compositions and base changes.

We also prove that universally injective is equivalent to being injective with
purely inseparable residue field extensions (also known as a radical morphism), see
 and Stacks tag 01S4.

A morphism of schemes  is universally injective if the base change
along any morphism  is injective (on points).

# Noetherian and Locally Noetherian Schemes

We introduce the concept of (locally) Noetherian schemes,
giving definitions, equivalent conditions, and basic properties.

## Main definitions

* : A scheme is locally Noetherian
  if the components of the structure sheaf at each affine open are Noetherian rings.

* : A scheme is Noetherian if it is locally Noetherian
  and quasi-compact as a topological space.

## Main results

* : A scheme is locally Noetherian
  if and only if it is covered by affine opens whose sections are Noetherian rings.

* : A locally Noetherian scheme is
  quasi-separated.

* : A scheme is Noetherian
  if and only if it is covered by finitely many affine opens whose sections are Noetherian rings.

* : A Noetherian scheme is
  topologically a Noetherian space.

* Robin Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*

# The pro-étale site

In this file we define the big and small pro-étale site. The big pro-étale site is
the category of schemes equipped with the pro-étale topology, which is the topology
generated by fpqc covers of weakly étale morphisms.

We prefer to work with weakly étale morphisms instead of pro-étale morphisms, since the property
of being pro-étale is not well-behaved: it is not local on the target.

We also define the small pro-étale site of a scheme  to be the category of schemes weakly-étale
over  and equip it with the induced topology.

# Quasi-compact precoverage

by a finite union of images of quasi-compact opens of the components.

# The structure sheaf on .

We define the structure sheaf on , for an -module  and prove
basic properties about it. We define this as a subsheaf of the sheaf of dependent functions into the
localizations, cut out by the condition that the function must be locally equal to a quotient of
an element of  by an element of .

Because the condition "is equal to a fraction" passes to smaller open subsets,
the subset of functions satisfying this condition is automatically a subpresheaf.
Because the condition "is locally equal to a fraction" is local,
it is also a subsheaf.

(It may be helpful to refer back to ,
where we show that dependent functions into any type family form a sheaf,
and also , where we characterise the predicates
which pick out sub-presheaves and sub-sheaves of these sheaves.)

When , the structure sheaf is furthermore a sheaf of commutative rings, which we bundle as
.

We then obtain two key descriptions of the structure sheaf. We show that the stalks  is the
localization of  at the prime corresponding to , and we show that the sections
is the localization of  away from .

Note that the results of this file are packaged into schemes and sheaf of modules in later files,
and one usually should not directly use the results in this file to respect the abstraction
boundaries.

## References

* Robin Hartshorne, *Algebraic Geometry*

The prime spectrum as an object of .

The type family over  consisting of the localization over each point.

The predicate saying that a dependent function on an open  is realised as a fixed fraction
in each of the stalks (which are localizations at various prime ideals).

The predicate  is "prelocal",
in the sense that if it holds on  it holds on any open subset  of .

We will define the structure sheaf as
the subsheaf of all dependent functions in
consisting of those functions which can locally be expressed as a ratio of
(the images in the localization of) elements of .

Quoting Hartshorne:

For an open set $U ⊆ Spec A$, we define $𝒪(U)$ to be the set of functions
$s : U → ⨆_{𝔭 ∈ U} A_𝔭$, such that $s(𝔭) ∈ A_𝔭$ for each $𝔭$,
and such that $s$ is locally a quotient of elements of $A$:
to be precise, we require that for each $𝔭 ∈ U$, there is a neighborhood $V$ of $𝔭$,
contained in $U$, and elements $a, f ∈ A$, such that for each $𝔮 ∈ V, f ∉ 𝔮$,
and $s(𝔮) = a/f$ in $A_𝔮$.

# Valuative criterion

## Main results

- :
  A morphism is universally closed if and only if
  it is quasi-compact and satisfies the existence part of the valuative criterion.
- :
  A morphism is separated if and only if
  it is quasi-separated and satisfies the uniqueness part of the valuative criterion.
- :
  A morphism is proper if and only if
  it is qcqs and of finite type and satisfies the valuative criterion.

# The Dold-Kan correspondence

The Dold-Kan correspondence states that for any abelian category , there is
an equivalence between the category of simplicial objects in  and the
category of chain complexes in  (with degrees indexed by  and the
homological convention that the degree is decreased by the differentials).

In this file, we finish the construction of this equivalence by providing
 which is of type
 for any abelian category .
The functor  of this equivalence is
definitionally equal to .

## Overall strategy of the proof of the correspondence

Before starting the implementation of the proof in Lean, the author noticed
that the Dold-Kan equivalence not only applies to abelian categories, but
should also hold generally for any pseudoabelian category
(i.e. a category with instances
 and ): this is
.

When the alternating face map complex  of a simplicial object  in an
abelian is studied, it is shown that it decomposes as a direct sum of the
normalized subcomplex and of the degenerate subcomplex. The crucial observation
is that in this decomposition, the projection on the normalized subcomplex can
be defined in each degree using simplicial operators. Then, the definition
of this projection  can be carried out for any
 when  is a preadditive category.

The construction of the endomorphism  is done in the files
, ,  and .
Eventually, as we would also like to show that the inclusion of the normalized
Moore complex is a homotopy equivalence (cf. file ),
this projection  needs to be homotopic to the identity. In our
construction, we get this for free because  is obtained by altering
the identity endomorphism by null homotopic maps. More details about this
aspect of the proof are in the file .

When the alternating face map complex  is equipped with the idempotent
endomorphism , it becomes an object in
which is the idempotent completion of the category . In ,
we obtain this functor ,
which is formally extended as
. (Here, some functors
have an index which is the number of occurrences of  at the source or the
target.)

In , assuming that the category  is additive,
we define the functor in the other direction
 as the formal
extension of a functor  which is
defined similarly as in *Simplicial Homotopy Theory* by Goerss-Jardine.
In , we show that  vanishes on the image of degeneracy
operators, which is one of the key properties that makes it possible to construct
the isomorphism .

The rest of the proof follows the strategy in the original paper by Dold. We show
that the functor  reflects isomorphisms in : this relies on a
decomposition of the identity of  using  and degeneracies obtained in
. Then, in , we construct a natural transformation
. It is shown that it is an
isomorphism using the fact that  reflects isomorphisms, and because we can show
that the composition  is the identity (see ). The fact
that  is defined as a formal direct factor makes the proof easier because we only
have to compare endomorphisms of an alternating face map complex  and we do not
have to worry with inclusions of kernel subobjects.

# Construction of homotopies for the Dold-Kan correspondence

(The general strategy of proof of the Dold-Kan correspondence is explained
in .)

The purpose of the files , ,
and  is to construct an idempotent endomorphism
 of the alternating face map complex
for each  when  is a preadditive category.
In the case  is abelian, this  shall be the projection on the
normalized Moore subcomplex of  associated to the decomposition of the
complex  as a direct sum of this normalized subcomplex and of the
degenerate subcomplex.

In , this endomorphism  shall be obtained by
passing to the limit idempotent endomorphisms  for all .
These endomorphisms  are defined by induction. The idea is to
start from the identity endomorphism  of  and to ensure by
induction that the  higher face maps (except $d_0$) vanish on the
image of . Then, in a certain degree , the image of  for
a big enough  will be contained in the normalized subcomplex. This
construction is done in .

It would be easy to define the  degreewise (similarly as it is done
in *Simplicial Homotopy Theory* by Goerss-Jardine p. 149), but then we would
have to prove that they are compatible with the differential (i.e. they
are chain complex maps), and also that they are homotopic to the identity.
These two verifications are quite technical. In order to reduce the number
of such technical lemmas, the strategy that is followed here is to define
a series of null homotopic maps  (attached to families of maps )
and use these in order to construct  : the endomorphisms
shall basically be obtained by altering the identity endomorphism by adding
null homotopic maps, so that we get for free that they are morphisms
of chain complexes and that they are homotopic to the identity. The most
technical verifications that are needed about the null homotopic maps

# Simply connected spaces

This file defines simply connected spaces.
A topological space is simply connected if its fundamental groupoid is equivalent to .

We also define the corresponding predicate for sets.

## Main theorems
  -  - A space is simply connected if and only if it is
    nonempty and there is a unique path up to homotopy between any two points

  -  - A contractible space is simply connected

A simply connected space is one whose fundamental groupoid is equivalent to

In a simply connected space, any two paths are homotopic

A space is simply connected iff it is path connected, and there is at most one path
 up to homotopy between any two points.

Another version of

A space is simply connected if and only if it is path-connected and every loop
   at any basepoint is null-homotopic (i.e., homotopic to the constant loop).

Forward: all paths homotopic implies all loops null-homotopic

Backward: all loops null-homotopic implies all paths homotopic

# Model categories

We introduce a typeclass  expressing that  is equipped with
classes of morphisms named "fibrations", "cofibrations" and "weak equivalences"
which satisfy the axioms of (closed) model categories as they appear for example
in *Simplicial Homotopy Theory* by Goerss and Jardine. We also provide an
alternate constructor  which uses a formulation of the axioms
using weak factorization systems.

As a given category  may have several model category structures, it is advisable
to define only local instances of , or to set these instances on type synonyms.

## References
* Daniel G. Quillen, Homotopical algebra
* Paul G. Goerss, John F. Jardine, Simplicial Homotopy Theory
*

A model category is a category equipped with classes of morphisms named cofibrations,
fibrations and weak equivalences which satisfy the axioms CM1/CM2/CM3/CM4/CM5
of (closed) model categories.

Constructor for  which assumes a formulation of axioms
using weak factorization systems.

BEGIN FILE: Mathlib/AlgebraicTopology/ModelCategory/JoyalTrick.lean
================================================================================

# A trick by Joyal

In order to construct a model category, we may sometimes have basically
proven all the axioms with the exception of the left lifting property
of cofibrations with respect to trivial fibrations. A trick by Joyal
allows to obtain this lifting property under suitable assumptions,
namely that cofibrations are stable under composition and cobase change.
(The dual result is also formalized.)

## References
* John F. Jardine, Simplicial presheaves

Joyal's trick: that cofibrations have the left lifting property
with respect to trivial fibrations follows from the left lifting property
of trivial cofibrations with respect to fibrations and a few other
consequences of the model categories axioms.

Joyal's trick (dual): that trivial cofibrations have the left lifting
property with respect to fibrations follows from the left lifting property
of cofibrations with respect to trivial fibrations and a few other
consequences of the model categories axioms.

# Anodyne extensions

Anodyne extensions form a property of morphisms in the category of simplicial
sets. It contains horn inclusions and it is closed under coproducts, pushouts,
transfinite compositions and retracts. Equivalently, using the small
object argument, anodyne extensions can be defined (and are defined here)
as the class of morphisms that satisfy the left lifting property with respect
to the class of fibrations (for the Quillen model category structure:
fibrations are morphisms that have the right lifting property with respect
to horn inclusions). When the Quillen model category structure is fully
upstreamed (TODO @joelriou), it can be shown that a morphism  is an
anodyne extension iff  is a cofibration that is also a weak equivalence.

We also introduce the class of strong anodyne extensions that could be defined
as a closure similarly as anodyne extensions, but without taking the closure
under retracts. Sean Moss has given a combinatorial description of these
strong anodyne extensions: the inclusion  of a subcomplex
of a simplicial set  is a strong anodyne extension iff there exists
a regular pairing for . In this file, we define strong anodyne extensions
in terms of such regular pairings, and using the main result of the file

we show that a strong anodyne extension is an anodyne extension.

## TODO
* introduce inner variants of these definitions
* show that strong anodyne extensions are indeed stable under coproducts,
  transfinite compositions and pushouts (the proof should reduce to the
  construction of pairings)
* study the interaction between anodyne extension and binary products:
  the critical case consists in showing that inclusions
   are strong anodyne extensions (@joelriou)
* show that anodyne extensions are stable under the subdivision functor (@joelriou)

## References
* P. Gabriel, M. Zisman, *Calculus of fractions and homotopy theory*, IV.2
* Sean Moss, *Another approach to the Kan-Quillen model structure*

In the category of simplicial sets, an anodyne extension is a morphism
that has the left lifting property with respect to fibrations, where
a fibration is a morphism that has the right lifting property with respect
to horn inclusions. We do not introduce a typeclass for anodyne extensions
because when the Quillen model structure is fully upstreamed (TODO @joelriou),
the assumption  can be spelled as
.

In the category of simplicial sets, a strong anodyne extension is a morphism
which belongs to the closure of horn inclusions by pushouts, coproducts,
transfinite compositions (but not by retracts). We define this class here
by saying that  is a strong anodyne extension if  is a monomorphism
and there exists a regular pairing (in the sense of Moss) for the subcomplex
 of .

# Inner anodyne extensions

Much of this file is mirrored from
.

*Inner* anodyne extensions form a property of morphisms in the category of simplicial
sets. It contains *inner* horn inclusions and it is closed under coproducts, pushouts,
transfinite compositions and retracts. Equivalently, using the small
object argument, inner anodyne extensions can be defined (and are defined here)
as the class of morphisms that satisfy the left lifting property with respect
to the class of inner fibrations.

In the category of simplicial sets, an *inner* anodyne extension is a morphism
that has the left lifting property with respect to *inner* fibrations, where
an inner fibration is a morphism that has the right lifting property with respect
to inner horn inclusions.

In the category of simplicial sets, a strong *inner* anodyne extension is a morphism
which belongs to the closure of *inner* horn inclusions by pushouts, coproducts,
transfinite compositions (but not by retracts). We define this class here
by saying that  is a strong inner anodyne extension if  is a monomorphism
and there exists a regular, *inner* pairing (in the sense of Moss) for the subcomplex
 of .

# Pairings

In this file, we introduce the definition of a pairing for a subcomplex
of a simplicial set , following the ideas by Sean Moss,
*Another approach to the Kan-Quillen model structure*, who gave a
complete combinatorial characterization of strong (inner) anodyne extensions.
Strong (inner) anodyne extensions are transfinite compositions of pushouts of coproducts
of (inner) horn inclusions, i.e. this is similar to (inner) anodyne extensions but
without the stability property under retracts.

A pairing for  consists in the data of a partition of the nondegenerate
simplices of  not in  into type (I) simplices and type (II) simplices,
and of a bijection between the types of type (I) and type (II) simplices.
Indeed, the main observation is that when we attach a simplex along a horn
inclusion, exactly two nondegenerate simplices are added: this simplex,
and the unique face which is not in the image of the horn. The former shall be
considered as of type (I) and the latter as type (II).

We say that a pairing is *regular* (typeclass ) when
- it is proper (), i.e. any type (II) simplex is uniquely
  a face of the corresponding type (I) simplex.
- a certain ancestrality relation is well founded.

When these conditions are satisfied, the inclusion  is
a strong anodyne extension (TODO @joelriou), and the converse is also true
(if  is a strong anodyne extension, then there is a regular pairing for  (TODO)).

of the nondegenerate simplices of  not in  in two types (I) and (II) of simplices,
and a bijection between the type (II) simplices and the type (I) simplices.

underlying reflexive quiver (equivalently its one truncation). The quotient imposes an additional
hom relation on this free category, asserting that  whenever , , and  are
respectively the 2nd, 0th, and 1st faces of a 2-simplex.

analogously defined  implemented relative to
the syntax of the 2-truncated simplex category.

# The adjunction between the nerve and the homotopy category functor

We define an adjunction  between the functor that
takes a simplicial set to its homotopy category and the functor that takes a category to its nerve.

Up to natural isomorphism, this is constructed as the composite of two other adjunctions,
namely  between analogously-defined functors involving
the category of 2-truncated simplicial sets and . The
aforementioned natural isomorphism



exists because nerves of categories are 2-coskeletal.

We also prove that  is fully faithful, demonstrating that  is
reflective. Since the category of simplicial sets is cocomplete, we conclude in
 that the category of categories has colimits.

Finally we show that  preserves finite cartesian products; note
that it fails to preserve infinite products.

# The Nerve of a Codiscrete Category

In the codiscrete category on a type , every hom-type is given by .
When we take the nerve of such a category, the -simplices become equivalent to
-vectors of length .
Therefore, if  has decidable equality, so does the type of -simplices in this nerve.

Since the morphisms in a codiscrete category do not carry information, an n-simplex of
coherentIso is equivalent to an X-vector of length (n + 1).

If a type  has decidable equality, the nerve of the codiscrete category on
has decidable equality as well.

# Analytic functions

A function is analytic in one dimension around  if it can be written as a converging power series
. This definition can be extended to any dimension (even in infinite dimension) by
requiring that  is a continuous -multilinear map. In general,  is not unique (in two
dimensions, taking  or  gives the same map when applied to a
vector ). A way to guarantee uniqueness is to take a symmetric , but this is not
always possible in nonzero characteristic (in characteristic 2, the previous example has no
symmetric representative). Therefore, we do not insist on symmetry or uniqueness in the definition,
and we only require the existence of a converging series.

The general framework is important to say that the exponential map on bounded operators on a Banach
space is analytic, as well as the inverse on invertible operators.

# Properties of continuously polynomial functions

We expand the API around continuously polynomial functions. Notably, we show that this class is
stable under the usual operations (addition, subtraction, negation).

We also prove that continuous multilinear maps are continuously polynomial, and so
are continuous linear maps into continuous multilinear maps. In particular, such maps are
analytic.

### Continuous multilinear maps

We show that continuous multilinear maps are continuously polynomial, and therefore analytic.

### Continuous linear maps into continuous multilinear maps

We show that a continuous linear map into continuous multilinear maps is continuously polynomial
(as a function of two variables, i.e., uncurried). Therefore, it is also analytic.

Formal multilinear series associated to a linear map into multilinear maps.

# Changing origin in a power series

If a function is analytic in a disk , then it is analytic in any disk contained in that
one. Indeed, one can write
$$
f (x + y + z) = \sum_{n} p_n (y + z)^n = \sum_{n, k} \binom{n}{k} p_n y^{n-k} z^k
= \sum_{k} \Bigl(\sum_{n} \binom{n}{k} p_n y^{n-k}\Bigr) z^k.
$$
The corresponding power series has thus a -th coefficient equal to
$\sum_{n} \binom{n}{k} p_n y^{n-k}$. In the general case where  is a multilinear map, this has
to be interpreted suitably: instead of having a binomial coefficient, one should sum over all
possible subsets  of  of cardinality , and attribute  to the indices in  and
 to the indices outside of .

In this file, we implement this. The new power series is called . Then, we
check its convergence and the fact that its sum coincides with the original sum. The outcome of this
discussion is that the set of points where a function is analytic is open. All these arguments
require the target space to be complete, as otherwise the series might not converge.

# Composition of analytic functions

In this file we prove that the composition of analytic functions is analytic.

The argument is the following. Assume  and . Then


= ∑' qₙ (p_{i₁} (y, ..., y), ..., p_{iₙ} (y, ..., y))

For each  and , define a  multilinear function mapping
 to
.
Then  is obtained by summing all these multilinear functions.

To formalize this, we use compositions of an integer , i.e., its decompositions into
a sum  of positive integers. Given such a composition  and two formal
multilinear series  and , let  be the above multilinear
function. Then the -th coefficient in the power series expansion of  is the sum of these
terms over all .

To complete the proof, we need to show that this power series has a positive radius of convergence.
This follows from the fact that  has cardinality  and estimates on
the norm of  and , which give summability. We also need to show that it indeed converges to
. For this, we note that the composition of partial sums converges to , and that it
corresponds to a part of the whole sum, on a subset that increases to the whole space. By
summability of the norms, this implies the overall convergence.

## Main results

*  is the formal composition of the formal multilinear series  and .
*  states that if two functions  and  admit power series expansions
   and , then  admits a power series expansion given by .
*  states that the composition of analytic functions is analytic.
*  states that composition is associative on formal
  multilinear series.

## Implementation details

The main technical difficulty is to write down things. In particular, we need to define precisely
 and to show that it is indeed a continuous multilinear
function. This requires a whole interface built on the class . Once this is set,
the main difficulty is to reorder the sums, writing the composition of the partial sums as a sum
over some subset of . We need to check that the reordering is a bijection,
running over difficulties due to the dependent nature of the types under consideration, that are
controlled thanks to the interface for .

The associativity of composition on formal multilinear series is a nontrivial result: it does not
follow from the associativity of composition of analytic functions, as there is no uniqueness for
the formal multilinear series representing a function (and also, it holds even when the radius of
convergence of the series is ). Instead, we give a direct proof, which amounts to reordering
double sums in a careful way. The change of variables is a canonical (combinatorial) bijection
 between  and
, and is described
in more details below in the paragraph on associativity.

### Convergence of the inverse of a power series

Assume that  is a convergent multilinear series, and let  be its (left or right) inverse.
Using the left-inverse formula gives
$$
q_n = - (p_1)^{-n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \sum_{i_1 + \dotsc + i_k = n} q_k (p_{i_1}, \dotsc, p_{i_k}).
$$
Assume for simplicity that we are in dimension  and . In the formula for , the term
 appears with a multiplicity of  (choosing the index  for which  while
all the other indices are equal to ), which indicates that  might grow like . This is
bad for summability properties.

It turns out that the right-inverse formula is better behaved, and should instead be used for this
kind of estimate. It reads
$$
q_n = - (p_1)^{-1} \sum_{k=2}^n \sum_{i_1 + \dotsc + i_k = n} p_k (q_{i_1}, \dotsc, q_{i_k}).
$$
Here,  can only appear in the term with , and it only appears twice, so there is
hope this formula can lead to an at most geometric behavior.

Let . Bounding  with  gives an inequality
$$
Q_n ≤ C' \sum_{k=2}^n r^k \sum_{i_1 + \dotsc + i_k = n} Q_{i_1} \dotsm Q_{i_k}.
$$

This formula is not enough to prove by naive induction on  a bound of the form .
However, assuming that the inequality above were an equality, one could get a formula for the
generating series of the :

$$
\begin{align}
Q(z) & := \sum Q_n z^n = Q_1 z + C' \sum_{2 \leq k \leq n} \sum_{i_1 + \dotsc + i_k = n}
  (r z^{i_1} Q_{i_1}) \dotsm (r z^{i_k} Q_{i_k})
\\ & = Q_1 z + C' \sum_{k = 2}^\infty (\sum_{i_1 \geq 1} r z^{i_1} Q_{i_1})
  \dotsm (\sum_{i_k \geq 1} r z^{i_k} Q_{i_k})
\\ & = Q_1 z + C' \sum_{k = 2}^\infty (r Q(z))^k
= Q_1 z + C' (r Q(z))^2 / (1 - r Q(z)).
\end{align}
$$

One can solve this formula explicitly. The solution is analytic in a neighborhood of  in ,
hence its coefficients grow at most geometrically (by a contour integral argument), and therefore
the original , which are bounded by these ones, are also at most geometric.

This classical argument is not really satisfactory, as it requires an a priori bound on a complex
analytic function. Another option would be to compute explicitly its terms (with binomial
coefficients) to obtain an explicit geometric bound, but this would be very painful.

Instead, we will use the above intuition, but in a slightly different form, with finite sums and an
induction. I learnt this trick in [poeschel2017siegelsternberg]. Let
$S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n Q_k a^k$ (where  is a positive real parameter to be chosen suitably small).
The above computation but with finite sums shows that

$$
S_n \leq Q_1 a + C' \sum_{k=2}^n (r S_{n-1})^k.
$$

In particular, $S_n \leq Q_1 a + C' (r S_{n-1})^2 / (1- r S_{n-1})$.
Assume that $S_{n-1} \leq K a$, where  is fixed and  is small enough so that
 (to control the denominator). Then this equation gives a bound
$S_n \leq Q_1 a + 2 C' r^2 K^2 a^2$.
If  is small enough, this is bounded by  as the second term is quadratic in , and
therefore negligible.

By induction, we deduce  for all , which gives in particular the fact that
remains bounded.

in a general abstract setup.

# Delone sets

A **Delone set**  in a metric space is a set which is both:

* **Uniformly Discrete**: there exists  such that distinct points of
  are separated by a distance strictly greater than ;
* **Relatively Dense**: there exists  such that every point of
  lies within distance  of some point of .

The  structure stores the set together with explicit radii witnessing
these properties. The definitions use metric entourages so that the theory fits
naturally into the uniformity framework.

Delone sets appear in discrete geometry, crystallography, aperiodic order, and tiling theory.

## Main definitions

* : The main structure representing a Delone set in a metric space .
* : Transports a Delone set along a bilipschitz equivalence,
  scaling the radii.
*  Preserves the packing and covering radii exactly.

## Basic properties

*  : Distinct points in a Delone set are further apart than
  the packing radius.
*  : Every point of the space lies within the covering radius
  of the set.
*  : Any ball of sufficiently small radius contains at most one point of
  the set.

## Implementation notes

* **Bundled Structure**:  is bundled as a structure rather than a predicate
  (e.g., ). This facilitates dynamical systems constructions like hulls and patches by
  ensuring operations automatically preserve the required properties, eliminating the need to
  manually pass around proofs that the set remains Delone.
* **Explicit Data**: Since radii are stored as explicit data, the map from  to
  is not injective. We provide a  instance and  to allow the convenience
  of  notation while ensuring radii remain bundled, computationally accessible, and tracked by
  extensionality.

A **Delone set** consists of a set together with explicit radii
witnessing uniform discreteness and relative denseness.

The underlying set.

Radius such that every point of the space is within  of .

# Asymptotics in a Topological Vector Space

This file defines , , and
as generalizations of , , and
from normed spaces to topological vector spaces.

Given two functions  and  taking values in topological vector spaces
over a normed field ,
we say that $f = o(g)$ (resp., $f = O(g)$)
if for any neighborhood of zero  in the codomain of
there exists a neighborhood of zero  in the codomain of
such that $\operatorname{gauge}_{K, U} (f(x)) = o(\operatorname{gauge}_{K, V} (g(x)))$
(resp., $\operatorname{gauge}_{K, U} (f(x)) = O(\operatorname{gauge}_{K, V} (g(x)))$),
where $\operatorname{gauge}_{K, U}(y) = \inf \{‖c‖ \mid y ∈ c • U\}$.

We say that $f=Θ(g)$, if both $f=O(g)$ and $g=O(f)$.

In a normed space, we can use balls of positive radius as both  and ,
thus reducing the definition to the classical one.

These modifications of the definitions free the user from having to chose a canonical norm,
at the expense of having to pick a specific base field.
This is exactly the tradeoff we want in ,
as there the base field is already chosen,
and this removes the choice of norm being part of the statement.

These definitions were added to the library in order to migrate Fréchet derivatives
from normed vector spaces to topological vector spaces.
The definitions are motivated by

but the definition there doesn't work for topological vector spaces over general normed fields.
This Zulip discussion
led to the current choice of the definition of ,
and  was defined in a similar manner.

## Main results

* : the equivalence between these two definitions in the case of a
  normed space.

* : the equivalence to convergence of the ratio to zero
  in case of a topological vector space.

# Almost everywhere differentiability of functions with locally bounded variation

This implies that Lipschitz functions from the real line into finite-dimensional vector spaces
are also differentiable almost everywhere.

We prove that f is integrable by proving that we can ensure that the integrals over any
    two tagged prepartitions π₁ and π₂ can be made ε-close by making the partitions
    sufficiently fine.

    Start by defining some constants C, ε₁, ε₂ that will be useful later.

The set of discontinuities of f is contained in an open set U with μ U < ε₂.

Box.Icc I \ U is compact and avoids discontinuities of f, so there exists r > 0 such that for
    every x ∈ Box.Icc I \ U, the oscillation (within Box.Icc I) of f on the ball of radius r
    centered at x is ≤ ε₁

We prove the claim for partitions π₁ and π₂ subordinate to r/2, by writing the difference as
    an integralSum over π₁ ⊓ π₂ and considering separately the boxes of π₁ ⊓ π₂ which are/aren't
    fully contained within U.

If a box J is not contained within U, then the oscillation of f on J is small, which bounds
    the contribution of J to the overall sum.

The contribution of the boxes contained within U is bounded because f is bounded and μ U < ε₂.

# Filters used in box-based integrals

First we define a structure . This structure will be used as an
argument in the definition of  in order to use the same definition for a few
well-known definitions of integrals based on partitions of a rectangular box into subboxes (Riemann
integral, Henstock-Kurzweil integral, and McShane integral).

This structure holds three Boolean values (see below), and encodes eight different sets of
parameters; only four of these values are used somewhere in . Three of them correspond to
the integration theories listed above, and one is a generalization of the one-dimensional
Henstock-Kurzweil integral such that the divergence theorem works without additional integrability
assumptions.

Finally, for each set of parameters  and a rectangular box
, we define several s that will be used either in the definition of
the corresponding integral, or in the proofs of its properties. We equip
 with a  structure such that larger
 produce larger filters.

## Main definitions

### Integration parameters

The structure  has 3 Boolean fields with the following meaning:

* : the value  means that the filter corresponds to a Riemann-style integral, i.e.
  in the definition of integrability we require a constant upper estimate  on the size of boxes
  of a tagged partition; the value  means that the estimate may depend on the position of the
  tag.

* : the value  means that we require that each tag belongs to its own closed box;
  the value  means that we only require that tags belong to the ambient box.

* : the value  means that  can depend on the maximal ratio of sides of the
  same box of a partition. Presence of this case make quite a few proofs harder but we can prove the
  divergence theorem only for the filter
  {bRiemann := false, bHenstock := true, bDistortion := true}

### Well-known sets of parameters

Out of eight possible values of , the following four are used in
the library.

*  (, ,
  ): this value corresponds to the Riemann integral; in the corresponding
  filter, we require that the diameters of all boxes  of a tagged partition are bounded from
  above by a constant upper estimate that may not depend on the geometry of , and each tag
  belongs to the corresponding closed box.

*  (, ,
  ): this value corresponds to the most natural generalization of
  Henstock-Kurzweil integral to higher dimension; the only (but important!) difference between this
  theory and Riemann integral is that instead of a constant upper estimate on the size of all boxes
  of a partition, we require that the partition is *subordinate* to a possibly discontinuous
  function , i.e. each box  is included in a closed ball with
  center  and radius .

*  (, ,
  ): this value corresponds to the McShane integral; the only difference with
  the Henstock integral is that we allow tags to be outside of their boxes; the tags still have to
  be in the ambient closed box, and the partition still has to be subordinate to a function.

*  (, ,
  ): this is the least integration theory in our list, i.e., all functions
  integrable in any other theory is integrable in this one as well.  This is a non-standard
  generalization of the Henstock-Kurzweil integral to higher dimension.  In dimension one, it
  generates the same filter as . In higher dimension, this generalization defines an
  integration theory such that the divergence of any Fréchet differentiable function  is
  integrable, and its integral is equal to the sum of integrals of  over the faces of the box,
  taken with appropriate signs.

  A function  is -integrable if for any  and  there exists
   such that for any tagged partition  subordinate to , if each
  tag belongs to the corresponding closed box and for each box , the maximal ratio of its
  sides is less than or equal to , then the integral sum of  over  is -close to the
  integral.

## Implementation details

* Later we define the integral of a function over a rectangular box as the limit (if it exists) of
  the integral sums along . While it is
  possible to define the integral with a general filter on  as a
  parameter, many lemmas (e.g., Sacks-Henstock lemma and most results about integrability of
  functions) require the filter to have a predictable structure. So, instead of adding assumptions
  about the filter here and there, we define this auxiliary type that can encode all integration
  theories we need in practice.

* While the definition of the integral only uses the filter
   and partitions of a box, some lemmas
  (e.g., the Henstock-Sacks lemmas) are best formulated in terms of the predicate  and
  other filters defined above.

* We use  instead of  for the fields of  in order to have decidable
  equality and inequalities.

polynomial functional calculus (i.e., ).

# Continuity of the continuous functional calculus in each variable

The continuous functional calculus is a map which takes a pair  ( is a C⋆-algebra) and
a function  where  satisfies some predicate , depending on  and
returns another element of the algebra . This is the map . The class
 declares that  is a continuous map from
to . However, users generally interact with the continuous functional calculus through ,
which operates on bare functions  instead and takes a junk value when  is not
continuous on the spectrum of .  In this file we provide some lemma concerning the continuity
of , subject to natural hypotheses.

However, the continuous functional calculus is *also* continuous in the variable , but there
are some conditions that must be satisfied. In particular, given a function  the map
 is continuous so long as  varies over a collection of elements satisfying the
predicate  and their spectra are collectively contained in a compact set on which  is
continuous. Moreover, it is required that the continuous functional calculus be the isometric
variant.

Under the assumption of , we show that the continuous
functional calculus is Lipschitz with constant 1 in the variable
on the set of functions which are continuous on the spectrum of . Combining this with the
continuity of the continuous functional calculus in the variable , we obtain a joint continuity
result for  in both variables.

Finally, all of this is developed for both the unital and non-unital functional calculi.
The continuity results in the function variable are valid for all scalar rings, but the continuity
results in the variable  come in two flavors: those for  and those for .

# Instances of the continuous functional calculus

## Main theorems

* : the continuous functional calculus for
  selfadjoint elements in a -algebra with a continuous functional calculus for normal elements
  and where every element has compact spectrum. In particular, this includes unital C⋆-algebras
  over .
* : the continuous functional calculus for nonnegative
  elements in an -algebra with a continuous functional calculus for selfadjoint elements,
  where every element has compact spectrum, and where nonnegative elements have nonnegative
  spectrum. In particular, this includes unital C⋆-algebras over .

## Tags

continuous functional calculus, normal, selfadjoint

### Pull back a non-unital instance from a unital one on the unitization

This is an auxiliary definition used for constructing an instance of the non-unital continuous
functional calculus given an instance of the unital one on the unitization.

This is the natural non-unital star homomorphism obtained from the chain
This range of this map is contained in the range of  (see ),
and so we may restrict it to  to get the necessary homomorphism for the non-unital continuous
functional calculus.

### Continuous functional calculus for selfadjoint elements

An element in a non-unital C⋆-algebra is selfadjoint if and only if it is normal and its
quasispectrum is contained in .

A normal element whose -quasispectrum is contained in  is selfadjoint.

### Continuous functional calculus for nonnegative elements

In a C⋆-algebra, commuting nonnegative elements have nonnegative products.

### The restriction of a continuous functional calculus is equal to the original one

# Isometric continuous functional calculus

This file adds a class for an *isometric* continuous functional calculus. This is separate from the
usual  class because we prefer not to require a metric (or a norm) on
the algebra for reasons discussed in the module documentation for that file.

Of course, with a metric on the algebra and an isometric continuous functional calculus, the
algebra must *be* a C⋆-algebra already. As such, it may seem like this class is not useful. However,
the main purpose is to allow for the continuous functional calculus to be an isometry for the other
scalar rings  and  too.

### Isometric continuous functional calculus for unital algebras

An extension of the  requiring that  is an isometry.

### Isometric continuous functional calculus for non-unital algebras

An extension of the  requiring that  is an
isometry.

### Instances of isometric continuous functional calculi

The instances for  and  can be found in
, as those require an actual
 instance on , whereas the one for  is simply inherited from an existing
instance for .

### Properties specific to

### Non-unital instance for unital algebras

An isometric continuous functional calculus on a unital algebra yields to a non-unital one.

# The continuous functional calculus for non-unital algebras

This file defines a generic API for the *continuous functional calculus* in *non-unital* algebras
which is suitable in a wide range of settings. The design is intended to match as closely as
possible that for unital algebras in
.  Changes to either file
should be mirrored in its counterpart whenever possible. The underlying reasons for the design
decisions in the unital case apply equally in the non-unital case. See the module documentation in
that file for more information.

A continuous functional calculus for an element  in a non-unital topological -algebra is
a continuous extension of the polynomial functional calculus (i.e., ) for
polynomials with no constant term to continuous -valued functions on  which
vanish at zero. More precisely, it is a continuous star algebra homomorphism
 that sends
to . In all cases of interest (e.g., when  is compact and  is , ,
or ), this is sufficient to uniquely determine the continuous functional calculus which is
encoded in the  class.

## Main declarations

+ : a class stating that every
  satisfying  has a non-unital star algebra homomorphism from the continuous -valued
  functions on the -quasispectrum of  vanishing at zero into the algebra . This map is a
  closed embedding, and satisfies the **spectral mapping theorem**.
+ : the underlying non-unital star algebra
  homomorphism for an element satisfying property .
+ : an unbundled version of  which takes the junk value  when
   is not defined.

# Documentation concerning the continuous functional calculus

A library note giving advice on developing and using the continuous functional calculus, as well
as the organizational structure within Mathlib.

# The continuous functional calculus

In Mathlib, there are two classes ---  and
, indexed by the scalar ring  and the predicate
which must be satisfied --- which are used to provide the interface to the continuous functional
calculus. This allows us to reason about the continuous functional calculus in both unital and
non-unital algebras, using functions, , , or , as appropriate.

These classes are designed to be used even in contexts where no norm is present, such as for
, and indeed, an instance of  already
exists in this context. However, when a norm is present (i.e., in the context of C⋆-algebras), the
continuous functional calculus is an isometry. In order not to lose this information, we provide
two additional classes  and
, extending the classes above. We encode this as a class
for two reasons:

1. to provide a uniform interface for multiple scalar rings
2. to allow for generalization to real C⋆-algebras

This means that there are twelve different classes, corresponding to the choices of scalar ring
(, , or ), unital or non-unital algebras, isometric or not. The relationship between
these is documented in the diagram below, with arrows indicating always available instances.
The dotted arrow requires the presence of instances ,  and
. Note that the instances which change scalar rings occur *within* each
class (i.e., , , etc.), so a
more accurate diagram would have the chain on the left embedded within each node of the graph
on the right.


## Developing general theory

When developing general theory of the continuous functional calculus, users should work in the
appropriate general class. For example, the positive and negative parts of a selfadjoint element
are defined using the continuous functional calculus via the functions  and
. These functions both take the value  at , and so work equally well in the
non-unital setting. Moreover, the only scalar ring needed is , not . Therefore, the correct
context in which to develop the basic theory of positive and negative parts is:


One pattern that should *never* be used is to directly assume
(or the non-unital version) over the scalar ring . Doing so only complicates the setup, for
no benefit. Indeed, in practice the only available instance of

with , , . Therefore, directly assuming
the  version makes Lean do more work in type class inference, and makes the structure of the
source code less readable. Instead, the correct pattern is to assume the version over , and then
add these extra three classes as needed to get the instance over .

There are three questions that an author should ask themselves when developing general theory
in order to determine the correct s to have in context. These are:

1. Does this work for arbitrary scalar (semi)rings? Only , or is  sufficient?

  For arbitrary scalar rings, use  with a predicate , and assume that  is an
  -algebra. For  use  and assume  is a -algebra. For  use
   and assume  is an -algebra. Reminder, if you need the functional calculus
  over , simply use the  setup with the three extra classes.

2. Does this work in non-unital algebras?

  This determines whether you should use the unital or  variation, and whether your
  algebra should be unital or non-unital.

3. Does this require norm properties of the algebra?

  This determines whether you should use the standard version or the  variation.
  If you are not using the  variation, you should generally only assume that  is a
   (or potentially a topological algebra). If you are using the

Of course, sometimes one needs to have different sections which make different assumptions, even
for the same functions considered. For instance, although theory of positive and negative parts

## Using

Mathlib makes heavy use of s in the continuous functional calculus. There are three
different tactics which are used:

1.  for proving goals of the form ,  or .
2.  for proving goals of the form .
3.  for proving goals of the form .

In general, lemmas about the continuous functional calculus should be written using s
wherever possible for these kinds of goals. These arguments should be placed *last*, at least among
the explicit arguments. Moreover, if the arguments  and  cannot be inferred from other
explicit arguments (i.e., those which are not s), then they should also be *explicit*
rather than implicit, despite the fact that they appear in the types of the  arguments.
The reason is that it is often necessary to supply these arguments in order for the
arguments to fire.

As to argument order, we generally prefer functions before elements of the algebra (i.e.,  and
then ) to match the order of application (i.e., ). Likewise, we generally place the
s for the continuity conditions before the others because these are the most likely to
require manual intervention.

# The continuous functional calculus

This file defines a generic API for the *continuous functional calculus* which is suitable in a wide
range of settings.

A continuous functional calculus for an element  in a topological -algebra is a continuous
extension of the polynomial functional calculus (i.e., ) to continuous -valued
functions on . More precisely, it is a continuous star algebra homomorphism
 that sends  to
. In all cases of interest (e.g., when  is compact and  is , , or ),
this is sufficient to uniquely determine the continuous functional calculus which is encoded in the
 class.

Although these properties suffice to uniquely determine the continuous functional calculus, we
choose to bundle more information into the class itself. Namely, we include that the star algebra
homomorphism is a closed embedding, and also that the spectrum of the image of
 under this morphism is the range of . In addition, the class specifies
a collection of continuous functional calculi for elements satisfying a given predicate
, and we require that this predicate is preserved by the functional calculus.

Although  is a necessity for getting the full power
out of the continuous functional calculus, this declaration will generally not be accessed directly
by the user. One reason for this is that  requires a proof of  (indeed, if the
spectrum is empty, there cannot exist a star algebra homomorphism like this). Instead, we provide
the completely unbundled  which operates on bare functions and provides junk
values when either  does not satisfy the property , or else when the function which is the
argument to  is not continuous on the spectrum of .

This completely unbundled approach may give up some conveniences, but it allows for tremendous
freedom. In particular,  makes sense for *any*  and . This is quite
useful in a variety of settings, but perhaps the most important is the following.
Besides being a star algebra homomorphism sending the identity to , the key property enjoyed
by the continuous functional calculus is the *composition property*, which guarantees that
 under suitable hypotheses on ,  and . Note that this
theorem is nearly impossible to state nicely in terms of  (see ). An
additional advantage of the unbundled approach is that expressions like  are valid
arguments to , and a bundled continuous counterpart can only make sense when the spectrum of
 does not contain zero and when we have an  operation on the domain.

A reader familiar with C⋆-algebra theory may be somewhat surprised at the level of abstraction here.
For instance, why not require  to be an actual C⋆-algebra? Why define separate continuous
functional calculi for ,  or  instead of simply using the continuous functional
calculus for normal elements? The reason for both can be explained with a simple example,
. In Mathlib, matrices are not equipped with a norm (nor even a metric), and so
requiring  to be a C⋆-algebra is far too stringent. Likewise,  is not a -algebra, and so
it is impossible to consider the -spectrum of .

There is another, more practical reason to define separate continuous functional calculi for
different scalar rings. It gives us the ability to use functions defined on these types, and the
algebra of functions on them. For example, for  it is quite natural to consider the
functions  and  because the functions  form a lattice ordered
group. If  is selfadjoint, and we define , and likewise for ,
then the properties  and  are trivial consequences of the
corresponding facts for functions. In contrast, if we had to do this using functions on , the
proofs of these facts would be much more cumbersome.

## Implementation details

Instead of defining a class depending on a term , we register it for an  predicate
, and then any element of  satisfying this predicate has the associated star
algebra homomorphism with the specified properties. In so doing we avoid a common pitfall:
dependence of the class on a term. This avoids annoying situations where  are
propositionally equal, but not definitionally so, and hence Lean would not be able to automatically
identify the continuous functional calculi associated to these elements. In order to guarantee
the necessary properties, we require that the continuous functional calculus preserves this
predicate. That is,  for any function  continuous on the spectrum of .

As stated above, the unbundled approach to  has its advantages. For instance, given an
expression , the user is free to rewrite either  or  as desired with no possibility
of the expression ceasing to be defined. However, this unbundling also has some potential downsides.
In particular, by unbundling, proof requirements are deferred until the user calls the lemmas, most
of which have hypotheses both of  and of .

In order to minimize burden to the user, we provide  in terms of two tactics. Goals
related to continuity are dispatched by (a small wrapper around) . As for goals involving
the predicate , it should be noted that these will only ever be of the form ,
 or . For the moment we provide a rudimentary tactic to deal with these
goals, but it can be modified to become more sophisticated as the need arises.

# Spectral properties in C⋆-algebras

In this file, we establish various properties related to the spectrum of elements in C⋆-algebras.
In particular, we show that the spectrum of a unitary element is contained in the unit circle in
, the spectrum of a selfadjoint element is real, the spectral radius of a selfadjoint element
or normal element is its norm, among others.

An essential feature of C⋆-algebras is **spectral permanence**. This is the property that the
spectrum of an element in a closed subalgebra is the same as the spectrum of the element in the
whole algebra. For Banach algebras more generally, and even for Banach ⋆-algebras, this fails.

A consequence of spectral permanence is that one may always enlarge the C⋆-algebra (via a unital
embedding) while preserving the spectrum of any element. In addition, it allows us to make sense of
the spectrum of elements in non-unital C⋆-algebras by considering them as elements in the
 of the C⋆-algebra, or indeed *any* unital C⋆-algebra. Of course, one may do this
(that is, consider the spectrum of an element in a non-unital by embedding it in a unital algebra)
for any Banach algebra, but the downside in that setting is that embedding in different unital
algebras results in varying spectra.

In Mathlib, we don't *define* the spectrum of an element in a non-unital C⋆-algebra, and instead
simply consider the  so as to avoid depending on a choice of unital algebra. However,
we can still establish a form of spectral permanence.

## Main statements

+ : The spectrum of a unitary element is contained in the unit
  sphere in .
+ : The spectral radius of a selfadjoint element is equal
  to its norm.
+ : The spectral radius of a normal element is equal to
  its norm.
+ : The spectral radius of  is equal to
  the square of the norm of .
+ : Any element of the spectrum of a selfadjoint element is real.
* : for  in a C⋆-Subalgebra  of , then  is a Unit
  if and only if  is a unit.
* : **spectral permanence** for , where  is a C⋆-Subalgebra
  of , .

These functions have many uses in real analysis. E.g.,

### Composition of  functions

We show that the composition of  functions is . One way to do this would be to
use the following simple inductive proof. Assume it is done for .
Then, to check it for , one needs to check that the derivative of  is , i.e.,
that  is . The term  is the composition of two  functions, so
it is  by the inductive assumption. The term  is also . Then, the matrix
multiplication is the application of a bilinear map (which is , and therefore ) to
. As the composition of two  maps, it is again , and we are done.

There are two difficulties in this proof.

The first one is that it is an induction over all Banach
spaces. In Lean, this is only possible if they belong to a fixed universe. One could formalize this
by first proving the statement in this case, and then extending the result to general universes
by embedding all the spaces we consider in a common universe through .

The second one is that it does not work cleanly for analytic maps: for this case, we need to
exhibit a whole sequence of derivatives which are all analytic, not just finitely many of them, so
an induction is never enough at a finite step.

Both these difficulties can be overcome with some cost. However, we choose a different path: we
write down an explicit formula for the -th derivative of  in terms of derivatives of

## Implementation notes

The definitions in this file are designed to work on any field . They are sometimes slightly more
complicated than the naive definitions one would guess from the intuition over the real or complex
numbers, but they are designed to circumvent the lack of gluing properties and partitions of unity
in general. In the usual situations, they coincide with the usual definitions.

### Definition of  functions in domains

One could define  functions in a domain  by fixing an arbitrary choice of derivatives (this
is what we do with ) and requiring that all these derivatives up to  are
continuous. If the derivative is not unique, this could lead to strange behavior like two
functions  and  on  whose sum is not . A better definition is thus to say that a
function is  inside  if it admits a sequence of derivatives up to  inside .

This definition still has the problem that a function which is locally  would not need to
be , as different choices of sequences of derivatives around different points might possibly
not be glued together to give a globally defined sequence of derivatives. (Note that this issue
cannot happen over the real numbers, thanks to partitions of unity, but the behavior over a general
field is not so clear, and we want a definition for general fields). Also, there are locality
problems for the order parameter: one could image a function which, for each , has a nice
sequence of derivatives up to order , but they do not coincide for varying  and can therefore
not be glued to give rise to an infinite sequence of derivatives. This would give a function
which is  for all , but not . We solve this issue by putting locality conditions
in space and order in our definition of  and .
The resulting definition is slightly more complicated to work with (in fact not so much), but it
gives rise to completely satisfactory theorems.

For instance, with this definition, a real function which is  (but not better) on
for each natural  is by definition  at .

There is another issue with the definition of . We can
require the existence and good behavior of derivatives up to order  on a neighborhood of
within . However, this does not imply continuity or differentiability within  of the function
at  when  does not belong to . Therefore, we require such existence and good behavior on
a neighborhood of  within  (which appears as  in this file).

We also define a predicate  (and its localized version
), saying that a sequence of multilinear maps is *a* sequence of

## Main definitions and results

### Side of the composition, and universe issues

With a naïve direct definition, the -th derivative of a function belongs to the space
 where there are n iterations of . This space
may also be seen as the space of continuous multilinear functions on  copies of  with
values in , by uncurrying. This is the point of view that is usually adopted in textbooks,
and that we also use. This means that the definition and the first proofs are slightly involved,
as one has to keep track of the uncurrying operation. The uncurrying can be done from the
left or from the right, amounting to defining the -th derivative either as the derivative of
the -th derivative, or as the -th derivative of the derivative.
For proofs, it would be more convenient to use the latter approach (from the right),
as it means to prove things at the -th step we only need to understand well enough the
derivative in  (contrary to the approach from the left, where one would need to know
enough on the -th derivative to deduce things on the -th derivative).

However, the definition from the right leads to a universe polymorphism problem: if we define
 by induction, we need to
generalize over all spaces (as  and  don't take values in the same space). It is
only possible to generalize over all spaces in some fixed universe in an inductive definition.
For , then  is a map . Therefore, the definition will only
work if  and  are in the same universe.

This issue does not appear with the definition from the left, where one does not need to generalize
over all spaces. Therefore, we use the definition from the left. This means some proofs later on
become a little bit more complicated: to prove that a function is , the most efficient approach
is to exhibit a formula for its -th derivative and prove it is continuous (contrary to the
inductive approach where one would prove smoothness statements without giving a formula for the
derivative). In the end, this approach is still satisfactory as it is good to have formulas for the
iterated derivatives in various constructions.

One point where this explicit approach is particularly delicate is in the proof of smoothness of a
composition: there is a formula for the -th derivative of a composition (Faà di Bruno's formula),
but it is very complicated, while the inductive proof is very simple. The inductive proof would
be good enough for  functions with  (modulo polymorphism issues, i.e., one would
need to first prove inductively the result when all spaces belong to the same universe, and then
prove the general result by lifting all the spaces to a common universe). However, it would not
work for  functions. Therefore, we give the proof based on Faà di Bruno's formula, which is
more complicated but more general.

### Variables management

The textbook definitions and proofs use various identifications and abuse of notations, for instance
when saying that the natural space in which the derivative lives, i.e.,
, is the same as a space of multilinear maps. When doing things
formally, we need to provide explicit maps for these identifications, and chase some diagrams to see
everything is compatible with the identifications. In particular, one needs to check that taking the
derivative and then doing the identification, or first doing the identification and then taking the
derivative, gives the same result. The key point for this is that taking the derivative commutes
with continuous linear equivalences. Therefore, we need to implement all our identifications with
continuous linear equivs.

The Faa di Bruno formula gives the iterated derivative of  in terms of those of

The formula is straightforward to prove by induction, as differentiating

with  terms where one differentiates either , or one of the ,

by adding  to it. In this way, one obtains bijectively all partitions of ,
and the proof can go on (up to relabelling).

The main difficulty is to write things down in a precise language, namely to write

parts, we work with partitions in which the ordering is part of the data -- this is equivalent,
but much more convenient to implement. We call these .

Note that the implementation of  is very specific to the Faa di Bruno formula:
as testified by the formula above, what matters is really the embedding of the parts in ,
and moreover the parts have to be ordered by  for the formula to hold

# Continuously  times differentiable functions with pointwise Hölder continuous derivatives

We say that a function is of class $C^{k+(α)}$ at a point ,
where  is a natural number and , if

- it is of class $C^k$ at  in the sense of ;
- its th derivative satisfies $D^kf(x)-D^kf(a) = O(‖x - a‖ ^ α)$ as .

Note that the Hölder condition used in this definition fixes one of the points at .
In different sources, it is called *pointwise*, *local*, or *weak* Hölder condition,
though the term "local" may also mean a stronger condition
saying that a function is Hölder continuous on a neighborhood of .

The immediate reason for adding this definition to the library
is its use in [Moreira2001], where Moreira proves a version of the Morse-Sard theorem
for functions that satisfy this condition on their critical set.

In this file, we define  to be the predicate
saying that a function is $C^{k+(α)}$ in the sense described above
and prove basic properties of this predicate.

## Implementation notes

In Moreira's paper,  is assumed to be a strictly positive number.
We define the predicate for any , then assume  whenever it is necessary.

if it is $C^k$ at this point and $D^kf(x)-D^kf(a) = O(‖x - a‖ ^ α)$ as .

When naming lemmas about this predicate,  is called "order", and  is called "exponent".

A $C^{k+(α)}$ map is a $C^k$ map.

A $C^n$ map is a $C^{k+(α)}$ map for any .

A function is $C^{0+(α)}$ at a point if and only if
it is $C^0$ at the point (i.e., it is continuous on a neighborhood of the point)
and $f(x) - f(a) = O(‖x - a‖ ^ α)$.

# Exterior derivative of a differential form on a normed space

and the second exterior derivative of a form is zero.

## Implementation notes

There are a few competing definitions of the exterior derivative of a differential form
that differ from each other by a normalization factor.
We use the following one:

$$
dω(x; v_0, \dots, v_n) = \sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i D_x ω(x; v_0, \dots, \widehat{v_i}, \dots, v_n) · v_i
$$

where $\widehat{v_i}$ means that we omit this element of the tuple, see .

# Evaluation of the derivative of differential forms on vector fields

In this file we prove the following formula and its corollaries.
If  is a differentiable -form and  are  differentiable vector fields, then

$$
  dω(V_0(x), \dots, V_n(x)) = \sum_{i=0}^k (-1)^i •
      D_x\left(ω\big(x; V_0(x), \dots, \widehat{V_i(x)}, \dots, V_k(x)\big)\right)(V_i(x)) +
    \sum_{0 \le i < j\le k} (-1)^{i + j}
        ω\big(x; V_i, V_j, V_0(x), …, \widehat{V_i(x)}, …, \widehat{V_j(x)}, …, V_k(x)\big),
$$
where $[V_i, V_j]$ is the commutator of the vector fields $V_i$ and $V_j$.
As usual, $\widehat{V_i(x)}$ means that this item is removed from the sequence.

There is no convenient way to write the second term in Lean for ,
so we only state this theorem for ,
see  and .

In this case, we write the second term as a sum over , ,
where the indexes  in our sum correspond to
(formally, ) in the formula above.
For this reason, we have  before the sum in our formal statement.

If  is a differentiable -form and  are  differentiable vector fields, then

$$
  dω(V_0(x), \dots, V_{n + 1}(x)) =
    \sum_{i=0}^{n + 1} (-1)^i •
      D_x\left(ω\big(x; V_0(x), \dots, \widehat{V_i(x)}, \dots, V_{n + 1}(x)\big)\right)(V_i(x)) -
      \sum_{0 \le i \le j\le n} (-1)^{i + j}
        ω\big(x; V_i, V_{j + 1},
          V_0(x), …, \widehat{V_i(x)}, …, \widehat{V_{j + 1}(x)}, …, V_k(x)\big),
$$

where $[V_i, V_{j + 1}]$ is the commutator of the vector fields $V_i$ and $V_{j + 1}$.
As usual, $\widehat{V_i(x)}$ means that this item is removed from the sequence.

In informal texts, this formula is usually written as

$$
  dω(V_0(x), \dots, V_{n + 1}(x)) =
    \sum_{i=0}^{n + 1} (-1)^i •
      D_x\left(ω\big(x; V_0(x), \dots, \widehat{V_i(x)}, \dots, V_{n + 1}(x)\big)\right)(V_i(x)) -
      \sum_{0 \le i < j\le n + 1} (-1)^{i + j}
        ω\big(x; V_i, V_j,
          V_0(x), …, \widehat{V_i(x)}, …, \widehat{V_j(x)}, …, V_k(x)\big).
$$

In the sum from our formalization,
each index  corresponds to the index
in the sum used in informal texts.

For this reason,  in our sum has the opposite parity compared to informal texts,
which changes the sign before the sum from  to .

# Fréchet derivatives of analytic functions.

A function expressible as a power series at a point has a Fréchet derivative there.
Also the special case in terms of  when the domain is 1-dimensional.

As an application, we show that continuous multilinear maps are smooth. We also compute their
iterated derivatives, in .

## Main definitions and results

*  : an analytic function at a point is differentiable there.
*  : in a complete space, if a function is analytic on a
  neighborhood of a set , so is its derivative.
*  : if a function is analytic on a neighborhood of an
  open set , so is its derivative.
*  : if a function is analytic on a set of unique differentiability,
  so is its derivative within this set.
*  : if an open partial homeomorphism  is analytic at a
  point , with invertible derivative, then its inverse is analytic at .

## Comments on completeness

Some theorems need a complete space, some don't, for the following reason.

(1) If a function is analytic at a point , then it is differentiable there (with derivative given
by the first term in the power series). There is no issue of convergence here.

(2) If a function has a power series on a ball , there is no guarantee that the power
series for the derivative will converge at , if the space is not complete. So, to deduce
that  is differentiable at , one needs completeness in general.

(3) However, if a function  has a power series on a ball , and is a priori known to be
differentiable at some point , then the power series for the derivative of  will
automatically converge at , towards the given derivative: this follows from the facts that this
is true in the completion (thanks to the previous point) and that the map to the completion is
an embedding.

(4) Therefore, if one assumes  where  is an open set, then  is analytic
therefore differentiable at every point of , by (1), so by (3) the power series for its
derivative converges on whole balls. Therefore, the derivative of  is also analytic on . The
same holds if  is merely a set with unique differentials.

(5) However, this does not work for , as we don't get for free
differentiability at points in a neighborhood of . Therefore, the theorem that deduces
 from  requires completeness of the space.

A function which is analytic within a set is strictly differentiable there. Since we
don't have a predicate , we spell out what it would mean.

For most binary operations we also define  and  theorems for the cases when

One can also interpret the derivative of a function  as an element of  (by identifying

derivative of polynomials is handled there, as it is naturally one-dimensional.

The simplifier is set up to prove automatically that some functions are differentiable, or
differentiable at a point (but not differentiable on a set or within a set at a point, as checking

The simplifier is not set up to compute the Fréchet derivative of maps (as these are in general
complicated multidimensional linear maps), but it will compute one-dimensional derivatives,
see .

## Implementation details

For a discussion of the definitions and their rationale, see the file docstring of
.

To make sure that the simplifier can prove automatically that functions are differentiable, we tag
many lemmas with the  attribute, for instance those saying that the sum of differentiable
functions is differentiable, as well as their product, their Cartesian product, and so on. A notable
exception is the chain rule: we do not mark as a simp lemma the fact that, if  and  are
differentiable, then their composition also is:  would always be able to match this lemma,
by taking  or  to be the identity. Instead, for every reasonable function (say, ),
we add a lemma that if  is differentiable then so is . This means adding
some boilerplate lemmas, but these can also be useful in their own right.

## Implementation details

The derivative is defined in terms of the  relation to ensure the definition does not
ingrain a choice of norm, and is then quickly translated to the more convenient  in the
subsequent theorems. It is also characterized in terms of the  relation.

We also introduce predicates  (where  is the base field,
 the function to be differentiated,  the point at which the derivative is asserted to exist,
and  the set along which the derivative is defined), as well as ,
 and  to express the existence of a derivative.

To be able to compute with derivatives, we write  and
for some choice of a derivative if it exists, and the zero function otherwise. This choice only
behaves well along sets for which the derivative is unique, i.e., those for which the tangent
directions span a dense subset of the whole space. The predicates  and
, defined in  express this property. We prove that indeed
they imply the uniqueness of the derivative. This is satisfied for open subsets, and in particular
for . This uniqueness only holds when the field is non-discrete, which we request at the very
beginning: otherwise, a derivative can be defined, but it has no interesting properties whatsoever.

# Extending differentiability to the boundary

We investigate how differentiable functions inside a set extend to differentiable functions
on the boundary. For this, it suffices that the function and its derivative admit limits there.

We prove that a function which is linearly approximated by a continuous linear map with a nonlinear
right inverse is locally onto. This will apply to the case where the approximating map is a linear
equivalence, for the local inverse theorem, but also whenever the approximating map is onto,
by Banach's open mapping theorem.

If a function is linearly approximated by a continuous linear map with a (possibly nonlinear)
right inverse, then it is locally onto: a ball of an explicit radius is included in the image
of the map.
