annihilator  is an L-summand of .

M-ideal, M-summands and L-summands were introduced by Alfsen and Effros in [alfseneffros1972] to
study the structure of general Banach spaces. When  is a JB\*-triple, the M-ideals of  are
exactly the norm-closed ideals of . When  is a JBW\*-triple with predual , the M-summands
of  are exactly the weak\*-closed ideals, and their pre-duals can be identified with the
L-summands of . In the special case when  is a C\*-algebra, the M-ideals are exactly the
norm-closed two-sided ideals of , when  is also a W\*-algebra the M-summands are exactly the
weak\*-closed two-sided ideals of .

one variable, by applying them to one variable after the other through currying. However, this
is only well defined when there is an order on the variables (for instance on ) although
the final result is independent of the order. While everything could be done following this
approach, it turns out that direct proofs are easier and more efficient.

Let  be a normed space over a field . This file is concerned with properties of the weak-\*
topology on the dual of . By the dual, we mean either of the type synonyms
 or , depending on whether it is viewed as equipped with its usual
operator norm topology or the weak-\* topology.

It is shown that the canonical mapping  is continuous, and
as a consequence the weak-\* topology is coarser than the topology obtained from the operator norm
(dual norm).

The file also equips  with the norm bornology inherited from , so
that  refers to operator-norm boundedness. This is a pragmatic choice discussed
further in the implementation notes.

(as well as sets of somewhat more general form) with respect to the weak-\* topology.

the weak-\* topology on (its type synonym) :
* : The weak-\* topology on the dual of a normed space is
  coarser (not necessarily strictly) than the operator norm topology.

## Implementation notes

* **Topology synonym:** When  is a vector space, the duals  and
  are type synonyms with different topology instances.
* **Bornology choice:** The  instance on  is inherited from
   via  and corresponds to the operator-norm bornology.
  While the natural bornology for a weak topology is technically the von Neumann bornology
  (pointwise boundedness), we use the norm bornology for several pragmatic reasons:
  1. **Practicality:** In the normed setting, "bounded" is almost universally synonymous with
     "norm-bounded". This allows  to be used directly in statements like Banach-Alaoglu.
  2. **Clarity:** It preserves a clear distinction between norm-boundedness () and
     topological weak-\* boundedness ().
  3. **Consistency:** By the Uniform Boundedness Principle, these notions coincide whenever
      is a Banach space ().
* **Polar sets:** The polar set  of a subset  of  is originally defined as a
  subset of the dual . We care about properties of these w.r.t. weak-\* topology,
  and for this purpose give the definition  for the "same" subset viewed as a
  subset of  (a type synonym of the dual but with a different topology instance).
* **Banach-Alaoglu Proof:** The weak dual of  is embedded in the space of functions
  with the topology of pointwise convergence.

# Banach open mapping theorem

This file contains the Banach open mapping theorem, i.e., the fact that a bijective
bounded linear map between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse.

in this sense, by Banach's open mapping theorem.

### Proof of the Banach open mapping theorem

First step of the proof of the Banach open mapping theorem (using completeness of ):
by Baire's theorem, there exists a ball in  whose image closure has nonempty interior.
Rescaling everything, it follows that any  is arbitrarily well approached by
images of elements of norm at most .
For further use, we will only need such an element whose image
is within distance  of , to apply an iterative process.

The Banach open mapping theorem: if a bounded linear map between Banach spaces is onto, then
any point has a preimage with controlled norm.

Second step of the proof: starting from , we want an exact preimage of . Let  be
   the approximate preimage of  given by the first step, and  the part that
   has no preimage yet. We will iterate this process, taking the approximate preimage of ,
   leaving only  without preimage yet, and so on. Let  be the approximate preimage
   of . Then  is a converging series, and by design the sum of the series is a
   preimage of . This uses completeness of .

The Banach open mapping theorem: a surjective bounded linear map between Banach spaces is
open.

### Applications of the Banach open mapping theorem

A surjective continuous linear map between Banach spaces admits a (possibly nonlinear)
controlled right inverse. In general, it is not possible to ensure that such a right inverse
is linear (take for instance the map from  to  where  is a closed subspace of
without a closed complement. Then it doesn't have a continuous linear right inverse.)

If a bounded linear map is a bijection, then its inverse is also a bounded linear map.

Associating to a linear equivalence between Banach spaces a continuous linear equivalence when
the direct map is continuous, thanks to the Banach open mapping theorem that ensures that the
inverse map is also continuous.

# The Banach-Steinhaus theorem: Uniform Boundedness Principle

Herein we prove the Banach-Steinhaus theorem for normed spaces: any collection of bounded linear
maps from a Banach space into a normed space which is pointwise bounded is uniformly bounded.

Note that we prove the more general version about barrelled spaces in
, and the usual version below is indeed deduced from the
more general setup.

This is the standard Banach-Steinhaus theorem, or Uniform Boundedness Principle.
If a family of continuous linear maps from a Banach space into a normed space is pointwise
bounded, then the norms of these linear maps are uniformly bounded.

See also  for the general statement in barrelled spaces.

This version of Banach-Steinhaus is stated in terms of suprema of
for convenience.

# Compact operators

In this file we define compact linear operators between two topological vector spaces (TVS).

## Main definitions

*  : predicate for compact operators

## Main statements

*  : the usual characterization of
  compact operators from a normed space to a T2 TVS.
*  : precomposing a compact operator by a continuous linear map gives
  a compact operator
*  : postcomposing a compact operator by a continuous linear map
  gives a compact operator
*  : compact operators are automatically continuous
*  : the set of compact operators is closed for the operator
  norm

Note that results linking compact operators with  are in a separate file
in order to avoid a heavy import. There, we prove :

*  : the identity of  is compact if and only if
   has finite dimension.

## Implementation details

We define  as a predicate, because the space of compact operators inherits all
of its structure from the space of continuous linear maps (e.g we want to have the usual operator
norm on compact operators).

The two natural options then would be to make it a predicate over linear maps or continuous linear
maps. Instead we define it as a predicate over bare functions, although it really only makes sense
for linear functions, because Lean is really good at finding coercions to bare functions (whereas
coercing from continuous linear maps to linear maps often needs type ascriptions).

## References

* N. Bourbaki, *Théories Spectrales*, Chapitre 3

# Strict linear maps with closed range are closed under finite-rank perturbation

Fix  a complete nontrivially normed field, and ,  two topological vector spaces
over . This file contains various results expressing that the set of continuous
linear maps  which are **strict** and have **closed range** is
"stable under finite-rank perturbations".

More precisely, we prove the following statements:
* : given a closed
  subspace  of  of finite codimension, we have that  is strict with closed range
  if and only if  is strict with closed range.
* : if
  differ by a finite rank continuous linear map, then  is strict with closed range if and only
  if  is strict with closed range.
* : given a *complemented*
  finite dimensional subspace  of , we have that  is strict with closed range
  if and only if  is strict with closed range.

These three results show up crucially when developing the theory of Fredholm operators
between topological vector spaces. Note that none of the results here use the Hahn-Banach
theorem, so there is no significant restriction on the field.

## Implementation details

This file covers almost exactly the content of
N. Bourbaki, *Théories Spectrales*, Chapitre III, § 3, n° 1. However,
there are two notable changes compared to Bourbaki :
* We treat all topological vector spaces over complete nontrivially normed fields,
  where Bourbaki restricts to locally convex spaces over  or . To do so, we have to
  tweak one statement by assuming that a finite dimensional subspace is complemented, which
  is always the case when you have Hahn-Banach available.
* We give a different proof, where we reduce the statement to
  . This gives a slightly longer proof, but we
  claim that it is more natural.

Note that these two changes are independent: the extra generality could have been achieved
with Bourbaki's proof.

## References

* N. Bourbaki, *Théories Spectrales*, Chapitre III, § 3, n° 1

subspace of . We want to show that  is strict with closed range if and only if
its restriction  is strict with closed range.

We do the proof in five steps. Note that we have commented the whole proof, so hopefully
you can follow the argument by reading the source code.

# The spectral norm and the norm extension theorem

This file shows that if  is a nonarchimedean normed field and  is an algebraic extension,
then there is a natural extension of the norm on  to a -algebra norm on , the so-called
*spectral norm*. The spectral norm of an element of  only depends on its minimal polynomial
over , so for  two extensions of , the spectral norm on  restricts to the
spectral norm on . This work can be used to uniquely extend the -adic norm on  to an
algebraic closure of , for example.

## Details

We define the spectral value and the spectral norm. We prove the norm extension theorem
[S. Bosch, U. Güntzer, R. Remmert, *Non-Archimedean Analysis* (Theorem 3.2.1/2)]
[bosch-guntzer-remmert] : given a nonarchimedean normed field  and an algebraic
extension , the spectral norm is a power-multiplicative -algebra norm on  extending
the norm on . All -algebra automorphisms of  are isometries with respect to this norm.
If  is finite, we get a formula relating the spectral norm on  with any other
power-multiplicative norm on  extending the norm on .

Moreover, we also prove the unique norm extension theorem: if  is a field complete with respect
to a nontrivial nonarchimedean multiplicative norm and  is an algebraic extension, then the
spectral norm on  is a nonarchimedean multiplicative norm, and any power-multiplicative
-algebra norm on  coincides with the spectral norm. More over, if  is finite, then
is a complete space. This result is S. Bosch, U. Güntzer, R. Remmert, *Non-Archimedean Analysis*
(Theorem 3.2.4/2).

As a prerequisite, we formalize the proof of S. Bosch, U. Güntzer, R. Remmert,
*Non-Archimedean Analysis* (Proposition 3.1.2/1).

## Main Definitions

*  : the spectral value of a polynomial in .
*  : the spectral norm  is the spectral value of the minimal polynomial
  of  over .
*  : the spectral norm is a -algebra norm on .
*  : the spectral norm is a multiplicative -algebra norm on .

## Main Results

*  : if  is a power-multiplicative -algebra norm on , then  is
  bounded above by .
*  : the -algebra automorphisms of  are isometries with respect to
  the spectral norm.
*  : if  is finite and normal, then
  .
*  : the spectral norm is power-multiplicative.
*  : the spectral norm is nonarchimedean.
*  : the spectral norm extends the norm on .
*  : any power-multiplicative -algebra norm on  coincides with the
  spectral norm.
*  : the spectral norm on  is multiplicative.
*  : if  is finite dimensional, then  is a complete space
  with respect to topology induced by the spectral norm.

## References
* S. Bosch, U. Güntzer, R. Remmert, *Non-Archimedean Analysis*

# Picard-Lindelöf (Cauchy-Lipschitz) Theorem

We prove the (local) existence of integral curves and flows to time-dependent vector fields.

Let  be a time-dependent (local) vector field on a Banach space, and let
and . If  is Lipschitz continuous in  within a closed ball around  of radius
 at every  and continuous in  at every , then there exists a (local) solution
 to the initial value problem  and  for all
, where .

We actually prove a more general version of this theorem for the existence of local flows. If there
is some  such that , then for every
, there exists a (local) solution  with the initial condition .
In other words, there exists a local flow  defined on  and
.

The proof relies on demonstrating the existence of a solution  to the following integral
equation:
$$\alpha(t) = x_0 + \int_{t_0}^t f(\tau, \alpha(\tau))\,\mathrm{d}\tau.$$
This is done via the contraction mapping theorem, applied to the space of Lipschitz continuous
functions from a closed interval to a Banach space. The needed contraction map is constructed by
repeated applications of the right-hand side of this equation.

## Main definitions and results

* : the Picard iteration, applied to the curve
* : the structure holding the assumptions of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem

The public-facing existence theorems stated using the integral curve API are in
.

## Implementation notes

* The structure  and theorems within this namespace are implementation details of the
  proof of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem and are not intended to be used outside of this file.
* Some sources, such as Lang, define  as the space of continuous functions from a closed
  interval to a closed ball. We instead define  here as the space of Lipschitz continuous
  functions from a closed interval. This slightly stronger condition allows us to postpone the usage
  of the completeness condition on the space  until the application of the contraction mapping
  theorem.
* We have chosen to formalise many of the real constants as , so that the non-negativity of
  certain quantities constructed from them can be shown more easily. When subtraction is involved,
  especially note whether it is the usual subtraction between two reals or the truncated subtraction
  between two non-negative reals.
* In this file, We only prove the existence of a solution. For uniqueness, see
   and related theorems in .

## Space of Lipschitz functions on a closed interval

We define the space of Lipschitz continuous functions from a closed interval. This will be shown to
be a complete metric space on which  is a contracting map, leading to a fixed point that
will serve as the solution to the ODE. The domain is a closed interval in order to easily inherit
the sup metric from continuous maps on compact spaces. We cannot use functions  with junk
values outside the domain, as the supremum within a closed interval will only be a pseudo-metric,
and the contracting map will fail to have a fixed point. In order to accommodate flows, we do not
require a specific initial condition. Rather,  contains curves whose initial condition is
within a closed ball.

### Estimates for the Mahler measure

If the leading coefficient of a polynomial has norm at least 1, then its Mahler measure
is at least 1. This holds in particular for nonzero polynomials with integer coefficients,
since their leading coefficient is a nonzero integer.

The Mahler measure of a polynomial is bounded above by the sum of the norms of its coefficients.

**Landau's inequality**: the Mahler measure of a polynomial is at most the ℓ² norm
of its coefficient vector, .

This is the classical inequality due to Landau (1905). Combined with the multiplicativity of the
Mahler measure (), it gives the Mignotte bound on coefficients of polynomial
factors.

# : a typeclass for ℝ or ℂ

This file defines the typeclass  intended to have only two instances:
ℝ and ℂ. It is meant for definitions and theorems which hold for both the real and the complex case,
and in particular when the real case follows directly from the complex case by setting  to ,
 to zero and so on. Its API follows closely that of ℂ.

Applications include defining inner products and Hilbert spaces for both the real and
complex case. One typically produces the definitions and proof for an arbitrary field of this
typeclass, which basically amounts to doing the complex case, and the two cases then fall out
immediately from the two instances of the class.

# Seminorms

This file defines seminorms.

A seminorm is a function to the reals which is positive-semidefinite, absolutely homogeneous, and
subadditive. They are closely related to convex sets, and a topological vector space is locally
convex if and only if its topology is induced by a family of seminorms.

## Main declarations

For a module over a normed ring:
* : A function to the reals that is positive-semidefinite, absolutely homogeneous, and
  subadditive.
* : The norm on  as a seminorm.

## References

* H. H. Schaefer, *Topological Vector Spaces*

# The arithmetic-geometric mean

Starting with two nonnegative real numbers, repeatedly replace them with their arithmetic and
geometric means. By the AM-GM inequality, the smaller number (geometric mean) will monotonically
increase and the larger number (arithmetic mean) will monotonically decrease.

The two monotone sequences converge to the same limit – the arithmetic-geometric mean (AGM).
This file defines the AGM in the  namespace and proves some of its basic properties.

## References

converging to the arithmetic-geometric mean starting from  and .

The AGM is also the supremum of the geometric means.

The AGM distributes over multiplication.

# Bernstein approximations and Weierstrass' theorem

We prove that the Bernstein approximations
for a continuous function  taking values in a locally convex vector space
converge uniformly to  as  tends to infinity.
This statement directly applies to the cases when the codomain is a (semi)normed space
or, more generally, has a topology defined by a family of seminorms.

Our proof follows Richard Beals' *Analysis, an introduction*, §7D.
The original proof, due to Bernstein in 1912, is probabilistic,
and relies on Bernoulli's theorem,
which gives bounds for how quickly the observed frequencies in a
Bernoulli trial approach the underlying probability.

The proof here does not directly rely on Bernoulli's theorem,
but can also be given a probabilistic account.
* Consider a weighted coin which with probability  produces heads,
  and with probability  produces tails.
* The value of  is the probability that
  such a coin gives exactly  heads in a sequence of  tosses.
* If such an appearance of  heads results in a payoff of ,
  the -th Bernstein approximation for  evaluated at  is the expected payoff.
* The main estimate in the proof bounds the probability that
  the observed frequency of heads differs from  by more than some ,
  obtaining a bound of , irrespective of .
* This ensures that for  large, the Bernstein approximation is (uniformly) close to the
  payoff function .

# Deligne's archimedean Gamma-factors

In the theory of L-series one frequently encounters the following functions (of a complex variable
) introduced in Deligne's landmark paper *Valeurs de fonctions L et périodes d'intégrales*:

$$ \Gamma_{\mathbb{R}}(s) = \pi ^ {-s / 2} \Gamma (s / 2) $$

and

$$ \Gamma_{\mathbb{C}}(s) = 2 (2 \pi) ^ {-s} \Gamma (s). $$

These are the factors that need to be included in the Dedekind zeta function of a number field
for each real, resp. complex, infinite place.

namespace NormNum

theorem cpow_pos (a b : ℂ) (b' : ℕ) (c : ℂ) (hb : b = b') (h : a ^ b' = c) : a ^ b = c := by
rw [← h, hb, Complex.cpow_natCast]

theorem cpow_neg (a b : ℂ) (b' : ℕ) (c c' : ℂ) (hb : b = b') (h : a ^ b' = c) (hc : c⁻¹ = c') :
a ^ (-b) = c' := by rw [← hc, ← h, hb, Complex.cpow_neg, Complex.cpow_natCast]

open Tactic

/-- Generalized version of , , . -/
unsafe def prove_rpow' (pos neg zero : Name) (α β one a b : expr) : tactic (expr × expr) := do
let na ← a.to_rat
let icα ← mk_instance_cache α
let icβ ← mk_instance_cache β
match match_sign b with
| Sum.inl b => do
let nc ← mk_instance_cache q(ℕ)
let (icβ, nc, b', hb) ← prove_nat_uncast icβ nc b
let (icα, c, h) ← prove_pow a na icα b'
let cr ← c
let (icα, c', hc) ← prove_inv icα c cr
pure (c', (expr.const neg []).mk_app [a, b, b', c, c', hb, h, hc])
| Sum.inr ff => pure (one, expr.const zero [] a)
| Sum.inr tt => do
let nc ← mk_instance_cache q(ℕ)
let (icβ, nc, b', hb) ← prove_nat_uncast icβ nc b
let (icα, c, h) ← prove_pow a na icα b'
pure (c, (expr.const Pos []).mk_app [a, b, b', c, hb, h])

/-- Evaluate  where  is a rational numeral and  is an integer. -/
unsafe def prove_cpow : expr → expr → tactic (expr × expr) :=
prove_rpow'  cpow_neg

/-- Evaluates expressions of the form  and  in the special case where
is an integer and  is a positive rational (so it's really just a rational power). -/
@[norm_num]
unsafe def eval_cpow : expr → tactic (expr × expr)
| q(@Pow.pow _ _ Complex.hasPow $(a) $(b)) => b.to_int >> prove_cpow a b
| q(Complex.cpow $(a) $(b)) => b.to_int >> prove_cpow a b
| _ => tactic.failed

end NormNum

end Tactics

a ^ b = c := by rw [← h, hb, ENNReal.rpow_natCast]

### Smoothness of

In this section we prove that the function  is infinitely smooth. To do
this, we show that $g_p(x)=p(x^{-1})f(x)$ is infinitely smooth for any polynomial  with real
coefficients. First we show that $g_p(x)$ tends to zero at zero, then we show that it is
differentiable with derivative $g_p'=g_{x^2(p-p')}$. Finally, we prove smoothness of $g_p$ by
induction, then deduce smoothness of $f$ by setting $p=1$.

# Stirling's formula

This file proves Stirling's formula for the factorial.
It states that $n!$ grows asymptotically like $\sqrt{2\pi n}(\frac{n}{e})^n$.

Also some _global_ bounds on the factorial function and the Stirling sequence are proved.

## Proof outline

The proof follows: .

We proceed in two parts.

**Part 1**: We consider the sequence $a_n$ of fractions $\frac{n!}{\sqrt{2n}(\frac{n}{e})^n}$
and prove that this sequence converges to a real, positive number $a$. For this the two main
ingredients are
- taking the logarithm of the sequence and
- using the series expansion of $\log(1 + x)$.

**Part 2**: We use the fact that the series defined in part 1 converges against a real number $a$
and prove that $a = \sqrt{\pi}$. Here the main ingredient is the convergence of Wallis' product
formula for .

# Euler's infinite product for the sine function

This file proves the infinite product formula

$$ \sin \pi z = \pi z \prod_{n = 1}^\infty \left(1 - \frac{z ^ 2}{n ^ 2}\right) $$

for any real or complex . Our proof closely follows the article
Salwinski, *Euler's Sine Product Formula: An Elementary Proof*: the basic strategy
is to prove a recurrence relation for the integrals ,
generalising the arguments used to prove Wallis' limit formula for .

# Comparing sums and integrals

## Summary

It is often the case that error terms in analysis can be computed by comparing
an infinite sum to the improper integral of an antitone function.

It contains several lemmas in this direction, for antitone or monotone functions
(or products of antitone and monotone functions), formulated for sums on  or .

  values at integer steps aligning with the right-hand side of the interval.

  the left-hand side of the interval is at most the integral of the function along that interval

# Abelian categories

This file contains the definition and basic properties of abelian categories.

There are many definitions of abelian category. Our definition is as follows:
A category is called abelian if it is preadditive,
has finite products, kernels, and cokernels,
and if every monomorphism and epimorphism is normal.

It should be noted that if we also assume finite coproducts, then preadditivity is
actually a consequence of the other properties, as we show in
. However, this fact is of little practical
relevance, since essentially all interesting abelian categories come with a
preadditive structure. In this way, by requiring preadditivity, we allow the
user to pass in the "native" preadditive structure for the specific category they are
working with.

## Main definitions

*  is the type class indicating that a category is abelian. It extends .
*  is , and
*  is .

## Main results

* In an abelian category, mono + epi = iso.
* If , then the map  is an epimorphism, and the map
   is a monomorphism.
* Factoring through the image and coimage is a strong epi-mono factorisation. This means that
  * every abelian category has images. We provide the isomorphism
    .
  * the canonical morphism
    is an isomorphism.
* We provide the alternate characterisation of an abelian category as a category with
  (co)kernels and finite products, and in which the canonical coimage-image comparison morphism
  is always an isomorphism.
* Every epimorphism is a cokernel of its kernel. Every monomorphism is a kernel of its cokernel.
* The pullback of an epimorphism is an epimorphism. The pushout of a monomorphism is a monomorphism.
  (This is not to be confused with the fact that the pullback of a monomorphism is a monomorphism,
  which is true in any category).

However, the limits we can construct at this level of generality will most likely be less nice than
the ones that can be created in specific applications. For this reason, we adopt the following
convention:

* If the statement of a theorem involves limits, the existence of these limits should be made an
  explicit typeclass parameter.
* If a limit only appears in a proof, but not in the statement of a theorem, the limit should not
  be a typeclass parameter, but instead be created using  or a similar

# The Freyd-Mitchell embedding theorem

Let  be an abelian category. We construct a ring  and a functor
 which is full, faithful and
exact.

## Overview of the proof

The usual strategy to prove the Freyd-Mitchell embedding theorem is as follows:

1. Prove that if  is a Grothendieck abelian category and  is a functor from a
   small category, then there is a functor  for a suitable  such that
   is faithful and exact and  is full.
2. Find a suitable Grothendieck abelian category  and a full, faithful and exact functor
   .

To prove (1), we proceed as follows:

1. Using the Special Adjoint Functor Theorem and the duality between subobjects and quotients in
   abelian categories, we have that Grothendieck abelian categories have all limits (this is shown
   in ).
2. Using the small object argument, it is shown that Grothendieck abelian categories have enough
   injectives (see ).
3. Putting these two together, it follows that Grothendieck abelian categories have an injective
   cogenerator (see ).
4. By taking a coproduct of copies of the injective cogenerator, we find a projective separator
   in  such that every object in the image of  is a quotient of . Then the additive Hom
   functor  is faithful (because  is a separator), left
   exact (because it is a hom functor), right exact (because  is projective) and full (because of
   a combination of the aforementioned properties, see
   ).
   We put this all together in the file
   .

To prove (2), there are multiple options.

* Some sources (for example Freyd's "Abelian Categories") choose . The
  main difficulty with this approach is that it is not obvious that  is abelian. This approach
  has a very algebraic flavor and requires a relatively large amount of ad-hoc reasoning.
* In the Stacks project, it is suggested to choose  for a suitable Grothendieck
  topology on  and there are reasons to believe that this  is in fact equivalent to
  . This approach translates many of the interesting properties along the
  sheafification adjunction from a category of -valued presheaves, which in turn inherits many
  interesting properties from the category of abelian groups.
* Kashiwara and Schapira choose , which can be shown to be equivalent to
   (see the file ).
  This approach deduces most interesting properties from the category of types.

When work on this theorem commenced in early 2022, all three approaches were quite out of reach.
By the time the theorem was proved in early 2025, both the  approach and the  approach
were available in mathlib. The code below uses .

## Implementation notes

In the literature you will generally only find this theorem stated for small categories . In
Lean, we can work around this limitation by passing from  to , thereby
enlarging the category of modules that we land in (which should be inconsequential in most
applications) so that our embedding theorem applies to all abelian categories. If  was already a
small category, then this does not change anything.

Let  be a Grothendieck abelian category. In this file, we formalize

We recall that injective objects can be characterized in terms of
lifting properties (see the file ):
an object  is injective iff the morphism  has the right lifting
property with respect to all monomorphisms.

The main technical lemma in this file is the lemma
 which states that
if  is a generator of , then a morphism  has the right
lifting property with respect to the inclusions of subobjects of
iff it has the right lifting property with respect to all
monomorphisms. Then, we can apply the small object argument
to the family of morphisms
which consists of the inclusions of subobjects of . When it is
applied to the morphism , the factorization given by the
small object is a factorization  where  is
injective (because  has the expected right lifting properties),
and  is a monomorphism because it is a transfinite composition
of monomorphisms (this uses the axiom AB5).

The proof of the technical lemma  that
was formalized is not exactly the same as in the mathematical literature.
Assume that  has the lifting property with respect to
monomorphisms in the family .
We would like to show that  has the right lifting property with
respect to any monomorphism . In various sources,
given a commutative square with  on the left and  on the right,
the ordered set of subobjects  of  containing  equipped
with a lifting  is introduced. The existence of a lifting
is usually obtained by applying Zorn's lemma in this situation.
Here, we split the argument into two separate facts:
* any monomorphism  is a transfinite composition of pushouts of monomorphisms in
   (see );
* the class of morphisms that have the left lifting property with respect to  is stable under
  transfinite composition (see the file ).

# Every NonPreadditiveAbelian category is preadditive

In mathlib, we define an abelian category as a preadditive category with finite products,
kernels and cokernels, and in which every monomorphism and epimorphism is normal.

While virtually every interesting abelian category has a natural preadditive structure (which is why
it is included in the definition), preadditivity is not actually needed: Every category that has
all of the other properties appearing in the definition of an abelian category admits a preadditive
structure. This is the construction we carry out in this file.

The proof proceeds in roughly five steps:
1. Prove some results (for example that all equalizers exist) that would be trivial if we already
   had the preadditive structure but are a bit of work without it.
2. Develop images and coimages to show that every monomorphism is the kernel of its cokernel.

The results of the first two steps are also useful for the "normal" development of abelian
categories, and will be used there.

3. For every object , define a "subtraction" morphism  and use it to define
   subtraction on morphisms as .
4. Prove a small number of identities about this subtraction from the definition of .
5. From these identities, prove a large number of other identities that imply that defining
    indeed gives an abelian group structure on morphisms such that composition
   is bilinear.

The construction is non-trivial and it is quite remarkable that this abelian group structure can
be constructed purely from the existence of a few limits and colimits. Even more remarkably,
since abelian categories admit exactly one preadditive structure (see
), the construction manages to exactly
reconstruct any natural preadditive structure the category may have.

## References

* F. Borceux, *Handbook of Categorical Algebra 2*

We call a category  if it has a zero object, kernels, cokernels, finite
products and coproducts, and every monomorphism and every epimorphism is normal.

Notice that every such category is abelian (see ),
so in practice it is preferable to work directly with .

# Pseudoelements in abelian categories

A *pseudoelement* of an object  in an abelian category  is an equivalence class of arrows
ending in , where two arrows are considered equivalent if we can find two epimorphisms with a
common domain making a commutative square with the two arrows. While the construction shows that
pseudoelements are actually subobjects of  rather than "elements", it is possible to chase these
pseudoelements through commutative diagrams in an abelian category to prove exactness properties.
This is done using some "diagram-chasing metatheorems" proved in this file. In many cases, a proof
in the category of abelian groups can more or less directly be converted into a proof using
pseudoelements.

A classic application of pseudoelements is diagram lemmas like the four lemma or the snake lemma.

Pseudoelements are in some ways weaker than actual elements in a concrete category. The most
important limitation is that there is no extensionality principle: If , then
 does not necessarily imply that  (however, if  or ,
it does). A corollary of this is that we cannot define arrows in abelian categories by dictating
their action on pseudoelements. Thus, a usual style of proofs in abelian categories is this:
First, we construct some morphism using universal properties, and then we use diagram chasing
of pseudoelements to verify that it has some desirable property such as exactness.

It should be noted that the Freyd-Mitchell embedding theorem
(see ) gives a vastly stronger notion of
pseudoelement (in particular one that gives extensionality) and this file should be updated to
go use that instead!

## Main results

We define the type of pseudoelements of an object and, in particular, the zero pseudoelement.

We prove that every morphism maps the zero pseudoelement to the zero pseudoelement ()
and that a zero morphism maps every pseudoelement to the zero pseudoelement ().

Here are the metatheorems we provide:
* A morphism  is zero if and only if it is the zero function on pseudoelements.
* A morphism  is an epimorphism if and only if it is surjective on pseudoelements.
* A morphism  is a monomorphism if and only if it is injective on pseudoelements
  if and only if .
* A sequence  of morphisms is exact if and only if

  pseudoelement  such that  and for every  we have

# Refinements

In order to prove injectivity/surjectivity/exactness properties for diagrams
in the category of abelian groups, we often need to do diagram chases.
Some of these can be carried out in more general abelian categories:
for example, a morphism  in an abelian category  is a
monomorphism if and only if for all , the induced map
 of abelian groups is a monomorphism, i.e. injective.
Alternatively, the Yoneda presheaf functor which sends  to the
presheaf of maps  for all  preserves and reflects
monomorphisms.

However, if  is an epimorphism in  and ,
 may fail to be surjective (unless  is a split
epimorphism).

In this file, the basic result is
which states that if  is a morphism in an abelian category,
then it is an epimorphism if and only if for all ,
there exists an epimorphism  and  such
that . In other words, if we allow a precomposition
with an epimorphism, we may lift a morphism to  to a morphism to .
Following unpublished notes by George Bergman, we shall say that the
precomposition by an epimorphism  is a refinement of . Then,
we get that an epimorphism is a morphism that is "surjective up to refinements".
(This result is similar to the fact that a morphism of sheaves on
a topological space or a site is epi iff sections can be lifted
locally. Then, arguing "up to refinements" is very similar to
arguing locally for a Grothendieck topology (TODO: indeed,
show that it corresponds to the "refinements" topology on an
abelian category  that is defined by saying that
a sieve is covering if it contains an epimorphism)).

Similarly, it is possible to show that a short complex in an abelian
category is exact if and only if it is exact up to refinements
(see ).

As it is outlined in the documentation of the file
, the Freyd-Mitchell
embedding theorem implies the existence of a faithful and exact functor
from an abelian category  to the category of abelian groups. If we
define a pseudo-element of  to be an element in , one
may do diagram chases in any abelian category using these pseudo-elements.
However, using this approach would require proving this embedding theorem!
Currently, mathlib contains a weaker notion of pseudo-elements
. Some theorems can be obtained
using this notion, but there is the issue that for this notion
of pseudo-elements a morphism  in  is not determined by
its action on pseudo-elements (see also ).
On the contrary, the approach consisting of working up to refinements
does not require the introduction of other types: we only need to work
with morphisms  in  which we may consider as being
"sort of elements of ". One may carry diagram-chasing by tracking
these morphisms and sometimes introducing an auxiliary epimorphism .

## References
* George Bergman, A note on abelian categories – translating element-chasing proofs,
  and exact embedding in abelian groups (1974)

# Adhesive categories

## Main definitions
- : A convenience formulation for a pushout being
  a van Kampen colimit.
- : A category is adhesive if it has pushouts and pullbacks along
  monomorphisms, and such pushouts are van Kampen.

## Main Results
- : The category of  is adhesive.
- : In adhesive categories,
  pushouts along monomorphisms are pullbacks.
- : In adhesive categories,
  monomorphisms are stable under pushouts.
- : Monomorphisms in adhesive categories are
  regular (this implies that adhesive categories are balanced).
- : The category  is adhesive if
  has all pullbacks and all pushouts and is adhesive

## References
-
- Stephen Lack and Paweł Sobociński, Adhesive Categories

This only makes sense when the original diagram is a pushout.
A convenient formulation for a pushout being a van Kampen colimit. For any commutative cube of
which a van Kampen pushout forms the bottom face and the back faces are pullbacks, the front faces
are pullbacks if and only if the top face is a pushout. See  below.

If a van Kampen pushout forms the bottom face of a commutative "half-cube" whose front faces
are pullbacks, then there exist two back faces which are pullbacks and a top face which is a
pushout.

A pushout is van Kampen if and only if whenever it forms the bottom face of a commutative
"half-cube", the front faces are pullbacks if and only if there exist back faces which are pullbacks
and a top face which is a pushout.

A category is adhesive if it has pushouts and pullbacks along monomorphisms,
and such pushouts are van Kampen.

If  and  are monomorphisms in an adhesive category, then the map
 induced by their pullback is a monomorphism.
See Theorem 5.1 in Lack and Sobociński.

First, take the pullback of  and  and then form the pushout of the projection maps:

* If  preserves limits and  has limits, and satisfies the solution set condition,

# Compatibilities for left adjoints from compatibilities satisfied by right adjoints

In this file, given isomorphisms between compositions of right adjoint functors,
we obtain isomorphisms between the corresponding compositions of the left adjoint functors,
and show that the left adjoint functors satisfy properties similar to the left/right
unitality and the associativity of pseudofunctors if the right adjoint functors
satisfy the corresponding properties.

This is used in  to study
the behaviour with respect to composition of the pullback functors on presheaves
of modules, by reducing these definitions and properties to the (obvious) case of the
pushforward functors. Similar results are obtained for sheaves of modules
in .

If a right adjoint functor is isomorphic to the identity functor,
so is the left adjoint.

A natural transformation  involving right adjoint functors
induces a natural transformation  between the corresponding
left adjoint functors.

A natural isomorphism  involving right adjoint functors
induces a natural isomorphism  between the corresponding
left adjoint functors.

# Adjoints of fully faithful functors

A left adjoint is
* faithful, if and only if the unit is a monomorphism
* full, if and only if the unit is a split epimorphism
* fully faithful, if and only if the unit is an isomorphism

A right adjoint is
* faithful, if and only if the counit is an epimorphism
* full, if and only if the counit is a split monomorphism
* fully faithful, if and only if the counit is an isomorphism

This is Lemma 4.5.13 in Riehl's *Category Theory in Context* [riehl2017].
See also  for the statements about fully faithful functors.

In the file , we prove that in fact, if there exists
an isomorphism , then the unit is an isomorphism, and similarly for the counit.
See  and
.

If the left adjoint is faithful, then each component of the unit is a monomorphism.

If the left adjoint is full, then each component of the unit is a split epimorphism.

If the right adjoint is full, then each component of the counit is a split monomorphism.

If the left adjoint is fully faithful, then the unit is an isomorphism.

If the right adjoint is faithful, then each component of the counit is an epimorphism.

If the right adjoint is full, then each component of the counit is a split monomorphism.

If the right adjoint is full, then each component of the counit is a split monomorphism.

If the right adjoint is fully faithful, then the counit is an isomorphism.

If the unit of an adjunction is an isomorphism, then its inverse on the image of L is given
by L whiskered with the counit.

If the unit of an adjunction is an isomorphism, then one has an isomorphism .

If the counit of an adjunction is an isomorphism, then its inverse on the image of R is given
by R whiskered with the unit.

If the counit of an adjunction is an isomorphism, then one has an isomorphism
.

If each component of the unit is a monomorphism, then the left adjoint is faithful.

If each component of the unit is a split epimorphism, then the left adjoint is full.

If the unit is an isomorphism, then the left adjoint is fully faithful.

If each component of the counit is an epimorphism, then the right adjoint is faithful.

If each component of the counit is a split monomorphism, then the right adjoint is full.

If the counit is an isomorphism, then the right adjoint is fully faithful.

If  is an isomorphism, then  is in the essential image of .

# Balanced categories

A category is called balanced if any morphism that is both monic and epic is an isomorphism.

Balanced categories arise frequently. For example, categories in which every monomorphism
(or epimorphism) is strong are balanced. Examples of this are abelian categories and toposes, such
as the category of types.

A category is called balanced if any morphism that is both monic and epic is an isomorphism.

Given two adjunctions  and  both between objects , , there is a

defined as a special case of , where the two "vertical" 1-morphisms are identities.
This bijection is ; the image of a 2-morphism under it is called its conjugate.

Furthermore, this bijection preserves (and reflects) isomorphisms, i.e. a 2-morphism is an iso
iff its image under the bijection is an iso.

When all four morphisms in a square are left adjoints, the mates operation can be iterated:
In this case the iterated mate equals the conjugate of the original 2-morphism and is thus an
isomorphism if and only if the original 2-morphism is. This explains why some Beck-Chevalley
2-morphisms are isomorphisms.

### Simp-normal form for 2-morphisms

Rewriting involving associators and unitors could be very complicated. We try to ease this
complexity by putting carefully chosen simp lemmas that rewrite any 2-morphisms into simp-normal
form defined below. Rewriting into simp-normal form is also useful when applying (forthcoming)
 tactic.

The simp-normal form of 2-morphisms is defined to be an expression that has the minimal number of
parentheses. More precisely,
1. it is a composition of 2-morphisms like  such that each  is
  either a structural 2-morphisms (2-morphisms made up only of identities, associators, unitors)
  or non-structural 2-morphisms, and
2. each non-structural 2-morphism in the composition is of the form ,
  where each  is a 1-morphism that is not the identity or a composite and  is a
  non-structural 2-morphisms that is also not the identity or a composite.

Note that  is actually .

The following simp attributes are put in order to rewrite any 2-morphisms into normal forms. There
are associators and unitors in the RHS in the several simp lemmas here (e.g. ),
which at first glance look more complicated than the LHS, but they will be eventually reduced by
the pentagon or the triangle identities, and more generally, (forthcoming)  tactic.

The left whiskering of a 2-isomorphism is a 2-isomorphism.

The right whiskering of a 2-isomorphism is a 2-isomorphism.

# The coherence theorem for bicategories

In this file, we prove the coherence theorem for bicategories, stated in the following form: the
free bicategory over any quiver is locally thin.

The proof is almost the same as the proof of the coherence theorem for monoidal categories that
has been previously formalized in mathlib, which is based on the proof described by Ilya Beylin
and Peter Dybjer. The idea is to view a path on a quiver as a normal form of a 1-morphism in the
free bicategory on the same quiver. A normalization procedure is then described by
, which is a
pseudofunctor from the free bicategory to the locally discrete bicategory on the path category.
It turns out that this pseudofunctor is locally an equivalence of categories, and the coherence
theorem follows immediately from this fact.

## Main statements

*  : the free bicategory is locally thin, that is, there is at most one
  2-morphism between two fixed 1-morphisms.

## References

* Ilya Beylin and Peter Dybjer, Extracting a proof of coherence for monoidal categories from a
  proof of normalization for monoids

# Extensions and lifts in bicategories

We introduce the concept of extensions and lifts within the bicategorical framework. These concepts
are defined by commutative diagrams in the (1-)categorical context. Within the bicategorical
framework, commutative diagrams are replaced by 2-morphisms. Depending on the orientation of the
2-morphisms, we define both left and right extensions (likewise for lifts). The use of left and
right here is a common one in the theory of Kan extensions.

## Implementation notes
We define extensions and lifts as objects in certain comma categories ( for left,
and  for right). See the file  for properties
about these categories. We introduce some intuitive aliases. For example,
is an alias for .

# Free bicategories

We define the free bicategory over a quiver. In this bicategory, the 1-morphisms are freely
generated by the arrows in the quiver, and the 2-morphisms are freely generated by the formal
identities, the formal unitors, and the formal associators modulo the relation derived from the
axioms of a bicategory.

# Strictly unitary lax functors and pseudofunctors

In this file, we define strictly unitary lax functors and
strictly unitary pseudofunctors between bicategories.

A lax functor  is said to be *strictly unitary* (sometimes, it is also
called *normal*) if there is an equality  and the
unit 2-morphism  is the identity 2-morphism induced
by this equality.

A pseudofunctor is called *strictly unitary* (or a *normal homomorphism*) if it
satisfies the same condition (i.e. its "underlying" lax functor is strictly
unitary).

# Transformations between lax functors

Just as there are natural transformations between functors, there are transformations
between lax functors. The equality in the naturality condition of a natural transformation gets
replaced by a specified 2-morphism. Now, there are three possible types of transformations (between
lax functors):
* lax natural transformations;
* oplax natural transformations;
* strong natural transformations.

These differ in the direction (and invertibility) of the 2-morphisms involved in the naturality
condition.

* : lax transformations between lax functors  and . The naturality
  condition is given by a 2-morphism  for each 1-morphism
  .
* : oplax transformations between lax functors  and . The naturality
  condition is given by a 2-morphism  for each 1-morphism
  .
* : strong transformations between lax functors  and . The naturality
  condition is given by a 2-isomorphism  for each 1-morphism
  .

## Remarks
There are multiple notions of opposite categories for bicategories.
- There is 1-cell dual  as defined above.
- There is the 2-cell dual,  where only the 2-morphisms are reversed

# Promoting a monoidal category to a single object bicategory.

A monoidal category can be thought of as a bicategory with a single object.

The objects of the monoidal category become the 1-morphisms,
with composition given by tensor product,
and the morphisms of the monoidal category become the 2-morphisms.

We verify that the endomorphisms of that single object recovers the original monoidal category.

One could go much further: the bicategory of monoidal categories
(equipped with monoidal functors and monoidal natural transformations)
is equivalent to the bicategory consisting of
* single object bicategories,
* pseudofunctors, and
* (oplax) natural transformations  such that .

Promote a monoidal category to a bicategory with a single object.
(The objects of the monoidal category become the 1-morphisms,
with composition given by tensor product,
and the morphisms of the monoidal category become the 2-morphisms.)

The monoidal functor from the endomorphisms of the single object
when we promote a monoidal category to a single object bicategory,
to the original monoidal category.

We subsequently show this is an equivalence.

when we promote a monoidal category to a single object bicategory,
and the original monoidal category.

# Strict bicategories

A bicategory is called  if the left unitors, the right unitors, and the associators are
isomorphisms given by equalities.

## Implementation notes

In the literature of category theory, a strict bicategory (usually called a strict 2-category) is
often defined as a bicategory whose left unitors, right unitors, and associators are identities.
We cannot use this definition directly here since the types of 2-morphisms depend on 1-morphisms.
For this reason, we use , which gives isomorphisms from equalities, instead of
identities.

A bicategory is called  if the left unitors, the right unitors, and the associators are
isomorphisms given by equalities.

Identity morphisms are left identities for composition.

Identity morphisms are right identities for composition.

Composition in a bicategory is associative.

The left unitors are given by equalities

The right unitors are given by equalities

The associators are given by equalities

# Categories

Defines a category, as a type class parametrised by the type of objects.

## Notation

Introduces notations in the  scope
*  for the morphism spaces (type as ),
*  for the identity morphism on  (type as ),
*  for composition in the 'arrows' convention (type as ).

Users may like to add  for composition in the standard convention, using

The typeclass  describes morphisms associated to objects of type .

The universe levels of the objects and morphisms are independent, and will often need to be
specified explicitly, as .

Typically any concrete example will either be a , where ,
which can be introduced as
or a , where , which can be introduced as

In order for the library to handle these cases uniformly,
we generally work with the unconstrained ,
for which objects live in  and morphisms live in .

Because the universe parameter  for the objects can be inferred from
when we write , while the universe parameter  for the morphisms
cannot be automatically inferred, through the category theory library
we introduce universe parameters with morphism levels listed first,
as in
or
when multiple independent universes are needed.

This has the effect that we can simply write
(that is, only specifying a single parameter) while  will be inferred.

Often, however, it's not even necessary to include the .
(Although it was in earlier versions of Lean.)
If it is omitted a "free" universe will be used.

Many classes in Mathlib have universe parameters that do not appear in their
input parameter types. For example:
*  — the morphism universe  is not determined by
*  — the shape universes
  are not determined by
*  — the target universe  is not determined by
  (but  is determined by , so  *is* an output)
*  — the sheaf type universe  is not determined
  by , ,
*  — has no input parameters at all

By default (since ), Lean treats any universe
parameter not occurring in input types as an output parameter, and erases it from typeclass
resolution cache keys. This means that queries differing only in such a universe share a
cache entry — the first result found is reused.

This is correct when the universe truly is determined by the inputs (e.g.,  in
), but incorrect when the universe is part of the *question*
(e.g.,  in ). Cache collisions cause "stuck at solving universe constraint"
errors or silent misresolution.

The  attribute
(from ) overrides the default:
*  — no universe parameters are output (all kept in cache key)
*  — only  is output

**Rule of thumb:** if the class is typically used with explicit universe annotations
(e.g., ) or is marked , its "extra" universe
parameters are likely inputs, not outputs, and the class should be annotated with
.

# The category of types with partial functions

This defines , the category of types equipped with partial functions.

This category is classically equivalent to the category of pointed types. The reason it doesn't hold
constructively stems from the difference between  and . Both can model partial
functions, but the latter forces a decidable domain.

Precisely,  turns a partial function  into a function
 by sending to  the undefined values (and  to ). But being
defined is (generally) undecidable while being sent to  is decidable. So it can't be
constructive.

# Computation of  for a presheaf

Let  be a presheaf. In this file, we construct an equivalence
 and show that there is a quasi-commutative
diagram


where the top arrow is the forgetful functor forgetting the yoneda-costructure, the right arrow is
the aforementioned equivalence and the diagonal arrow is the Yoneda embedding.

In the notation of Kashiwara-Schapira, the type of the equivalence is written , where
 is  (with the functor  being either the identity or the Yoneda
embedding) and  is taking presheaves. The equivalence is a key ingredient in various results in
Kashiwara-Schapira.

The proof is somewhat long and technical, in part due to the construction inherently involving a
sigma type which comes with the usual DTT issues. However, a user of this result should not need
to interact with the actual construction, the mere existence of the equivalence and the commutative
triangle should generally be sufficient.

## Main results
* :
  the equivalence
* : the natural isomorphism


## Implementation details

The proof needs to introduce "correction terms" in various places in order to overcome DTT issues,
and these need to be canceled against each other when appropriate. It is important to deal with
these in a structured manner, otherwise you get large goals containing many correction terms which
are very tedious to manipulate. We avoid this blowup by carefully controlling which definitions
 is allowed to unfold and stating many lemmas explicitly before they are required. This
leads to manageable goals containing only a small number of correction terms. Generally, we use
the form  for these correction terms and try to push them as far outside as
possible.

## Future work
* If needed, it should be possible to show that the equivalence is natural in .

## References
* M. Kashiwara, P. Schapira, *Categories and Sheaves*, Lemma 1.4.12

## Tags

# Epi and mono in concrete categories

In this file, we relate epimorphisms and monomorphisms in a concrete category
to surjective and injective morphisms, and we show that if  has
strong epi mono factorizations and is such that  preserves
both epi and mono, then any morphism in  can be factored in a
functorial manner as a composition of a surjective morphism followed
by an injective morphism.

In any concrete category, injective morphisms are monomorphisms.

A concrete category with strong epi mono factorizations and such that
the forget functor preserves mono and epi admits functorial surjective/injective
factorizations.

In any concrete category, surjective morphisms are epimorphisms.

If the forgetful functor of a concrete category reflects isomorphisms, being an isomorphism
is equivalent to being bijective.

# Dialectica category

We define the category  of the Dialectica interpretation, after [dialectica1989].

## Background

Dialectica categories are important models of linear type theory. They satisfy most of the
distinctions that linear logic was meant to introduce and many models do not satisfy, like the
independence of constants. Many linear type theories are being used at the
moment--[nLab] describes some of them: for quantum systems, for effects in programming, for linear
dependent types. In particular, dialectica categories are connected to polynomial functors, being a
slightly more sophisticated version of polynomial types, as discussed, for instance, in Moss and
von Glehn's [*Dialectica models of type theory*]. As such they are related to the polynomial
constructions being developed by Awodey, Riehl, and Hazratpour. For the non-dependent
version developed here several applications are known to Petri Nets, small cardinals
in Set Theory, state in imperative programming, and others, see [Dialectica Categories].

# Dinatural transformations

Dinatural transformations are special kinds of transformations between
functors  which depend both covariantly and contravariantly
on the same category (also known as difunctors).

A dinatural transformation is a family of morphisms given only on *the diagonal* of the two
functors, and is such that a certain naturality hexagon commutes.
Note that dinatural transformations cannot be composed with each other (since the outer
hexagon does not commute in general), but can still be "pre/post-composed" with
ordinary natural transformations.

# Distributive monoidal categories

## Main definitions

A monoidal category  with binary coproducts is left distributive if the left tensor product
preserves binary coproducts. This means that, for all objects , , and  in ,
the cogap map  can be promoted to an isomorphism. We refer to
this isomorphism as the left distributivity isomorphism.

A monoidal category  with binary coproducts is right distributive if the right tensor product
preserves binary coproducts. This means that, for all objects , , and  in ,
the cogap map  can be promoted to an isomorphism. We refer to
this isomorphism as the right distributivity isomorphism.

A distributive monoidal category is a monoidal category that is both left and right distributive.

## Main results

- A symmetric monoidal category is left distributive if and only if it is right distributive.

- A closed monoidal category is left distributive.

- For a category  the category of endofunctors  is left distributive (but almost
  never right distributive). The left distributivity is tantamount to the fact that the coproduct
  in the functor categories is computed pointwise.

- We show that any preadditive monoidal category with coproducts is distributive. This includes the
  examples of abelian groups, R-modules, and vector bundles.

## TODO

Show that the category of pointed types with the monoidal structure given by the smash product of
pointed types and the coproduct given by the wedge sum is distributive.

## References

* Hans-Joachim Baues, Mamuka Jibladze, Andy Tonks, Cohomology of
  monoids in monoidal categories, in: Operads: Proceedings of Renaissance
  Conferences, Contemporary Mathematics 202, AMS (1997) 137-166

# Effective epimorphisms

We define the notion of effective epimorphism and effective epimorphic family of morphisms.

A morphism is an *effective epi* if it is a joint coequalizer of all pairs of
morphisms which it coequalizes.

A family of morphisms with fixed target is *effective epimorphic* if it is initial among families
of morphisms with its sources and a general fixed target, coequalizing every pair of morphisms it
coequalizes (here, the pair of morphisms coequalized can have different targets among the sources
of the family).

We have defined the notion of effective epi for morphisms and families of morphisms in such a
way that avoids requiring the existence of pullbacks. However, if the relevant pullbacks exist
then these definitions are equivalent, see the file

See nlab: *Effective Epimorphism* and
Stacks 00WP for the standard definitions. Note that
our notion of  is often called "strict epi" in the literature.

# Equivalence of categories

An equivalence of categories  and  is a pair of functors  and  such
that  and . In many situations, equivalences are a better
notion of "sameness" of categories than the stricter isomorphism of categories.

Recall that one way to express that two functors  and  are adjoint is using
two natural transformations  and , called the unit and the
counit, such that the compositions  and  are the identity. Unfortunately,
it is not the case that the natural isomorphisms  and  in the definition of an equivalence
automatically give an adjunction. However, it is true that
* if one of the two compositions is the identity, then so is the other, and
* given an equivalence of categories, it is always possible to refine  in such a way that the
  identities are satisfied.

For this reason, in mathlib we define an equivalence to be a "half-adjoint equivalence", which is
a tuple  as in the first paragraph such that the composite  is the
identity. By the remark above, this already implies that the tuple is an "adjoint equivalence",
i.e., that the composite  is also the identity.

We also define essentially surjective functors and show that a functor is an equivalence if and only
if it is full, faithful and essentially surjective.

## Main definitions

* : bundled (half-)adjoint equivalences of categories
* : type class on a functor  containing the data of the preimages
  and the isomorphisms .
* : type class on a functor  which is full, faithful and
  essentially surjective.

## Main results

* : upgrade an equivalence to a (half-)adjoint equivalence
* : when  and  are isomorphic functors,
   is an equivalence iff  is.
* : construction of an equivalence of categories from
  a functor  which satisfies the property  (i.e.  is full, faithful
  and essentially surjective).

# Essential image of a functor

The essential image  of a functor consists of the objects in the target category which
are isomorphic to an object in the image of the object function.
This, for instance, allows us to talk about objects belonging to a subcategory expressed as a
functor rather than a subtype, preserving the principle of equivalence. For example this lets us
define exponential ideals.

The essential image can also be seen as a subcategory of the target category, and witnesses that
a functor decomposes into an essentially surjective functor and a fully faithful functor.
(TODO: show that this decomposition forms an orthogonal factorisation system).

under isomorphism of the function .

# Extremal epimorphisms

An extremal epimorphism  is an epimorphism which does not factor
through any proper subobject of . In case the category has equalizers,
we show that a morphism  which does not factor through
any proper subobject of  is automatically an epimorphism, and also
an extremal epimorphism. We also show that a strong epimorphism
is an extremal epimorphism, and that both notions coincide when
the category has pullbacks.

# Filtered categories

A category is filtered if every finite diagram admits a cocone.
We give a simple characterisation of this condition as
1. for every pair of objects there exists another object "to the right",
2. for every pair of parallel morphisms there exists a morphism to the right so the compositions
   are equal, and
3. there exists some object.

An important example of filtered category is given by nonempty directed types;
actually, filtered categories may be considered as a generalization of nonempty directed types.
In the file , we show that "conversely"
if  is a filtered category, there exists a final functor  from
a nonempty directed type ().

Filtered colimits are often better behaved than arbitrary colimits.
See  for some details.

Filtered categories are nice because colimits indexed by filtered categories tend to be
easier to describe than general colimits (and more often preserved by functors).

In this file we show that any functor from a finite category to a filtered category admits a cocone:
*

More generally,
for any finite collection of objects and morphisms between them in a filtered category
(even if not closed under composition) there exists some object  receiving maps from all of them,
so that all the triangles (one edge from the finite set, two from morphisms to ) commute.
This formulation is often more useful in practice and is available via ,
which takes a finset of objects, and an indexed family (indexed by source and target)
of finsets of morphisms.

We also prove the converse of  as .

Furthermore, we give special support for two diagram categories: The  and the .
This is because these shapes show up in the proofs that forgetful functors of algebraic categories
(e.g. , , ...) preserve filtered colimits.

All of the above API, except for the  and the , is also provided for cofiltered
categories.

# A functor from a small category to a filtered category factors through a small filtered category

A consequence of this is that if  is filtered and finally small, then  is also
"finally filtered-small", i.e., there is a final functor from a small filtered category to .
This is occasionally useful, for example in the proof of the recognition theorem for ind-objects
(Proposition 6.1.5 in [Kashiwara2006]).

The "filtered closure" of an -indexed family of objects in  is the set of objects in
obtained by starting with the family and successively adding maxima and coequalizers.

The full subcategory induced by the filtered closure of a family of objects is filtered.

Our goal for this section is to show that the size of the filtered closure of an -indexed
   family of objects in  only depends on the size of  and the morphism types of , not on
   the size of the objects of . More precisely, if  lives in , the objects of
   live in  and the morphisms of  live in , then we want
   .

   The strategy is to define a type  which should be an inductive type
   similar to , which lives in the correct universe and surjects onto the full
   subcategory. The difficulty with this is that we need to define it at the same time as the map
   , as the coequalizer constructor depends on the actual morphisms
   in . This would require some kind of inductive-recursive definition, which Lean does not
   allow. Our solution is to define a function  by (strong)
   induction and then take the union over all natural numbers, mimicking what one would do in a
   set-theoretic setting.

One step of the inductive procedure consists of adjoining all maxima and coequalizers of all
objects and morphisms obtained so far. This is quite redundant, picking up many objects which we
already hit in earlier iterations, but this is easier to work with later.

The realization function sends the abstract maxima and weak coequalizers to the corresponding
objects in .

as a function of .

The surjection from the abstract filtered closure to the actual filtered closure in .

# Representably flat functors

We define representably flat functors as functors such that the category of structured arrows
over  is cofiltered for each . This concept is also known as flat functors as in [Elephant]
Remark C2.3.7, and this name is suggested by Mike Shulman in
 to avoid
confusion with other notions of flatness (e.g. see the notion of flat type-valued
functor in the file ).

This definition is equivalent to left exact functors (functors that preserves finite limits) when
 has all finite limits.

# Separating and detecting sets

There are several non-equivalent notions of a generator of a category. Here, we consider two of
them:

* We say that  is a separating set if the functors
    for  such that  are collectively faithful, i.e., if
     for all  with domain satisfying  implies .
* We say that  is a detecting set if the functors
    collectively reflect isomorphisms, i.e., if any  with domain satisfying
    uniquely factors through , then  is an isomorphism.

There are, of course, also the dual notions of coseparating and codetecting sets.

## Main results

We
* define predicates , ,  and  on
  ;
* show that equivalences of categories preserve these notions;
* show that separating and coseparating are dual notions;
* show that detecting and codetecting are dual notions;
* show that if  has equalizers, then detecting implies separating;
* show that if  has coequalizers, then codetecting implies coseparating;
* show that if  is balanced, then separating implies detecting and coseparating implies
  codetecting;
* show that  is separating if and only if  is coseparating if and only if  is thin;
* show that  is detecting if and only if  is codetecting if and only if  is a groupoid;
* define predicates , ,  and  as the
  singleton counterparts to the definitions for sets above and restate the above results in this
  situation;
* show that  is a separator if and only if  is faithful (and the dual);
* show that  is a detector if and only if  reflects isomorphisms (and the
  dual);
* show that  is  if it admits small pullbacks and a detector;
* define corresponding typeclasses , ,
  and  on categories and prove analogous results for these.

# Connected category

Define a connected category as a _nonempty_ category for which every functor
to a discrete category is isomorphic to the constant functor.

NB. Some authors include the empty category as connected, we do not.
We instead are interested in categories with exactly one 'connected
component'.

  transitive closure of the relation "there is a morphism in some direction
  from  to ".

# Isomorphisms of categories

An  is an isomorphism of categories: a pair of functors  and
whose composites are *equal* (not merely naturally isomorphic) to the identity functors.
This is a strict notion, stronger than an equivalence of categories .
We also define  as a property saying that a functor is fully faithful and
bijective on objects. We develop basic api for these two concepts.

Unless the application explicitly demands an isomorphism, the equivalence of categories is
to be preferred.

# Constructing limits from products and equalizers.

If a category has all products, and all equalizers, then it has all limits.
Similarly, if it has all finite products, and all equalizers, then it has all finite limits.

If a functor preserves all products and equalizers, then it preserves all limits.
Similarly, if it preserves all finite products and equalizers, then it preserves all finite limits.

# Constructing pullbacks from binary products and equalizers

If a category has binary products and equalizers, then it has pullbacks.
Also, if a category has binary coproducts and coequalizers, then it has pushouts.

If the product  and the equalizer of  and  exist, then the
pullback of  and  exists: It is given by composing the equalizer with the projections.

If a category has all binary products and all equalizers, then it also has all pullbacks.
As usual, this is not an instance, since there may be a more direct way to construct
pullbacks.

If the coproduct  and the coequalizer of  and  exist, then the
pushout of  and  exists: It is given by composing the inclusions with the coequalizer.

If a category has all binary coproducts and all coequalizers, then it also has all pushouts.
As usual, this is not an instance, since there may be a more direct way to construct pushouts.

# Constructions related to weakly initial objects

This file gives constructions related to weakly initial objects, namely:
* If a category has small products and a small weakly initial set of objects, then it has a weakly
  initial object.
* If a category has wide equalizers and a weakly initial object, then it has an initial object.

These are primarily useful to show the General Adjoint Functor Theorem.

If  has (small) products and a small weakly initial set of objects, then it has a weakly initial
object.

If  has (small) wide equalizers and a weakly initial object, then it has an initial object.

The initial object is constructed as the wide equalizer of all endomorphisms on the given weakly

# Final and initial functors

A functor  is final if for every ,
the comma category of morphisms  is connected.

Dually, a functor  is initial if for every ,
the comma category of morphisms  is connected.

We show that right adjoints are examples of final functors, while
left adjoints are examples of initial functors.

For final functors, we prove that the following three statements are equivalent:
1.  is final.
2. Every functor  has a colimit if and only if  does,
   and these colimits are isomorphic via .
3. .

Starting at 1. we show (in ) that
the categories of cocones over  and over  are equivalent.
(In fact, via an equivalence which does not change the cocone point.)
This readily implies 2., as , , and .

From 2. we can specialize to  to obtain 3., as .

From 3., we prove 1. directly in .

Dually, we prove that if a functor  is initial, then any functor  has a
limit if and only if  does, and these limits are isomorphic via .

In the end of the file, we characterize the finality of some important induced functors on the
(co)structured arrow category ( and ) and on the
Grothendieck construction ( and ).

## Naming
There is some discrepancy in the literature about naming; some say 'cofinal' instead of 'final'.
The explanation for this is that the 'co' prefix here is *not* the usual category-theoretic one
indicating duality, but rather indicating the sense of "along with".

(),

morphism levels before object levels. See note [category theory universes].

The evaluation functors jointly reflect limits: that is, to show a cone is a limit of
it suffices to show that each evaluation cone is a limit. In other words, to prove a cone is
limiting you can show it's pointwise limiting.

Given a functor  and a collection of limit cones for each diagram , we can stitch
them together to give a cone for the diagram .
 shows that the new cone is limiting, and  shows it is
(essentially) made up of the original cones.

The stitched together cones each project down to the original given cones (up to iso).

Stitching together limiting cones gives a limiting cone.

The evaluation functors jointly reflect colimits: that is, to show a cocone is a colimit of
it suffices to show that each evaluation cocone is a colimit. In other words, to prove a cocone is
colimiting you can show it's pointwise colimiting.

Given a functor  and a collection of colimit cocones for each diagram , we can stitch
them together to give a cocone for the diagram .
 shows that the new cocone is colimiting, and  shows it is
(essentially) made up of the original cocones.

The stitched together cocones each project down to the original given cocones (up to iso).

Stitching together colimiting cocones gives a colimiting cocone.

# Existence of limits and colimits

In  we defined ,
the data showing that a cone  is a limit cone.

The two main structures defined in this file are:
* , which consists of a choice of cone for  and the fact it is a limit cone, and
* , asserting the mere existence of some limit cone for .

 is a propositional typeclass
(it's important that it is a proposition merely asserting the existence of a limit,
as otherwise we would have non-defeq problems from incompatible instances).

While  only asserts the existence of a limit cone,
we happily use the axiom of choice in mathlib,
so there are convenience functions all depending on :
* , producing some limit object (of course all such are isomorphic)
* , the morphisms out of the limit,
* , the universal morphism from any other , etc.

Key to using the  interface is that there is an  lemma stating that
to check , for , it suffices to check
for every .
This, combined with  lemmas, makes it possible to prove many easy facts about limits using
automation (e.g. ).

There are abbreviations  and
asserting the existence of classes of limits.
Later more are introduced, for finite limits, special shapes of limits, etc.

Ideally, many results about limits should be stated first in terms of ,
and then a result in terms of  derived from this.
At this point, however, this is far from uniformly achieved in mathlib ---
often statements are only written in terms of .

## Implementation
At present we simply say everything twice, in order to handle both limits and colimits.
It would be highly desirable to have some automation support,
e.g. a  attribute that behaves similarly to .

Adopting the theorem numbering of [Kashiwara2006], we show the following properties:

Limits:
* If  has products indexed by , then  has products indexed by , and the functor
   creates such products (6.1.17),
* if  has equalizers, then  has equalizers, and the functor
  creates them (6.1.17)
* if  has small limits (resp. finite limits), then  has small limits (resp. finite limits)
  and the functor  creates them (6.1.17),

Colimits:
*  has filtered colimits (6.1.8), and the functor  preserves filtered
  colimits,
* if  has coproducts indexed by a finite type , then  has coproducts indexed by
  (6.1.18(ii)),
* if  has finite coproducts, then  has small coproducts (6.1.18(ii)),
* if  has coequalizers, then  has coequalizers (6.1.18(i)),
* if  has finite colimits, then  has small colimits (6.1.18(iii)).
*  preserves finite colimits (6.1.6),

Note that:
* the functor  does not preserve any kind of colimit in general except for
  filtered colimits and
* the functor  preserves finite colimits, but not infinite colimits in general.
