# Ind-objects

For a presheaf  we define the type  of presentations
of  as a small filtered colimit of representable presheaves and define the predicate
 asserting that there is at least one such presentation.

A presheaf is an ind-object if and only if the category  is filtered
and finally small. In this way,  can be thought of the universal
indexing category for the representation of  as a small filtered colimit of representable
presheaves.

## Future work

of their presentations.

The ind-objects form a locally -small category  which has numerous interesting
properties.

as a property of presheaves . This comes with significant technical hurdles.
The recommended alternative is to consider ind-objects over  instead.

# Preservation and reflection of (co)limits.

There are various distinct notions of "preserving limits". The one we
aim to capture here is: A functor F : C ⥤ D "preserves limits" if it
sends every limit cone in C to a limit cone in D. Informally, F
preserves all the limits which exist in C.

Note that:

* Of course, we do not want to require F to *strictly* take chosen
  limit cones of C to chosen limit cones of D. Indeed, the above
  definition makes no reference to a choice of limit cones so it makes
  sense without any conditions on C or D.

* Some diagrams in C may have no limit. In this case, there is no
  condition on the behavior of F on such diagrams. There are other
  notions (such as "flat functor") which impose conditions also on
  diagrams in C with no limits, but these are not considered here.

In order to be able to express the property of preserving limits of a
certain form, we say that a functor F preserves the limit of a
diagram K if F sends every limit cone on K to a limit cone. This is
vacuously satisfied when K does not admit a limit, which is consistent
with the above definition of "preserves limits".

morphism levels before object levels. See note [category theory universes].

A functor  preserves limits of  (written as )
if  maps any limit cone over  to a limit cone.

A functor  preserves colimits of  (written as )
if  maps any colimit cocone over  to a colimit cocone.

We say that  preserves limits of shape  if  preserves limits for every diagram
, i.e.,  maps limit cones over  to limit cones.

We say that  preserves colimits of shape  if  preserves colimits for every diagram
, i.e.,  maps colimit cocones over  to colimit cocones.

# Preservation of (co)limits in the functor category

  for  preserves colimits.

  pointwise, so pointwise preservation implies general preservation.

# Finite-limit-preserving presheaves

In this file we prove that if  is a small finitely cocomplete category and
is a presheaf, then  is filtered (equivalently, the category of
elements of  is cofiltered) if and only if  preserves finite limits.

This is one of the keys steps of establishing the equivalence  (here,
 is the category of left exact functors) for a *small* finitely cocomplete category
.

## Implementation notes

In the entire file, we are careful about details like functor associativity to ensure that we do
not end up in situations where we have morphisms like , where the domain of
is  where  and  are definitionally equal but not syntactically equal. In these
situations, lemmas about  cannot be applied using  and , forcing the
use of . In particular, for us this means that  is better
than  and that we should be very particular about functor associativity.

The theorem is also true for large categories and the proof given here generalizes to this case on
paper. However, our infrastructure for commuting finite limits of shape  and filtered colimits
of shape  is fundamentally not equipped to deal with the case where not all limits of shape
exist. In fact, not even the definition  can be written down if not
all limits of shape  exist. Refactoring this to the level of generality we need would be a major
undertaking. Since the application to the category of Ind-objects only require the case where
is small, we leave this as a TODO.

* F. Borceux, *Handbook of Categorical Algebra 1*, Proposition 6.1.2

# Preservation of zero objects and zero morphisms

We define the class  and show basic properties.

## Main results

We provide the following results:
* Left adjoints and right adjoints preserve zero morphisms;
* full functors preserve zero morphisms;
* if both categories involved have a zero object, then a functor preserves zero morphisms if and
  only if it preserves the zero object;
* functors which preserve initial or terminal objects preserve zero morphisms.

These are slightly unusual relative to the other shapes in the library,

# Multi-(co)equalizers

A *multiequalizer* is an equalizer of two morphisms between two products.
Since both products and equalizers are limits, such an object is again a limit.
This file provides the diagram whose limit is indeed such an object.
In fact, it is well-known that any limit can be obtained as a multiequalizer.
The dual construction (multicoequalizers) is also provided.

## Projects

Prove that a multiequalizer can be identified with
an equalizer between products (and analogously for multicoequalizers).

Prove that the limit of any diagram is a multiequalizer (and similarly for colimits).

# Reflexive coequalizers

This file deals with reflexive pairs, which are pairs of morphisms with a common section.

A reflexive coequalizer is a coequalizer of such a pair. These kind of coequalizers often enjoy
nicer properties than general coequalizers, and feature heavily in some versions of the monadicity
theorem.

We also give some examples of reflexive pairs: for an adjunction  with counit , the pair
 is reflexive. If a pair  is a kernel pair for some morphism, then it is
reflexive.

## Main definitions

*  is the predicate that f and g have a common section.

   to . It acts on reflexive pairs as forgetting
  the common section.
*  is the predicate that a category has all colimits of reflexive pairs.
* : an isomorphism promoting the coequalizer of a reflexive pair
  to the colimit of a diagram out of the walking reflexive pair.

## Main statements

* : A kernel pair is a reflexive pair
* : The inclusion functor is final.
* : A category has coequalizers of reflexive pairs if and only if it
  has all colimits of shape .

# Strict initial objects

This file sets up the basic theory of strict initial objects: initial objects where every morphism
to it is an isomorphism. This generalises a property of the empty set in the category of sets:
namely that the only function to the empty set is from itself.

We say  has strict initial objects if every initial object is strict, i.e. given any morphism
 where  is initial, then  is an isomorphism.
Strictly speaking, this says that *any* initial object must be strict, rather than that strict
initial objects exist, which turns out to be a more useful notion to formalise.

If the binary product of  with a strict initial object exists, it is also initial.

To show a category  with an initial object has strict initial objects, the most convenient way
is to show any morphism to the (chosen) initial object is an isomorphism and use
.

The dual notion (strict terminal objects) occurs much less frequently in practice so is ignored.

# Strong epimorphisms

In this file, we define strong epimorphisms. A strong epimorphism is an epimorphism
which has the (unique) left lifting property with respect to monomorphisms. Similarly,
a strong monomorphism is a monomorphism which has the (unique) right lifting property
with respect to epimorphisms.

## Main results

Besides the definition, we show that
* the composition of two strong epimorphisms is a strong epimorphism,
* if  is a strong epimorphism, then so is ,
* if  is both a strong epimorphism and a monomorphism, then it is an isomorphism

We also define classes  and  for categories in which
every monomorphism or epimorphism is strong, and deduce that these categories are balanced.

# Zero morphisms and zero objects

A category "has zero morphisms" if there is a designated "zero morphism" in each morphism space,
and compositions of zero morphisms with anything give the zero morphism. (Notice this is extra
structure, not merely a property.)

A category "has a zero object" if it has an object which is both initial and terminal. Having a
zero object provides zero morphisms, as the unique morphisms factoring through the zero object.

# Sifted categories

A category  is sifted if  is nonempty and the diagonal functor  is final.
Sifted categories can be characterized as those such that the colimit functor
preserves finite products. We achieve this characterization in this file.

## Main results
- : A nonempty category with binary coproducts is
  sifted.
- : The -valued colimit functor for sifted
  diagrams preserves finite products.
- : The converse: if the -valued colimit functor
  preserves finite products, the category is sifted.
- : A category admitting a final functor from a sifted
  category is itself sifted.

# Weak limits

If  is a functor and , we say that  is a weak limit of  if
every cone over  admits a (not necessarily unique) morphism to . In other words, a
weak limit satisfies the same "versal property" as a limit, without the uniqueness
condition. In particular, weak limits are not unique, and they are not functorial.

We set up some API for weak limits, mostly copied from that for limits, prove that any
limit cone is a weak limit cone, and that, if a limit exists, then it is a retract of any
weak limit (see ).

In the files ,  and , we specialize
to weak equalizers, weak kernels and weak pullbacks, and give some API for those shapes,
again inspired from the non-weak case. We prove that a category with weak equalizers and
pullbacks has weak pullbacks, and that a preadditive category has weak equalizers if and only
if it has weak kernels.

## References

* Peter J Freyd, *Representations in Abelian categories*, p. 99

cone morphism to .

## Locally directed gluing

We say that a diagram of sets is "locally directed" if for any  in the diagram,
 is a union of elements in the diagram. Equivalently, for every  in the diagram,
the set of elements containing  is directed (and hence the name).

This is the condition needed to show that a colimit (in ) of open embeddings is the
gluing of the open sets. See  for an actual application.

We say that a functor  to  is locally directed if for every , the
set of  containing  is (co)directed.
That is, for each diagram
there exists
that commutes with it.

# Markov Categories

Copy-discard categories where deletion is natural for all morphisms.

## Main definitions

*  - Copy-discard category with natural deletion

## Main results

*  - Any morphism to the unit equals discard
*  - The monoidal unit is terminal

## Implementation notes

Natural discard forces probabilistic interpretation: morphisms preserve normalization. The unit
being terminal follows from naturality of discard.

The key property  means discard "erases" any preceding
morphism, a distinguishing feature of Markov categories in categorical probability.

## References

* Cho and Jacobs, *Disintegration and Bayesian inversion via string diagrams*
* Fritz, *A synthetic approach to Markov kernels, conditional independence
  and theorems on sufficient statistics*

## Tags

Markov category, probability, categorical probability

Copy-discard category where discard is natural.

Process then discard equals discard directly.

Any morphism to the unit equals discard.

The monoidal unit is a terminal object.

There is a unique morphism to the unit (it is terminal).

# Positive Categories

Markov categories where deletion is natural for all morphisms.

## Main definitions

* : Markov category where copy is natural given deterministic composition of
  morphisms.

## Main results

*  - Given morphisms  and , if their composition is
  deterministic, then process , copy and then process  equals copy and process  and
  independently.

* All isomorphisms in a positive Markov category are deterministic.

## Implementation notes

The key property , given
, means that after processing , copying and then processing  is the
same as copying and processing  and  independently. The probabilistic interpretation is that
given a deterministic process that has a stochastic intermediate result, the same distribution over
both results can be obtained by computing the intermediate result independently of the
deterministic process.

## References

* Fritz, *A synthetic approach to Markov kernels, conditional independence
  and theorems on sufficient statistics*, Def. 11.22
* Moss and Perrone, *A category-theoretic proof of the ergodic decomposition theorem*

# Day's reflection theorem

Let  be a symmetric monoidal closed category and let  be a reflective subcategory. Day's
reflection theorem proves the equivalence of four conditions, which are all of the form that a
map obtained by acting on the unit of the reflective adjunction, with the internal hom and
tensor functors, is an isomorphism.

Suppose that  is itself monoidal and that the reflector is a monoidal functor. Then we can
apply Day's reflection theorem to prove that  is also closed monoidal.

# Monoidal categories

A monoidal category is a category equipped with a tensor product, unitors, and an associator.
In the definition, we provide the tensor product as a pair of functions
*
*

and allow use of the overloaded notation  for both.
The unitors and associator are provided componentwise.

The tensor product can be expressed as a functor via .
The unitors and associator are gathered together as natural
isomorphisms in ,  and .

Some consequences of the definition are proved in other files after proving the coherence theorem,
e.g.  in .

## Implementation notes

In the definition of monoidal categories, we also provide the whiskering operators:
* , denoted by ,
* , denoted by .

These are products of an object and a morphism (the terminology "whiskering"
is borrowed from 2-category theory). The tensor product of morphisms  can be defined
in terms of the whiskerings. There are two possible such definitions, which are related by
the exchange property of the whiskerings. These two definitions are accessed by
and . By default,  is defined so that  holds
definitionally.

If you want to provide  and define  and  in terms of it,
you can use the alternative constructor .

The whiskerings are useful when considering simp-normal forms of morphisms in monoidal categories.

### Simp-normal form for morphisms

Rewriting involving associators and unitors could be very complicated. We try to ease this
complexity by putting carefully chosen simp lemmas that rewrite any morphisms into the simp-normal
form defined below. Rewriting into simp-normal form is especially useful in preprocessing
performed by the  tactic.

The simp-normal form of morphisms is defined to be an expression that has the minimal number of
parentheses. More precisely,
1. it is a composition of morphisms like  such that each  is
  either a structural morphism (morphisms made up only of identities, associators, unitors)
  or a non-structural morphism, and
2. each non-structural morphism in the composition is of the form ,
  where each  is an object that is not the identity or a tensor and  is a non-structural
  morphism that is not the identity or a composite.

Note that  is actually .

Currently, the simp lemmas don't rewrite  and  into  and ,
respectively, since it requires a huge refactoring. We hope to add these simp lemmas soon.

## Implementation notes

Verifying the various axioms directly requires tedious rewriting.
Using the  tactic may make the proofs marginally more readable.

More exciting, however, would be to make possible one of the following options:
1. Integration with homotopy.io / globular to give "picture proofs".
2. The monoidal coherence theorem, so we can ignore associators
   (after which most of these proofs are trivial).
3. Automating these proofs using  or some relative.

In this file, we take the second approach using the monoidal composition  and the
 tactic.

monoidally natural in .

-morphism to .

# Cartesian closed functors

Define the exponential comparison morphisms for a functor which preserves binary products, and use
them to define a Cartesian closed functor: one which (naturally) preserves exponentials.

Define the Frobenius morphism, and show it is an isomorphism iff the exponential comparison is an
isomorphism.

## TODO
Some of the results here are true more generally for closed objects and for closed monoidal
categories, and these could be generalised.

## References



## Tags
Frobenius reciprocity, Cartesian closed functor

The Frobenius morphism for an adjunction  at  is given by the morphism

    L(FA ⨯ B) ⟶ LFA ⨯ LB ⟶ A ⨯ LB

natural in , where the first morphism is the product comparison and the latter uses the counit

# A Cartesian closed category with zero object is trivial

A Cartesian closed category with zero object is trivial: it is equivalent to the category with one
object and one morphism.

## References

*

If a Cartesian closed category has an initial object which is isomorphic to the terminal object,
then each homset has exactly one element.

If a Cartesian closed category has a zero object, each homset has exactly one element.

A Cartesian closed category with a zero object is equivalent to the category with one object and
one morphism.

# Braidings for Day convolution

In this file, we show that if  is a braided monoidal category and
 also a braided monoidal category, then the Day convolution monoidal structure
on  is also braided monoidal. We prove it by constructing an explicit
braiding isomorphism whenever sufficient Day convolutions exist, and we
prove that it satisfies the forward and reverse hexagon identities.

Furthermore, we show that when both  and  are symmetric monoidal
categories, then the Day convolution monoidal structure is symmetric as well.

# The free monoidal category over a type

Given a type , the free monoidal category over  has as objects formal expressions built from
(formal) tensor products of terms of  and a formal unit. Its morphisms are compositions and
tensor products of identities, unitors and associators.

In this file, we construct the free monoidal category and prove that it is a monoidal category. If
 is a monoidal category, we construct the functor  associated to
a function .

The free monoidal category has two important properties: it is a groupoid and it is thin. The former
is obvious from the construction, and the latter is what is commonly known as the monoidal coherence
theorem. Both of these properties are proved in the file .

Don't generate unnecessary  or  lemmas
which the  linter will complain about.

Given a type , the free monoidal category over  has as objects formal expressions built from
(formal) tensor products of terms of  and a formal unit. Its morphisms are compositions and
tensor products of identities, unitors and associators.

Formal compositions and tensor products of identities, unitors and associators. The morphisms
of the free monoidal category are obtained as a quotient of these formal morphisms by the
relations defining a monoidal category.

The morphisms of the free monoidal category satisfy 21 relations ensuring that the resulting
category is in fact a category and that it is monoidal.

We say that two formal morphisms in the free monoidal category are equivalent if they become
equal if we apply the relations that are true in a monoidal category. Note that we will prove
that there is only one equivalence class -- this is the monoidal coherence theorem.

# The monoidal coherence theorem

In this file, we prove the monoidal coherence theorem, stated in the following form: the free
monoidal category over any type  is thin.

We follow a proof described by Ilya Beylin and Peter Dybjer, which has been previously formalized
in the proof assistant ALF. The idea is to declare a normal form (with regard to association and
adding units) on objects of the free monoidal category and consider the discrete subcategory of
objects that are in normal form. A normalization procedure is then just a functor
, where
functoriality says that two objects which are related by associators and unitors have the
same normal form. Another desirable property of a normalization procedure is that an object is
isomorphic (i.e., related via associators and unitors) to its normal form. In the case of the
specific normalization procedure we use we not only get these isomorphisms, but also that they
assemble into a natural isomorphism .
But this means that any two parallel morphisms in the free monoidal category factor through a
discrete category in the same way, so they must be equal, and hence the free monoidal category
is thin.

## References

* Ilya Beylin and Peter Dybjer, Extracting a proof of coherence for monoidal categories from a
  proof of normalization for monoids

 is braided, then the category of monoids is naturally monoidal.

In this section, we prove that the category of monoids in a braided monoidal category is monoidal.

Given two monoids  and  in a braided monoidal category ,
the multiplication on the tensor product  is defined in the obvious way:
it is the tensor product of the multiplications on  and ,
except that the tensor factors in the source come in the wrong order,
which we fix by pre-composing with a permutation isomorphism constructed from the braiding.

(There is a subtlety here: in fact there are two ways to do these,
using either the positive or negative crossing.)

A more conceptual way of understanding this definition is the following:
The braiding on  gives rise to a monoidal structure on
the tensor product functor from  to .
A pair of monoids in  gives rise to a monoid in ,
which the tensor product functor by being monoidal takes to a monoid in .
The permutation isomorphism appearing in the definition of
the multiplication on the tensor product of two monoids is
an instance of a more general family of isomorphisms
which together form a strength that equips the tensor product functor with a monoidal structure,
and the monoid axioms for the tensor product follow from the monoid axioms for the tensor factors
plus the properties of the strength (i.e., monoidal functor axioms).
The strength  of the tensor product functor has been defined in
.
Its properties, stated as independent lemmas in that module,
are used extensively in the proofs below.
Notice that we could have followed the above plan not only conceptually
but also as a possible implementation and
could have constructed the tensor product of monoids via ,
but we chose to give a more explicit definition directly in terms of .

To complete the definition of the monoidal category structure on the category of monoids,
we need to provide definitions of associator and unitors.
The obvious candidates are the associator and unitors from ,
but we need to prove that they are monoid morphisms, i.e., compatible with unit and multiplication.
These properties translate to the monoidality of the associator and unitors
(with respect to the monoidal structures on the functors they relate),
which have also been proved in .

The proofs that associators and unitors preserve monoid units don't require braiding.

We don't want  to be simp as it would loop with  applied
to .

The skeleton of a monoidal category can be viewed as a monoid, where the multiplication is given by
the tensor product, and satisfies the monoid axioms since it is a skeleton.

the equivalence.

# Artinian and Noetherian categories

An Artinian category is a category in which objects do not
have infinite decreasing sequences of subobjects.

A Noetherian category is a category in which objects do not
have infinite increasing sequences of subobjects.

Note: In the file, ,
it is shown that any nonzero Artinian object has a simple subobject.

## Future work
The Jordan-Hölder theorem, following .

A category is Noetherian if it is essentially small and all objects are Noetherian.

A category is Artinian if it is essentially small and all objects are Artinian.

# Additive Functors

A functor between two preadditive categories is called *additive*
provided that the induced map on hom types is a morphism of abelian
groups.

An additive functor between preadditive categories creates and preserves biproducts.
Conversely, if  is a functor between preadditive categories, where  has binary
biproducts, and if  preserves binary biproducts, then  is additive.

A preadditive category is a category in which  is an abelian group in such a way that
composition of morphisms is linear in both variables.

This file contains a definition of preadditive category that directly encodes the definition given
above. The definition could also be phrased as follows: A preadditive category is a category

available, the contents of this file should become obsolete.

# Hom orthogonal families.

A family of objects in a category with zero morphisms is "hom orthogonal" if the only
morphism between distinct objects is the zero morphism.

We show that in any category with zero morphisms and finite biproducts,
a morphism between biproducts drawn from a hom orthogonal family
can be decomposed into a block diagonal matrix with entries in the endomorphism rings of the .

When the category is preadditive, this decomposition is an additive equivalence,
and intertwines composition and matrix multiplication.
When the category is -linear, the decomposition is an -linear equivalence.

If every object in the hom orthogonal family has an endomorphism ring with invariant basis number
(e.g. if each object in the family is simple, so its endomorphism ring is a division ring,
or otherwise if each endomorphism ring is commutative),
then decompositions of an object as a biproduct of the family have uniquely defined multiplicities.
We state this as:

This is preliminary to defining semisimple categories.

A family of objects is "hom orthogonal" if
there is at most one morphism between distinct objects.

(In a category with zero morphisms, that must be the zero morphism.)

Morphisms between two direct sums over a hom orthogonal family
are equivalent to block diagonal matrices,
with blocks indexed by ,
and matrix entries in -th block living in the endomorphisms of .

as an additive equivalence.

as an -linear equivalence.

The hypothesis that  has invariant basis number is automatically satisfied
if  is simple (as then  is a division ring).

Given a hom orthogonal family
for which each  is a ring with invariant basis number (e.g. if each  is simple),
if two direct sums over  are isomorphic, then they have the same multiplicities.

# Left exactness of functors between preadditive categories

We show that a functor is left exact in the sense that it preserves finite limits, if it
preserves kernels. The dual result holds for right exact functors and cokernels.

## Main results

* We first derive preservation of binary products in the lemma
  ,
* then show the preservation of equalizers in ,
* and then derive the preservation of all finite limits with the usual construction.

A functor between preadditive categories which preserves kernels preserves that an
arbitrary binary fan is a limit.

A kernel-preserving functor between preadditive categories preserves any pair being a limit.

A kernel-preserving functor between preadditive categories preserves binary products.

A functor between preadditive categories preserves the equalizer of two
morphisms if it preserves all kernels.

A functor between preadditive categories preserves all equalizers if it preserves all kernels.

A functor between preadditive categories which preserves kernels preserves all finite limits.

A functor between preadditive categories which preserves cokernels preserves finite coproducts.

A cokernel-preserving functor between preadditive categories preserves any pair being
a colimit.

A cokernel-preserving functor between preadditive categories preserves binary coproducts.

A functor between preadditive categories preserves the coequalizer of two
morphisms if it preserves all cokernels.

A functor between preadditive categories preserves all coequalizers if it preserves all
cokernels.

A functor between preadditive categories which preserves cokernels preserves all finite
colimits.

# Schur's lemma

We first prove the part of Schur's Lemma that holds in any preadditive category with kernels,
that any nonzero morphism between simple objects
is an isomorphism.

Second, we prove Schur's lemma for -linear categories with finite-dimensional hom spaces,
over an algebraically closed field :
the hom space  between simple objects  and  is at most one dimensional,
and is 1-dimensional iff  and  are isomorphic.

See also , which does not require .

The part of **Schur's lemma** that holds in any preadditive category with kernels:
that a nonzero morphism between simple objects is an isomorphism.

As a corollary of Schur's lemma for preadditive categories,
any morphism between simple objects is (exclusively) either an isomorphism or zero.

In any preadditive category with kernels,
the endomorphisms of a simple object form a division ring.

Part of **Schur's lemma** for -linear categories:
the hom space between two non-isomorphic simple objects is 0-dimensional.

We prove this with the explicit  assumption,
rather than just , as this form is useful for
Müger's formulation of semisimplicity.
An auxiliary lemma for Schur's lemma.

If  is finite dimensional, and every nonzero endomorphism is invertible,
then  is 1-dimensional.

**Schur's lemma** for endomorphisms in -linear categories.

Endomorphisms of a simple object form a field if they are finite dimensional.
This can't be an instance as  would be undetermined.

There is a symmetric argument that uses  instead,
but we don't bother proving that here.
**Schur's lemma** for -linear categories:
if hom spaces are finite dimensional, then the hom space between simples is at most 1-dimensional.

See  and  below
for the refinements when we know whether or not the simples are isomorphic.

of -presentable objects is a dense functor. This expresses canonically

In this file, we define the notion of locally presentable and accessible
categories. We first define these notions for a category  relative to a
fixed regular cardinal  (typeclasses
and ). The existence of such a regular
cardinal  is asserted in the typeclasses  and
. We show that in a locally presentable or

## References
* Adámek, J. and Rosický, J., *Locally presentable and accessible categories*

Given a regular cardinal , a category  is -locally presentable
if it is cocomplete and admits a (small) family  of -presentable
objects such that any object identifies as a -filtered colimit of these objects.

Given a regular cardinal , a category  is -accessible
if it has -filtered colimits and admits a (small) family  of -presentable
objects such that any object identifies as a -filtered colimit of these objects.

A category is locally finitely presentable if it is locally -presentable.

A category is finitely accessible if it is -accessible.

A category  is locally presentable if it is -locally presentable
for some regular cardinal .

A category  is accessible if it is -accessible
for some regular cardinal .

# Regular categories

A regular category is a category with finite limits such that each kernel pair has a coequalizer
and such that regular epimorphisms are stable under pullback.

These categories provide a good ground to develop the calculus of relations, as well as being the
semantics for regular logic.

## Main results

* We show that every regular category has strong epi-mono factorisations, following Theorem 1.11
  in [Gran2021].
* We show that every regular category satisfies Frobenius reciprocity. That is, that in their
  internal language, we have  iff , for a proposition  not
  depending on .

## Future work
* Show that every topos is regular
* Show that regular logic has an interpretation in regular categories

## References
* Marino Gran, An Introduction to Regular Categories
*

# Simple objects

We define simple objects in any category with zero morphisms.
A simple object is an object  such that any monomorphism
is either an isomorphism or zero (but not both).

This is formalized as a -valued typeclass .

In some contexts, especially representation theory, simple objects are called "irreducibles".

If a morphism  out of a simple object is nonzero and has a kernel, then that kernel is zero.
(We state this as , but should add .)

When the category is abelian, being simple is the same as being cosimple (although we do not
state a separate typeclass for this).
As a consequence, any nonzero epimorphism out of a simple object is an isomorphism,
and any nonzero morphism into a simple object has trivial cokernel.

We show that any simple object is indecomposable.

An object is simple if monomorphisms into it are (exclusively) either isomorphisms or zero.

A nonzero monomorphism to a simple object is an isomorphism.

See also , which requires .
A nonzero morphism  to a simple object is an epimorphism
(assuming  has an image, and  has equalizers).

We don't want the definition of 'simple' to include the zero object, so we check that here.

We next make the dual arguments, but for this we must be in an abelian category.

In an abelian category, an object satisfying the dual of the definition of a simple object is
simple.

A nonzero epimorphism from a simple object is an isomorphism.

means that  is not an iso, and hence zero, and hence  is a mono.

There are another three potential variations of this lemma,
but as any one suffices to prove  we will not give them all.

Any simple object in a preadditive category is indecomposable.

If  has subobject lattice , then  is simple.

is simple iff it has subobject lattice .

A subobject is simple iff it is an atom in the subobject lattice.

# Closed sieves

A natural closure operator on sieves is a closure operator on  for each  which commutes
with pullback.
We show that a Grothendieck topology  induces a natural closure operator, and define what the
closed sieves are. The collection of -closed sieves forms a presheaf which is a sheaf for ,
and further this presheaf can be used to determine the Grothendieck topology from the sheaf
predicate.
Finally we show that a natural closure operator on sieves induces a Grothendieck topology, and hence
that natural closure operators are in bijection with Grothendieck topologies.

# The Coherent, Regular and Extensive Grothendieck Topologies

This file defines three related Grothendieck topologies on a category .

The first one is called the *coherent* topology. For that to exist, the category  must satisfy a
condition called , which is essentially the minimal requirement for the coherent
coverage to exist. It means that finite effective epimorphic families can be "pulled back".
Given such a category, the coherent coverage is  and the corresponding
Grothendieck topology is . The covering sieves of this coverage are generated by
presieves consisting of finite effective epimorphic families.

The second one is called the *regular* topology and for that to exist, the category  must satisfy
a condition called . This means that effective epimorphisms can be "pulled back".
The regular coverage is  and the corresponding Grothendieck topology is
. The covering sieves of this coverage are generated by presieves consisting of
a single effective epimorphism.

The third one is called the *extensive* coverage and for that to exist, the category  must
satisfy a condition called . This means  has finite coproducts and that
those are preserved by pullbacks. This condition is weaker than , where in
addition finite coproducts are disjoint. The extensive coverage is  and the
corresponding Grothendieck topology is . The covering sieves of this coverage
are generated by presieves consisting of finitely many arrows that together induce an isomorphism
from the coproduct to the target.

- nLab, *Coherent Coverage*

# Coverages

A coverage  on a category  is a set of presieves associated to every object ,
called "covering presieves".
This collection must satisfy a certain "pullback compatibility" condition, saying that
whenever  is a covering presieve on  and  is a morphism, then there exists
some covering sieve  on  such that  factors through  along .

The main difference between a coverage and a Grothendieck pretopology is that we *do not*
require  to have pullbacks.
This is useful, for example, when we want to consider the Grothendieck topology on the category
of extremally disconnected sets in the context of condensed mathematics.

# Induced Topology

We say that a functor  is locally dense if for each covering sieve  in  of
some ,  generates a covering sieve of  in . A locally dense fully faithful
functor then induces a topology on  via . Note that this is equal to
the collection of sieves on  whose image generates a covering sieve. This construction would
make  both cover-lifting and cover-preserving.

Some typical examples are full and cover-dense functors (for example the functor from a basis of a
topological space  into ). The functor  is also locally dense, and the
induced topology can then be used to construct the big sites associated to a scheme.

Given a fully faithful cover-dense functor  between small sites, we then have
. This is known as the comparison lemma.

# Prestacks: descent of morphisms

Let  be a category and .
Given , and objects  and  in ,
we define a presheaf of types  on the category :
its sections on an object  corresponding to a morphism
are the type of morphisms . We shall say that
 satisfies the descent of morphisms for a Grothendieck topology
if these presheaves are all sheaves (typeclass ).

## Terminological note

In this file, we use the language of pseudofunctors to formalize prestacks.
Similar notions could also be phrased in terms of fibered categories.
In the mathematical literature, various uses of the words "prestacks" and
"stacks" exists. Our definitions are consistent with Giraud's definition II 1.2.1
in *Cohomologie non abélienne*: a prestack is defined by the descent of morphisms
condition with respect to a Grothendieck topology, and a stack by the effectiveness
of the descent. However, contrary to Laumon and Moret-Bailly in *Champs algébriques* 3.1,
we do not require that target categories are groupoids.

## References
* Jean Giraud, *Cohomologie non abélienne*
* Gérard Laumon and Laurent Moret-Bailly, *Champs algébriques*

notion with the notions of effective epimorphism and effective epimorphic family.

More precisely, if  is a morphism, then  is an effective epi if and only if the sieve
it generates is effective epimorphic; see .
The analogous statement for a family of morphisms is in the theorem
.

is a colimit cocone.

# Morphisms of sheaves factor as a locally surjective followed by a locally injective morphism

When morphisms in a concrete category  factor in a functorial manner as a surjective map
followed by an injective map, we obtain that any morphism of sheaves in
factors in a functorial manner as a locally surjective morphism (which is epi) followed by
a locally injective morphism (which is mono).

Moreover, if we assume that the category of sheaves  is balanced
(see ), then epimorphisms are exactly locally surjective morphisms.

# Grothendieck topologies

Definition and lemmas about Grothendieck topologies.
A Grothendieck topology for a category  is a set of sieves on each object  satisfying
certain closure conditions.

Alternate versions of the axioms (in arrow form) are also described.
Two explicit examples of Grothendieck topologies are given:
* The dense topology
* The atomic topology

as well as the complete lattice structure on Grothendieck topologies (which gives two additional
explicit topologies: the discrete and trivial topologies.)

A pretopology, or a basis for a topology is defined in
. The topology associated
to a topological space is defined in .

## Tags

Grothendieck topology, coverage, pretopology, site

## References

* nLab, *Grothendieck topology*
* S. MacLane, I. Moerdijk, *Sheaves in Geometry and Logic*

## Implementation notes

We use the definition of [nlab] and MM92 (Chapter III, Section 2), where Grothendieck topologies
are saturated collections of morphisms, rather than the notions of the Stacks project (00VG) and
the Elephant, in which topologies are allowed to be unsaturated, and are then completed.
TODO (BM): Add the definition from Stacks, as a pretopology, and complete to a topology.

This is so that we can produce a bijective correspondence between Grothendieck topologies on a
small category and Lawvere-Tierney topologies on its presheaf topos, as well as the equivalence
between Grothendieck topoi and left exact reflective subcategories of presheaf toposes.

three axioms:

    in  is in , we have that  itself is in .

# Defining precoverages via pre--hypercovers

A precoverage is a condition on all presieves. In some applications, it is practical
to instead define a condition on all pre--hypercovers. Such a condition
for every object is a pre--hypercover family if these conditions are
invariant under deduplication.

A pre--hypercover family on  is a property on the category of pre--hypercovers
for every  that is invariant under deduplication.
The data of a pre--hypercover family is the same as the data of a precoverage
(see: ).

The condition on pre--hypercovers for every object.

The induced condition on presieves in , given by a pre--hypercover family.

The associated precoverage to a pre--hypercover family.

The associated pre--hypercover family to a precoverage.

Giving a precoverage on a category is the same as giving a predicate
on every pre--hypercover that is stable under deduplication.

# The jointly surjective precoverage

In the category of types, the jointly surjective precoverage has the jointly surjective
families as coverings. We show that this precoverage is stable under the standard constructions.

(forgetful) functor  is stable under base change if the canonical map
 is surjective.

# Local sites

A site is called local if it has a terminal object whose only covering sieve is trivial -
this makes it possible to define coconstant sheaves on it, giving its sheaf topos the structure
of a local topos. This is one of the conditions of cohesive sites.

Sheaves of types on any local site form a local topos (i.e. a topos whose global sections functor
has a fully faithful right adjoint), and a subcanonical site is local if and only if its topos of
sheaves of types is (see TODOs).

* : typeclass stating that  makes the category it is defined on into a local site.

  presheaves and sheaves.
* : the coconstant sheaf functor  for any local site and
  sufficiently nice target category , defined as the skyscraper sheaf functor of the canonical
  point.
* : the adjunction between the global sections functor  and
  .
* :  is fully faithful.
* : on local sites, the constant sheaf functor is fully faithful.

# Locally bijective morphisms of presheaves

Let  be a category equipped with a Grothendieck topology .
Let  be a concrete category.
In this file, we introduce a type class  which says
that the class  (of morphisms of presheaves which become isomorphisms
after sheafification) is the class of morphisms that are both locally injective
and locally surjective (i.e. locally bijective). We prove that this holds iff
for any presheaf , the sheafification map  is locally bijective.
We show that this holds under certain universe assumptions.

A morphism of sheaves of types is locally bijective iff it is an isomorphism.
(This is generalized below as .)

Given a category  equipped with a Grothendieck topology  and a concrete category ,
this property holds if a morphism in  satisfies  (i.e. becomes an iso after
sheafification) iff it is both locally injective and locally surjective.

# Precoverages

A precoverage  on a category  is a set of presieves associated to every object ,
called "covering presieves".
There are no conditions on this set. Common extensions of a precoverage are:

- : A coverage is a precoverage that satisfies a pullback compatibility
  condition, saying that whenever  is a covering presieve on  and  is a morphism,
  then there exists some covering sieve  on  such that  factors through  along .
- : If  has pullbacks, a pretopology on  is a precoverage that
  has isomorphisms and is stable under pullback and refinement.

These two are defined in later files. For precoverages, we define stability conditions:

- : Singleton presieves by isomorphisms are covering.
- : The pullback of a covering presieve is again
  covering.
- : Refining a covering presieve by covering
  presieves yields a covering presieve.

A precoverage is a collection of *covering* presieves on every object .
See  and  for common extensions of this.

The collection of covering presieves for an object .

A precoverage has isomorphisms if singleton presieves by isomorphisms are covering.

A precoverage is stable under base change if pullbacks of covering presieves
are covering presieves.
Use  for less universe restrictions.
Note: This is stronger than the analogous requirement for a , because
 does not imply equality with the (arbitrarily) chosen pullbacks in .

A precoverage is stable under composition if the indexed composition
of coverings is again a covering.
Use  for less universe restrictions.
Note: This is stronger than the analogous requirement for a , because
this is in general not equal to a .

also  is a covering.

A precoverage has pullbacks, if every covering presieve has pullbacks along arbitrary
morphisms.

# Grothendieck pretopologies

Definition and lemmas about Grothendieck pretopologies.
A Grothendieck pretopology for a category  is a set of families of morphisms with fixed codomain,
satisfying certain closure conditions.

We show that a pretopology generates a genuine Grothendieck topology, and every topology has
a maximal pretopology which generates it.

The pretopology associated to a topological space is defined in .

## Tags

coverage, pretopology, site

## References

* nLab, *Grothendieck pretopology*
* S. MacLane, I. Moerdijk, *Sheaves in Geometry and Logic*
* Stacks, *00VG*

A (Grothendieck) pretopology on  consists of a collection of families of morphisms with a fixed
target  for every object  in , called "coverings" of , which satisfies the following
three axioms:
1. Every family consisting of a single isomorphism is a covering family.
2. The collection of covering families is stable under pullback.
3. Given a covering family, and a covering family on each domain of the former, the composition
   is a covering family.

In some sense, a pretopology can be seen as Grothendieck topology with weaker saturation conditions,
in that each covering is not necessarily downward closed.

See:  or [MM92] Chapter III,
Section 2, Definition 2.

For all , the coverings of  (sets of families of morphisms with target )

# The category of type-valued sheaves is a regular epi category

## Main results

: Let  be a Grothendieck topology on , and suppose that
 is a regular epi category which has pushouts and pullbacks, and that sheafification of
-valued -sheaves exists. Suppose further that the category  is balanced, and
that the underlying morphism of presheaves of every epimorphism in  can be factored
as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism. Then  is a regular epi category.

Note: This is not an instance because of the factorisation requirement, but it can in principle be
turned into an instance whenever  has equalizers and  has images. This holds in
particular when  is  or any abelian category. We add it as an instance for ,
but the fact that  is a regular epi category when  is an abelian category
already follows from the sheaf category being abelian.

## References

*Handbook of Categorical Algebra: Volume 3, Sheaf Theory*, by Borceux, 1994.

.

    is an epimorphism.

    isomorphism.

    regular epimorphism.

    sheafification preserves colimits,  exhibits its target  as a coequalizer of this
    kernel pair. The result follows.

# Skeleton of a category

Define skeletal categories as categories in which any two isomorphic objects are equal.

Construct the skeleton of an arbitrary category by taking isomorphism classes, and show it is a
skeleton of the original category.

In addition, construct the skeleton of a thin category as a partial ordering, and (noncomputably)
show it is a skeleton of the original category. The advantage of this special case being handled
separately is that lemmas and definitions about orderings can be used directly, for example for the
subobject lattice. In addition, some of the commutative diagrams about the functors commute
definitionally on the nose which is convenient in practice.

# The small object argument

Let  be a category. A class of morphisms
permits the small object argument (typeclass
where  is an auxiliary universe) if there exists a regular
cardinal  such that
holds. This technical condition is defined in the file
. It involves certain
smallness conditions relative to , the existence of certain colimits in ,
and for each object  which is the source of a morphism in ,
the  functor () should commute
to transfinite compositions of pushouts of coproducts of morphisms in
(this condition is automatically satisfied for a suitable  when  is a
presentable object of , see the file ).

## Main results

Assuming  permits the small object argument, the two main results
obtained in this file are:
* the class  of morphisms that have the left lifting property with
  respect to the maps that have the right lifting property with respect
  to  are exactly the retracts of transfinite compositions (indexed
  by a suitable well-ordered type ) of pushouts of coproducts of
  morphisms in ;
* morphisms in  have a functorial factorization as a morphism in
   followed by a morphism in .

In the context of model categories, these results are known as Quillen's small object
argument (originally for ). Actually, the more general construction by
transfinite induction already appeared in the proof of the existence of enough
injectives in abelian categories with AB5 and a generator by Grothendieck, who then
wrote that the "proof was essentially known". Indeed, the argument appeared
in *Homological algebra* by Cartan and Eilenberg (p. 9-10) in the case of modules,
and they mention that the result was initially obtained by Baer.

## Structure of the proof

The main part in the proof is the construction of the functorial factorization.
This involves a construction by transfinite induction. A general
procedure for constructions by transfinite
induction in categories (including the iteration of a functor)
is done in the file .
The factorization of the small object argument is obtained by doing
a transfinite iteration of a specific functor  which
is defined in the file  (this definition
involves coproducts and a pushout). These ingredients are combined
in the file
where the main results are obtained under a
assumption. The fact that the left lifting property with respect to
a class of morphisms is stable by transfinite compositions was obtained in
the file .

## References

- Henri Cartan and Samuel Eilenberg, *Homological algebra*
- Alexander Grothendieck, *Sur quelques points d'algèbre homologique*
- Daniel G. Quillen, *Homotopical algebra*
-

# Subterminal objects

Subterminal objects are the objects which can be thought of as subobjects of the terminal object.
In fact, the definition can be constructed to not require a terminal object, by defining  to be
subterminal iff for any , there is at most one morphism .
An alternate definition is that the diagonal morphism  is an isomorphism.
In this file we define subterminal objects and show the equivalence of these three definitions.

We also construct the subcategory of subterminal objects.

# Thin categories

A thin category (also known as a sparse category) is a category with at most one morphism between
each pair of objects.
Examples include posets, but also some indexing categories (diagrams) for special shapes of
(co)limits.
To construct a category instance one only needs to specify the  part,
as the axioms hold for free.
If  is thin, then the category of functors to  is also thin.
Further, to show two objects are isomorphic in a thin category, it suffices only to give a morphism
in each direction.

Construct a category instance from a , using the fact that
   hom spaces are subsingletons to prove the axioms.

We don't assume anything about where the category instance on  came from.
In particular this allows  to be a preorder, with the category instance inherited from the
preorder structure.

If  is a thin category, then  is a thin category.

To show  in a thin category, it suffices to just give any morphism in each direction.

# The adjoint functor is triangulated

If a functor  between pretriangulated categories is triangulated, and if we
have an adjunction , then  is also a triangulated functor. We deduce the
symmetric statement (if  is a triangulated functor, then so is ) using opposite
categories.

We then introduce a class  for adjunctions: an adjunction
is called triangulated if both  and  are triangulated, and if the adjunction
is compatible with the shifts by  on  and  (in the sense of );
we prove that this is compatible with composition and that the identity adjunction is
triangulated.
Thanks to the results above, an adjunction carrying an  instance
is triangulated as soon as one of the adjoint functors is triangulated.

We finally specialize these structures to equivalences of categories, and prove that,
if  is an equivalence of pretriangulated categories, then
 is triangulated if and only if  is triangulated.

# Triangulated subcategories

In this file, given a pretriangulated category  and ,

is a triangulated subcategory of . When  is a triangulated
subcategory, we introduce a class of morphisms
consisting of the morphisms whose "cone" belongs to  (up to isomorphisms),
and we show that it has both calculus of left and right fractions.

We also show that  is equipped with a pretriangulated structure,
which is triangulated if  is.

## Implementation notes

In the definition of , we do not assume that the predicate
on objects is closed under isomorphisms (i.e. that the subcategory is "strictly full").
Part of the theory would be more convenient under this stronger assumption
(e.g. the subtype of  consisting of triangulated subcategories
would be a lattice), but some applications require this:
for example, the subcategory of bounded below complexes in the homotopy category
of an additive category is not closed under isomorphisms.

# Behrend's bound on Roth numbers

This file proves Behrend's lower bound on Roth numbers. This says that we can find a subset of
 of size  which does not contain arithmetic progressions of
length .

The idea is that the sphere (in the -dimensional Euclidean space) doesn't contain arithmetic
progressions (literally) because the corresponding ball is strictly convex. Thus we can take
integer points on that sphere and map them onto  in a way that preserves arithmetic progressions
().

* Wikipedia, *Salem-Spencer set*

## Tags

3AP-free, Salem-Spencer, Behrend construction, arithmetic progression, sphere, strictly convex

The frontier of a closed strictly convex set only contains trivial arithmetic progressions.
The idea is that an arithmetic progression is contained on a line and the frontier of a strictly
convex set does not contain lines.

### Turning the sphere into 3AP-free set

We define , the intersection of the $L^2$ sphere with the positive quadrant of
integer points. Because the $L^2$ closed ball is strictly convex, the $L^2$ sphere and

an additive monoid homomorphism.

sets.

The Roth number of a finset is the size of its biggest 3AP-free subset. This is a more general
definition than the one often found in mathematical literature, where the -th Roth number is
the size of the biggest 3AP-free subset of .

# Approximate subgroups

This file defines approximate subgroups of a group, namely symmetric sets  such that  can
be covered by a small number of translates of .

## Main results

Approximate subgroups are a central concept in additive combinatorics, as a natural weakening and
flexible substitute of genuine subgroups. As such, they share numerous properties with subgroups:
* : Group homomorphisms send approximate subgroups to approximate
  subgroups
* : The intersection of (non-trivial powers of) two approximate
  subgroups is an approximate subgroup. Warning: The intersection of two approximate subgroups isn't
  an approximate subgroup in general.

Approximate subgroups are close qualitatively and quantitatively to other concepts in additive
combinatorics:
* : An approximate subgroup has small powers.
* : A set of small tripling can be made an approximate
  subgroup by squaring.

It can be readily confirmed that approximate subgroups are a weakening of subgroups:
* : A 1-approximate subgroup is the same thing as a subgroup.

An approximate subgroup in a group is a symmetric set  containing the identity and such that
 can be covered by a small number of translates of .

In practice, we will take  fixed and  large but finite.

An approximate subgroup in a group is a symmetric set  containing the identity and such that
 can be covered by a small number of translates of .

In practice, we will take  fixed and  large but finite.

A -approximate subgroup is the same thing as a subgroup.

A -approximate subgroup is the same thing as a subgroup.

A configuration is nondegenerate if:

 4) any two lines have at most one intersection point.

# Incidence algebras

Given a locally finite order  the incidence algebra over  is the type of functions from
non-empty intervals of  to some algebraic codomain.

This algebra has a natural multiplication operation whereby the product of two such functions
is defined on an interval by summing over all divisions into two subintervals the product of the
values of the original pair of functions.

This structure allows us to interpret many natural invariants of the intervals (such as their
cardinality) as elements of the incidence algebra. For instance the cardinality function, viewed as
an element of the incidence algebra, is simply the square of the function that takes constant value
one on all intervals. This constant function is called the zeta function, after
its connection with the Riemann zeta function.

The incidence algebra is a good setting for proving many inclusion-exclusion type principles, these
go under the name Möbius inversion, and are essentially due to the fact that the zeta function has
a multiplicative inverse in the incidence algebra, an inductively definable function called the
Möbius function that generalizes the Möbius function in number theory.

## Main definitions

*  is the delta function, defined analogously to the identity matrix.
*  is the incidence algebra product, defined analogously to the matrix product.
*  is the zeta function, defined analogously to the upper triangular matrix
  of ones.
*  is the inverse of the zeta function.

## Implementation notes

One has to define  as either the left or right inverse of . We define it as the left
inverse, and prove it is also a right inverse by defining  as the right inverse and using that
left and right inverses agree if they exist.

# Inclusion-exclusion principle

This file proves several variants of the inclusion-exclusion principle.

The inclusion-exclusion principle says that the sum/integral of a function over a finite union of
sets can be calculated as the alternating sum over  of the sum/integral of the function over
the intersection of  of the sets.

By taking complements, it also says that the sum/integral of a function over a finite intersection
of complements of sets can be calculated as the alternating sum over  of the sum/integral of
the function over the intersection of  of the sets.

By taking the function to be constant , we instead get a result about the cardinality/measure of
the sets.

## Main declarations

Per the above explanation, this file contains the following variants of inclusion-exclusion:
* : Sum of a function over a finite union of sets
* : Cardinality of a finite union of sets
* : Sum of a function over a finite intersection of
  complements of sets
* : Cardinality of a finite intersection of
  complements of sets

See also  for the version with integrals, and
 for the version with measures.

# Partitions

A partition of a natural number  is a way of writing  as a sum of positive integers, where the
order does not matter: two sums that differ only in the order of their summands are considered the
same partition. This notion is closely related to that of a composition of , but in a composition
of  the order does matter.
A summand of the partition is called a part.

## Main functions

*  is a structure, made of a multiset of integers which are all positive and

# Generating functions for partitions

This file defines generating functions related to partitions. Given a character function $f(i, c)$
of a part $i$ and the number of occurrences of the part $c$, the related generating function is
$$
G_f(X) = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \left(\sum_{p \in P_{n}} \prod_{i \in p} f(i, \#i)\right) X^n
= \prod_{i = 1}^{\infty}\left(1 + \sum_{j = 1}^{\infty} f(i, j) X^{ij}\right)
$$
where $P_n$ is all partitions of $n$, $\#i$ is the count of $i$ in the partition $p$.
We give the definition  using the first equation, and prove the second
equation in  (with shifted indices).

This generating function can be specialized to
* When $f(i, c) = 1$, this is the generating function for partition function $p(n)$
  (TODO: prove this).
* When $f(i, 1) = 1$ and $f(i, c) = 0$ for $c > 1$, this is the generating function for
  . More generally, setting $f(i, c) = 1$ only for $c < m$ gives
  the generating function for .
  (See ).
* When $f(i, c) = 1$ for odd $i$ and $f(i, c) = 0$ for even $i$, this is the generating function for
  . More generally, setting $f(i, c) = 1$ only for $i$ satisfying certain
   gives the generating function for .
  (See )

The definition of  ignores the value of $f(0, c)$ and $f(i, 0)$. The formula
can be interpreted as assuming $f(i, 0) = 1$ and $f(0, c) = 0$ for $c \ne 0$. In theory we could
respect the actual value of $f(0, c)$ and $f(i, 0)$, but it makes the otherwise finite sum and
product potentially infinite.

Generating function associated with character $f(i, c)$ for partition functions, where $i$ is a
part of the partition, and $c$ is the count of that part in the partition. The character function is
multiplied within one , and summed among all  for a fixed . This way,
each  is assigned a value, which we use as the coefficients of the power series.

See the module docstring of  for more details.

The summands in the formula  tends to infinity in their order.

The infinite sum in the formula  always converges.

# Glaisher's theorem

This file proves Glaisher's theorem: the number of partitions of an integer $n$ into parts not
divisible by $d$ is equal to the number of partitions in which no part is repeated $d$ or more
times.

## Main declarations
* : Glaisher's theorem.
* : Euler's partition theorem, a special case
  of Glaisher's theorem when . This is also Theorem 45 from the
  100 Theorems List.

## Proof outline

The proof is based on the generating functions for  and  partitions,
which turn out to be equal:

$$\prod_{i=1,i\nmid m}^\infty\frac{1}{1-X^i}=\prod_{i=0}^\infty (1+X^{i+1}+\cdots+X^{(m-1)(i+1)})$$

## References

The generating function of  is
$$
\prod_{i \in p} \sum_{j = 0}^{\infty} X^{ij}
$$

The generating function of  is
$$
\prod_{i = 1}^{\infty} \sum_{j = 0}^{m - 1} X^{ij}
$$

# Pentagonal number theorem for power series

This file proves the pentagonal number theorem for power series:

$$ \prod_{n = 0}^{\infty} (1 - x^{n + 1}) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} (-1)^k x^{a_k} $$

where $a_k = k(3k - 1)/2$ are the pentagonal numbers. We state the theorem in two parts by
introducing the intermediate power series , whose coefficients are
defined using pentagonal numbers. We then show that this series is equal to both sides.

# Pentagonal number theorem

This is an intermediate file that proves the pentagonal number theorem in a general topological ring
modulo summability and multipliability. The complete proof for formal power series is in
. TODO: also prove for real/complex numbers.

## Declarations

* : pentagonal number theorem with a few summability and
  multipliability assumptions.

## References

We define an auxiliary sequence

$$ a_{k, n} = x^{(k+1)n} \prod_{i=0}^{n} (1 - x^{k + i + 1}) $$

We will also use its sum

$$ A_k = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_{k, n} $$

And a second auxiliary sequence

$$ b_{k, n} = x^{(k+1)n} (x^{2k + n + 3} - 1) \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} (1 - x^{k + i + 2}) $$

and  have relation

$$ a_{k,n} + x^{3k + 5}a_{k + 1, n} = b_{k, n+1} - b_{k, n} $$

By summing with telescoping, we get a recurrence formula for $A$

$$ A_k = 1 - x^{2k + 3} - x^{3k + 5}A_{k + 1} $$

The Euler function is related to $A_0$ by

$$ \prod_{n = 0}^{\infty} (1 - x^{n + 1}) = 1 - x - x^2 A_0 $$

Applying the recurrence formula repeatedly, we get

$$ \prod_{n = 0}^{\infty} (1 - x^{n + 1}) =
\left(\sum_{k=0}^{j} (-1)^k \left(x^{k(3k+1)/2} - x^{(k+1)(3k+2)/2}\right) \right) +
(-1)^{j+1}x^{(j+1)(3j+4)/2}A_j $$

**Pentagonal number theorem**, assuming appropriate multipliability and summability.

$$ \prod_{n = 0}^{\infty} (1 - x^{n + 1}) =
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} (-1)^k \left(x^{k(3k+1)/2} - x^{(k+1)(3k+2)/2}\right) $$

# The Ruzsa-Szemerédi problem

This file proves the lower bound of the Ruzsa-Szemerédi problem. The problem is to find the maximum
number of edges that a graph on  vertices can have if all edges belong to at most one triangle.

The lower bound comes from turning the big 3AP-free set from Behrend's construction into a graph
that has the property that every triangle gives a (possibly trivial) arithmetic progression on the
original set.

## Main declarations

* : Maximum number of edges a graph on  vertices can have such that
  each edge belongs to exactly one triangle.
* : There exists a graph with  vertices and
   edges such that each edge belongs to exactly one triangle.

### The Ruzsa-Szemerédi number

The **Ruzsa-Szemerédi number** of a fintype is the maximum number of edges a locally linear
graph on that type can have.

In other words,  is the maximum number of edges a graph on  can have such
that each edge belongs to exactly one triangle.

 vertices can have.

can have such that each edge belongs to exactly one triangle.

# Multigraphs

A multigraph is a set of vertices and a set of edges,
together with incidence data that associates each edge
with an unordered pair  of vertices called the *ends* of .
The pair of  and  is called a *link*.
The vertices  and  may be equal, in which case  is a *loop*.
There may be more than one edge with the same ends.

If a multigraph has no loops and has at most one edge for every given ends, it is called *simple*,
and these objects are also formalized as .

This module defines  for a vertex type  and an edge type ,
and gives basic API for incidence, adjacency and extensionality.
The design broadly follows [Chou1994].

## Implementation notes

Unlike the design of , the vertex and edge sets of  are modelled as sets
 and , within ambient types, rather than being types themselves.
This mimics the 'embedded set' design used in , which seems to be more convenient for
formalizing real-world proofs in combinatorics.

A specific advantage is that this allows subgraphs of  to also exist on
an equal footing with  as terms in ,
and so there is no need for a  type and all the associated
definitions and canonical coercion maps. The same will go for minors and the various other
partial orders on multigraphs.

The main tradeoff is that parts of the API will need to care about whether a term
 or  is a 'real' vertex or edge of the graph, rather than something outside
the vertex or edge set. This is an issue, but is likely amenable to automation.

# The Hales-Jewett theorem

We prove the Hales-Jewett theorem. We deduce Van der Waerden's theorem and the multidimensional
Hales-Jewett theorem as corollaries.

The Hales-Jewett theorem is a result in Ramsey theory dealing with *combinatorial lines*. Given
an 'alphabet'  and , an example of a combinatorial line in  is
. See  for a precise general definition. The
Hales-Jewett theorem states that for any fixed finite types  and , there exists a (potentially
huge) finite type  such that whenever  is -colored (i.e. for any coloring
), there exists a monochromatic line. We prove the Hales-Jewett theorem using
the idea of *color focusing* and a *product argument*. See the proof of
 for details.

*Combinatorial subspaces* are higher-dimensional analogues of combinatorial lines. See
. The multidimensional Hales-Jewett theorem generalises the statement above
from combinatorial lines to combinatorial subspaces of a fixed dimension.

The version of Van der Waerden's theorem in this file states that whenever a commutative monoid
is finitely colored and  is a finite subset, there exists a monochromatic homothetic copy of .
This follows from the Hales-Jewett theorem by considering the map  sending
to , which sends a combinatorial line to a homothetic copy of .

## Main results

- : The Hales-Jewett theorem.
- : The multidimensional Hales-Jewett theorem.
- : A generalization of Van der Waerden's theorem.

allows us to work directly with , , , and  instead of ,

The **Hales-Jewett theorem**. This version has a restriction on universe levels which is
necessary for the proof. See  for a fully universe-polymorphic

The proof proceeds by induction on .

We have to show that the theorem is invariant under  for the induction to work.

This deals with the degenerate case where  is empty.

Now we have to show that the theorem holds for  if it holds for .

Later we'll need  to be nonempty. So we first deal with the trivial case where  is
    empty.
    Then  has only one element, so any line is monochromatic.

The key idea is to show that for every , in high dimension we can either find
    color focused lines or a monochromatic line.

# Hall's Marriage Theorem

Given a list of finite subsets $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ of some given set
$S$, P. Hall in [Hall1935] gave a necessary and sufficient condition for
there to be a list of distinct elements $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ with
$x_i\in X_i$ for each $i$: it is when for each $k$, the union of every
$k$ of these subsets has at least $k$ elements.

Rather than a list of finite subsets, one may consider indexed families
 of finite subsets with  a , and then the list
of distinct representatives is given by an injective function
such that , called a *matching*.
This version is formalized as

As observed in [Halpern1966], one may use the constrained version of the theorem
in a compactness argument to remove this constraint.

are nonempty (), which uses the
Tychonoff theorem.

We prove Hindman's theorem on finite sums, using idempotent ultrafilters.

Given an infinite sequence  of positive integers, the set  is the set
of positive integers that can be expressed as a finite sum of 's, without repetition. Hindman's
theorem asserts that whenever the positive integers are finitely colored, there exists a sequence
 such that  is monochromatic. There is also a stronger version, saying
that whenever a set of the form  is finitely colored, there exists a sequence
 such that  is monochromatic and contained in . We prove both
these versions for a general semigroup  instead of  since it is no harder, although this
special case implies the general case.

The idea of the proof is to extend the addition  to addition

(see  or ) and consists of a set of
*vertices*, usually denoted  or , and a set of *hyperedges*, here called *edges* and
denoted  or . In contrast with a graph, where edges are unordered pairs of vertices, in
hypergraphs, edges are unordered sets of vertices; i.e., they are subsets of the vertex set .

A hypergraph where  and  is *empty*, denoted . A hypergraph with a nonempty
vertex set () and empty edge set is *trivial*. A hypergraph where the edge set is the power
set of the vertex set (or, equivalently, where all possible subsets of the vertex sets are in the

# Matroids

A  is a structure that combinatorially abstracts
the notion of linear independence and dependence;
matroids have connections with graph theory, discrete optimization,
additive combinatorics and algebraic geometry.
Mathematically, a matroid  is a structure on a set  comprising a
collection of subsets of  called the bases of ,
where the bases are required to obey certain axioms.

This file gives a definition of a matroid  in terms of its bases,
and some API relating independent sets (subsets of bases) and the notion of a
basis of a set  (a maximal independent subset of ).

## Implementation details

There are a few design decisions worth discussing.

### Finiteness
  The first is that our matroids are allowed to be infinite.
  Unlike with many mathematical structures, this isn't such an obvious choice.
  Finite matroids have been studied since the 1930's,
  and there was never controversy as to what is and isn't an example of a finite matroid -
  in fact, surprisingly many apparently different definitions of a matroid
  give rise to the same class of objects.

  However, generalizing different definitions of a finite matroid
  to the infinite in the obvious way (i.e. by simply allowing the ground set to be infinite)
  gives a number of different notions of 'infinite matroid' that disagree with each other,
  and that all lack nice properties.
  Many different competing notions of infinite matroid were studied through the years;
  in fact, the problem of which definition is the best was only really solved in 2013,
  when Bruhn et al. [2] showed that there is a unique 'reasonable' notion of an infinite matroid
  (these objects had previously defined by Higgs under the name 'B-matroid').
  These are defined by adding one carefully chosen axiom to the standard set,
  and adapting existing axioms to not mention set cardinalities;
  they enjoy nearly all the nice properties of standard finite matroids.

  Even though at least 90% of the literature is on finite matroids,
  B-matroids are the definition we use, because they allow for additional generality,
  nearly all theorems are still true and just as easy to state,
  and (hopefully) the more general definition will prevent the need for a costly future refactor.
  The disadvantage is that developing API for the finite case is harder work
  (for instance, it is harder to prove that something is a matroid in the first place,
  and one must deal with  rather than ).
  For serious work on finite matroids, we provide the typeclasses
   and  and associated API.

### Cardinality
  Just as with bases of a vector space,
  all bases of a finite matroid  are finite and have the same cardinality;
  this cardinality is an important invariant known as the 'rank' of .
  For infinite matroids, bases are not in general equicardinal;
  in fact the equicardinality of bases of infinite matroids is independent of ZFC [3].
  What is still true is that either all bases are finite and equicardinal,
  or all bases are infinite. This means that the natural notion of 'size'
  for a set in matroid theory is given by the function , which
  is the cardinality as a term in . We use this function extensively
  in building the API; it is preferable to both  and
  because it allows infinite sets to be handled without splitting into cases.

### The ground
  A last place where we make a consequential choice is making the ground set of a matroid
  a structure field of type  (where  is the type of 'possible matroid elements')
  rather than just having a type  of all the matroid elements.
  This is because of how common it is to simultaneously consider
  a number of matroids on different but related ground sets.
  For example, a matroid  on ground set  can have its structure
  'restricted' to some subset  to give a smaller matroid  with ground set .
  A statement like  is mathematically obvious.
  But if the ground set of a matroid is a type, this doesn't typecheck,
  and is only true up to canonical isomorphism.
  Restriction is just the tip of the iceberg here;
  one can also 'contract' and 'delete' elements and sets of elements
  in a matroid to give a smaller matroid,
  and in practice it is common to make statements like  and
  .
  Such things are a nightmare to work with unless  is actually propositional equality
  (especially because the relevant coercions are usually between sets and not just elements).

  So the solution is that the ground set  has type ,
  and there are elements of type  that aren't in the matroid.
  The tradeoff is that for many statements, one now has to add
  hypotheses of the form  to make sure than  is actually 'in the matroid',
  rather than letting a 'type of matroid elements' take care of this invisibly.
  It still seems that this is worth it.
  The tactic  exists specifically to discharge such goals
  with minimal fuss (using default values).
  The tactic works fairly well, but has room for improvement.

  A related decision is to not have matroids themselves be a typeclass.
  This would make things be notationally simpler
  (having  in the presence of  rather than  for a term )
  but is again just too awkward when one has multiple matroids on the same type.
  In fact, in regular written mathematics,
  it is normal to explicitly indicate which matroid something is happening in,
  so our notation mirrors common practice.

### Notation
  We use a few nonstandard conventions in theorem names that are related to the above.
  First, we mirror common informal practice by referring explicitly to the  set rather
  than the notation . (Writing  everywhere in a proof term would be unwieldy, and
  writing  in theorem names would be unnatural to read.)

  Second, because we are typically interested in subsets of the ground set ,
  using  is inconvenient, since  is typically false for .
  On the other hand (especially when duals arise), it is common to complement
  a set  *within* the ground set, giving .
  For this reason, we use the term  in theorem names to refer to taking a set difference
  with respect to the ground set, rather than a complement within a type. The lemma
   is one of the many examples of this.

  Finally, in theorem names, matroid predicates that apply to sets
  (such as , , ) are typically used as suffixes rather than prefixes.
  For instance, we have  rather than .
