# Matroid Independence and Basis axioms

Matroids in mathlib are defined axiomatically in terms of bases,
but can be described just as naturally via their collections of independent sets,
and in fact such a description, being more 'verbose', can often be useful.
As well as this, the definition of a  uses an unwieldy 'maximality'
axiom that can be dropped in cases where there is some finiteness assumption.

This file provides several ways to do define a matroid in terms of its independence or base
predicates, using axiom sets that are appropriate in different settings,
and often much simpler than the general definition.
It also contains  lemmas and typeclasses as appropriate.

All the independence axiom sets need nontriviality (the empty set is independent),
monotonicity (subsets of independent sets are independent),
and some form of 'augmentation' axiom, which allows one to enlarge a non-maximal independent set.
This augmentation axiom is still required when there are finiteness assumptions, but is simpler.
It just states that if  is a finite independent set and  is a larger finite
independent set, then there exists  for which  is independent.
This is the axiom that appears in most of the definitions.

## Implementation Details

To facilitate building a matroid from its independent sets, we define a structure
which has a ground set , an independence predicate , and some axioms as its fields.
This structure is another encoding of the data in a ; the function
constructs a  from an .

This is convenient because if one wants to define  from a known independence
predicate , it is easier to define an  so that  and
then set  than it is to directly define  with the base axioms.
The simp lemma  is important here; it shows that ,
so the  constructed is the right one, and the intermediate  can be
made essentially invisible by the simplifier when working with .

Because of this setup, we don't define any API for , as it would be
a redundant copy of the existing API for .
(In particular, one could define a natural equivalence
with , but this would be pointless, as there is no need
for the inverse of ).

# Matroid loops and coloops

## Loops
A 'loop' of a matroid  is an element  satisfying one of the following equivalent conditions:
* ;
*  is dependent in ;
*  is a circuit of ;
* no base of  contains .

In many mathematical contexts, loops can be thought of as 'trivial' or 'zero' elements;
For linearly representable matroids, they correspond to the zero vector,
and for graphic matroids, they correspond to edges incident with just one vertex (aka 'loops').
As trivial as they are, loops can be created from matroids with no loops by taking minors or duals,
so in many contexts it is unreasonable to simply forbid loops from appearing.
For , this file defines a set ,
as well as predicates  and ,
and provides API for interacting with them.

## Coloops
The dual notion of a loop is a 'coloop'. Geometrically, these can be thought of elements that are
skew to the remainder of the matroid. Coloops in graphic matroids are 'bridge' edges of the graph,
and coloops in linearly representable matroids are vectors not spanned by the other vectors
in the matroid.
Coloops also have many equivalent definitions in abstract matroid language;
a coloop is an element of  if any of the following equivalent conditions holds :
*  is a loop of ;
*  is a cocircuit of ;
*  is in no circuit of ;
*  is in every base of ;
* for all , ,
*  is nonspanning.

## Notes

For finite matroids, both maps and comaps are a special case of a construction of
Perfect [perfect1969matroid] in which a matroid structure can be transported across an arbitrary
bipartite graph that may not correspond to a function at all (See [oxley2011], Theorem 11.2.12).
It would have been nice to use this more general construction as a basis for the definition
of both  and .

Unfortunately, we can't do this, because the construction doesn't extend to infinite matroids.
Specifically, if  and  are matroids on the same type ,
and  is the natural function from  to ,
then the images under  of the independent sets of the direct sum  are
the independent sets of a matroid if and only if the union of  and  is a matroid,
and unions do not exist for some pairs of infinite matroids: see [aignerhorev2012infinite].
For this reason,  requires injectivity to be well-defined in general.

## Notes

It is not (provably) the case that all matroids are ,

Lemmas like  become true for all matroids

The -valued rank and rank functions  and ,

independently of the  typeclass,

and its value may differ on a set  and the closure of .
We state and prove theorems without  whenever possible,

# -valued rank

If the 'cardinality' of  is taken to mean the -valued term ,
then all bases of any  have the same cardinality,
and for each  with , all -bases for  have the same cardinality.
The 'rank' of a matroid is the cardinality of all its bases,
and the 'rank' of a set  in a matroid  is the cardinality of each -basis of .
This file defines these two concepts as a term
and a function  respectively.

The rank function  satisfies three properties, often known as (R1), (R2), (R3):
* ,
*  for all ,
*  for all .

In fact, if  is finite, then any function  satisfying these properties
is the rank function of a ; in other words, properties (R1) - (R3) give an alternative
definition of finite matroids, and a finite matroid is determined by its rank function.
Because of this, and the convenient quantitative language of these axioms,
the rank function is often the preferred perspective on matroids in the literature.
(The above doesn't work as well for infinite matroids,
which is why mathlib defines matroids using bases/independence. )

# Sums of matroids

The *sum*  of a collection  of matroids is a matroid on the disjoint union of
the ground sets of the summands, in which the independent sets are precisely the unions of
independent sets of the summands.

We can ask for such a sum both for pairs and for arbitrary indexed collections of matroids,
and we can also ask for the 'disjoint union' to be either set-theoretic or type-theoretic.
To this end, we define five separate versions of the sum construction.

General-Valued CSP is a very broad class of problems in discrete optimization.
General-Valued CSP subsumes Min-Cost-Hom (including 3-SAT for example) and Finite-Valued CSP.

# Pigeonhole principles

Given pigeons (possibly infinitely many) in pigeonholes, the
pigeonhole principle states that, if there are more pigeons than
pigeonholes, then there is a pigeonhole with two or more pigeons.

There are a few variations on this statement, and the conclusion can
be made stronger depending on how many pigeons you know you might
have.

The basic statements of the pigeonhole principle appear in the
following locations:

*  has
*  has
*  has
*  has
*  has

This module gives access to these pigeonhole principles along with 20 more.
The versions vary by:

* using a function between s or a function between possibly infinite types restricted to
  s;
* counting pigeons by a general weight function () or by heads ();
* using strict or non-strict inequalities;
* establishing upper or lower estimate on the number (or the total weight) of the pigeons in one
  pigeonhole;
* in case when we count pigeons by some weight function  and consider a function  between
  s  and , we can either assume that each pigeon is in one of the pigeonholes
  (), or assume that for , the total weight of the pigeons in this
  pigeonhole  is nonpositive or nonnegative depending on
  the inequality we are proving.
* in the case where the "holes" are not necessarily disjoint, that is, a pigeon could be in multiple
  holes at the same time, a set-valued version is provided.

Lemma names follow  convention (e.g.,
); "pigeonhole principle" is mentioned in the
docstrings instead of the names.

### The pigeonhole principles on s, pigeons counted by weight

In this section we prove the following version of the pigeonhole principle: if the total weight of a
finite set of pigeons is greater than , and they are sorted into  pigeonholes, then for
some pigeonhole, the total weight of the pigeons in this pigeonhole is greater than , and a few
variations of this theorem.

The principle is formalized in the following way, see
: if  is a function which maps all
elements of  to  and , where  is
a weight function taking values in a linearly ordered cancellative monoid, then for
some , the sum of the weights of all  such that  is greater than .

There are a few bits we can change in this theorem:

* reverse all inequalities, with obvious adjustments to the name;
* replace the assumption  with ,
  and replace  with  in the name;
* use non-strict inequalities assuming  is nonempty.

We can do all these variations independently, so we have eight versions of the theorem.

#### Strict inequality versions


The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, strict inequality version:
if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is greater than , and they are sorted into
 pigeonholes, then for some pigeonhole, the total weight of the pigeons in this pigeonhole is
greater than .

The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, strict inequality version:
if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is less than , and they are sorted into
pigeonholes, then for some pigeonhole, the total weight of the pigeons in this pigeonhole is less
than .

The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, strict inequality version:
if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is greater than , they are sorted into some
pigeonholes, and for all but  pigeonholes the total weight of the pigeons there is nonpositive,
then for at least one of these  pigeonholes, the total weight of the pigeons in this pigeonhole
is greater than .

The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, strict inequality version:
if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is less than , they are sorted into some
pigeonholes, and for all but  pigeonholes the total weight of the pigeons there is nonnegative,
then for at least one of these  pigeonholes, the total weight of the pigeons in this pigeonhole
is less than .

#### Non-strict inequality versions


The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, non-strict inequality
version: if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is greater than or equal to , and
they are sorted into  pigeonholes, then for some pigeonhole, the total weight of the pigeons
in this pigeonhole is greater than or equal to .

The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, non-strict inequality
version: if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is less than or equal to , and they
are sorted into  pigeonholes, then for some pigeonhole, the total weight of the pigeons in
this pigeonhole is less than or equal to .

The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, non-strict inequality
version: if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is greater than or equal to , they
are sorted into some pigeonholes, and for all but  pigeonholes the total weight of the
pigeons there is nonpositive, then for at least one of these  pigeonholes, the total weight of
the pigeons in this pigeonhole is greater than or equal to .

The pigeonhole principle for finitely many pigeons counted by weight, non-strict inequality
version: if the total weight of a finite set of pigeons is less than or equal to , they are
sorted into some pigeonholes, and for all but  pigeonholes the total weight of the pigeons
there is nonnegative, then for at least one of these  pigeonholes, the total weight of the
pigeons in this pigeonhole is less than or equal to .

### The pigeonhole principles on s, pigeons counted by heads

In this section we formalize a few versions of the following pigeonhole principle: there is a
pigeonhole with at least as many pigeons as the ceiling of the average number of pigeons across all
pigeonholes.

First, we can use strict or non-strict inequalities. While the versions with non-strict inequalities
are weaker than those with strict inequalities, sometimes it might be more convenient to apply the
weaker version. Second, we can either state that there exists a pigeonhole with at least
pigeons, or state that there exists a pigeonhole with at most  pigeons. In the latter case we do
not need the assumption .

# Kleitman's bound on the size of intersecting families

An intersecting family on  elements has size at most , so we could naïvely think that two
intersecting families could cover all  sets. But actually that's not case because for example
none of them can contain the empty set. Intersecting families are in some sense correlated.
Kleitman's bound stipulates that  intersecting families cover at most  sets.

## Main declarations

* : Kleitman's theorem.

## References

* D. J. Kleitman, *Families of non-disjoint subsets*

**Kleitman's theorem**. An intersecting family on  elements contains at most  sets, and
each further intersecting family takes at most half of the sets that are in no previous family.

This file proves the Kruskal-Katona theorem. This is a sharp statement about how many sets of size

The key results proved here are:
* : The basic Kruskal-Katona theorem. Given a set family  consisting of

  achieved by initial segments of colex.

This is important for iterating Kruskal-Katona: the shadow of an initial segment is also an

This is a pretty painful proof, with lots of cases.

First show that if t ∪ a ≤ s, then t ≤ s - min s

Now show that if t ≤ s - min s, there is j such that t ∪ j ≤ s
  We choose j as the smallest thing not in t

If t = s - min s, then use j = min s so t ∪ j = s

Assume first t < s - min s, and take k as the colex witness for this

Cases on j < k or j = k

if j < k, k is our colex witness for t ∪ {j} < s

if j = k, all of range k is in t so by sizes t ∪ {j} = s

The shadow of an initial segment is also an initial segment.

Applying the compression makes the set smaller in colex. This is intuitive since a portion of
the set is being "shifted down" as .

These are the compressions which we will apply to decrease the "measure" of a family of sets.

Applying a good compression will decrease measure, keep cardinality, keep sizes and decrease
shadow. In particular, 'good' means it's useful, and every smaller compression won't make a
difference.

If we're compressed by all useful compressions, then we're an initial segment. This is the other
key Kruskal-Katona part.

This measures roughly how compressed the family is.

Note that this does depend on the order of the ground set, unlike the Kruskal-Katona theorem itself
(although  currently is stated in an order-dependent manner).

Applying a compression strictly decreases the measure. This helps show that "compress until we
can't any more" is a terminating process.

The main Kruskal-Katona helper: use induction with our measure to keep compressing until
we can't any more, which gives a set family which is fully compressed and has the nice properties we
want.

Are there any compressions we can make now?

No. Then where we are is the required set family.

Yes. Then apply the smallest compression, then keep going

Finally we can prove Kruskal-Katona.

### Bridge edges

An edge of a graph is a *bridge* if without it, its incident vertices
are not reachable from one another.

decompose c into
  puw     pwv     pvu
  u ----> w ----> v ----> u

We have two walks from v to w
  pvu     puw
  v ----> u ----> w
  |               ^

pwv.reverse
  so they both contain the edge s(v, w), but that's a contradiction since c is a trail.

Deleting a non-bridge edge from a connected graph preserves connectedness.

Connecting two unreachable vertices by an edge preserves existing bridges,
provided the bridge is already an edge.

### 2-reachability

In this section, we prove results about 2-connected components of a graph, but without naming them.

A walk between two vertices separated by an edge must go through that edge.

A trail doesn't go through an edge that disconnects one of its endpoints from the endpoints of
the trail.

A trail doesn't go through a vertex that is disconnected from its endpoints by an edge.

A trail doesn't go through any leaf vertex, except possibly at its endpoints.

Removing leaves from a connected graph keeps it connected.

# Darts in graphs

A  or half-edge or bond in a graph is an ordered pair of adjacent vertices, regarded as an
oriented edge. This file defines darts and proves some of their basic properties.

A  is an oriented edge, implemented as an ordered pair of adjacent vertices.
This terminology comes from combinatorial maps, and they are also known as "half-edges"
or "bonds."

The edge associated to the dart.

The dart with reversed orientation from a given dart.

Two darts are said to be adjacent if they could be consecutive
darts in a walk -- that is, the first dart's second vertex is equal to
the second dart's first vertex.

For a given vertex , this is the bijective map from the neighbor set at
to the darts  with .

# Degree-sum formula and handshaking lemma

The degree-sum formula is that the sum of the degrees of the vertices in
a finite graph is equal to twice the number of edges.  The handshaking lemma,
a corollary, is that the number of odd-degree vertices is even.

## Main definitions

-  is the degree-sum formula.
-  is the handshaking lemma.
-  is that the number of odd-degree
  vertices different from a given odd-degree vertex is odd.
-  is that the existence of an
  odd-degree vertex implies the existence of another one.

## Implementation notes

We give a combinatorial proof by using the facts that (1) the map from
darts to vertices is such that each fiber has cardinality the degree
of the corresponding vertex and that (2) the map from darts to edges is 2-to-1.

## Tags

simple graphs, sums, degree-sum formula, handshaking lemma

The degree-sum formula.  This is also known as the handshaking lemma, which might
more specifically refer to .

The degree-sum formula only counting over the vertices that form edges.

See  for the general version.

The handshaking lemma.  See also .

The eccentricity of a vertex is the greatest distance between it and any other vertex.

The extended diameter is the greatest distance between any two vertices, with the value  in
case the distances are not bounded above, or the graph is not connected.

Note: Neither  nor  implies the other.

Note: Neither  nor  implies the other.

the finiteness assumptions

The diameter is the greatest distance between any two vertices, with the value  in

# Turán's theorem

In this file we prove Turán's theorem, the first important result of extremal graph theory,
which states that the -cliquefree graph on  vertices with the most edges is the complete
-partite graph with part sizes as equal as possible ().

The forward direction of the proof performs "Zykov symmetrisation", which first shows
constructively that non-adjacency is an equivalence relation in a maximal graph, so it must be
complete multipartite with the parts being the equivalence classes. Then basic manipulations
show that the graph is isomorphic to the Turán graph for the given parameters.

For the reverse direction we first show that a Turán-maximal graph exists, then transfer
the property through  using the isomorphism provided by the forward direction.

## Main declarations

* :  means that  has the most number of edges for
  its number of vertices while still being -cliquefree.
* : The canonical -cliquefree Turán graph on  vertices.
* : The result of Zykov symmetrisation, a finpartition of
  the vertices such that two vertices are in the same part iff they are non-adjacent.
* : The forward direction, an isomorphism
  between  satisfying  and .
* : the reverse direction,  given the isomorphism.
* : Turán's theorem in full.

# Matchings

A *matching* for a simple graph is a set of disjoint pairs of adjacent vertices, and the set of all
the vertices in a matching is called its *support* (and sometimes the vertices in the support are
said to be *saturated* by the matching). A *perfect matching* is a matching whose support contains
every vertex of the graph.

In this module, we represent a matching as a subgraph whose vertices are each incident to at most
one edge, and the edges of the subgraph represent the paired vertices.

## Main definitions

* :  means that  is a matching of its
  underlying graph.

*  defines when a subgraph  of a simple graph is a
  perfect matching, denoted .

*  means that a graph  has no perfect matchings.

*  means that a graph consists of cycles (including cycles of length 0,
  also known as isolated vertices)

*  means that edges in a graph  are alternatingly
  included and not included in some other graph

# Graph partitions

This module provides an interface for dealing with partitions on simple graphs. A partition of
a graph , with vertices , is a set  of disjoint nonempty subsets of  such that:

* The union of the subsets in  is .

* Each element of  is an independent set. (Each subset contains no pair of adjacent vertices.)

Graph partitions are graph colorings that do not name their colors.  They are adjoint in the
following sense. Given a graph coloring, there is an associated partition from the set of color
classes, and given a partition, there is an associated graph coloring from using the partition's
subsets as colors. Going from graph colorings to partitions and back makes a coloring "canonical":
all colors are given a canonical name and unused colors are removed. Going from partitions to
graph colorings and back is the identity.

## Main definitions

*  is a structure to represent a partition of a simple graph.

*  is whether a given partition is an -partition.
  (a partition with at most  parts).

*  is whether a given graph is -partite.

*  creates colorings from partitions.

*  creates partitions from colorings.

  -colorability are equivalent.

* : a proof that  is a proper partition of .
* : a proof that each element of  doesn't have a pair of adjacent vertices.

# Trail, Path, and Cycle

In a simple graph,

* A *trail* is a walk whose edges each appear no more than once.

* A *circuit* is a nonempty trail whose first and last vertices are the
  same.

* A *path* is a trail whose vertices appear no more than once.

* A *cycle* is a nonempty trail whose first and last vertices are the
  same and whose vertices except for the first appear no more than once.

**Warning:** graph theorists mean something different by "path" than
do homotopy theorists.  A "walk" in graph theory is a "path" in
homotopy theory.  Another warning: some graph theorists use "path" and
"simple path" for "walk" and "path."

Some definitions and theorems have inspiration from multigraph
counterparts in [Chou1994].

# Energy of a partition

This file defines the energy of a partition.

The energy is the auxiliary quantity that drives the induction process in the proof of Szemerédi's
Regularity Lemma. As long as we do not have a suitable equipartition, we will find a new one that
has an energy greater than the previous one plus some fixed constant.

## References

Yaël Dillies, Bhavik Mehta, *Formalising Szemerédi’s Regularity Lemma in Lean*

The energy of a partition, also known as index. Auxiliary quantity for Szemerédi's regularity
lemma.

# Szemerédi's Regularity Lemma

In this file, we prove Szemerédi's Regularity Lemma (aka SRL). This is a landmark result in
combinatorics roughly stating that any sufficiently big graph behaves like a random graph. This is
useful because random graphs are well-behaved in many aspects.

More precisely, SRL states that for any  and integer  there exists a bound  such that
any graph on at least  vertices can be partitioned into at least  parts and at most  parts
such that the resulting partitioned graph is -uniform.

This statement is very robust to tweaking and many different versions exist. Here, we prove the
version where the resulting partition is equitable (aka an *equipartition*), namely all parts have
the same size up to a difference of .

The proof we formalise goes as follows:
1. Define an auxiliary measure of edge density, the *energy* of a partition.
2. Start with an arbitrary equipartition of size .
3. Repeatedly break up the parts of the current equipartition in a big but controlled number of
  parts. The key point is to break along the witnesses of non-uniformity, so that a lesser portion
  of the pairs of parts are non--uniform.
4. Check that this results in an equipartition with an energy greater than the energy of the current
  partition, plus some constant.
5. Since the energy is between zero and one, we can't run this process forever. Check that when the
  process stops we have an -uniform equipartition.

This file only contains the final result. The supporting material is spread across the
 folder:
* : Definition of the bound on the number of parts.
  Numerical inequalities involving the lemma constants.
* : Definition of the energy of a simple graph along a
  partition.
* : Definition of uniformity of a simple graph along
  a pair of parts and along a partition.
* : Construction of an equipartition with
  a prescribed number of parts of each size and almost refining a given partition.
* : Break up one part of the current equipartition.
  Check that density between non-uniform parts increases, and that density between uniform parts
  doesn't decrease too much.
* : Gather all those broken up parts into the new
  equipartition (aka *increment partition*). Check that energy increases by at least a fixed amount.
* : Wrap everything up into an induction on the energy.

## TODO

We currently only prove the equipartition version of SRL.

* Prove the diagonal version.

# Unit-distance graph embeddings

An embedding of a graph into some metric space is _unit-distance_ if the distance between any two
adjacent vertices is 1. The space in question is usually the Euclidean plane, but can also be
higher-dimensional Euclidean space or the sphere (cf. [Frankl_2020]). We do not require nonadjacent
vertices to not be distance 1 apart as [hong2014] does.

## Main definitions

# Tiles for tilings

This file defines some basic concepts related to individual tiles for tilings in a discrete context
(with definitions in a continuous context to be developed separately but analogously).

Work in the field of tilings does not generally try to define or state things in any kind of maximal
generality, so it is necessary to adapt definitions and statements from the literature to produce
something that seems appropriately general for mathlib, covering a wide range of tiling-related
concepts found in the literature. Nevertheless, further generalization may prove of use as this work
is extended in future.

We work in the context of a space  acted on by a group ; the action is not required to be
faithful, although typically it is. In a discrete context, tiles are expected to cover the space, or
a subset of it being tiled when working with tilings not of the whole space, and the tiles are
pairwise disjoint. In a continuous context, definitions in the literature vary; the tiles may be
closed and cover the space with interiors required to be disjoint (as used by Grünbaum and Shephard
or Goodman-Strauss), or they may be required to be measurable and to partition it up to null sets
(as used by Greenfeld and Tao).

In general we are concerned not with a tiling in isolation but with tilings by some protoset of
tiles; thus we make definitions in the context of such a protoset, where copies of the tiles in the
tiling must be images of those tiles under the action of an element of the given group.

Where there are matching rules that say what combinations of tiles are considered as valid, these
are provided as separate hypotheses where required. Tiles in a protoset are commonly considered in
the literature to be marked in some way. When this is simply to distinguish two otherwise identical
tiles, this is represented by the use of different indices in the protoset. When this is to give a
tile fewer symmetries than it would otherwise have under the action of the given group, this is
represented by the symmetries specified in the  being less than its full stabilizer.

The group  is throughout here a multiplicative group. Additive groups are also used in the
literature, typically when based on ; to support the use of additive groups,  could
be used with the theory here.

## Main definitions

* : A prototile in  as acted on by , carrying the information of a subgroup of
  the stabilizer that says when two copies of the prototile are considered the same.

* : An indexed family of prototiles.

* : An image of a tile in the protoset .

* Chaim Goodman-Strauss, *Open Questions in Tiling*
* Rachel Greenfeld and Terence Tao, *A counterexample to the periodic tiling
  conjecture*

tilings. Two copies related by an element of  are considered the same; two copies not so
related, even if they have the same points, are considered distinct.

A divide-and-conquer recurrence is a function  that satisfies a recurrence relation of
the form  for sufficiently large , where  is
a function such that  for every , the coefficients
are positive, and the coefficients  are real numbers in . (This assumption can be
relaxed to , for some ; we leave this as future work.) These
recurrences arise mainly in the analysis of divide-and-conquer algorithms such as mergesort or
Strassen's algorithm for matrix multiplication. This class of algorithms works by dividing an
instance of the problem of size , into  smaller instances, where the -th instance is of
size roughly , and calling itself recursively on those smaller instances.  then
represents the running time of the algorithm, and  represents the running time required to
divide the instance and process the answers produced by the recursive calls. Since virtually all
such algorithms produce instances that are only approximately of size  (they must round up
or down, at the very least), we allow the instance sizes to be given by a function  that
approximates .

A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) is a state machine which
decides membership in a particular , by following a path
uniquely determined by an input string.

We define regular languages to be ones for which a DFA exists, other formulations
are later proved equivalent.

Note that this definition allows for automata with infinite states,
a  instance must be supplied for true DFAs.

# Myhill–Nerode theorem

This file proves the Myhill–Nerode theorem using left quotients.

Given a language  and a word , the *left quotient* of  by  is the set of suffixes
such that  is in . The *Myhill–Nerode theorem* shows that each left quotient, in fact,
corresponds to the state of an automaton that matches , and that  is regular if and only if
there are finitely many such states.

# Nondeterministic Finite Automata

A Nondeterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) is a state machine which
decides membership in a particular , by following every
possible path that describes an input string.

We show that DFAs and NFAs can decide the same languages, by constructing
an equivalent DFA for every NFA, and vice versa.

As constructing a DFA from an NFA uses an exponential number of states,
we re-prove the pumping lemma instead of lifting ,
in order to obtain the optimal bound on the minimal length of the string.

Like , this definition allows for automata with infinite states;

# The primitive recursive functions

The primitive recursive functions are the least collection of functions
 which are closed under projections (using the
pairing function), composition, zero, successor, and primitive recursion
(i.e.  where the motive is ).

We can extend this definition to a large class of basic types by
using canonical encodings of types as natural numbers (Gödel numbering),
which we implement through the type class . (More precisely,
we need that the composition of encode with decode yields a
primitive recursive function, so we have the  type class
for this.)

In the above, the pairing function is primitive recursive by definition.
This deviates from the textbook definition of primitive recursive functions,
which instead work with *-ary* functions. We formalize the textbook
definition in .  then proves it is
equivalent to our chosen formulation. For more discussion of this and
other design choices in this formalization, see [carneiro2019].

## Main definitions

- :  is primitive recursive, for functions
- :  is primitive recursive, for functions between  types
- : well-behaved encoding of  into , i.e. one such that roundtripping through
  the encoding functions adds no computational power

## Implementation notes

To count the execution time of a Turing machine, we have decided to count the number of times the
 function is used. Each step executes a statement (of type ); this is a function, and
generally contains multiple "fundamental" steps (pushing, popping, and so on).
However, as functions only contain a finite number of executions and each one is executed at most
once, this execution time is up to multiplication by a constant the amount of fundamental steps.

## From compositional semantics to sequential semantics

Our initial sequential model is designed to be as similar as possible to the compositional
semantics in terms of its primitives, but it is a sequential semantics, meaning that rather than
defining an  function for each program, defined by recursion on
programs, we have a type  with a step function  that provides a
deterministic evaluation order. In order to do this, we introduce the notion of a *continuation*,
which can be viewed as a  with a hole in it where evaluation is currently taking place.
Continuations can be assigned a  semantics as well, with the interpretation
being that given a  result returned from the code in the hole, the remainder of the
program will evaluate to a  final value.

# Turing machines

The files  and  define

## Naming conventions

Each model of computation in this file shares a naming convention for the elements of a model of
computation. These are the parameters for the language:

*  is the alphabet on the tape.
*  is the set of labels, or internal machine states.
*  is the type of internal memory, not on the tape. This does not exist in the TM0 model, and
  later models achieve this by mixing it into .
*  is used in the TM2 model, which has multiple stacks, and denotes the number of such stacks.

All of these variables denote "essentially finite" types, but for technical reasons it is
convenient to allow them to be infinite anyway. When using an infinite type, we will be interested
in proving that only finitely many values of the type are ever interacted with.

Given these parameters, there are a few common structures for the model that arise:

*  is the set of all actions that can be performed in one step. For the TM0 model this set is
  finite, and for later models it is an infinite inductive type representing "possible program
  texts".
*  is the set of instantaneous configurations, that is, the state of the machine together with
  its environment.
*  is the set of all machines in the model. Usually this is approximately a function
  , although different models have different ways of halting and other actions.
*  is the function that describes how the state evolves over one step.
  If , then  is a terminal state, and the result of the computation is read off
  from . Because of the type of , these models are all deterministic by construction.
*  sets up the initial state. The type  depends on the model;
  in most cases it is .
* , given a machine  and input , starts from
  , runs  until it reaches an output, and then applies a function  to
  the final state to obtain the result. The type  depends on the model.
*  asserts that a machine  starts in , and
  can only ever jump to other states inside . This implies that the behavior of  on any input
  cannot depend on its values outside . We use this to allow  to be an infinite set when
  convenient, and prove that only finitely many of these states are actually accessible. This
  formalizes "essentially finite" mentioned above.

## The TM1 model

The TM1 model is a simplification and extension of TM0 (Post-Turing model) in the direction of
Wang B-machines. The machine's internal state is extended with a (finite) store  of variables
that may be accessed and updated at any time.

A machine is given by a  indexed set of procedures or functions. Each function has a body which
is a . Most of the regular commands are allowed to use the current value  of the local
variables and the value  on the tape to calculate what to write or how to change local
state, but the statements themselves have a fixed structure. The s can be as follows:

* : move left or right, and then do
* : write  to the tape, then do
* : change the internal state to
* : If  is true, do , else
* : Go to label
* : Transition to the halting state, which halts on the following step

Note that here most statements do not have labels;  commands can only go to a new function.
Only the  and  statements actually take a step; the rest is done by recursion on
statements and so take 0 steps. (There is a uniform bound on how many statements can be executed
before the next , so this is an  speedup with the constant depending on the machine.)

The  command has a one step stutter before actually halting so that any changes made before
the halt have a chance to be "committed", since the  relation uses the final configuration
before the halt as the output, and  and  etc. take 0 steps in this model.

## TM2 emulator in TM1

To prove that TM2 computable functions are TM1 computable, we need to reduce each TM2 program to a
TM1 program. So suppose a TM2 program is given. This program has to maintain a whole collection of
stacks, but we have only one tape, so we must "multiplex" them all together. Pictorially, if stack
1 contains  and stack 2 contains  then the tape looks like this:


where a tape element is a vertical slice through the diagram. Here the alphabet is
, where:

*  is marked only in one place, the initial position of the TM, and represents the
  tail of all stacks. It is never modified.
*  is the value of the -th stack, if in range, otherwise  (which is
  the blank value). Note that the head of the stack is at the far end; this is so that push and pop
  don't have to do any shifting.

In "resting" position, the TM is sitting at the position marked . For non-stack actions,
it operates in place, but for the stack actions , , and , it must shuttle to the
end of the appropriate stack, make its changes, and then return to the bottom. So the states are:

* : waiting at  to execute function
* : travelling to the right to get to the end of stack  in
  order to perform stack action , and later continue with executing
* : travelling to the left after having performed a stack action, and executing
   once we arrive

Because of the shuttling, emulation overhead is , where  is the current maximum of the
length of all stacks. Therefore a program that takes  steps to run in TM2 takes
steps to run when emulated in TM1, where  is the length of the input.

A displaced lemma proved in unnecessary generality

The alphabet of the TM2 simulator on TM1 is a marker for the stack bottom,
plus a vector of stack elements for each stack, or none if the stack does not extend this far.

The bottom marker is fixed throughout the calculation, so we use the  function
to express the program state in terms of a tape with only the stacks themselves.

A stack action is a command that interacts with the top of a stack. Our default position
is at the bottom of all the stacks, so we have to hold on to this action while going to the end
to modify the stack.

stack actions into one.

The machine states of the TM2 emulator. We can either be in a normal state when waiting for the

# Modelling partial recursive functions using Turing machines

The files  and  define a simplified basis for partial recursive functions,
and a  model
Turing machine for evaluating these functions. This amounts to a constructive proof that every
 function can be evaluated by a Turing machine.

## Main definitions

* : A TM2 Turing machine which can evaluate  programs

## Simulating sequentialized partial recursive functions in TM2

At this point we have a sequential model of partial recursive functions: the  type and
 function from . The key feature of this model is that
it does a finite amount of computation (in fact, an amount which is statically bounded by the size
of the program) between each step, and no individual step can diverge (unlike the compositional
semantics, where every sub-part of the computation is potentially divergent). So we can utilize the
same techniques as in the other TM simulations in  to prove that
each step corresponds to a finite number of steps in a lower level model. (We don't prove it here,
but in anticipation of the complexity class P, the simulation is actually polynomial-time as well.)

The target model is , which has a fixed finite set of stacks, a bit of local storage,
with programs selected from a potentially infinite (but finitely accessible) set of program
positions, or labels , each of which executes a finite sequence of basic stack commands.

# Condensed Objects

This file defines the category of condensed objects in a category , following the work
of Clausen-Scholze and Barwick-Haine.

## Implementation Details

We use the coherent Grothendieck topology on , and define condensed objects in  to
be -valued sheaves, with respect to this Grothendieck topology.

Note: Our definition more closely resembles "Pyknotic objects" in the sense of Barwick-Haine,
as we do not impose cardinality bounds, and manage universes carefully instead.

## References

- [barwickhaine2019]: *Pyknotic objects, I. Basic notions*, 2019.
- [scholze2019condensed]: *Lectures on Condensed Mathematics*, 2019.

# Sheaves on CompHaus are equivalent to sheaves on Stonean

The forgetful functor from extremally disconnected spaces  to compact
Hausdorff spaces  has the marvellous property that it induces an equivalence of categories
between sheaves on these two sites. With the terminology of nLab,  is a
*dense subsite* of : see

Since Stonean spaces are the projective objects in , which has enough projectives,
and the notions of effective epimorphism, epimorphism and surjective continuous map are equivalent
in  and , we can use the general setup in
 to deduce the equivalence of
categories. We give the corresponding statements for  as well.

## Implementation Notes

- We use a custom structure for the total space of a bundle instead of using a type synonym for the
  canonical disjoint union  because the total space usually has a different topology and
  Lean 4  fails to apply lemmas about  to elements of the total space.

  trivializations of original fiber bundles to construct the topology on the total space of the new
  fiber bundle.

## Implementation notes

The support is internally represented (in the primed ) as a  that
represents a superset of the true support of the function, quotiented by the always-true relation so
that this does not impact equality. This approach has computational benefits over storing a
; it allows us to add together two finitely-supported functions without
having to evaluate the resulting function to recompute its support (which would required
decidability of  for ).

The true support of the function can still be recovered with ; but these
decidability obligations are now postponed to when the support is actually needed. As a consequence,
there are two ways to sum a : with  which works over an arbitrary function
but requires recomputation of the support and therefore a  argument; and with
 which requires an additive morphism, using its properties to show that
summing over a superset of the support is sufficient.

 takes an altogether different approach here; it uses  and declares
the  instance as noncomputable. This design difference is independent of the fact that
 is dependently-typed and  is not; in future, we may want to align these two
definitions, or introduce two more definitions for the other combinations of decisions.

Evaluation at a point is an . This is the finitely-supported version of
.

is the sum of  over the support of .

The product over two dfinsupps agree if the functions agree and are well-behaved within the
shared support.

The sum over two dfinsupps agree if the functions agree and are well-behaved within the
shared support.

When summing over an , the decidability assumption is not needed, and the result is
also an .

## Implementation notes

The support is internally represented (in the primed ) as a  that
represents a superset of the true support of the function, quotiented by the always-true relation so
that this does not impact equality. This approach has computational benefits over storing a
; it allows us to add together two finitely-supported functions without
having to evaluate the resulting function to recompute its support (which would required
decidability of  for ).

The true support of the function can still be recovered with ; but these
decidability obligations are now postponed to when the support is actually needed. As a consequence,
there are two ways to sum a : with  which works over an arbitrary function
but requires recomputation of the support and therefore a  argument; and with
 which requires an additive morphism, using its properties to show that
summing over a superset of the support is sufficient.

 takes an altogether different approach here; it uses  and declares
the  instance as noncomputable. This design difference is independent of the fact that
 is dependently-typed and  is not; in future, we may want to align these two
definitions, or introduce two more definitions for the other combinations of decisions.

# Definition of the  typeclass

This file defines a typeclass  saying that  is finite. A type is  if it
is equivalent to  for some . We also define  as a typeclass equivalent to
.

The  predicate has no computational relevance and, being -valued, gets to enjoy proof
irrelevance -- it represents the mere fact that the type is finite.  While the  class also
represents finiteness of a type, a key difference is that a  instance represents finiteness
in a computable way: it gives a concrete algorithm to produce a  whose elements enumerate
the terms of the given type. As such, one generally relies on congruence lemmas when rewriting
expressions involving  instances.

Every  instance automatically gives a  instance, see , but not vice
versa. Every  instance should be computable since they are meant for computation. If it's
not possible to write a computable  instance, one should prefer writing a  instance
instead.

## Main definitions

*  denotes that  is an infinite type.

## Implementation notes

The definition of  is not just  since  requires
that , and the definition in this module allows for . This means
we can write the instance .

A finite set is defined to be a set whose coercion to a type has a  instance.

There are two components to finiteness constructions. The first is  instances for each
construction. This gives a way to actually compute a  that represents the set, and these
may be accessed using . This gets the  in the correct form, since otherwise
 is a  for the subtype for . The second component is
"constructors" for  that give proofs that  instances exist classically given
other  proofs. Unlike the  instances, these *do not* use any decidability
instances since they do not compute anything.

# Finite sets

Terms of type  are one way of talking about finite subsets of  in Mathlib.
Below,  is defined as a structure with 2 fields:

  1.  is a  of elements;
  2.  is a proof that  has no duplicates.

Finsets in Lean are constructive in that they have an underlying  that enumerates their
elements. In particular, any function that uses the data of the underlying list cannot depend on its
ordering. This is handled on the  level by multiset API, so in most cases one needn't
worry about it explicitly.

Finsets give a basic foundation for defining finite sums and products over types:

  1. ;
  2. .

Lean refers to these operations as big operators.
More information can be found in .

Finsets are directly used to define fintypes in Lean.
A  instance for a type  consists of a universal  containing every term of

# Density of a finite set

This defines the density of a  and provides induction principles for finsets.

## Main declarations

* : Density of  in  as a nonnegative rational number.

## Implementation notes

There are many other ways to talk about the density of a finset and provide its API:
1. Use the uniform measure
2. Define finitely additive functions and generalise the  API to it. This could either
  be done with
  a. A structure
  b. A typeclass

Solution 1 would mean importing measure theory in simple files (not necessarily bad, but not
amazing), and every single API lemma would require the user to prove that all the sets they are
talking about are measurable in the trivial sigma-algebra (quite terrible user experience).

Solution 2 would mean that some API lemmas about density don't contain  in their name because
they are general results about finitely additive functions. But not all lemmas would be like that
either since some really are -specific. Hence the user would need to think about whether the
lemma they are looking for is generally true for finitely additive measure or whether it is
-specific.

On top of this, solution 2.a would break dot notation on  (possibly fixable by
introducing notation for ) and solution 2.b would run the risk of being bad
performance-wise.

These considerations more generally apply to  and  and demonstrate that
overengineering basic definitions is likely to hinder user experience.

# Monomial orders

## Monomial orders

A *monomial order* is well ordering relation on a type of the form  which
is compatible with addition and for which  is the smallest element.
Since several monomial orders may have to be used simultaneously, one cannot
get them as instances.

In this formalization, they are presented as a structure  which encapsulates
, an additive and monotone isomorphism to a linearly ordered cancellative
additive commutative monoid.
The entry  asserts that  is well founded.

The terminology comes from commutative algebra and algebraic geometry, especially Gröbner bases,
where  are exponents of monomials.

Given a monomial order , we provide the notation
 and  to compare  with respect to .
It is activated using .

## Examples

Commutative algebra defines many monomial orders, with different usefulness ranges.
In this file, we provide the basic example of lexicographic ordering.
For the graded lexicographic ordering, see

The  design provides further benefits if you put in a bit more work.
The first step is to extend  to create a class of those types satisfying
the axioms of your new type of morphisms.
Continuing the example above:


Note that  are marked as  even though they are not purely required to be so
due to the  parameter already filling them in. This is required to see through
type synonyms, which is important in the category theory library. Also, it appears having them as
 is slightly faster.

The second step is to add instances of your new  for all types extending .
Typically, you can just declare a new class analogous to :


Then any declaration taking a specific type of morphisms as parameter can instead take the
class you just defined:

This means anything set up for s will automatically work for es,
and defining  only takes a constant amount of effort,
instead of linearly increasing the work per -related declaration.

## Design rationale

The current form of FunLike was set up in pull request :

We made  *unbundled*: child classes don't extend , they take a
parameter instead. This suits the instance synthesis algorithm better: it's easy to verify a type
does **not** have a  instance by checking the discrimination tree once instead of searching
the entire  hierarchy.

injective coercion to (dependent) functions from  to .

# Basic properties of holors

Holors are indexed collections of tensor coefficients. Confusingly,
they are often called tensors in physics and in the neural network
community.

A holor is simply a multidimensional array of values. The size of a
holor is specified by a , whose length is called the dimension
of the holor.

The tensor product of  and  is the
holor given by . A holor is "of
rank at most 1" if it is a tensor product of one-dimensional holors.
The CP rank of a holor  is the smallest N such that  is the sum
of N holors of rank at most 1.

A slice is a subholor consisting of all entries with initial index i.

The 1-dimensional "unit" holor with 1 in the th position.

Two holors are equal if all their slices are equal.

The original holor can be recovered from its slices by multiplying with unit vectors and
summing up.

# Association Lists

This file defines association lists. An association list is a list where every element consists of
a key and a value, and no two entries have the same key. The type of the value is allowed to be
dependent on the type of the key.

This type dependence is implemented using : The elements of the list are of type ,
for some type index .

Association lists are represented by the  structure. This file defines this structure and
provides ways to access, modify, and combine s.

# Palindromes

This module defines *palindromes*, lists which are equal to their reverse.

The main result is the  inductive type, and its associated  induction
principle. Also provided are conversions to and from other equivalent definitions.

## References

* Pierre Castéran, *On palindromes*

[casteran]:

## Tags

palindrome, reverse, induction

asserts that  is a palindrome. This is defined inductively:

* The empty list is a palindrome;
* A list with one element is a palindrome;
* Adding the same element to both ends of a palindrome results in a bigger palindrome.

# Lists as finsupp

## Main definitions

- : Interpret a list as a finitely supported function, where the indexing type is
  , and the values are either the elements of the list (accessing by indexing) or  outside of
  the list.

## Main theorems

- : A  over  an , when interpreted
  as a finitely supported function, is equal to the sum of  produced by mapping over
  .

## Implementation details

The functions defined here rely on a decidability predicate that each element in the list
can be decidably determined to be not equal to zero or that one can decide one is out of the
bounds of a list. For concretely defined lists that are made up of elements of decidable terms,
this holds. More work will be needed to support lists over non-dec-eq types like , where the
elements are beyond the dec-eq terms of casted values from .

Indexing into a , as a finitely-supported function,
where the support are all the indices within the length of the list
that index to a non-zero value. Indices beyond the end of the list are sent to 0.

This is a computable version of the  construction.

map from R^m → R^n represented by the same function. The transpose of this matrix is the right
inverse of this map, sending anything not in the image to zero.

# Dershowitz-Manna ordering

In this file we define the _Dershowitz-Manna ordering_ on multisets. Specifically, for two multisets
 and  in a partial order ,  is smaller than  in the Dershowitz-Manna ordering if
 can be obtained from  by replacing one or more elements in  by some finite number of
elements from , each of which is smaller (in the underling ordering over ) than one of the
replaced elements from . We prove that, given a well-founded partial order on the underlying set,
the Dershowitz-Manna ordering defined over multisets is also well-founded.

Whenever you state a lemma about the coercion , check that Lean inserts , not
. Else your lemma will never apply.

It sometimes happens that a  lemma declared early in the library can be proved by
using later, more general simp lemmas. In that case, the following reasons might be arguments for

un-ed):
1. There is a significant portion of the library which needs the early lemma to be available via
   and which doesn't have access to the more general lemmas.
2. The more general lemmas have more complicated typeclass assumptions, causing rewrites with them
  to be slower.

open NormNum

namespace Tactic

namespace NormNum

 A predicate representing partial progress in a proof of .
def SquarefreeHelper (n k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  0 < k → (∀ m, Nat.Prime m → m ∣ bit1 n → bit1 k ≤ m) → Squarefree (bit1 n)

theorem squarefree_bit10 (n : ℕ) (h : SquarefreeHelper n 1) : Squarefree (bit0 (bit1 n)) := by
  refine' @Nat.minSqFacProp_div _ _ Nat.prime_two two_dvd_bit0 _ none _
  · rw [bit0_eq_two_mul (bit1 n), mul_dvd_mul_iff_left (two_ne_zero' ℕ)]
    exact Nat.not_two_dvd_bit1 _
  · rw [bit0_eq_two_mul, Nat.mul_div_right _ (by decide : 0 < 2)]
    refine' h (by decide) fun p pp dp => Nat.succ_le_of_lt (lt_of_le_of_ne pp.two_le _)
    rintro rfl
    exact Nat.not_two_dvd_bit1 _ dp

theorem squarefree_bit1 (n : ℕ) (h : SquarefreeHelper n 1) : Squarefree (bit1 n) := by
  refine' h (by decide) fun p pp dp => Nat.succ_le_of_lt (lt_of_le_of_ne pp.two_le _)
  rintro rfl; exact Nat.not_two_dvd_bit1 _ dp

theorem squarefree_helper_0 {k} (k0 : 0 < k) {p : ℕ} (pp : Nat.Prime p) (h : bit1 k ≤ p) :
    bit1 (k + 1) ≤ p ∨ bit1 k = p := by
  rcases lt_or_eq_of_le h with ((hp : _ + 1 ≤ _) | hp)
  · rw [bit1, bit0_eq_two_mul] at hp
    change 2 * (_ + 1) ≤ _ at hp
    rw [bit1, bit0_eq_two_mul]
    refine' Or.inl (lt_of_le_of_ne hp _)
    rintro rfl
    exact Nat.not_prime_mul (by decide) (lt_add_of_pos_left _ k0) pp
  · exact Or.inr hp

theorem squarefreeHelper_1 (n k k' : ℕ) (e : k + 1 = k')
    (hk : Nat.Prime (bit1 k) → ¬bit1 k ∣ bit1 n) (H : SquarefreeHelper n k') :
    SquarefreeHelper n k := fun k0 ih => by
  subst e
  refine' H (Nat.succ_pos _) fun p pp dp => _
  refine' (squarefree_helper_0 k0 pp (ih p pp dp)).resolve_right fun hp => _
  subst hp; cases hk pp dp

theorem squarefreeHelper_2 (n k k' c : ℕ) (e : k + 1 = k') (hc : bit1 n % bit1 k = c) (c0 : 0 < c)
    (h : SquarefreeHelper n k') : SquarefreeHelper n k := by
  refine' squarefree_helper_1 _ _ _ e (fun _ => _) h
  refine' mt _ (ne_of_gt c0); intro e₁
  rwa [← hc, ← Nat.dvd_iff_mod_eq_zero]

theorem squarefreeHelper_3 (n n' k k' c : ℕ) (e : k + 1 = k') (hn' : bit1 n' * bit1 k = bit1 n)
    (hc : bit1 n' % bit1 k = c) (c0 : 0 < c) (H : SquarefreeHelper n' k') : SquarefreeHelper n k :=
  fun k0 ih => by
  subst e
  have k0' : 0 < bit1 k := bit1_pos (Nat.zero_le _)
  have dn' : bit1 n' ∣ bit1 n := ⟨_, hn'.symm⟩
  have dk : bit1 k ∣ bit1 n := ⟨_, ((mul_comm _ _).trans hn').symm⟩
  have : bit1 n / bit1 k = bit1 n' := by rw [← hn', Nat.mul_div_cancel _ k0']
  have k2 : 2 ≤ bit1 k := Nat.succ_le_succ (bit0_pos k0)
  have pk : (bit1 k).Prime := by
    refine' Nat.prime_def_minFac.2 ⟨k2, le_antisymm (Nat.minFac_le k0') _⟩
    exact ih _ (Nat.minFac_prime (ne_of_gt k2)) (dvd_trans (Nat.minFac_dvd _) dk)
  have dkk' : ¬bit1 k ∣ bit1 n' := by
    rw [Nat.dvd_iff_mod_eq_zero, hc]
    exact ne_of_gt c0
  have dkk : ¬bit1 k * bit1 k ∣ bit1 n := by rwa [← Nat.dvd_div_iff_mul_dvd dk, this]
  refine' @Nat.minSqFacProp_div _ _ pk dk dkk none _
  rw [this]
  refine' H (Nat.succ_pos _) fun p pp dp => _
  refine' (squarefree_helper_0 k0 pp (ih p pp <| dvd_trans dp dn')).resolve_right fun e => _
  subst e
  contradiction

theorem squarefreeHelper_4 (n k k' : ℕ) (e : bit1 k * bit1 k = k') (hd : bit1 n < k') :
    SquarefreeHelper n k := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos n with h | h
  · subst n
    exact fun _ _ => squarefree_one
  subst e
  refine' fun k0 ih => Irreducible.squarefree (Nat.prime_def_le_sqrt.2 ⟨bit1_lt_bit1.2 h, _⟩)
  intro m m2 hm md
  obtain ⟨p, pp, hp⟩ := Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd (ne_of_gt m2)
  have :=
    (ih p pp (dvd_trans hp md)).trans
      (le_trans (Nat.le_of_dvd (lt_of_lt_of_le (by decide) m2) hp) hm)
  rw [Nat.le_sqrt] at this
  exact not_le_of_gt hd this

theorem not_squarefree_mul (a aa b n : ℕ) (ha : a * a = aa) (hb : aa * b = n) (h₁ : 1 < a) :
    ¬Squarefree n := by
  rw [← hb, ← ha]
  exact fun H => ne_of_gt h₁ (Nat.isUnit_iff.1 <| H _ ⟨_, rfl⟩)

 Given  a natural numeral and  with , return .
unsafe def prove_non_squarefree (e : expr) (n a : ℕ) : tactic expr := do
  let ea := reflect a
  let eaa := reflect (a * a)
  let c ← mk_instance_cache q(Nat)
  let (c, p₁) ← prove_lt_nat c q(1) ea
  let b := n / (a * a)
  let eb := reflect b
  let (c, eaa, pa) ← prove_mul_nat c ea ea
  let (c, e', pb) ← prove_mul_nat c eaa eb
  guard (e' == e)
  return <| q(@not_squarefree_mul).mk_app [ea, eaa, eb, e, pa, pb, p₁]

 Given ,,  the value of , ,
  returns .
unsafe def prove_squarefree_aux :
    ∀ (ic : instance_cache) (en en1 : expr) (n1 : ℕ) (ek : expr) (k : ℕ), tactic expr
  | ic, en, en1, n1, ek, k => do
    let k1 := bit1 k
    let ek1 := q((bit1 : ℕ → ℕ)).mk_app [ek]
    if n1 < k1 * k1 then do
        let (ic, ek', p₁) ← prove_mul_nat ic ek1 ek1
        let (ic, p₂) ← prove_lt_nat ic en1 ek'
        pure <| q(squarefreeHelper_4).mk_app [en, ek, ek', p₁, p₂]
      else do
        let c := n1 % k1
        let k' := k + 1
        let ek' := reflect k'
        let (ic, p₁) ← prove_succ ic ek ek'
        if c = 0 then do
            let n1' := n1 / k1
            let n' := n1' / 2
            let en' := reflect n'
            let en1' := q((bit1 : ℕ → ℕ)).mk_app [en']
            let (ic, _, pn') ← prove_mul_nat ic en1' ek1
            let c := n1' % k1
            guard (c ≠ 0)
            let (ic, ec, pc) ← prove_div_mod ic en1' ek1 tt
            let (ic, p₀) ← prove_pos ic ec
            let p₂ ← prove_squarefree_aux ic en' en1' n1' ek' k'
            pure <| q(squarefreeHelper_3).mk_app [en, en', ek, ek', ec, p₁, pn', pc, p₀, p₂]
          else do
            let (ic, ec, pc) ← prove_div_mod ic en1 ek1 tt
            let (ic, p₀) ← prove_pos ic ec
            let p₂ ← prove_squarefree_aux ic en en1 n1 ek' k'
            pure <| q(squarefreeHelper_2).mk_app [en, ek, ek', ec, p₁, pc, p₀, p₂]

 Given  a squarefree natural numeral, returns .
unsafe def prove_squarefree (en : expr) (n : ℕ) : tactic expr :=
  match match_numeral en with
  | match_numeral_result.one => pure q(@squarefree_one ℕ _)
  | match_numeral_result.bit0 en1 =>
    match match_numeral en1 with
    | match_numeral_result.one => pure q(Nat.squarefree_two)
    | match_numeral_result.bit1 en => do
      let ic ← mk_instance_cache q(ℕ)
      let p ← prove_squarefree_aux ic en en1 (n / 2) q((1 : ℕ)) 1
      pure <| q(squarefree_bit10).mk_app [en, p]
    | _ => failed
  | match_numeral_result.bit1 en' => do
    let ic ← mk_instance_cache q(ℕ)
    let p ← prove_squarefree_aux ic en' en n q((1 : ℕ)) 1
    pure <| q(squarefree_bit1).mk_app [en', p]
  | _ => failed

 Evaluates the  predicate on naturals.
@[norm_num]
unsafe def eval_squarefree : expr → tactic (expr × expr)
  | q(@Squarefree ℕ $(inst) $(e)) => do
    is_def_eq inst q(Nat.monoid)
    let n ← e.toNat
    match n with
      | 0 => false_intro q(@not_squarefree_zero ℕ _ _)
      | 1 => true_intro q(@squarefree_one ℕ _)
      | _ =>
        match n with
        | some d => prove_non_squarefree e n d >>= false_intro
        | none => prove_squarefree e n >>= true_intro
  | _ => failed

end NormNum

end Tactic

# Primality for binary natural numbers

This file defines versions of  and  for  and . As with other
 definitions, they are not intended for general use ( should be used instead of  in
most cases) but they can be used in contexts where kernel computation is required, such as proofs

The default decidable instance for  is optimized for VM evaluation, so it should be
preferred within  or in tactic execution, while for proofs the  tactic can be used
to construct primality and non-primality proofs more efficiently than kernel computation.

Nevertheless, sometimes proof by computational reflection requires natural number computations, and
 implements algorithms directly on binary natural numbers for this purpose.

An , defined in , is an inductive type which describes a
tree which stores the  at internal nodes.

In this file we define the correctness invariant of an , comprising:

* : All internal  fields must match the actual measured
  size of the tree. (This is not hard to satisfy.)
* : Unless the tree has the form  or  or
  (that is, nil or a single singleton subtree), the two subtrees must satisfy
   and , where  is a global
  parameter of the data structure (and this property must hold recursively at subtrees).
  This is why we say this is a "size balanced tree" data structure.
* : The members of the tree must be in strictly increasing order,
  meaning that if  is in the left subtree and  is the root, then  and
  . We enforce this using  which includes also a global
  upper and lower bound.

This whole file is in the  namespace, because we first have to prove the correctness of
all the operations (and defining what correctness means here is somewhat subtle).
The actual  operations are in .

a total preorder, meaning a  operation that is

* Reflexive:
* Total:

 (assuming that the key values are linearly ordered).

Two values  are equivalent if  and . An
maintains the invariant that it never stores two equivalent nodes;
the insertion operation comes with two variants depending on whether
you want to keep the old value or the new value in case you insert a value
that is equivalent to one in the set.

The operations in this file are not verified, in the sense that they provide
"raw operations" that work for programming purposes but the invariants
are not explicitly in the structure. See  for a verified version
of this data structure.

The advantage is that it is possible to, for example, prove that the result of  on

which may need to be revised if it turns out some operations violate these assumptions,
because there is a decent amount of slop in the actual data structure invariants, so the
theorem will go through with multiple choices of assumption.

* : polynomial functor
* : greatest fixed point of a polynomial functor

Specifically, we define the polynomial functor  as:

* A := a possibly infinite tree-like structure without information in the nodes
* B := given the tree-like structure ,  is a valid path
  from the root of  to any given node.

its valid paths to values of

that  is a possibly infinite tree.

below.

doesn't work for  instances

The multiset consisting of a single prime

We can forget the primality property and regard a multiset
of primes as just a multiset of positive integers, or a multiset
of natural numbers.  In the opposite direction, if we have a
multiset of positive integers or natural numbers, together with
a proof that all the elements are prime, then we can regard it
as a multiset of primes.  The next block of results records
obvious properties of these coercions.

naturals, promoted to an .

then factor it, we get back the original multiset.

monoid ℕ+ to the additive monoid of multisets.

We now have four different results that all encode the
idea that inequality of multisets corresponds to divisibility
of positive integers.

The gcd and lcm operations on positive integers correspond
to the inf and sup operations on multisets.

The number of occurrences of p in the factor multiset of m
is the same as the p-adic valuation of m.

The application of this type is finitary product measures, but it could be used in any
construction/theorem that is easier to define/prove on binary products than on finitary products.

* Once we have the construction on binary products (like binary product measures in
  ), we can easily define a finitary version on the type
  by iterating. Properties can also be easily extended from the binary case to the finitary case
  by iterating.
* Then we can use the equivalence  below (or enhanced versions of it,
  like a  for product measures) to get the construction on , at

# Multivariate quotients of polynomial functors.

Basic definition of multivariate QPF. QPFs form a compositional framework
for defining inductive and coinductive types, their quotients and nesting.

The idea is based on building ever larger functors. For instance, we can define
a list using a shape functor:


This shape can itself be decomposed as a sum of product which are themselves
QPFs. It follows that the shape is a QPF and we can take its fixed point
and create the list itself:


We can continue and define the quotient on permutation of lists and create
the multiset type:


And  is also a QPF. We can then create a novel data type (for Lean):


An unordered tree. This is currently not supported by Lean because it nests
an inductive type inside of a quotient. We can go further and define
unordered, possibly infinite trees:


by using the  construct. Those options can all be mixed and
matched because they preserve the properties of QPF. The latter example,
, combines fixed point, co-fixed point and quotients.

## Implementation notes

There is tension throughout the library between considering relations between  and  simply as
, or as a bundled object  with dedicated operations and API.

The former approach is used almost everywhere as it is very lightweight and has arguably native
support from core Lean features, but it cracks at the seams whenever one starts talking about
operations on relations. For example:
* composition of relations ,  is

* map of a relation  under ,  is
  .

The latter approach is embodied by , with the dedicated notation  for composition.
(Note that  is _not_ the same as function composition .)

Previously,  suffered from the leakage of its definition as
The fact that  wasn't an  confuses automation.
But simply making it an  would have killed the point of having a separate less see-through
type to perform relation operations on. So we instead redefined it as
This extra level of indirection guides automation correctly and prevents (some kinds of) leakage.

Simultaneously, uniform spaces need a theory of relations on a type  as elements of
, and the new definition of  fulfills this role quite well.

# Covers in a uniform space

This file defines covers, aka nets, which are a quantitative notion of compactness given an
entourage.

A -cover of a set  is a set  such that every element of  is -close to some element of
.

The concept of uniform covers is used to define two further notions of covering:
* Metric covers: , defined using the distance entourage.
* Dynamical covers: , defined using the dynamical entourage.

## References

R. Vershynin, *High Dimensional Probability*, Section 4.2.

For an entourage , a set  is a *-cover* of a set  if every point of  is -close
to some point of .

This is also called a *-net* in the literature.

# Uniform separation

This file defines a notion of separation of a set relative to a relation.

For a relation , an -separated set  is a set such that every pair of elements of  is
-unrelated.

The concept of uniformly separated sets is used to define two further notions of separation:
* Metric separation: , defined using the small distance relation.
* Dynamical nets: , defined using the dynamical relation.

# Semiquotients

A data type for semiquotients, which are classically equivalent to
nonempty sets, but are useful for programming; the idea is that
a semiquotient set  represents some (particular but unknown)
element of . This can be used to model nondeterministic functions,
which return something in a range of values (represented by the
predicate ) but are not completely determined.

A member of  is classically a nonempty ,
 and in the VM is represented by an element of ; the relation
 between these is that the VM element is required to be a member
 of the set . The specific element of  that the VM computes
 is hidden by a quotient construction, allowing for the representation
 of nondeterministic functions.

# Noncomputable Set Cardinality

We define the cardinality of set  as a term  and a term .
The latter takes the junk value of zero if  is infinite. Both functions are noncomputable, and
are defined in terms of  (which takes a type as its argument); this file can be seen
as an API for the same function in the special case where the type is a coercion of a ,
allowing for smoother interactions with the  API.

 never takes junk values, so is more mathematically natural than , even
though it takes values in a less convenient type. It is probably the right choice in settings where
one is concerned with the cardinalities of sets that may or may not be infinite.

 has a nicer codomain, but when using it,  hypotheses are normally needed to
make sure its values are meaningful.  More generally,  is intended to be used over the
obvious alternative  when finiteness is 'propositional' rather than 'structural'.
When working with sets that are finite by virtue of their definition, then  probably
makes more sense. One setting where  works nicely is in a type  with ,
where every set is automatically finite. In this setting, we use default arguments and a simple
tactic so that finiteness goals are discharged automatically in  theorems.

## Implementation Notes

The theorems in this file are very similar to those in , but with
 operations instead of . We first prove all the theorems for , and then
derive most of the  results as a consequence. Things are done this way to avoid reliance
on the  API for theorems about infinite sets, and to allow for a refactor that removes or
modifies  in the future.

Nearly all the theorems for  require finiteness of one or more of their arguments. We
provide this assumption with a default argument of the form ,
where  will find an  term in the cases where  is a set in a
type.

Often, where there are two set arguments  and , the finiteness of one follows from the other
in the context of the theorem, in which case we only include the ones that are needed, and derive
the other inside the proof. A few of the theorems, such as  do not require
finiteness arguments; they are true by coincidence due to junk values.

## Implementation

A finite set is defined to be a set whose coercion to a type has a  instance.

There are two components to finiteness constructions. The first is  instances for each
construction. This gives a way to actually compute a  that represents the set, and these
may be accessed using . This gets the  in the correct form, since otherwise
 is a  for the subtype for . The second component is
"constructors" for  that give proofs that  instances exist classically given
other  proofs. Unlike the  instances, these *do not* use any decidability
instances since they do not compute anything.

## Implementation notes

The complete lattice instance for equivalence relations could have been defined by lifting
the Galois insertion of equivalence relations on α into binary relations on α, and then using
 to define a complete lattice instance with more appropriate
definitional equalities (a similar example is  in
). This does not save space, however, and is less clear.

Partitions are not defined as a separate structure here; users are encouraged to
reason about them using the existing  and its infrastructure.

# Stars and bars

In this file, we prove (in ) that the function
defined in  counts the number of multisets of cardinality  over an
alphabet of cardinality . In conjunction with  proved in
, which shows that ,
this is central to the "stars and bars" technique in combinatorics, where we switch between
counting multisets of size  over an alphabet of size  to counting strings of  elements
("stars") separated by  dividers ("bars").

## Informal statement

Many problems in mathematics are of the form of (or can be reduced to) putting  indistinguishable
objects into  distinguishable boxes; for example, the problem of finding natural numbers
 whose sum is . This is equivalent to forming a multiset of cardinality  from
an alphabet of cardinality  -- for each box  the multiset contains as many copies
of  as there are items in the th box.

The "stars and bars" technique arises from another way of presenting the same problem. Instead of
putting  items into  boxes, we take a row of  items (the "stars") and separate them by
inserting  dividers (the "bars").  For example, the pattern  exhibits 4 items
distributed into 6 boxes -- note that any box, including the first and last, may be empty.
Such arrangements of  stars and  bars are in 1-1 correspondence with multisets of size
over an alphabet of size , and are counted by .

Note that this problem is one component of Gian-Carlo Rota's "Twelvefold Way"


## Formal statement

Here we generalise the alphabet to an arbitrary fintype , and we use  as the type of
multisets of size  over . Thus the statement that these are counted by  is:

while the "stars and bars" technique gives

# Two-pointings

This file defines , the type of two pointings of . A two-pointing is the data of
two distinct terms.

This is morally a Type-valued . Another type which is quite close in essence is .
Categorically speaking,  is a cospan in the category of types. This forms the category of
bipointed types. Two-pointed types form a full subcategory of those.

is illustrated in the example found in the file  in the  folder of

# Partially defined possibly infinite lists

This file provides a  type representing partially defined possibly infinite lists
(referred here as weak sequences).

Weak sequences.

 While the  structure allows for lists which may not be finite,
 a weak sequence also allows the computation of each element to
 involve an indeterminate amount of computation, including possibly
 an infinite loop. This is represented as a regular  interspersed
 with  elements to indicate that computation is ongoing.

 This model is appropriate for Haskell style lazy lists, and is closed
 under most interesting computation patterns on infinite lists,
 but conversely it is difficult to extract elements from it.

# Productive weak sequences

This file defines the property of a weak sequence being productive as never stalling – the next
output always comes after a finite time. Given a productive weak sequence, a regular sequence
() can be derived from it using .

A weak sequence is *productive* if it never stalls forever - there are
always a finite number of s between  constructors.
The sequence itself is allowed to be infinite though.

Given a productive weak sequence, we can collapse all the s to
 produce a sequence.

# Relations between and equivalence of weak sequences

This file defines a relation between weak sequences as a relation between their  elements,
ignoring computation time ( elements). Equivalence is then defined in the obvious way.

## Main definitions

* : Lift a relation to a relation over weak sequences.
* : Two sequences are -related if their corresponding
  elements are -related.
* : Two sequences are equivalent if they are -related.

lift a relation to a relation over weak sequences

Definition of bisimilarity for weak sequences

Two weak sequences are  related if they are either both empty,
 or they are both nonempty and the heads are  related and the tails are
  related. (This is a coinductive definition.)

If two sequences are equivalent, then they have the same values and
 the same computational behavior (i.e. if one loops forever then so does
 the other), although they may differ in the number of s needed to
 arrive at the answer.

Let  be measure preserving with respect to a measure . We say  is ergodic with

  strict invariance condition to almost invariance in the ergodicity condition.

strictly invariant set is either almost empty or full.
