# Semirings and rings of sets

A semi-ring of sets  (in the sense of measure theory) is a family of sets containing ,
stable by intersection and such that for all ,  is equal to a disjoint union of
finitely many sets in . Note that a semi-ring of sets may not contain unions.

An important example of a semi-ring of sets is intervals in . The intersection of two intervals
is an interval (possibly empty). The union of two intervals may not be an interval.
The set difference of two intervals may not be an interval, but it will be a disjoint union of
two intervals.

A ring of sets is a set of sets containing , stable by union, set difference and intersection.

This file proves the Hahn decomposition theorem (signed version). The Hahn decomposition theorem
states that, given a signed measure , there exist complementary, measurable sets  and ,
such that  is positive and  is negative with respect to ; that is,  restricted on
is non-negative and  restricted on  is non-positive.

The Hahn decomposition theorem leads to many other results in measure theory, most notably,
the Jordan decomposition theorem, the Lebesgue decomposition theorem and the Radon-Nikodym theorem.

## Main results

*  : the Hahn decomposition
  theorem.
*  : A measurable set of negative
  measure contains a negative subset.

## Notation

being positive/negative with respect to the signed measure .

## Tags

Hahn decomposition theorem

###

In this section we will prove that a set  whose measure is negative contains a negative subset
 with respect to the signed measure  (i.e. ), whose measure is negative. This lemma
is used to prove the Hahn decomposition theorem.

To prove this lemma, we will construct a sequence of measurable sets $(A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$,
such that, for all $n$, $s(A_{n + 1})$ is close to maximal among subsets of
$i \setminus \bigcup_{k \le n} A_k$.

This sequence of sets does not necessarily exist. However, if this sequence terminates; that is,
there does not exist any set satisfying the property, the last $A_n$ will be a negative subset
of negative measure, hence proving our claim.

In the case that the sequence does not terminate, it is easy to see that
$i \setminus \bigcup_{k = 0}^\infty A_k$ is the required negative set.

To implement this in Lean, we define several auxiliary definitions.

The Jordan decomposition theorem states that, given a signed measure , there exists a

# The semivariation of a vector measure

The semivariation of a vector measure is the supremum of the variations of its push-forwards
to  through all linear forms of norm at most . The interest of this notion is that, in the
reals, any set has nonnegative or nonpositive measure, so that the variation is realized by
a subset (up to a factor of at most ). This property is inherited by the semivariation in
general: one has the inequalities

# Presburger definability and semilinear sets

This file formalizes the classical result that Presburger definable sets are the same as semilinear
sets. As an application of this result, we show that the graph of multiplication is not Presburger
definable.

## Main Results

- : a set is Presburger definable in  if and only if it
  is semilinear.
- : in the 1-dimensional case, a set is Presburger
  arithmetic definable in  if and only if it is ultimately periodic, i.e. periodic after some
  number .
- : the graph of multiplication is not Presburger definable in .

  Languages*

# Linear and semilinear sets

This file defines linear and semilinear sets. In an , a linear set is a coset of a
finitely generated additive submonoid, and a semilinear set is a finite union of linear sets.

We prove that semilinear sets are closed under union, projection, set addition and additive closure.
We also prove that any semilinear set can be decomposed into a finite union of proper linear sets,
which are linear sets with linearly independent submonoid generators (periods).

## Main Definitions

- : a set is linear if it is a coset of a finitely generated additive submonoid.
- : a set is semilinear if it is a finite union of linear sets.
- : a linear set is proper if its submonoid generators (periods) are linearly
  independent.
- : a semilinear set is proper if it is a finite union of proper linear sets.

# Fraïssé Classes and Fraïssé Limits

This file pertains to the ages of countable first-order structures. The age of a structure is the
class of all finitely-generated structures that embed into it.

Of particular interest are Fraïssé classes, which are exactly the ages of countable
ultrahomogeneous structures. To each is associated a unique (up to nonunique isomorphism)
Fraïssé limit - the countable ultrahomogeneous structure with that age.

## Main Definitions

-  is the class of finitely-generated structures that embed into a
  particular structure.
- A class  is  when all finitely-generated
  structures that embed into structures in  are also in .
- A class  has  when for every ,  in
  , there is another structure in  into which both  and  embed.
- A class  has  when for any pair of embeddings
  of a structure  in  into other structures in , those two structures can be embedded into
  a fourth structure in  such that the resulting square of embeddings commutes.
-  indicates that a class is nonempty, essentially countable,
  and satisfies the hereditary, joint embedding, and amalgamation properties.
-  indicates that a structure is a Fraïssé limit for a given
  class.

## Main Results

- We show that the age of any structure is isomorphism-invariant and satisfies the hereditary and
  joint-embedding properties.
-  shows that the age of any countable structure is
  essentially countable.
-  gives necessary and sufficient conditions
  for a class to be the age of a countable structure in a language with countably many functions.
-  shows that any class which is Fraïssé has
  at most one Fraïssé limit up to equivalence.
-  shows that any countably infinite
  structure in the empty language is a Fraïssé limit of the class of finite structures.
-  shows that the class of finite structures in the
  empty language is Fraïssé.

## Implementation Notes

- Classes of structures are formalized with .
- Some results pertain to countable limit structures, others to countably-generated limit
  structures. In the case of a language with countably many function symbols, these are equivalent.

### The Age of a Structure and Fraïssé Classes


The age of a structure  is the class of finitely-generated structures that embed into it.

A class  has the hereditary property when all finitely-generated structures that embed into
 structures in  are also in .

A class  has the joint embedding property when for every ,  in , there is another
 structure in  into which both  and  embed.

A class  has the amalgamation property when for any pair of embeddings of a structure  in
  into other structures in , those two structures can be embedded into a fourth structure in
  such that the resulting square of embeddings commutes.

A Fraïssé class is a nonempty, essentially countable class of structures satisfying the
hereditary, joint embedding, and amalgamation properties.

Any class in the age of a structure has a representative which is a finitely generated
substructure.

The age of a countable structure is essentially countable (has countably many isomorphism
classes).

This is not a simp-lemma because it does not apply to itself.
The age of a direct limit of structures is the union of the ages of the structures.

# Bernoulli numbers

The Bernoulli numbers are a sequence of rational numbers that frequently show up in
number theory.

## Mathematical overview

The Bernoulli numbers $(B_0, B_1, B_2, \ldots)=(1, -1/2, 1/6, 0, -1/30, \ldots)$ are
a sequence of rational numbers. They show up in the formula for the sums of $k$th
powers. They are related to the Taylor series expansions of $x/\tan(x)$ and
of $\coth(x)$, and also show up in the values that the Riemann Zeta function
takes both at both negative and positive integers (and hence in the
theory of modular forms). For example, if $1 \leq n$ then

$$\zeta(2n)=\sum_{t\geq1}t^{-2n}=(-1)^{n+1}\frac{(2\pi)^{2n}B_{2n}}{2(2n)!}.$$

This result is formalised in Lean: .

The Bernoulli numbers can be formally defined using the power series

$$\sum B_n\frac{t^n}{n!}=\frac{t}{1-e^{-t}}$$

although that happens to not be the definition in mathlib (this is an *implementation
detail* and need not concern the mathematician).

Note that $B_1=-1/2$, meaning that we are using the $B_n^-$ of
from Wikipedia.

## Implementation detail

The Bernoulli numbers are defined using well-founded induction, by the formula
$$B_n=1-\sum_{k\lt n}\frac{\binom{n}{k}}{n-k+1}B_k.$$
This formula is true for all $n$ and in particular $B_0=1$. Note that this is the definition
for positive Bernoulli numbers, which we call . The negative Bernoulli numbers are
then defined as .

The proof of von Staudt-Clausen's theorem follows Rado's JLMS 1934 paper
"A New Proof of a Theorem of v. Staudt".

## Main theorems

*

### The von Staudt-Clausen Theorem

Here we formalize Rado's proof of von Staudt-Clausen's theorem, which states that for any $k \ge 0$,
$$B_{2k} + \sum_{p \text{ prime}, (p - 1) \mid 2k} \frac{1}{p} \in \mathbb{Z}.$$
Rado's proof is based on Faulhaber's theorem and induction on $k$.

# Bernoulli polynomials

The Bernoulli polynomials
are an important tool obtained from Bernoulli numbers.

## Mathematical overview

The $n$-th Bernoulli polynomial is defined as
$$ B_n(X) = ∑_{k = 0}^n {n \choose k} (-1)^k B_k X^{n - k} $$
where $B_k$ is the $k$-th Bernoulli number. The Bernoulli polynomials are generating functions,
$$ \frac{t e^{tX} }{ e^t - 1} = ∑_{n = 0}^{\infty} B_n(X) \frac{t^n}{n!} $$

## Implementation detail

Bernoulli polynomials are defined using , the Bernoulli numbers.

  coefficients up to  is .
- : The Bernoulli polynomials act as generating functions

# Bertrand's Postulate

This file contains a proof of Bertrand's postulate: That between any positive number and its
double there is a prime.

The proof follows the outline of the Erdős proof presented in "Proofs from THE BOOK": One considers
the prime factorization of , and splits the constituent primes up into various
groups, then upper bounds the contribution of each group. This upper bounds the central binomial
coefficient, and if the postulate does not hold, this upper bound conflicts with a simple lower
bound for large enough . This proves the result holds for large enough , and for smaller
an explicit list of primes is provided which covers the remaining cases.

As in the Metamath implementation, we rely on some optimizations from
Shigenori Tochiori. In particular we use the cleaner bound on the central
binomial coefficient given in .

## References

* M. Aigner and G. M. Ziegler _Proofs from THE BOOK_
* S. Tochiori, _Considering the Proof of “There is a Prime between n and 2n”_
* M. Carneiro, _Arithmetic in Metamath, Case Study: Bertrand's Postulate_

## Tags

Bertrand, prime, binomial coefficients

# Diophantine functions and Matiyasevic's theorem

Hilbert's tenth problem asked whether there exists an algorithm which for a given integer polynomial
determines whether this polynomial has integer solutions. It was answered in the negative in 1970,
the final step being completed by Matiyasevic who showed that the power function is Diophantine.

Here a function is called Diophantine if its graph is Diophantine as a set. A subset  in
turn is called Diophantine if there exists an integer polynomial on  such that  iff

# Diophantine Approximation

The first part of this file gives proofs of various versions of
**Dirichlet's approximation theorem** and its important consequence that when $\xi$ is an
irrational real number, then there are infinitely many rationals $x/y$ (in lowest terms)
such that
$$\left|\xi - \frac{x}{y}\right| < \frac{1}{y^2} \,.$$
The proof is based on the pigeonhole principle.

The second part of the file gives a proof of **Legendre's Theorem** on rational approximation,
which states that if $\xi$ is a real number and $x/y$ is a rational number such that
$$\left|\xi - \frac{x}{y}\right| < \frac{1}{2y^2} \,,$$
then $x/y$ must be a convergent of the continued fraction expansion of $\xi$.

## Main statements

The main results are three variants of Dirichlet's approximation theorem:
* , which states that for all real  and natural ,

  a natural number ,
* , which says that there is a rational number
  satisfying  and ,

and
* , which states that
  for irrational , the set  is infinite.

We also show a converse,
* , which states that the set above is finite
  when  is a rational number.

Both statements are combined to give an equivalence,
.

There are two versions of Legendre's Theorem. One, , uses
, a simple recursive definition of the convergents that is also defined
in this file, whereas the other,  defined in the file

### Finitely many good approximations to rational numbers

We now show that a rational number  has only finitely many good rational
approximations.

If  is rational, then the good rational approximations to  have bounded
numerator and denominator.

A rational number has only finitely many good rational approximations.

The set of good rational approximations to a real number  is infinite if and only if
is irrational.

### Legendre's Theorem on Rational Approximation

We prove **Legendre's Theorem** on rational approximation: If $\xi$ is a real number and
$x/y$ is a rational number such that $|\xi - x/y| < 1/(2y^2)$,
then $x/y$ is a convergent of the continued fraction expansion of $\xi$.

The proof is by induction. However, the induction proof does not work with the
statement as given, since the assumption is too weak to imply the corresponding
statement for the application of the induction hypothesis. This can be remedied
by making the statement slightly stronger. Namely, we assume that $|\xi - x/y| < 1/(y(2y-1))$
when $y \ge 2$ and $-\frac{1}{2} < \xi - x < 1$ when $y = 1$.

## Implementation notes

The elliptic relator is identical to the elliptic net recurrence defined by Stange, except that the
final term in the latter is negated. This unifies the definitions of Stange's elliptic nets and
Ward's elliptic sequences without requiring the sequence to be an odd function.

The normalised EDS  is defined in terms of the auxiliary sequence
, which are equal when  is odd, and which differ by a factor of
when  is even. This coincides with the definition in the references since both agree for
 and for , and the correct factors of  are removed in
 and in .

One reason is to avoid the necessity for ring division by  in the inductive definition of
. The idea is that it can be shown that
always contains a factor of , so it is possible to remove a factor of  *a posteriori*, but
stating this lemma requires first defining , which requires having this
factor of  *a priori*. Another reason is to allow the definition of univariate -division
polynomials of elliptic curves, omitting a factor of the bivariate -division polynomial.

* M Ward, *Memoir on Elliptic Divisibility Sequences*

## History

Fermat's Last Theorem was an open problem in number theory for hundreds of years, until it was
finally solved by Andrew Wiles, assisted by Richard Taylor, in 1994 (see
A. Wiles, *Modular elliptic curves and Fermat's last theorem* and
R. Taylor and A. Wiles, *Ring-theoretic properties of certain Hecke algebras*).
An ongoing Lean formalisation of the proof, using mathlib as a dependency, is taking place at
 .

# Factorisation properties of natural numbers

This file defines abundant, pseudoperfect, deficient, and weird numbers and formalizes their
relations with prime and perfect numbers.

## Main Definitions

* : a natural number  is _abundant_ if the sum of its proper divisors is greater
  than
* : a natural number  is _pseudoperfect_ if the sum of a subset of its proper
  divisors equals
* : a natural number  is _deficient_ if the sum of its proper divisors is less
  than
* : a natural number is _weird_ if it is abundant but not pseudoperfect

## Main Results

* : A positive natural number is either deficient,
  perfect, or abundant.
* : All prime natural numbers are deficient.
* : There are infinitely many deficient numbers.
* : Any natural number power of a prime is deficient.

## Implementation Notes
* Zero is not included in any of the definitions and these definitions only apply to natural
  numbers greater than zero.

## References
* R. W. Prielipp, *PERFECT NUMBERS, ABUNDANT NUMBERS, AND DEFICIENT NUMBERS*

## Tags

abundant, deficient, weird, pseudoperfect

"probable prime") if  divides .  is a Fermat pseudoprime to base  if
is a composite number that passes the Fermat primality test to base  and is coprime with .

Fermat pseudoprimes can also be seen as composite numbers for which Fermat's little theorem holds
true.

Numbers which are Fermat pseudoprimes to all bases are known as Carmichael numbers (not yet defined
in this file).

# Frobenius Number

In this file we first define a predicate for Frobenius numbers, then solve the 2-variable variant
of this problem. We also show the Frobenius number exists for any set of coprime natural numbers
that doesn't contain 1. This is closely related to the fact that all ideals of ℕ are finitely
generated, which we also prove in this file.

## Theorem Statement

Given a finite set of relatively prime integers all greater than 1, their Frobenius number is the
largest positive integer that cannot be expressed as a sum of nonnegative multiples of these
integers. Here we show the Frobenius number of two relatively prime integers  and  greater
than 1 is . This result is also known as the Chicken McNugget Theorem.

## Implementation Notes

First we define Frobenius numbers in general using  and . Then
we proceed to compute the Frobenius number of  and .

For the upper bound, we begin with an auxiliary lemma showing  is not attainable, then show
 is not attainable. Then for the construction, we create a  which is
and , then show it is at most . Then  is a multiple of , so
is a multiple of n, and we're done.

A set of natural numbers has a Frobenius number iff their gcd is 1; if 1 is in the set,
the Frobenius number is -1, so the Frobenius number doesn't exist as a natural number.
Wikipedia seems to attribute this to
Issai Schur, but Schur's theorem
is a more precise statement about asymptotics of the number of ℕ-linear combinations, and the
existence of the Frobenius number for a set with gcd 1 is probably well known before that.

The nth Harmonic number is not an integer. We formalize the proof using
2-adic valuations. This proof is due to Kürschák.

Reference:

The 2-adic valuation of the n-th harmonic number is the negative of the logarithm of n.

The 2-adic norm of the n-th harmonic number is 2 raised to the logarithm of n in base 2.

The n-th harmonic number is not an integer for n ≥ 2.

This is an attempt at formalizing some basic properties of height functions.

We aim at a level of generality that allows to apply the theory to algebraic number fields
and to function fields (and possibly beyond).

# The Marica-Schönheim special case of Graham's conjecture

Graham's conjecture states that if $0 < a_1 < \dots a_n$ are integers, then
$\max_{i, j} \frac{a_i}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)} \ge n$. This file proves the conjecture when the $a_i$ are
squarefree as a corollary of the Marica-Schönheim inequality.

## References

*Applications of the FKG Inequality and Its Relatives*, Graham

Statement of Graham's conjecture (which is now a theorem in the literature).

Graham's conjecture states that if $0 < a_1 < \dots a_n$ are integers, then
$\max_{i, j} \frac{a_i}{\gcd(a_i, a_j)} \ge n$.

The special case of Graham's conjecture where all numbers are squarefree.

# Pell's Equation

*Pell's Equation* is the equation $x^2 - d y^2 = 1$, where $d$ is a positive integer
that is not a square, and one is interested in solutions in integers $x$ and $y$.

In this file, we aim at providing all of the essential theory of Pell's Equation for general $d$
(as opposed to the contents of , which is specific to the case
$d = a^2 - 1$ for some $a > 1$).

We begin by defining a type  for solutions of the equation,
show that it has a natural structure as an abelian group, and prove some basic
properties.

We then prove the following

**Theorem.** Let $d$ be a positive integer that is not a square. Then the equation
$x^2 - d y^2 = 1$ has a nontrivial (i.e., with $y \ne 0$) solution in integers.

See  and .

We then define the *fundamental solution* to be the solution
with smallest $x$ among all solutions satisfying $x > 1$ and $y > 0$.
We show that every solution is a power (in the sense of the group structure mentioned above)
of the fundamental solution up to a (common) sign,
see , and that a (positive) solution has this property
if and only if it is fundamental, see .

## References

* [K. Ireland, M. Rosen, *A classical introduction to modern number theory* (Section 17.5)]
  [IrelandRosen1990]

# Pell's equation and Matiyasevic's theorem

This file solves Pell's equation, i.e. integer solutions to
*in the special case that *.
This is then applied to prove Matiyasevic's theorem that the power
function is Diophantine, which is the last key ingredient in the solution to Hilbert's tenth
problem. For the definition of Diophantine function, see .

For results on Pell's equation for arbitrary (positive, non-square) , see
.

## Main definition

*  is a function assigning to a natural number  the -th solution to Pell's equation
  constructed recursively from the initial solution .

## Main statements

*  shows that every solution to Pell's equation is recursively obtained using
*  shows that a certain system of Diophantine equations has a solution if and only if
  the first variable is the -component in a solution to Pell's equation - the key step towards
  Hilbert's tenth problem in Davis' version of Matiyasevic's theorem.
*  shows that the power function is Diophantine.

## Implementation notes

The proof of Matiyasevic's theorem doesn't follow Matiyasevic's original account of using Fibonacci
numbers but instead Davis' variant of using solutions to Pell's equation.

## References

* M. Davis, _Hilbert's tenth problem is unsolvable_

# The Selberg Sieve

We set up the working assumptions of the Selberg sieve, define the notion of an upper bound sieve
and show that every upper bound sieve yields an upper bound on the size of the sifted set. We also
define the Λ² sieve and prove that Λ² sieves are upper bound sieves. We then diagonalise the main
term of the Λ² sieve.

We mostly follow the treatment outlined by Heath-Brown in the notes to an old graduate course. One
minor notational difference is that we write $\nu(n)$ in place of $\frac{\omega(n)}{n}$.

## Results
*  - Every upper bound sieve gives an upper bound
  on the size of the sifted set in terms of  and
*  - Lambda squared weights produce upper bound sieves
*  - The main sum of a Λ² sieve has a nice diagonalisation

* Koukoulopoulos, *The Distribution of Prime Numbers*

# Liouville constants

This file contains a construction of a family of Liouville numbers, indexed by a natural number $m$.
The most important property is that they are examples of transcendental real numbers.
This fact is recorded in .

More precisely, for a real number $m$, Liouville's constant is
$$
\sum_{i=0}^\infty\frac{1}{m^{i!}}.
$$
The series converges only for $1 < m$. However, there is no restriction on $m$, since,
if the series does not converge, then the sum of the series is defined to be zero.

We prove that, for $m \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfying $2 \le m$, Liouville's constant associated to $m$
is a transcendental number. Classically, the Liouville number for $m = 2$ is the one called
"Liouville's constant".

## Implementation notes

The indexing $m$ is eventually a natural number satisfying $2 ≤ m$. However, we prove the first few
lemmas for $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

\sum_{i=0}^\infty\frac{1}{m^{i!}}.

if the series does not converge, then the sum of the series is defined to be zero.

# Volume of the set of Liouville numbers

In this file we prove that the set of Liouville numbers with exponent (irrationality measure)
strictly greater than two is a set of Lebesgue measure zero, see
.

Since this set is a residual set, we show that the filters  and  are disjoint.
These filters correspond to two common notions of genericity on : residual sets and sets of full
measure. The fact that the filters are disjoint means that two mutually exclusive properties can be
“generic” at the same time (in the sense of different “genericity” filters).

## Tags

Liouville number, Lebesgue measure, residual, generic property

The set of numbers satisfying the Liouville condition with some exponent  has Lebesgue
measure zero.

The set of Liouville numbers has Lebesgue measure zero.

The filters  and  are disjoint. This means that there exists a residual
set of Lebesgue measure zero (e.g., the set of Liouville numbers).

# Well-approximable numbers and Gallagher's ergodic theorem

Gallagher's ergodic theorem is a result in metric number theory. It thus belongs to that branch of
mathematics concerning arithmetic properties of real numbers which hold almost everywhere with
respect to the Lebesgue measure.

Gallagher's theorem concerns the approximation of real numbers by rational numbers. The input is a
sequence of distances , and the theorem concerns the set of real numbers  for which
there are infinitely many solutions to:
$$
  |x - m/n| < δₙ,
$$
where the rational number  is in lowest terms. The result is that for any , this set is
either almost all  or almost no .

This result was proved by Gallagher in 1959
P. Gallagher, *Approximation by reduced fractions*. It is formalised here as
 except with  belonging to the circle
since this turns out to be more natural.

Given a particular , the Duffin-Schaeffer conjecture (now a theorem) gives a criterion for
deciding which of the two cases in the conclusion of Gallagher's theorem actually occurs. It was
proved by Koukoulopoulos and Maynard in 2019
D. Koukoulopoulos, J. Maynard, *On the Duffin-Schaeffer conjecture*.
We do *not* include a formalisation of the Koukoulopoulos-Maynard result here.

# Birkhoff representation

This file proves two facts which together are commonly referred to as "Birkhoff representation":
1. Any nonempty finite partial order is isomorphic to the partial order of sup-irreducible elements
  in its lattice of lower sets.
2. Any nonempty finite distributive lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of lower sets of its
  partial order of sup-irreducible elements.

## Main declarations

For a finite nonempty partial order :
* :  is isomorphic to the order of its irreducible lower sets.

If  is moreover a distributive lattice:
* :  is isomorphic to the lattice of lower sets of its irreducible
  elements.
* , : Order embedding of  into the
  powerset lattice of its irreducible elements.
* , : Same as the previous two, but bundled as
  an injective lattice homomorphism.
* :  embeds into some powerset algebra. You should prefer using
  this over the explicit Birkhoff embedding because the Birkhoff embedding is littered with
  decidability footguns that this existential-packaged version can afford to avoid.

## See also

These results form the object part of finite Stone duality: the functorial contravariant
equivalence between the category of finite distributive lattices and the category of finite
partial orders. TODO: extend to morphisms.

## References

* G. Birkhoff, *Rings of sets*

## Tags

birkhoff, representation, stone duality, lattice embedding

lattice of lower sets.

lattice of lower sets.

to the partial order of sup-irreducible elements in its lattice of lower sets.

**Birkhoff Representation for partial orders.** Any partial order is isomorphic
to the partial order of inf-irreducible elements in its lattice of upper sets.

**Birkhoff Representation for finite distributive lattices**. Any nonempty finite distributive
lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of lower sets of its sup-irreducible elements.

**Birkhoff's Representation Theorem**. Any finite distributive lattice can be embedded in a
powerset lattice.

# (Generalized) Boolean algebras

This file sets up the theory of (generalized) Boolean algebras.

A Boolean algebra is a bounded distributive lattice with a complement operator. Boolean algebras
generalize the (classical) logic of propositions and the lattice of subsets of a set.

Generalized Boolean algebras may be less familiar, but they are essentially Boolean algebras which
do not necessarily have a top element () (and hence not all elements may have complements). One
example in mathlib is , the type of all finite subsets of an arbitrary
(not-necessarily-finite) type .

a *relative* complement operator, written using "set difference" notation as  ().
For convenience, the  type class is defined to extend
so that it is also bundled with a  operator.

(A terminological point:  is the complement of  relative to the interval . We do
not yet have relative complements for arbitrary intervals, as we do not even have lattice
intervals.)

The intuition is that a circular order is a circle and  means that going around
clockwise from  you reach  before  ( is between  and  is meaningless on an
unoriented circle). A circular partial order is several, potentially intersecting, circles. A
circular preorder is like a circular partial order, but several points can coexist.

Note that the relations between ,  and
are subtler than between , , . In particular, one cannot
simply extend the  of a  to make it a .

One can translate from usual orders to circular ones by "closing the necklace at infinity". See
 and . Going the other way involves "cutting the necklace" or
"rolling the necklace open".

# Complete Sublattices

This file defines complete sublattices. These are subsets of complete lattices which are closed
under arbitrary suprema and infima. As a standard example one could take the complete sublattice of
invariant submodules of some module with respect to a linear map.

* : an alternate constructor for a complete sublattice, demanding fewer
  hypotheses

* : complete sublattices pull back under complete lattice morphisms.

A complete sublattice is a subset of a complete lattice that is closed under arbitrary suprema
and infima.

under binary  since this follows from the stronger  condition. Likewise for infima.

# Dedekind-MacNeille completion

The Dedekind-MacNeille completion of a partial order is the smallest complete lattice into which it
embeds.

The theory of concept lattices allows for a simple construction. In fact,  is simply
an abbreviation for . This means we don't need to reprove that this is a
complete lattice; instead, the file simply proves that any order embedding into another complete
lattice factors through it.

# Formal concept analysis

This file defines concept lattices. A concept of a relation  is a pair of sets
 and  such that  is the set of all  that are related to all elements
of , and  is the set of all  that are related to all elements of .

Ordering the concepts of a relation  by inclusion on the first component gives rise to a
*concept lattice*. Every concept lattice is complete and in fact every complete lattice arises as
the concept lattice of its .

## Implementation notes

Concept lattices are usually defined from a *context*, that is the triple , but the type
of  determines  and  already, so we do not define contexts as a separate object.

# Conditionally complete partial orders

This file defines *conditionally complete partial orders* with suprema, infima or both. These are
partial orders where every nonempty, upwards (downwards) directed set which is
bounded above (below) has a least upper bound (greatest lower bound). This class extends
() and the requirement is that  () must be the least upper bound.

The three classes defined herein are:

+  for partial orders with suprema,
+  for partial orders with infima, and
+  for partial orders with both suprema and infima

One common use case for these classes is the order on a von Neumann algebra, or W⋆-algebra.
This is the strongest order-theoretic structure satisfied by a von Neumann algebra;
in particular it is *not* a conditionally complete *lattice*, and indeed it is a lattice if and only
if the algebra is commutative. In addition,  can be made to satisfy this class (one must provide
a suitable  instance), with the order , which is
available in the  namespace.

These use cases are the motivation for defining three classes, as compared with other parts of the
order theory library, where only the supremum versions are defined (e.g.,  and
). We note that, if these classes are used outside of order theory, then
it is more likely that the infimum versions would be useful. Indeed, whenever the underlying type
has an antitone involution (e.g., if it is an ordered ring, then negation would be such a map),
then any  is automatically a
. Because of the  attribute, the additional overhead
required to add and maintain the infimum version is minimal.

Conditionally complete partial orders (with infima) are partial orders
where every nonempty, directed set which is bounded below has a greatest lower bound.

For each nonempty, directed set  which is bounded below,  is
 the greatest lower bound of .

Conditionally complete partial orders (with suprema) are partial orders
where every nonempty, directed set which is bounded above has a least upper bound.

For each nonempty, directed set  which is bounded above,  is
 the least upper bound of .

Conditionally complete partial orders (with suprema and infima) are partial orders
where every nonempty, directed set which is bounded above (respectively, below) has a
least upper (respectively, greatest lower) bound.

# Sets closed under directed suprema

We say that a set  is closed under directed suprema whenever it contains all least upper bounds
for nonempty, directed subsets. Conversely, a set  is inaccessible by directed suprema whenever
its complement is closed under directed suprema. Equivalently, if the least upper bound of a
nonempty directed set  is contained in , then  and  must have nonempty intersection.

# Definition of direct systems, inverse systems, and cardinalities in specific inverse systems

The first part of this file concerns directed systems:  is defined as the quotient
of the disjoint union ( type) by an equivalence relation (): compare
, which is a quotient by a plain relation.
Recursion and induction principles for constructing functions from and to  and
proving things about elements in .

In the second part we compute the cardinality of each node in an inverse system  indexed by a
well-order in which every map between successive nodes has constant fiber , and every limit
node is the  of the inverse subsystem formed by all previous nodes.
(To avoid importing , we in fact construct a bijection rather than
stating the result in terms of .)

The most tricky part of the whole argument happens at limit nodes: if  is a limit,
what we have in hand is a family of bijections  for every ,
which we would like to "glue" up to a bijection . We denote
 by , and they form an inverse system just like the .
Observe that at a limit node ,  is actually the inverse limit of  over
all  (). If the family of bijections  is natural (),
we immediately obtain a bijection between the limits  (),
and we just need an additional bijection  to obtain the desired
extension  to the limit node . (We do have such a bijection, for example, when
we consider a directed system of algebraic structures (say fields) , and  is
the inverse system of homomorphisms  into a specific field .)

Now our task reduces to the recursive construction of a *natural* family of bijections for each .
We can prove that a natural family over all  () extends to a natural family over
 (where ), but at a limit node, recursion stops working: we have natural
families over all  for each , but we need to know that they glue together to form a
natural family over all  (). This intricacy did not occur to the author when he
thought he had a proof and set out to formalize it. Fortunately he was able to figure out an
additional  condition (compatibility with the bijections  in the
component) that guarantees uniqueness () and hence gluability (well-definedness):
see . Instead of just a family of natural families, we actually construct a family of
the stronger s that bundles the  condition, in order for the inductive argument
to work.

It is possible to circumvent the introduction of the  condition using Zorn's lemma;
if there is a chain of natural families (i.e. for any two families in the chain, one is an
extension of the other) over lower sets (which are all of the form , , or ),
we can clearly take the union to get a natural family that extends them all. If a maximal
natural family has domain  or  ( a limit), we already know how to extend it
one step further to  or  respectively, so it must be the case that the domain
is everything. However, the author chose the  approach in the end because it constructs
the distinguished bijection that is compatible with the projections to all .

# Extend a well-founded order to a well-order

This file constructs a well-order (linear well-founded order) which is an extension of a given
well-founded order.

## Proof idea

We can map our order into two well-orders:
* the first map respects the order but isn't necessarily injective. Namely, this is the *rank*
  function .
* the second map is injective but doesn't necessarily respect the order. This is an arbitrary
  embedding into  given by .

Then their lexicographic product is a well-founded linear order which our original order injects in.

## Implementation note

The definition in  3 used an auxiliary well-founded order on  lifted from ,
instead of using  directly. The new definition is definitionally equal
to the  3 version but avoids non-standard instances.

## Tags

well-founded relation, well order, extension

An arbitrary well order on  that extends .

The construction maps  into two well-orders: the first map is , which is not
necessarily injective but respects the order ; the other map is the identity (with an arbitrarily
chosen well-order on ), which is injective but doesn't respect .

By taking the lexicographic product of the two, we get both properties, so we can pull it back and
get a well-order that extend our original order . Another way to view this is that we choose an
arbitrary well-order to serve as a tiebreak between two elements of same rank.

Any well-founded relation can be extended to a well-ordering on that type.

A type alias for , intended to extend a well-founded order on  to a well-order.

"Identity" equivalence between a well-founded order and its well-order extension.

# Theory of filters on sets

A *filter* on a type  is a collection of sets of  which contains the whole ,
is upwards-closed, and is stable under intersection. They are mostly used to
abstract two related kinds of ideas:
* *limits*, including finite or infinite limits of sequences, finite or infinite limits of functions
  at a point or at infinity, etc...
* *things happening eventually*, including things happening for large enough , or near enough
  a point , or for close enough pairs of points, or things happening almost everywhere in the
  sense of measure theory. Dually, filters can also express the idea of *things happening often*:
  for arbitrarily large , or at a point in any neighborhood of given a point etc...

## Main definitions

In this file, we endow  it with a complete lattice structure.
This structure is lifted from the lattice structure on  using the Galois
insertion which maps a filter to its elements in one direction, and an arbitrary set of sets to
the smallest filter containing it in the other direction.
We also prove  is a monadic functor, with a push-forward operation
 and a pull-back operation  that form a Galois connections for the
order on filters.

The examples of filters appearing in the description of the two motivating ideas are:
*  : made of sets of  containing  for some
*  : made of neighborhoods of  in a topological space (defined in topology.basic)
*  : made of entourages of a uniform space (those space are generalizations of metric spaces
  defined in )
*  : made of sets whose complement has zero measure with respect to
  (defined in )

The predicate "happening eventually" is , and "happening often" is
, whose definitions are immediate after  is defined (but they come
rather late in this file in order to immediately relate them to the lattice structure).

# Convergence of intervals

## Motivation

If a function tends to infinity somewhere, then its derivative is not integrable around this place.
One should be careful about this statement: "somewhere" could mean a point, but also convergence
from the left or from the right, or it could also be infinity, and "around this place" will refer
to these directed neighborhoods. Therefore, the above theorem has many variants. Instead of stating
all these variants, one can look for the common abstraction and have a single version. One has to
be careful: if one considers convergence along a sequence, then the function may tend to infinity
but have a derivative which is small along the sequence (with big jumps in between), so in the end
the derivative may be integrable on a neighborhood of the sequence. What really matters for such
calculus issues in terms of derivatives is that whole intervals are included in the sets we
consider.

The right common abstraction is provided in this file, as the  typeclass.
It takes as parameters a class of bounded intervals and two real filters  and .
An instance  registers that, if  and  are converging towards
the filter , then the intervals  are eventually contained in any given set
belonging to . For instance, for  and , the strict and large right
neighborhoods of  respectively, then given any large right neighborhood  and any two
sequences  and  converging strictly to the right of ,
then the interval  is eventually contained in . Therefore, the instance
 holds. Note that one could have taken as
well , but that  and  wouldn't work.

With this formalism, the above theorem would read: if  and  tends
to infinity along , then its derivative is not integrable on any element of .
Beyond this simple example, this typeclass plays a prominent role in generic formulations of
the fundamental theorem of calculus.

## Main definition

#  for relations and partial functions

## Considering functions and partial functions as relations

A function  can be considered as the relation  which relates  and  for
all , and nothing else. This relation is called .

A partial function  can be considered as the relation  which relates  and
 for all  for which  exists, and nothing else. This relation is called
.

In this regard, a function is a relation for which every element in  is related to exactly one
element in  and a partial function is a relation for which every element in  is related to at
most one element in .

This file leverages this analogy to generalize  definitions from functions to partial
functions and relations.

## Notes

 can be generalized to relations in two ways:
*  returns the image of the set under the inverse relation.
*  returns the set of elements that are only related to those in the set.

Both generalizations are sensible in the context of filters, so  and
get two generalizations each.

We first take care of relations. Then the definitions for partial functions are taken as special
cases of the definitions for relations.

# Galois connections, insertions and coinsertions

This file contains basic results on Galois connections, insertions and coinsertions in various
order structures, and provides constructions that lift order structures from one type to another.

## Implementation details

Galois insertions can be used to lift order structures from one type to another.
For example, if  is a complete lattice, and  and  form a Galois insertion,
then  is also a complete lattice.  is the lower adjoint and  is the upper adjoint.

An example of a Galois insertion is in group theory. If  is a group, then there is a Galois
insertion between the set of subsets of , , and the set of subgroups of ,
. The lower adjoint is , taking the  generated by a ,
and the upper adjoint is the coercion from  to , taking the underlying set
of a subgroup.

Naively lifting a lattice structure along this Galois insertion would mean that the definition
of  on subgroups would be . This is an undesirable definition
because the intersection of subgroups is already a subgroup, so there is no need to take the
closure. For this reason a  function is added as a field to the
structure. It has type . When , then
 is already a subgroup, so this function can be defined using  and not .
This means the infimum of subgroups will be defined to be the intersection of sets, paired
with a proof that intersection of subgroups is a subgroup, rather than the closure of the
intersection.

# Graded orders

This file defines graded orders, also known as ranked orders.

An -graded order is an order  equipped with a distinguished "grade" function  which
should be understood as giving the "height" of the elements. Usual graded orders are -graded,
cograded orders are -graded, but we can also grade by , and polytopes are naturally
-graded.

Visually,  is the height of  in the Hasse diagram of .

## Main declarations

* : Graded order.
* : Graded order where minimal elements have minimal grades.
* : Graded order where maximal elements have maximal grades.
* : Graded order where minimal elements have minimal grades and maximal
  elements have maximal grades.
* : The grade of an element. Because an order can admit several gradings, the first argument
  is the order we grade by.

## How to grade your order

Here are the translations between common references and our :
* Stanley defines a graded order of rank  as an order where all maximal chains
  have "length"  (so the number of elements of a chain is ). This corresponds to
  .
* Engel's ranked orders are somewhere between  and
  , in that he requires  rather than
  . He defines a graded order as an order where all minimal elements
  have grade  and all maximal elements have the same grade. This is roughly a less bundled
  version of , assuming we discard orders with infinite chains.

## Implementation notes

One possible definition of graded orders is as the bounded orders whose flags (maximal chains)
all have the same finite length (see Stanley p. 99). However, this means that all graded orders must
have minimal and maximal elements and that the grade is not data.

Instead, we define graded orders by their grade function, without talking about flags yet.

## References

* Konrad Engel, *Sperner Theory*
* Richard Stanley, *Enumerative Combinatorics*

# Heyting algebras

This file defines Heyting, co-Heyting and bi-Heyting algebras.

A Heyting algebra is a bounded distributive lattice with an implication operation  such that
. It also comes with a pseudo-complement , such that .

Co-Heyting algebras are dual to Heyting algebras. They have a difference  and a negation
such that  and .

Bi-Heyting algebras are Heyting algebras that are also co-Heyting algebras.

From a logic standpoint, Heyting algebras precisely model intuitionistic logic, whereas Boolean
algebras model classical logic.

Heyting algebras are the order-theoretic equivalent of Cartesian closed categories.

## Main declarations

* : Heyting algebra without a top element (nor negation).
* : Co-Heyting algebra without a bottom element (nor complement).
* : Heyting algebra.
* : Co-Heyting algebra.
* : Bi-Heyting algebra.

## Implementation notes

Aligning the  and  API with  is kind of awkward, because they are
unfortunately quite different. One reason is that the arguments of sup/inf are often swapped
in the dual version, which is not compatible with . We work around this with extensive
use of .

* Francis Borceux, *Handbook of Categorical Algebra III*

# Co-Heyting boundary

The boundary of an element of a co-Heyting algebra is the intersection of its Heyting negation with
itself. The boundary in the co-Heyting algebra of closed sets coincides with the topological
boundary.

## Main declarations

# Heyting regular elements

This file defines Heyting regular elements, elements of a Heyting algebra that are their own double
complement, and proves that they form a Boolean algebra.

From a logic standpoint, this means that we can perform classical logic within intuitionistic logic
by simply double-negating all propositions. This is practical for synthetic computability theory.

## Main declarations

* :  is Heyting-regular if .
* : The subtype of Heyting-regular elements.
* : Heyting-regular elements form a Boolean algebra.

## References

* Francis Borceux, *Handbook of Categorical Algebra III*

We want the theorems in this file to be intuitionistic.

An element of a Heyting algebra is regular if its double complement is itself.

arbitrary relations, they're intended for use with well orders.

An initial segment is simply a lower set, i.e. if  belongs to the range, then any  also
belongs to the range. A principal segment is a set of the form  for some .

An initial segment embedding  is an order embedding  such that its range is an
initial segment. Likewise, a principal segment embedding  has a principal segment for a
range.

# Locally finite orders

This file defines locally finite orders.

A locally finite order is an order for which all bounded intervals are finite. This allows to make
sense of /// as lists, multisets, or finsets.
Further, if the order is bounded above (resp. below), then we can also make sense of the
"unbounded" intervals / (resp. /).

Many theorems about these intervals can be found in .

## Examples

Naturally occurring locally finite orders are , , , ,  the product of two
locally finite orders,  the finitely supported functions to a locally finite order ...

# Irreducible and prime elements in an order

This file defines irreducible and prime elements in an order and shows that in a well-founded
lattice every element decomposes as a supremum of irreducible elements.

An element is sup-irreducible (resp. inf-irreducible) if it isn't  and can't be written as the
supremum of any strictly smaller elements. An element is sup-prime (resp. inf-prime) if it isn't
and is greater than the supremum of any two elements less than it.

Primality implies irreducibility in general. The converse only holds in distributive lattices.
Both hold for all (non-minimal) elements in a linear order.

## Main declarations

* : Sup-irreducibility,  isn't minimal and
* : Inf-irreducibility,  isn't maximal and
* : Sup-primality,  isn't minimal and
* : Inf-primality,  isn't maximal and
* /: Decomposition into irreducibles
  in a well-founded semilattice.

### Irreducible and prime elements

A sup-irreducible element is a non-bottom element which isn't the supremum of anything smaller.

A sup-prime element is a non-bottom element which isn't less than the supremum of anything
smaller.

In a well-founded lattice, any element is the supremum of finitely many sup-irreducible
elements. This is the order-theoretic analogue of prime factorisation.

An inf-irreducible element is a non-top element which isn't the infimum of anything bigger.

An inf-prime element is a non-top element which isn't bigger than the infimum of anything
bigger.

In a cowell-founded lattice, any element is the infimum of finitely many inf-irreducible
elements. This is the order-theoretic analogue of prime factorisation.

# Normal functions

A normal function between well-orders is a strictly monotonic continuous function. Normal functions
arise chiefly in the context of cardinal and ordinal-valued functions.

We opt for an equivalent definition that's both simpler and often more convenient: a normal function
is a strictly monotonic function  such that at successor limits ,  is the least upper
bound of  with .

See  for a proof that these notions are equivalent.

A normal function between well-orders is a strictly monotonic continuous function.

This condition is the RHS of the  predicate, which is sufficient

two self-maps that commute with each other.

Current selection of inequalities is motivated by formalization of the rotation number of
a circle homeomorphism.

### Comparison of two sequences

If $f$ is a monotone function, then $∀ k, x_{k+1} ≤ f(x_k)$ implies that $x_k$ grows slower than
$f^k(x_0)$, and similarly for the reversed inequalities. If $x_k$ and $y_k$ are two sequences such
that $x_{k+1} ≤ f(x_k)$ and $y_{k+1} ≥ f(y_k)$ for all $k < n$, then $x_0 ≤ y_0$ implies
$x_n ≤ y_n$, see .

If some of the inequalities in this lemma are strict, then we have $x_n < y_n$. The rest of the
lemmas in this section formalize this fact for different inequalities made strict.

# Kőnig's infinity lemma

Kőnig's infinity lemma is most often stated as a graph theory result:
every infinite, locally finite connected graph contains an infinite path.
It has links to computability and proof theory, and it has a number of formulations.

In practice, most applications are not to an abstract graph,
but to a concrete collection of objects that are organized in a graph-like way,
often where the graph is a rooted tree representing a graded order.
In fact, the lemma is most easily stated and proved
in terms of covers in a strongly atomic order rather than a graph;
in this setting, the proof is almost trivial.

A common formulation of Kőnig's lemma is in terms of directed systems,
with the grading explicitly represented using an -indexed family of types,
which we also provide in this module.
This is a specialization of the much more general ,
which goes through topology and category theory,
but here it is stated and proved independently with much fewer dependencies.

We leave the explicitly graph-theoretic version of the statement as TODO.

## Main Results

*  : Kőnig's lemma for strongly atomic orders.

*  : Kőnig's lemma, where the sequence
  is given as an  instead of a function.

*  : Kőnig's lemma where the sequence
  starts at the minimum of an infinite type.

*  : Kőnig's lemma for inverse systems,
  proved using the above applied to an order on a sigma-type .

## Design notes

Krull dimensions are defined to take value in  so that  is
also negative infinity. This is because we want Krull dimensions to be additive with respect
to product of varieties so that  being the Krull dimension of empty variety is equal to
sum of  and the Krull dimension of any other varieties.

We could generalize the notion of Krull dimension to an arbitrary binary relation; many results
in this file would generalize as well. But we don't think it would be useful, so we only define
Krull dimension of a preorder.

The **Krull dimension** of a preorder  is the supremum of the rightmost index of all relation
series of  ordered by . If there is no series  in , then its Krull
dimension is defined to be negative infinity; if the length of all series  is
unbounded, its Krull dimension is defined to be positive infinity.

The **height** of an element  in a preorder  is the supremum of the rightmost index of all
relation series of  ordered by  and ending below or at . In other words, it is
the largest  such that there's a series  (or  if there is
no largest ).

The **coheight** of an element  in a preorder  is the supremum of the rightmost index of all
relation series of  ordered by  and beginning with . In other words, it is
the largest  such that there's a series  (or  if there is
no largest ).

The definition of  is via the  in the dual order, in order to easily transfer
theorems between  and . See  for the definition with a
series ordered by  and beginning with .

# (Semi-)lattices

Semilattices are partially ordered sets with join (least upper bound, or ) or meet (greatest
lower bound, or ) operations. Lattices are posets that are both join-semilattices and
meet-semilattices.

Distributive lattices are lattices which satisfy any of four equivalent distributivity properties,
of  over , on the left or on the right.

  commutative, associative and idempotent.

* : a type class for lattices
* : an alternative constructor for  via proofs that  and  are
  commutative, associative and satisfy a pair of "absorption laws".

* : a type class for distributive lattices.

# liminfs and limsups of functions and filters

Defines the liminf/limsup of a function taking values in a conditionally complete lattice, with
respect to an arbitrary filter.

lattice.  is the smallest element  such that, eventually,  (and vice versa for
). To work with the Limsup along a function  use .

Usually, one defines the Limsup as  where the Inf is taken over all sets in the filter.
For instance, in ℕ along a function , this is  (and the latter quantity
decreases with , so this is in fact a limit.). There is however a difficulty: it is well possible
that  is not bounded on the whole space, only eventually (think of  on ℝ).
Then there is no guarantee that the quantity above really decreases (the value of the
beforehand is not really well defined, as one cannot use ∞), so that the Inf could be anything.
So one cannot use this  definition in conditionally complete lattices, and one has
to use a less tractable definition.

In conditionally complete lattices, the definition is only useful for filters which are eventually
bounded above (otherwise, the Limsup would morally be +∞, which does not belong to the space) and
which are frequently bounded below (otherwise, the Limsup would morally be -∞, which is not in the
space either). We start with definitions of these concepts for arbitrary filters, before turning to
the definitions of Limsup and Liminf.

In complete lattices, however, it coincides with the  definition.

# Minimality and Maximality

This file proves basic facts about minimality and maximality
of an element with respect to a predicate  on an ordered type .

## Implementation Details

This file underwent a refactor from a version where minimality and maximality were defined using
sets rather than predicates, and with an unbundled order relation rather than a  instance.

A side effect is that it has become less straightforward to state that something is minimal
with respect to a relation that is *not* defeq to the default .
One possible way would be with a type synonym,
and another would be with an ad hoc  instance and  notation.
This was not an issue in practice anywhere in mathlib at the time of the refactor,
but it may be worth re-examining this to make it easier in the future; see the TODO below.

# Nucleus

Locales are the dual concept to frames. Locale theory is a branch of point-free topology, where
intuitively locales are like topological spaces which may or may not have enough points.

# Omega Complete Partial Orders

An omega-complete partial order is a partial order with a supremum
operation on increasing sequences indexed by natural numbers (which we
call ). In this sense, it is strictly weaker than join complete
semi-lattices as only ω-sized totally ordered sets have a supremum.

The concept of an omega-complete partial order (ωCPO) is useful for the
formalization of the semantics of programming languages. Its notion of
supremum helps define the meaning of recursive procedures.

# Order continuity

We say that a function is *left order continuous* if it sends all least upper bounds
to least upper bounds. The order dual notion is called *right order continuity*.

For monotone functions  these notions correspond to the usual left and right continuity.

We prove some basic lemmas (,  etc) and prove that a  is both left
and right order continuous.

### Definitions


A function  between preorders is left order continuous if it preserves all suprema of
nonempty sets. We define it using  instead of  so that the proof works both for
complete lattices and conditionally complete lattices.

A function  between preorders is right order continuous if it preserves all infima of
nonempty sets.  We define it using  instead of  so that the proof works both for
complete lattices and conditionally complete lattices.

Convert an injective left order continuous function to an order embedding.

Convert an injective right order continuous function to an order embedding.

A left adjoint in a Galois connection is left-continuous in the order-theoretic sense.

A right adjoint in a Galois connection is right-continuous in the order-theoretic sense.

# Partitions

of .

## Main declarations

## Representative functions ()

 means that  sends each element of the support to a representative in its
-class, agrees on related elements, and is the identity outside the support.

This is useful whenever a construction must pick one distinguished element per part of a partition.
For example, in graph theory one may partition edges into parallel classes or vertices into
connected components; a representative function can specify which edge remains when simplifying
parallel edges, or how supervertices are labeled after contraction. Similar uses arise in matroid
theory and in the definition of minors.

Tempting alternatives are to use  or fix a global well-order and take minimal
representatives. However, these lead to issues with inconsistencies: independent choices need not
respect relations between different instances (e.g. monotonicity of simplifications with respect
to subgraph order), a global order can clash with structure already carried by the type, and maps
between different types need not intertwine two separate canonical choices. Stating hypotheses with
 keeps the chosen representatives explicit; existence under suitable conditions can be
proved separately.

# Separating prime filters and ideals

In a distributive lattice, if $F$ is a filter, $I$ is an ideal, and $F$ and $I$ are
disjoint, then there exists a prime ideal $J$ containing $I$ with $J$ still disjoint from $F$.
This theorem is a crucial ingredient to Stone's duality for bounded distributive
lattices. The construction of the separator relies on Zorn's lemma.

## Tags

ideal, filter, prime, distributive lattice

## References

* M. H. Stone, Topological representations of distributive lattices and Brouwerian logics
  (1938)

Let S be the set of ideals containing I and disjoint from F.

Then I is in S...

...and S contains upper bounds for any non-empty chains.

Thus, by Zorn's lemma, we can pick a maximal ideal J in S.

By construction, J contains I and is disjoint from F. It remains to prove that J is prime.

First note that J is proper: ⊤ ∈ F so ⊤ ∉ J because F and J are disjoint.

Suppose that a₁ ∉ J, a₂ ∉ J. We need to prove that a₁ ⊔ a₂ ∉ J.

Consider the ideals J₁, J₂ generated by J ∪ {a₁} and J ∪ {a₂}, respectively.

For each i, Jᵢ is an ideal that contains aᵢ, and is not equal to J.

Therefore, since J is maximal, we must have Jᵢ ∉ S.

Since Jᵢ is an ideal that contains I, we have that Jᵢ is not disjoint from F.

Thus, pick cᵢ ∈ F ∩ Jᵢ.

Using the definition of Jᵢ, we can pick bᵢ ∈ J such that cᵢ ≤ bᵢ ⊔ aᵢ.

Since J is an ideal, we have b := b₁ ⊔ b₂ ∈ J.

We now prove a key inequality, using crucially that the lattice is distributive.

Note that c₁ ⊓ c₂ ∈ F, since c₁ and c₂ are both in F and F is a filter.
  Since F is an upper set, it now follows that b ⊔ (a₁ ⊓ a₂) ∈ F.

Now, if we would have a₁ ⊓ a₂ ∈ J, then, since J is an ideal and b ∈ J, we would also get
  b ⊔ (a₁ ⊓ a₂) ∈ J. But this contradicts that J is disjoint from F.

### Order instances on quotients

We define a  instance on a general , as the transitive closure of the
 relation. This is the quotient object in the category of preorders.

We show that in the case of a linear order with  equivalence classes, this
relation is automatically transitive (we don't need to take the transitive closure), and gives a
 structure on the quotient. In that case, the resulting order is sometimes called a
**condensation**.

# Scott continuity

A function  between preorders is Scott continuous (referring to Dana Scott) if it
distributes over . Scott continuity corresponds to continuity in Scott topological spaces
(defined in ). It is distinct from the (more commonly
used) continuity from topology (see ).

## Implementation notes

Given a set  of directed sets, we define say  is  if it distributes over
 for all elements of . This allows us to consider Scott Continuity on all directed sets
in this file, and ωScott Continuity on chains later in
.

* Gierz et al, *A Compendium of Continuous Lattices*

First, if an order isomorphism  is semiconjugate to an order embedding  by

.

Second, consider two actions  of a group on a complete lattice by order
isomorphisms. Then the map  semiconjugates each  to ,
see .  In the case of a conditionally complete lattice, a similar
statement holds true under an additional assumption that each set  is
bounded above, see .

The lemmas come from Étienne Ghys, Groupes d'homéomorphismes du cercle et cohomologie
bornée, Proposition 2.1 and 5.4 respectively. In the paper they are formulated for
homeomorphisms of the circle, so in order to apply results from this file one has to lift these
homeomorphisms to the real line first.

generated automatically.

## Implementation notes

This module's job is to take a bunch of autoparams filled in with all the ways we could synthesize
order typeclasses from  and bundle them into a Mathlib order typeclass. We also need
inheritance of sets of autoparams, because  takes all the autoparams of
 and then some.

To achieve this, each set of autoparams becomes a structure called  (thereby allowing it
to extend existing  structures), and the synthesization scripts are in the default field
values of this type. For the user, a simple  will synthesize all fields of the structure with
tactics, while individual fields that fail to synthesize may be specified using .

The autoparam tactic scripts prioritize existing instances if they exist, to prevent diamonds,
and in such cases require extra  typeclasses to ensure everyone agrees on the order.
Otherwise, those agreement typeclasses can be synthesized with tactics automatically.

Often, we write  in the type of the structure fields, followed by
in the tactic body. This is done to make sure that  is an instance that can be found by
typeclass search in the tactic body: in the case where  is generated by some means other
than typeclass inference, it does not exist as a local variable otherwise.

any others. They are so named since they can't be the successors of anything smaller. We define
 analogously, and prove basic results.

For some applications, it is desirable to exclude minimal elements from being successor limits, or
maximal elements from being predecessor limits. As such, we also provide  and
, which exclude these cases.

# Teichmuller-Tukey

This file defines the notion of being of finite character for a family of sets and proves the
Teichmuller-Tukey lemma.

## Main definitions

-  : A family of sets $F$ is of finite character iff for every set $X$,
  $X ∈ F$ iff every finite subset of $X$ is in $F$.

## Main results

-  : Teichmuller-Tukey lemma, saying that every nonempty
  family of finite character has a maximal element.

## References

-

A family of sets $F$ is of finite character iff for every set $X$, $X ∈ F$ iff every finite
subset of $X$ is in $F$

**Teichmuller-Tukey lemma**. Every nonempty family of finite character has a maximal element.

Apply Zorn's lemma. Take the union of the elements of a chain as its upper bound.

Prove that the union belongs to .

Use the finite character property and the fact that any finite subset of the union is also a
 subset of some element of the chain.

# Well quasi-orders

A well quasi-order (WQO) is a relation such that any infinite sequence contains an infinite
subsequence of related elements. For a preorder, this is equivalent to having a well-founded order
with no infinite antichains.

## Main definitions

* : a predicate for WQO unbundled relations
* : a typeclass for a bundled WQO  relation

## Tags

wqo, pwo, well quasi-order, partial well order, dickson order

A well quasi-order or WQO is a relation such that any infinite sequence contains an infinite
monotonic subsequence, or equivalently, two elements  and  with  and
.

For a preorder, this is equivalent to having a well-founded order with no infinite antichains.

Despite the nomenclature, we don't require the relation to be preordered. Moreover, a well
quasi-order will not in general be a well-order.

A version of **Dickson's lemma**: the Pi type  is well-quasi-ordered when  is
finite and each  is well-quasi-ordered. See  for the finite
product of well-quasi-ordered sets and  when the relation is .

A typeclass for an order with a well-quasi-ordered  relation.

Note that this is unlike , which instead takes a  relation.

This was previously a global instance,
but it doesn't appear to be used and has been implicated in slow typeclass resolutions.

A preorder is well quasi-ordered iff it's well-founded and has no infinite antichains.

A linear WQO is the same thing as a well-order.

A version of **Dickson's lemma**. See  for the finite product of
well-quasi-ordered sets.

# Zorn's lemmas

This file proves several formulations of Zorn's Lemma.

## Variants

The primary statement of Zorn's lemma is . Then it is specialized
to particular relations:
*  with
*  with
*  with

Lemma names carry modifiers:
* : Quantifies over a set, as opposed to over a type.
* : Doesn't ask to prove that the empty chain is bounded and lets you give an element
  that will be smaller than the maximal element found (the maximal element is no smaller than any
  other element, but it can also be incomparable to some).

## How-to

This file comes across as confusing to those who haven't yet used it, so here is a detailed
walkthrough:
1. Know what relation on which type/set you're looking for. See Variants above. You can discharge
  some conditions to Zorn's lemma directly using a  variant.
2. Write down the definition of your type/set, put a
  (or whatever you actually need) followed by an .
3. Fill in the details. This is where you start talking about chains.

A typical proof using Zorn could look like this

## Notes

Originally ported from Isabelle/HOL. The
original file was written by Jacques D.
Fleuriot, Tobias Nipkow, Christian Sternagel.

Local notation for the relation being considered.

**Zorn's lemma**

If every chain has an upper bound, then there exists a maximal element.

A variant of Zorn's lemma. If every nonempty chain of a nonempty type has an upper bound, then
there is a maximal element.

Every chain is contained in a maximal chain. This generalizes Hausdorff's maximality principle.

## Historical note

This is usually called the Erdős–Rényi model, but this name is historically inaccurate as Erdős and
Rényi introduced a closely related but different model. We therefore choose the name
"binomial random graph" to avoid confusion with this other model and because it is a more
descriptive name.

# Independence of Gaussian random variables

In this file we prove some results linking Gaussian random variables and independence. It is
a well known fact that if  is Gaussian, then  and  are independent if their covariance
is zero. We prove many versions of this theorem in different settings: in Banach spaces,
Hilbert spaces, and for families of real random variables.

We also prove that independent Gaussian random variables are jointly Gaussian.

## Main statements

* : Independent Gaussian random variables are jointly Gaussian,
  indexed version.
* : Independent Gaussian random variables are jointly Gaussian,
  product version.
* : If $(X_i)_{i \in \iota}$ are jointly Gaussian,
  then they are independent if for all $i \ne j$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = 0$.
* : If $(X, Y)$ is Gaussian,
  then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$.

# Independence of Gaussian processes

This file contains properties about independence of Gaussian processes. More precisely, we prove
different versions of the following statement: if some stochastic processes are jointly Gaussian,
then they are independent if their marginals are uncorrelated.

## Main statements

* : Assume that the processes $((X^t_s)_{s \in S_t})_{t \in T}$
  are jointly Gaussian. Then they are independent if for all $t_1, t_2 \in T$ with $t_1 \ne t_2$
  and $s_1 \in S_{t_1}$, $s_2 \in S_{t_2}$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X^{t_1}_{s_1}, X^{t_2}_{s_2} = 0$.

* : Two Gaussian processes $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ and $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$
  that are jointly Gaussian are independent if for all $s \in S$ and $t \in T$,
  $\mathrm{Cov}(X_s, Y_t) = 0$.

# Identically distributed random variables

Two random variables defined on two (possibly different) probability spaces but taking value in
the same space are *identically distributed* if their distributions (i.e., the image probability
measures on the target space) coincide. We define this concept and establish its basic properties
in this file.

## Main definitions and results

*  registers that the image of  under  coincides with the image of
  under  (and that  and  are almost everywhere measurable, as otherwise the image measures
  don't make sense). The measures can be kept implicit as in  if the spaces
  are registered as measure spaces.
* : being identically distributed is stable under composition with measurable
  maps.

There are two main kinds of lemmas, under the assumption that  and  are identically
distributed: lemmas saying that two quantities computed for  and  are the same, and lemmas
saying that if  has some property then  also has it. The first kind is registered as
, the second one as  (in the latter case, to deduce
a property of  from one of , use  where ). For
instance:

* : if  and  are identically distributed, then the probabilities
  that they belong to a given measurable set are the same.
* : if  and  are identically distributed, then their integrals
  are the same.
* : if  and  are identically distributed, then their variances
  are the same.

* : if  and  are identically distributed and
  is almost everywhere strongly measurable, then so is .
* : if  and  are identically distributed and
  belongs to , then so does .

We also register several dot notation shortcuts for convenience.
For instance, if , then  states that  and  are
identically distributed, and  states that  and  are identically distributed, and
so on.

Two functions defined on two (possibly different) measure spaces are identically distributed if
their image measures coincide. This only makes sense when the functions are ae measurable
(as otherwise the image measures are not defined), so we require this as well in the definition.

In a second countable topology, the first function in an identically distributed pair is a.e.
strongly measurable. So is the second function, but use  as
 has a different meaning.

Two families of random variables $(X_1, ..., X_p)$ and $(Y_1, ..., Y_q)$ are independent if
for all real bounded continuous functions $f$ and $g$,
$$P[f(X_1, ..., X_p) g(Y_1, ..., Y_q)] = P[f(X_1, ..., X_p)] * P[g(Y_1, ..., Y_q)].$$

Two random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent if
for all real bounded continuous functions $f$ and $g$,
$$P[f(X) g(Y)] = P[f(X)] * P[g(Y)].$$

The indicator of a set $A$ and a family of random variables $(X_1, ..., X_p)$ are independent
if for all real bounded continuous function $f$,
$$P[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_1, ..., X_p)] = P(A) P[f(X_1, ..., X_p)].$$

The indicator of a set $A$ and a random variable $X$ are independent
if for all real bounded continuous function $f$,
$$P[\mathbb{I}_A f(X)] = P(A) P[f(X)].$$

A sigma-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and a family of random variables $(X_1, ..., X_p)$ are independent
if for all set $A \in \mathcal{A}$ and for all real bounded continuous function $f$,
$$P[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_1, ..., X_p)] = P(A) P[f(X_1, ..., X_p)].$$

A sigma-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and a random variable $X$ are independent
if for all set $A \in \mathcal{A}$ and for all real bounded continuous function $f$,
$$P[\mathbb{I}_A f(X)] = P(A) P[f(X)].$$

Two stochastic processes $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ and $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$ are independent if
for all $s_1, ..., s_p \in S, t_1, ..., t_q \in T$ and
for all real bounded continuous functions $f$ and $g$,
$$P[f(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p}) g(Y_{t_1}, ..., Y_{t_q})] =
P[f(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p})] * P[g(Y_{t_1}, ..., Y_{t_q})].$$

The indicator of a set $A$ and a stochastic process $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ are independent if
for all $s_1, ..., s_p \in S$ and for all real bounded continuous function $f$,
$$P[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p})] =
P(A) P[f(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p})].$$

A sigma-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and a stochastic process $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ are independent if

for all real bounded continuous function $f$,
$$P[\mathbb{I}_A f(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p})] =

# Links between independence and characteristic function

Two random variables are independent if and only if their joint characteristic function is equal
to the product of the characteristic functions. More specifically, prove this in Hilbert spaces for
two variables and a finite family of variables. We prove the analogous statements in Banach spaces,
with an arbitrary Lp norm, for the dual characteristic function.

# Independence of stochastic processes

We prove that a stochastic process $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ is independent from a random variable $Y$ if
for all $s_1, ..., s_p \in S$ the family $(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p})$ is independent from $Y$.

We prove that two stochastic processes $(X_s)_{s \in S}$ and $(Y_t)_{t \in T}$ are independent if
for all $s_1, ..., s_p \in S$ and $t_1, ..., t_q \in T$ the two families
$(X_{s_1}, ..., X_{s_p})$ and $(Y_{t_1}, ..., Y_{t_q})$ are independent.
We prove an analogous condition for a family of stochastic processes.

# Stochastic processes with independent increments

A stochastic process  has independent increments if for any  and
, the random variables  are independent.

are independent.

## Main definition

   and , the random variables  are
  independent.

## Main statement

* : A stochastic process  has independent increments if
  and only if for any monotone sequence , the random variables  are

## Tags

independent increments

# Stoch

The category of measurable spaces with Markov kernels is a positive Markov category.

## Main definition

 is defined as the wide subcategory  of , where
 selects Markov kernels, and this construction provides in particular the instance
.

### Implementation notes

Among categories of measurable spaces and probability kernels,  stands out as the unique
positive Markov category. In contrast,  and the category of finite kernels (not
implemented) do not satisfy positivity. To see why, consider the counterexample with
$X = Y = \{\varnothing\}$, kernels $\kappa(\cdot | \varnothing) = 2\delta_{\varnothing}$ and
$\eta(\cdot | \varnothing) = (1/2)\delta_{\varnothing}$: although their composition is
deterministic, the positivity equation fails.

## Implementation details

This file is to a large extent a copy of part of .
The product of two measures is a particular case of composition-product of kernels and
it turns out that once the measurability of the Lebesgue integral of a kernel is proved,
almost all proofs about integrals against products of measures extend with minimal modifications
to the composition-product of two kernels.

The composition of kernels can also be expressed easily with the composition-product and therefore
the proofs about the composition are only simplified versions of the ones for the
composition-product. However it is necessary to do all the proofs once again because the
composition-product requires s-finiteness while the composition does not.
