 is true only when considering Markov kernels. To see why, consider

makes sense of composing infinitely many kernels together.

# Generalized Borel-Cantelli lemma

This file proves Lévy's generalized Borel-Cantelli lemma which is a generalization of the
Borel-Cantelli lemmas. With this generalization, one can easily deduce the Borel-Cantelli lemmas
by choosing appropriate filtrations. This file also contains the one-sided martingale bound which
is required to prove the generalized Borel-Cantelli.

### Lévy's generalization of the Borel-Cantelli lemma

Lévy's generalization of the Borel-Cantelli lemma states that: given a natural number indexed
filtration $(\mathcal{F}_n)$, and a sequence of sets $(s_n)$ such that for all
$n$, $s_n \in \mathcal{F}_n$, $limsup_n s_n$ is almost everywhere equal to the set for which
$\sum_n \mathbb{P}[s_n \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = \infty$.

The proof strategy follows by constructing a martingale satisfying the one-sided martingale bound.
In particular, we define
$$
  f_n := \sum_{k < n} \big(\mathbf{1}_{s_{k + 1}} - \mathbb{P}[s_{k + 1} \mid \mathcal{F}_k]\big).
$$
Then, as a martingale is both a sub- and a super-martingale, the set for which it is unbounded from
above must agree with the set for which it is unbounded from below almost everywhere. Thus, it
can only converge to $\pm \infty$ with probability 0. Thus, by considering
$$
  \limsup_n s_n = \{\sum_n \mathbf{1}_{s_n} = \infty\}
$$
almost everywhere, the result follows.

which we will take the martingale part.

An a.e. monotone strongly adapted process  with uniformly bounded differences converges to
if and only if its predictable part also converges to .

filtration  such that for all ,  is -measurable,  is almost
everywhere equal to the set for which .

# Martingale convergence theorems

The martingale convergence theorems are a collection of theorems characterizing the convergence
of a martingale provided it satisfies some boundedness conditions. This file contains the
almost everywhere martingale convergence theorem which provides an almost everywhere limit to
an L¹ bounded submartingale. It also contains the L¹ martingale convergence theorem which provides
an L¹ limit to a uniformly integrable submartingale. Finally, it also contains the Lévy upwards
theorems.

## Main results

* : the almost everywhere martingale
  convergence theorem: an L¹-bounded submartingale strongly adapted to the filtration
  converges almost everywhere to its limit process.
* : the limit process of an Lᵖ-bounded
  submartingale is Lᵖ.
* : part a of the L¹ martingale
  convergence theorem: a uniformly integrable submartingale strongly adapted to the filtration
  converges almost everywhere and in L¹ to an integrable function which is measurable with respect
  to the σ-algebra .
* : part b the L¹ martingale convergence
  theorem: if  is a uniformly integrable martingale strongly adapted to the filtration , then
   equals  almost everywhere where  is the limiting process of .
* : part c the L¹ martingale convergence theorem:
  given a -measurable function  where  is a filtration,  converges
  almost everywhere to .
* : part c the L¹ martingale convergence theorem:
  given a -measurable function  where  is a filtration,  converges in
  L¹ to .

### Almost everywhere martingale convergence theorem

We will now prove the almost everywhere martingale convergence theorem.

The a.e. martingale convergence theorem states: if  is an L¹-bounded -submartingale, then
it converges almost everywhere to an integrable function which is measurable with respect to
the σ-algebra .

Mathematically, we proceed by first noting that a real sequence $(x_n)$ converges if
(a) $\limsup_{n \to \infty} |x_n| < \infty$, (b) for all $a < b \in \mathbb{Q}$ we have the
number of upcrossings of $(x_n)$ from below $a$ to above $b$ is finite.
Thus, for all $\omega$ satisfying $\limsup_{n \to \infty} |f_n(\omega)| < \infty$ and the number of
upcrossings of $(f_n(\omega))$ from below $a$ to above $b$ is finite for all $a < b \in \mathbb{Q}$,
we have $(f_n(\omega))$ is convergent.

Hence, assuming $(f_n)$ is L¹-bounded, using Fatou's lemma, we have
$$
  \mathbb{E} \limsup_{n \to \infty} |f_n| \le \limsup_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}|f_n| < \infty
$$
implying $\limsup_{n \to \infty} |f_n| < \infty$ a.e. Furthermore, by the upcrossing estimate,
the number of upcrossings is finite almost everywhere implying $f$ converges pointwise almost
everywhere.

Thus, denoting $g$ the a.e. limit of $(f_n)$, $g$ is $\mathcal{F}_\infty$-measurable as for all
$n$, $f_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable and $\mathcal{F}_n \le \mathcal{F}_\infty$. Finally, $g$
is integrable as $|g| \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} |f_n|$ so
$$
  \mathbb{E}|g| \le \mathbb{E} \limsup_{n \to \infty} |f_n| \le
    \limsup_{n \to \infty} \mathbb{E}|f_n| < \infty
$$
as required.

In terms of implementation, we have  which shows that
a bounded sequence converges if it does not visit below $a$ and above $b$ infinitely often
for all $a, b ∈ s$ for some dense set $s$. So, we may skip the first step provided we can prove
that the realizations are bounded almost everywhere. Indeed, suppose $|f_n(\omega)|$ is not
bounded, then either $f_n(\omega) \to \pm \infty$ or one of $\limsup f_n(\omega)$ or
$\liminf f_n(\omega)$ equals $\pm \infty$ while the other is finite. But the first case
contradicts $\liminf |f_n(\omega)| < \infty$ while the second case contradicts finite upcrossings.

Furthermore, we introduce  which chooses the limiting random variable
of a stochastic process if it exists, otherwise returning 0. Hence, instead of showing an
existence statement, we phrase the a.e. martingale convergence theorem by showing that a
submartingale converges to its  almost everywhere.


If a stochastic process has a finite number of upcrossings from below  to above ,
then it does not frequently visit both below  and above .

A stochastic process that frequently visits below  and above  has infinite upcrossings.

A realization of a stochastic process with bounded upcrossings and bounded limit inferiors is
convergent.

We use the spelling  instead of the standard  in the assumptions since it is not as easy
to change  to  under binders.

An L¹-bounded submartingale has bounded upcrossings almost everywhere.

An L¹-bounded submartingale converges almost everywhere.

**Almost everywhere martingale convergence theorem**: An L¹-bounded submartingale converges
almost everywhere to a -measurable function.

The limiting process of an Lᵖ-bounded submartingale is Lᵖ.

### L¹ martingale convergence theorem

We will now prove the L¹ martingale convergence theorems.

The L¹ martingale convergence theorem states that:
(a) if  is a uniformly integrable (in the probability sense) submartingale strongly adapted to
  the filtration , it converges in L¹ to an integrable function  which is measurable with
  respect to  and
(b) if  is actually a martingale,  almost everywhere.
(c) Finally, if  is integrable and measurable with respect to ,  is a
  uniformly integrable martingale which converges to  almost everywhere and in L¹.

The proof is quite simple. (a) follows directly from the a.e. martingale convergence theorem
and the Vitali convergence theorem as our definition of uniform integrability (in the probability
sense) directly implies L¹-uniform boundedness. We note that our definition of uniform
integrability is slightly non-standard but is equivalent to the usual literary definition. This
equivalence is provided by .

(b) follows since given $n$, we have for all $m \ge n$,
$$
  \|f_n - \mathbb{E}[g \mid \mathcal{F}_n]\|_1 =
    \|\mathbb{E}[f_m - g \mid \mathcal{F}_n]\|_1 \le \|f_m - g\|_1.
$$
Thus, taking $m \to \infty$ provides the almost everywhere equality.

Finally, to prove (c), we define $f_n := \mathbb{E}[h \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$. It is clear that
$(f_n)_n$ is a martingale by the tower property for conditional expectations. Furthermore,
$(f_n)_n$ is uniformly integrable in the probability sense. Indeed, as a single function is
uniformly integrable in the measure theory sense, for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists some
$\delta > 0$ such that for all measurable set $A$ with $\mu(A) < δ$, we have
$\mathbb{E}|h|\mathbf{1}_A < \epsilon$. So, since for sufficiently large $\lambda$, by the Markov
inequality, we have for all $n$,
$$
  \mu(|f_n| \ge \lambda) \le \lambda^{-1}\mathbb{E}|f_n| \le \lambda^{-1}\mathbb{E}|h| < \delta,
$$
we have for sufficiently large $\lambda$, for all $n$,
$$
  \mathbb{E}|f_n|\mathbf{1}_{|f_n| \ge \lambda} \le
    \mathbb{E}|h|\mathbf{1}_{|f_n| \ge \lambda} < \epsilon,
$$
implying $(f_n)_n$ is uniformly integrable. Now, to prove $f_n \to h$ almost everywhere and in
L¹, it suffices to show that $h = g$ almost everywhere where $g$ is the almost everywhere and L¹
limit of $(f_n)_n$ from part (b) of the theorem. By noting that, for all $s \in \mathcal{F}_n$,
we have
$$
  \mathbb{E}g\mathbf{1}_s = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[g \mid \mathcal{F}_n]\mathbf{1}_s] =
    \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[h \mid \mathcal{F}_n]\mathbf{1}_s] = \mathbb{E}h\mathbf{1}_s
$$
where $\mathbb{E}[g \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = \mathbb{E}[h \mid \mathcal{F}_n]$ almost everywhere
by part (b); the equality also holds for all $s \in \mathcal{F}_\infty$ by Dynkin's theorem.
Thus, as both $h$ and $g$ are $\mathcal{F}_\infty$-measurable, $h = g$ almost everywhere as
required.

Similar to the a.e. martingale convergence theorem, rather than showing the existence of the
limiting process, we phrase the L¹-martingale convergence theorem by proving that a submartingale
does converge in L¹ to its . However, in contrast to the a.e. martingale convergence
theorem, we do not need to introduce an L¹ version of  as the L¹ limit
and the a.e. limit of a submartingale coincide.

strongly adapted to the filtration  converges a.e. and in L¹ to an integrable function which is
measurable with respect to the σ-algebra .

# Doob's upcrossing estimate

Given a discrete real-valued submartingale $(f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, denoting by $U_N(a, b)$ the
number of times $f_n$ crossed from below $a$ to above $b$ before time $N$, Doob's upcrossing
estimate (also known as Doob's inequality) states that
$$(b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_N(a, b)] \le \mathbb{E}[(f_N - a)^+].$$
Doob's upcrossing estimate is an important inequality and is central in proving the martingale
convergence theorems.

  taken to be ).
* : is the predictable process which is 1 if  is
  between a consecutive pair of lower and upper crossings and is 0 otherwise. Intuitively
  one might think of the  as the strategy of buying 1 share whenever the process
  crosses below  for the first time after selling and selling 1 share whenever the process
  crosses above  for the first time after buying.
* : is the number of times  crosses from below  to
  above  before time .
* : is the number of times  crosses from below  to above
  . This takes value in  and so is allowed to be .

## Main results

* :  is a
  stopping time whenever the process it is associated to is adapted.

### References

We mostly follow the proof from Kallenberg, *Foundations of modern probability*

## Proof outline

In this section, we will denote by $U_N(a, b)$ the number of upcrossings of $(f_n)$ from below $a$
to above $b$ before time $N$.

To define $U_N(a, b)$, we will construct two stopping times corresponding to when $(f_n)$ crosses
below $a$ and above $b$. Namely, we define
$$
  \sigma_n := \inf \{n \ge \tau_n \mid f_n \le a\} \wedge N;
$$
$$
  \tau_{n + 1} := \inf \{n \ge \sigma_n \mid f_n \ge b\} \wedge N.
$$
These are  and  in our formalization which are defined
using  allowing us to specify a starting and ending time.
Then, we may simply define $U_N(a, b) := \sup \{n \mid \tau_n < N\}$.

Fixing $a < b \in \mathbb{R}$, we will first prove the theorem in the special case that
$0 \le f_0$ and $a \le f_N$. In particular, we will show
$$
  (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_N(a, b)] \le \mathbb{E}[f_N].
$$
This is  in our formalization.

To prove this, we use the fact that given a non-negative, bounded, predictable process $(C_n)$
(i.e. $(C_{n + 1})$ is strongly adapted),
$(C \bullet f)_n := \sum_{k \le n} C_{k + 1}(f_{k + 1} - f_k)$ is a submartingale if $(f_n)$ is.

Define $C_n := \sum_{k \le n} \mathbf{1}_{[\sigma_k, \tau_{k + 1})}(n)$. It is easy to see that
$(1 - C_n)$ is non-negative, bounded and predictable, and hence, given a submartingale $(f_n)$,
$(1 - C) \bullet f$ is also a submartingale. Thus, by the submartingale property,
$0 \le \mathbb{E}[((1 - C) \bullet f)_0] \le \mathbb{E}[((1 - C) \bullet f)_N]$ implying
$$
  \mathbb{E}[(C \bullet f)_N] \le \mathbb{E}[(1 \bullet f)_N] = \mathbb{E}[f_N] - \mathbb{E}[f_0].
$$

Furthermore,
$$
\begin{align}
    (C \bullet f)_N & =
      \sum_{n \le N} \sum_{k \le N} \mathbf{1}_{[\sigma_k, \tau_{k + 1})}(n)(f_{n + 1} - f_n)\\
    & = \sum_{k \le N} \sum_{n \le N} \mathbf{1}_{[\sigma_k, \tau_{k + 1})}(n)(f_{n + 1} - f_n)\\
    & = \sum_{k \le N} (f_{\sigma_k + 1} - f_{\sigma_k} + f_{\sigma_k + 2} - f_{\sigma_k + 1}
      + \cdots + f_{\tau_{k + 1}} - f_{\tau_{k + 1} - 1})\\
    & = \sum_{k \le N} (f_{\tau_{k + 1}} - f_{\sigma_k})
      \ge \sum_{k < U_N(a, b)} (b - a) = (b - a) U_N(a, b)
\end{align}
$$
where the inequality follows since for all $k < U_N(a, b)$,
$f_{\tau_{k + 1}} - f_{\sigma_k} \ge b - a$ while for all $k > U_N(a, b)$,
$f_{\tau_{k + 1}} = f_{\sigma_k} = f_N$ and
$f_{\tau_{U_N(a, b) + 1}} - f_{\sigma_{U_N(a, b)}} = f_N - a \ge 0$. Hence, we have
$$
  (b - a) \mathbb{E}[U_N(a, b)] \le \mathbb{E}[(C \bullet f)_N]
  \le \mathbb{E}[f_N] - \mathbb{E}[f_0] \le \mathbb{E}[f_N],
$$
as required.

To obtain the general case, we simply apply the above to $((f_n - a)^+)_n$.

### Variant of the upcrossing estimate

Now, we would like to prove a variant of the upcrossing estimate obtained by taking the supremum
over $N$ of the original upcrossing estimate. Namely, we want the inequality
$$
  (b - a) \sup_N \mathbb{E}[U_N(a, b)] \le \sup_N \mathbb{E}[f_N].
$$
This inequality is central for the martingale convergence theorem as it provides a uniform bound
for the upcrossings.

We note that on top of taking the supremum on both sides of the inequality, we had also used
the monotone convergence theorem on the left-hand side to take the supremum outside of the
integral. To do this, we need to make sure $U_N(a, b)$ is measurable and integrable. Integrability
is easy to check as $U_N(a, b) ≤ N$ and so it suffices to show measurability. Indeed, by
noting that
$$
  U_N(a, b) = \sum_{i = 1}^N \mathbf{1}_{\{U_N(a, b) < N\}}
$$
$U_N(a, b)$ is measurable as $\{U_N(a, b) < N\}$ is a measurable set since $U_N(a, b)$ is a
stopping time.

in  and so is allowed to be ).

This presentation of sub-Gaussian random variables is inspired by section 2.5 of
[vershynin2018high]. Let  be a random variable. Consider the following five properties, in which

* (i) for all , ,

Properties (i) to (iv) are equivalent, in the sense that there exists a constant  such that
if  satisfies one of those properties with constant , then it satisfies any other one with
constant at most .

If  then properties (i)-(iv) are equivalent to (v) in that same sense.
Property (v) implies that  has expectation zero.

The name sub-Gaussian is used by various authors to refer to any one of (i)-(v). We will say that a
random variable has sub-Gaussian moment-generating function (mgf) with constant  to mean that
property (v) holds with that constant. The function  which appears in
property (v) is the mgf of a Gaussian with variance .
That property (v) is the most convenient one to work with if one wants to prove concentration
inequalities using Chernoff's method.

property.

# Classical probability

The classical formulation of probability states that the probability of an event occurring in a
finite probability space is the ratio of that event to all possible events.
This notion can be expressed with measure theory using
the counting measure. In particular, given the sets  and , we define the probability of
occurring in  to be . With this definition, we recover the probability over
the entire sample space when .

Classical probability is often used in combinatorics and we prove some useful lemmas in this file
for that purpose.

## Main definition

  conditioned on . This is a probability measure when  is finite and nonempty.

probability an element of a set  satisfies some predicate . Our current formulation still
allows us to describe this by abusing the definitional equality of sets and predicates by simply
writing . We should avoid this however as none of the lemmas are written for
predicates.

(or Lie algebra representations etc), we can deduce them as special cases of facts from this file.

, then any endomorphism of  is scalar.

closed field is one-dimensional.

# Continuous cohomology

# The group cohomology of a -linear -representation

Let  be a commutative ring and  a group. This file defines the group cohomology of
 to be the cohomology of the complex
$$0 \to \mathrm{Fun}(G^0, A) \to \mathrm{Fun}(G^1, A) \to \mathrm{Fun}(G^2, A) \to \dots$$
with differential $d^n$ sending $f: G^n \to A$ to the function mapping $(g_0, \dots, g_n)$ to
$$\rho(g_0)(f(g_1, \dots, g_n))$$
$$+ \sum_{i = 0}^{n - 1} (-1)^{i + 1}\cdot f(g_0, \dots, g_ig_{i + 1}, \dots, g_n)$$
$$+ (-1)^{n + 1}\cdot f(g_0, \dots, g_{n - 1})$$ (where  is the representation attached to ).

We have a -linear isomorphism
$\mathrm{Fun}(G^n, A) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(\bigoplus_{G^n} k[G], A)$, where
the right-hand side is morphisms in , and $k[G]$ is equipped with the left regular
representation. If we conjugate the $n$th differential in $\mathrm{Hom}(P, A)$ by this isomorphism,
where  is the bar resolution of  as a trivial -linear -representation, then the
resulting map agrees with the differential $d^n$ defined above, a fact we prove.

This gives us for free a proof that our $d^n$ squares to zero. It also gives us an isomorphism
$\mathrm{H}^n(G, A) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^n(k, A),$ where $\mathrm{Ext}$ is taken in the category
.

To talk about cohomology in low degree, please see the file
, which provides API
specialized to , , .

## Main definitions

* : a complex whose objects are
  $\mathrm{Fun}(G^n, A)$ and whose cohomology is the group cohomology $\mathrm{H}^n(G, A).$
* : an isomorphism between the above complex and the
  complex $\mathrm{Hom}(P, A),$ where  is the bar resolution of  as a trivial resolution.
* : this is $\mathrm{H}^n(G, A),$ defined as the $n$th cohomology of
  .
* : an isomorphism $\mathrm{H}^n(G, A) \cong \mathrm{Ext}^n(k, A)$
  (where $\mathrm{Ext}$ is taken in the category ) induced by .

Group cohomology is typically stated for -modules, or equivalently modules over the group ring
 However,  can be generalized to any commutative ring , which is what we use.

definition. We avoid using instances  so that we do not run into
possible scalar action diamonds.

# Hilbert's Theorem 90

Let  be a finite extension of fields. Then this file proves Noether's generalization of
Hilbert's Theorem 90: that the 1st group cohomology $H^1(Aut_K(L), L^\times)$ is trivial. We state
it both in terms of $H^1$ and in terms of cocycles being coboundaries.

Hilbert's original statement was that if $L/K$ is Galois, and $Gal(L/K)$ is cyclic, generated
by an element , then for every  such that $N_{L/K}(x) = 1,$ there exists  such
that $x = y/σ(y).$ Using the fact that  for any finite cyclic
group  with generator , we deduce the original statement from Noether's generalization.

Noether's generalization also holds for infinite Galois extensions.

# The group homology of a -linear -representation

Let  be a commutative ring and  a group. This file defines the group homology of
 to be the homology of the complex
$$\dots \to \bigoplus_{G^2} A \to \bigoplus_{G^1} A \to \bigoplus_{G^0} A$$
with differential $d_n$ sending $a\cdot (g_0, \dots, g_n)$ to
$$\rho(g_0^{-1})(a)\cdot (g_1, \dots, g_n)$$
$$+ \sum_{i = 0}^{n - 1}(-1)^{i + 1}a\cdot (g_0, \dots, g_ig_{i + 1}, \dots, g_n)$$
$$+ (-1)^{n + 1}a\cdot (g_0, \dots, g_{n - 1})$$ (where  is the representation attached to ).

We have a -linear isomorphism
$\bigoplus_{G^n} A \cong (A \otimes_k \left(\bigoplus_{G^n} k[G]\right))_G$ given by
. If we conjugate the $n$th differential in $(A \otimes_k P)_G$
by this isomorphism, where  is the bar resolution of  as a trivial -linear
-representation, then the resulting map agrees with the differential $d_n$ defined
above, a fact we prove.

Hence our $d_n$ squares to zero, and we get
$\mathrm{H}_n(G, A) \cong \mathrm{Tor}_n(A, k),$ where $\mathrm{Tor}$ is defined by deriving the
second argument of the functor $(A, B) \mapsto (A \otimes_k B)_G.$

To talk about homology in low degree, the file
 provides API specialized to
, , .

## Main definitions

* : the left-derived functors given by deriving the second argument of
  $(A, B) \mapsto (A \otimes_k B)_G$.
* : a complex whose objects are
  $\bigoplus_{G^n} A$ and whose homology is the group homology $\mathrm{H}_n(G, A).$
* : an isomorphism between the above two complexes.
* : this is $\mathrm{H}_n(G, A),$ defined as the $n$th homology of the
  second complex, .
* : an isomorphism $\mathrm{H}_n(G, A) \cong \mathrm{Tor}_n(A, k)$
  induced by .

## Implementation notes

Group homology is typically stated for -modules, or equivalently modules over the group ring
 However,  can be generalized to any commutative ring , which is what we use.
Moreover, we express -module structures on a module -module  using the  definition.
We avoid using instances  so that we do not run into possible scalar action diamonds.

Note that the existing definition of  in  is for monoidal
categories, and the bifunctor we need to derive here maps to . Hence we define
 by instead left-deriving the second argument of :
$(A, B) \mapsto (A \otimes_k B)_G$. The functor  is naturally
isomorphic to the functor sending  to , where we give  the -module
structure defined by , but currently mathlib's  is only defined
for commutative rings.

# Adjoining elements and being finitely generated in an algebra tower

## Main results

* : if  is finitely generated as -algebra and  as -algebra,
  then  is finitely generated as -algebra
* : **Artin--Tate lemma**: if C/B/A is a tower of rings, and A is Noetherian, and
  C is algebra-finite over A, and C is module-finite over B, then B is algebra-finite over A.

**Artin--Tate lemma**: if A ⊆ B ⊆ C is a chain of subrings of commutative rings, and
A is Noetherian, and C is algebra-finite over A, and C is module-finite over B,
then B is algebra-finite over A.

References: Atiyah--Macdonald Proposition 7.8; Altman--Kleiman 16.17.

# Algebraic independence persists to the algebraic closure

## Main results

* : if A/S/R is a tower of algebras with S/R algebraic,
  then a family of elements in A that are algebraically independent over R remains algebraically
  independent over S, provided that S has no zero divisors.

* : an algebraically independent family remains
  algebraically independent over the algebraic closure.

# Artinian rings and modules

A module satisfying these equivalent conditions is said to be an *Artinian* R-module
if every decreasing chain of submodules is eventually constant, or equivalently,
if the relation  on submodules is well founded.

A ring is said to be left (or right) Artinian if it is Artinian as a left (or right) module over
itself, or simply Artinian if it is both left and right Artinian.

## Main definitions

Let  be a ring and let  and  be -modules. Let  be an -submodule of .

  implemented as the predicate that the  relation on submodules is well founded.

* P. Samuel, *Algebraic Theory of Numbers*

# Instances related to Artinian rings

We show that every reduced Artinian ring and the polynomial ring over it
are decomposition monoids, and every reduced Artinian ring is semisimple.

If each  is a Artinian -module, then  satisfies the strong rank condition.

# Artinian rings and modules

A module satisfying these equivalent conditions is said to be an *Artinian* R-module
if every decreasing chain of submodules is eventually constant, or equivalently,
if the relation  on submodules is well founded.

A ring is said to be left (or right) Artinian if it is Artinian as a left (or right) module over
itself, or simply Artinian if it is both left and right Artinian.

## Main results

* , : there are only
  finitely prime ideals in a commutative Artinian ring, and each of them is maximal.

* : a reduced commutative Artinian ring  is isomorphic to a finite
  product of fields (and therefore is a semisimple ring and a decomposition monoid; moreover
   is also a decomposition monoid).

* : an Artinian module is semisimple
  iff its Jacobson radical is zero.

* : an Artinian ring  is semiprimary, in particular
  the Jacobson radical of  is a nilpotent ideal ().

## References

* M. F. Atiyah and I. G. Macdonald, *Introduction to commutative algebra*
* P. Samuel, *Algebraic Theory of Numbers*

algebra map, then  is an Artinian  module.

A ring is said to be left (or right) Artinian if it is Artinian as a left (or right) module over
itself, or simply Artinian if it is both left and right Artinian.

# Bézout rings

A Bézout ring (Bezout ring) is a ring whose finitely generated ideals are principal.
Notable examples include principal ideal rings, valuation rings, and the ring of algebraic integers.

## Main results
- : It suffices to verify every  is principal.
- : For a Bézout domain, Noetherian ↔ PID ↔ UFD ↔ ACCP

# Bialgebras

In this file we define s.

## Main definitions

* : the structure of a bialgebra on the -algebra ;
* : a commutative semiring is a bialgebra over itself.

## Implementation notes

Rather than the "obvious" axiom , the far
more convoluted  is used as a structure field; this says that
the corresponding two maps  are equal; a similar trick is
used for comultiplication as well. An alternative constructor  is provided
with the more easily-readable axioms. The argument for using the more convoluted axioms
is that in practice there is evidence that they will be easier to prove (especially
when dealing with things like tensor products of bialgebras). This does make the definition
more surprising to mathematicians, however mathlib is no stranger to definitions which
are surprising to mathematicians -- see for example its definition of a group.
Note that this design decision is also compatible with that of . The lengthy
docstring for these convoluted fields attempts to explain what is going on.

The constructor  is dual to the default constructor: For  is a commutative
semiring and  an -algebra, it consumes the counit and comultiplication as algebra
homomorphisms that satisfy the coalgebra axioms to define a bialgebra structure on .

# Binomial rings

In this file we introduce the binomial property as a mixin, and define the
and  functions generalizing binomial coefficients.

According to our main reference [elliott2006binomial] (which lists many equivalent conditions), a
binomial ring is a torsion-free commutative ring  such that for any  and any , the
product  is divisible by . The torsion-free condition lets us divide by
unambiguously, so we get uniquely defined binomial coefficients.

The defining condition doesn't require commutativity or associativity, and we get a theory with
essentially the same power by replacing subtraction with addition. Thus, we consider any additive
commutative monoid with a notion of natural number exponents in which multiplication by positive
integers is injective, and demand that the evaluation of the ascending Pochhammer polynomial
 at any element is divisible by . The quotient is called ,
because for  a natural number, it is the number of multisets of cardinality  taken from a type
of cardinality .

## Definitions

* : a mixin class specifying a suitable  function.
* : the quotient of an ascending Pochhammer evaluation by a factorial.
* : the quotient of a descending Pochhammer evaluation by a factorial.

## Results

* Basic results with choose and multichoose, e.g.,
* Relations between choose and multichoose, negated input.
* Fundamental recursion:
* Chu-Vandermonde identity:
* Pochhammer API

## References

* J. Elliott, *Binomial rings, integer-valued polynomials, and λ-rings*

A binomial ring is a ring for which ascending Pochhammer evaluations are uniquely divisible by
suitable factorials. We define this notion as a mixin for additive commutative monoids with natural
number powers, but retain the ring name. We introduce  as the uniquely defined
quotient.

This file defines the notion of a Dedekind ring (domain),

## Main definitions

-  defines a Dedekind ring as a commutative ring that is
  Noetherian, integrally closed in its field of fractions and has Krull dimension at most one.
   shows that this does not depend on the choice of field of fractions.
-  defines a Dedekind domain as a Dedekind ring that is a domain.

but are independent of that choice. The  lemmas express this independence.

# Dedekind domains

namely a Noetherian integral domain where the localization at every nonzero prime ideal is a DVR.

## Main definitions

-  alternatively defines a Dedekind domain as an integral domain that
  is Noetherian, and the localization at every nonzero prime ideal is a DVR.

## Main results
-  shows that
   implies the localization at each nonzero prime ideal is a DVR.
-  is one direction of the equivalence of definitions
  of a Dedekind domain

## Implementation notes

The definitions that involve a field of fractions choose a canonical field of fractions,
but are independent of that choice. The  lemmas express this independence.

Often, definitions assume that Dedekind domains are not fields. We found it more practical
to add a  assumption whenever this is explicitly needed.

# Selmer groups of fraction fields of Dedekind domains

Let $K$ be the field of fractions of a Dedekind domain $R$. For any set $S$ of prime ideals in the
height one spectrum of $R$, and for any natural number $n$, the Selmer group $K(S, n)$ is defined to
be the subgroup of the unit group $K^\times$ modulo $n$-th powers where each element has $v$-adic
valuation divisible by $n$ for all prime ideals $v$ away from $S$. In other words, this is precisely
$$ K(S, n) := \{x(K^\times)^n \in K^\times / (K^\times)^n \ \mid \
                \forall v \notin S, \ \mathrm{ord}_v(x) \equiv 0 \pmod n\}. $$

There is a fundamental short exact sequence
$$ 1 \to R_S^\times / (R_S^\times)^n \to K(S, n) \to \mathrm{Cl}_S(R)[n] \to 0, $$
where $R_S^\times$ is the $S$-unit group of $R$ and $\mathrm{Cl}_S(R)$ is the $S$-class group of
$R$. If the flanking groups are both finite, then $K(S, n)$ is finite by the first isomorphism
theorem. Such is the case when $R$ is the ring of integers of a number field $K$, $S$ is finite, and
$n$ is positive, in which case $R_S^\times$ is finitely generated by Dirichlet's unit theorem and
$\mathrm{Cl}_S(R)$ is finite by the class number theorem.

This file defines the Selmer group $K(S, n)$ and some basic facts.

## Main definitions

* : the Selmer group.
* TODO: maps in the sequence.

## Main statements

* TODO: proofs of exactness of the sequence.
* TODO: proofs of finiteness for global fields.

## Notation

* : the Selmer group with parameters , , and .

## Implementation notes

The Selmer group is typically defined as a subgroup of the Galois cohomology group $H^1(K, \mu_n)$
with certain local conditions defined by $v$-adic valuations, where $\mu_n$ is the group of $n$-th
roots of unity over a separable closure of $K$. Here $H^1(K, \mu_n)$ is identified with
$K^\times / (K^\times)^n$ by the long exact sequence from Kummer theory and Hilbert's theorem 90,
and the fundamental short exact sequence becomes an easy consequence of the snake lemma. This file
will define all the maps explicitly for computational purposes, but isomorphisms to the Galois
cohomological definition will be provided when possible.

# Discrete valuation rings

This file defines discrete valuation rings (DVRs) and develops a basic interface
for them.

## Important definitions

There are various definitions of a DVR in the literature; we define a DVR to be a local PID
which is not a field (the first definition in Wikipedia) and prove that this is equivalent
to being a PID with a unique non-zero prime ideal (the definition in Serre's
book "Local Fields").

Let R be an integral domain, assumed to be a principal ideal ring and a local ring.

# Modules of finite length

We define modules of finite length () to be finite iterated extensions of
simple modules, and show that a module is of finite length iff it is both Noetherian and Artinian,
iff it admits a composition series.

We do not make  a class, instead we use .

## Tags

Finite length, Composition series

A module of finite length is either trivial or a simple extension of a module known
to be of finite length.

The following instances are now automatic:
example [IsSemisimpleRing R] : IsNoetherianRing R := inferInstance
example [IsSemisimpleRing R] : IsArtinianRing R := inferInstance

(cf. [Katsov2004], [KatsovNam2011]).

submodules  into finitely generated modules , and  can be further assumed to lie in
the same universe as .

# The equational criterion for flatness

Let $M$ be a module over a commutative ring $R$. Let us say that a relation
$\sum_{i \in \iota} f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is *trivial* () if there exist a
finite index type $\kappa$ = , elements $(y_j)_{j \in \kappa}$ of $M$,
and elements $(a_{ij})_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}$ of $R$ such that for all $i$,
$$x_i = \sum_j a_{ij} y_j$$
and for all $j$,
$$\sum_i f_i a_{ij} = 0.$$

The *equational criterion for flatness* Stacks 00HK
() states that $M$ is flat if and only if every relation
in $M$ is trivial.

The equational criterion for flatness can be stated in the following form
(). Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Then the following two
conditions are equivalent:
* $M$ is flat.
* For finite free modules $R^l$, all elements $f \in R^l$, and all linear maps
  $x \colon R^l \to M$ such that $x(f) = 0$, there exist a finite free module $R^k$ and
  linear maps $a \colon R^l \to R^k$ and $y \colon R^k \to M$ such
  that $x = y \circ a$ and $a(f) = 0$.

Of course, the module $R^l$ in this statement can be replaced by an arbitrary free module
().

We also have the following strengthening of the equational criterion for flatness
(): Let $M$ be a
flat module. Let $K$ and $N$ be finite $R$-modules with $N$ free, and let $f \colon K \to N$ and
$x \colon N \to M$ be linear maps such that $x \circ f = 0$. Then there exist a finite free module
$R^k$ and linear maps $a \colon N \to R^k$ and $y \colon R^k \to M$ such
that $x = y \circ a$ and $a \circ f = 0$. We recover the usual equational criterion for flatness if
$K = R$ and $N = R^l$. This is used in the proof of Lazard's theorem.

We conclude that every linear map from a finitely presented module to a flat module factors
through a finite free module (), and
every finitely presented flat module is projective ().

## References

* Stacks: Flat modules and flat ring maps
* Stacks: Characterizing flatness

The proposition that the relation $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is trivial.
That is, there exist a finite index type $\kappa$ = , elements
$(y_j)_{j \in \kappa}$ of $M$, and elements $(a_{ij})_{i \in \iota, j \in \kappa}$ of $R$
such that for all $i$,
$$x_i = \sum_j a_{ij} y_j$$
and for all $j$,
$$\sum_i f_i a_{ij} = 0.$$
By , this condition implies $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$.

If the relation given by $(f_i)_{i \in \iota}$ and $(x_i)_{i \in \iota}$ is trivial, then
$\sum_i f_i x_i$ is actually equal to $0$.

**Equational criterion for flatness**, combined form.

Let $M$ be a module over a commutative ring $R$. The following are equivalent:
* $M$ is flat.
* For all ideals $I \subseteq R$, the map $I \otimes M \to M$ is injective.
* Every $\sum_i f_i \otimes x_i$ that vanishes in $R \otimes M$ vanishes trivially.
* Every relation $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is trivial.
* For all finite free modules $R^l$, all elements $f \in R^l$, and all linear maps
  $x \colon R^l \to M$ such that $x(f) = 0$, there exist a finite free module $R^k$ and
  linear maps $a \colon R^l \to R^k$ and $y \colon R^k \to M$ such
  that $x = y \circ a$ and $a(f) = 0$.

**Equational criterion for flatness**:
a module $M$ is flat if and only if every relation $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is trivial.

**Equational criterion for flatness**, forward direction.

If $M$ is flat, then every relation $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is trivial.

**Equational criterion for flatness**, backward direction.

If every relation $\sum_i f_i x_i = 0$ in $M$ is trivial, then $M$ is flat.

**Equational criterion for flatness**, alternate form.

A module $M$ is flat if and only if for all finite free modules $R^l$,
all $f \in R^l$, and all linear maps $x \colon R^l \to M$ such that $x(f) = 0$, there
exist a finite free module $R^k$ and linear maps $a \colon R^l \to R^k$ and
$y \colon R^k \to M$ such that $x = y \circ a$ and $a(f) = 0$.

**Equational criterion for flatness**, backward direction, alternate form.

Let $M$ be a module over a commutative ring $R$. Suppose that for all finite free modules $R^l$,
all $f \in R^l$, and all linear maps $x \colon R^l \to M$ such that $x(f) = 0$, there
exist a finite free module $R^k$ and linear maps $a \colon R^l \to R^k$ and
$y \colon R^k \to M$ such that $x = y \circ a$ and $a(f) = 0$. Then $M$ is flat.

**Equational criterion for flatness**, forward direction, second alternate form.

Let $M$ be a flat module over a commutative ring $R$. Let $N$ be a finite free module over $R$,
let $f \in N$, and let $x \colon N \to M$ be a linear map such that $x(f) = 0$. Then there exist a
finite free module $R^k$ and linear maps $a \colon N \to R^k$ and
$y \colon R^k \to M$ such that $x = y \circ a$ and $a(f) = 0$.

Let $M$ be a flat module. Let $K$ and $N$ be finite $R$-modules with $N$
free, and let $f \colon K \to N$ and $x \colon N \to M$ be linear maps such that
$x \circ f = 0$. Then there exist a finite free module $R^k$ and linear maps
$a \colon N \to R^k$ and $y \colon R^k \to M$ such that $x = y \circ a$ and
$a \circ f = 0$.

Every homomorphism from a finitely presented module to a flat module factors through a finite
free module.

# Grassmannians

## Main definitions

- :  is the ᵗʰ Grassmannian of the -module . It is defined
  to be the set of submodules of  whose **quotient** is locally free of rank . Note that there
  is another convention in literature where the ᵗʰ Grassmannian would instead be -dimensional
  subspaces of a given vector space over a field. See implementation notes below.

- : The Grassmannian functor that sends an -algebra  to the set
  .

## Implementation notes

In the literature, two conventions exist:

1. The ᵗʰ Grassmannian parametrises -dimensional **subspaces** of a given finite-dimensional
   vector space over a field.
2. The ᵗʰ Grassmannian parametrises **quotients** that are locally free of rank , of a given
   module over a ring.

For the purposes of Algebraic Geometry, the first definition here cannot be generalised to obtain
a scheme to represent the functor, which is why the second definition is the one chosen by
Grothendieck, EGA I.9.7.3 (Springer edition only), and in EGA V.11
(unpublished).

The first definition in the stated generality (i.e. over a field , and finite-dimensional vector
space ) can be recovered from the second definition by noting that -dimensional subspaces of
 are canonically equivalent to -dimensional quotients of , and also to -dimensional
quotients of , the dual of . In symbols, this means that the first definition is equivalent
to  and also to , where  is the dimension of .

*  is contained in the Jacobson radical of
* for every polynomial  over , with a *simple* root  over the quotient ring ,

unit. Warning: if  is not a field then it is not enough to assume that  has a factorization

of  over .)

A local ring  is *Henselian* if it is Henselian at its maximal ideal.

chains of prime ideals below it.

The height of an ideal is defined as the infimum of the heights of its minimal prime ideals.

For a prime ideal, its height equals its prime height.

An ideal has finite height if it is either the unit ideal or its height is finite.

A prime ideal of finite height is equal to any ideal that contains it with no greater height.

then J is a minimal prime over I

# Krull's Height Theorem

In this file, we prove **Krull's principal ideal theorem** (also known as
**Krullscher Hauptidealsatz**), and **Krull's height theorem** (also known as
**Krullscher Höhensatz**).

## Main Results

*  : This theorem is the
  **Krull's principal ideal theorem** (also known as **Krullscher Hauptidealsatz**), which states
  that: In a commutative Noetherian ring , any prime ideal that is minimal over a principal ideal
  has height at most 1.

*  : This theorem is the
  **Krull's height theorem** (also known as **Krullscher Höhensatz**), which states that:
  In a commutative Noetherian ring , any prime ideal that is minimal over an ideal generated by
   elements has height at most .

*  : This theorem is a corollary of the **Krull's height theorem**
  (also known as **Krullscher Höhensatz**). In a commutative Noetherian ring , the height of
  a (finitely-generated) ideal is smaller than or equal to the minimum number of generators for
  this ideal.

*  : In a commutative Noetherian ring , a prime ideal
   has height no greater than  if and only if it is a minimal ideal over some ideal generated
  by no more than  elements.

 In a commutative Noetherian ring , any prime ideal that is minimal over a principal ideal
 has height at most 1.

is one.

## Implementation notes

In the classical literature (e.g. Stenström), *right linear topologies* on a ring are often
described via filters of open **right** ideals, and the terminology is frequently abused by
identifying the topology with its filter of ideals.

In this development we work systematically with **left ideals**. Accordingly, Stenström’s
right-ideal construction  is replaced by the left ideal
.

With this convention, uniform filters correspond to linear (additive) topologies, while the
additional Gabriel condition (axiom T4) imposes an algebraic saturation property that does not
change the induced topology.

## References

* Bo Stenström, *Rings and Modules of Quotients*
* Bo Stenström, *Rings of Quotients*
* nLab: Uniform filter
* nLab: Gabriel filter
* nLab: Gabriel composition

# Predicate for Galois Groups

Given an action of a group  on an extension of fields , we introduce a predicate
 saying that  acts faithfully on  with fixed field . In particular,
we do not assume that  is an algebraic extension of .

## Implementation notes

We actually define  for extensions of rings , with the same definition
(faithful action on  with fixed ring ). This definition turns out to axiomatize a common
setup in algebraic number theory where a Galois group  acts on an extension of subrings
 (e.g., rings of integers). In particular, there are theorems in algebraic number theory that
naturally assume  and whose statements would otherwise require assuming
 (along with predicates relating
 and  to the rings  and ) despite  and  not appearing in the conclusion.

Unfortunately, this definition of  for extensions of rings  is
nonstandard and clashes with other notions such as the étale fundamental group. In particular, if
 is finite and  is integrally closed, then   is equivalent to
being integral and the fields of fractions  being Galois with Galois group
(see ), rather than  being étale for instance.

But in the absence of a more suitable name, the utility of the predicate  for
extensions of rings  seems to outweigh these terminological issues.

The Jacobson radical of a ring  is defined to be the intersection of all maximal ideals of .
This is similar to how the nilradical is equal to the intersection of all prime ideals of .

by letting the nilradical of an ideal  be the intersection of prime ideals containing .
Under this extension, the original nilradical is the radical of the zero ideal .
Here we define the Jacobson radical of an ideal  in a similar way,
as the intersection of maximal ideals containing .

# Jacobson Rings

The following conditions are equivalent for a ring :
1. Every radical ideal  is equal to its Jacobson radical
2. Every radical ideal  can be written as an intersection of maximal ideals
3. Every prime ideal  is equal to its Jacobson radical

Any ring satisfying any of these equivalent conditions is said to be Jacobson.
Some particular examples of Jacobson rings are also proven.
-  says that the quotient of a Jacobson ring is Jacobson.

# The Jacobi-Zariski exact sequence

Given algebras $R \to S \to T$, the Jacobi-Zariski exact sequence is a long exact sequence
relating the first homology of the naive cotangent complexes and the Kähler differentials of
the respective algebras. It takes the form:
$$
H_1(L_{T/R}) \to H_1(L_{T/S}) \to T \otimes_S \Omega_{S/R} \to \Omega_{T/R} \to \Omega_{T/S} \to 0
$$

T \otimes_S H_1(L_{S/R}) \to H_1(L_{T/R}) \to H_1(L_{T/S})
$$

# Krull dimensions of (commutative) rings

Given a commutative ring, its ring-theoretic Krull dimension is the order-theoretic Krull dimension
of its prime spectrum. Unfolding this definition, it is the length of the longest sequence(s) of
prime ideals ordered by strict inclusion.

The ring-theoretic Krull dimension is the Krull dimension of its spectrum ordered by inclusion.

# Wedderburn's Little Theorem

This file proves Wedderburn's Little Theorem.

## Main Declarations

* : a finite division ring is a field.

## Future work

A couple simple generalisations are possible:
* A finite ring is commutative iff all its nilpotents lie in the center.
  Chintala, Vineeth, *Sorry, the Nilpotents Are in the Center*
* A ring is commutative if all its elements have finite order.
  Dolan, S. W., *A Proof of Jacobson's Theorem*

When alternativity is added to Mathlib, one could formalise the Artin-Zorn theorem, which states
that any finite alternative division ring is in fact a field.


If interested, generalisations to semifields could be explored. The theory of semi-vector spaces is
not clear, but assuming that such a theory could be found where every module considered in the
below proof is free, then the proof works nearly verbatim.

Everything in this namespace is internal to the proof of Wedderburn's little theorem.

We proceed by contradiction; that is, we assume the center is strictly smaller than .

# Local isomorphisms

A ring homomorphism is a local isomorphism if source locally (in the geometric sense)
it is a standard open immersion.

## Main declarations

- : The class of algebras that are locally standard open immersions.

We show that local isomorphisms are local, stable under composition and base change.

Most results in this file follow purely formally from the corresponding property of
standard open immersion. We could use the  API to obtain them, but
it would yield results with less universe generality and we would have to replace
 by . In the future, we may consider refactoring the API
for  properties to allow for also treating properties of s
and then simplify the proofs in this file.

it is a standard open immersion.

ring homomorphism  satisfying 3 properties:
1. For all ,  is a unit;
2. For all , there exists  such that ;
3. For all  such that , there exists  such that .
   (The converse is a consequence of 1.)

and  be submonoids of  and  respectively, e.g.:

## Main definitions

* : if  is another localization of  at , then  and

## Implementation notes

In maths it is natural to reason up to isomorphism, but in Lean we cannot naturally  one
structure with an isomorphic one; one way around this is to isolate a predicate characterizing
a structure up to isomorphism, and reason about things that satisfy the predicate.

A previous version of this file used a fully bundled type of ring localization maps,
then used a type synonym  for  to instantiate the
-algebra structure on . This results in defining ad-hoc copies for everything already
defined on . By making  a predicate on the ,
we can ensure the localization map commutes nicely with other s.

To prove most lemmas about a localization map  in this file we invoke the
corresponding proof for the underlying  localization map
, which can be found in
and the namespace .

To reason about the localization as a quotient type, use  and associated lemmas.
These show the quotient map  equals the surjection
 induced by the map .
The lemma  hence gives you access to the results in the rest of the file,
which are about the  induced by any localization map.

The proof that "a   which is the localization of an integral domain  at
is a field" is a  rather than an , so if you want to reason about a field of
fractions , assume  instead of just .

# Cardinality of localizations

In this file, we establish the cardinality of localizations. In most cases, a localization has
cardinality equal to the base ring. If there are zero-divisors, however, this is no longer true -
for example,  localized at  is equal to , and if you have zero in your
submonoid, then your localization is trivial (see ).

## Main statements

* : A localization has cardinality no larger than the base ring.
* : If you don't localize at zero-divisors, the localization of a ring
  has cardinality equal to its base ring.

A localization always has cardinality less than or equal to the base ring.

If you do not localize at any zero-divisors, localization preserves cardinality.

The S-polynomial of two polynomials.

Denoting

- the leading monomial of polynomial $f$ and $g$ as $lm(f)$ and $lm(g)$,
- the leading coefficient of $f$ and $g$ as $lc(f)$ and $lc(g)$
  (formalized as  and ), and
- the least common multiple of $lm(f)$ and $lm(g)$ as $lcm(lm(f),lm(g))$,

the S-polynomial of $f$ and $g$ is defined as
$$sPoly(f,g) := (lcm(lm(f),lm(g)) / lm(f)) * lc(g) * f - (lcm(lm(f),lm(g)) / lm(g)) * lc(f) * g.$$

$(lcm(lm(f),lm(g)) / lm(f))$ and $lcm(lm(f),lm(g)) / lm(g)$ is formalized as
 and , while there is
also another more direct formalization in .

Notice that, when the polynomial ring is over a field, S-polynomial is usually defined as
$$sPoly'(f,g) :=
  (lcm(lm(f),lm(g)) / (lm(f) * lc(f))) * f - (lcm(lm(f),lm(g)) / (lm(g) * lc(g))) * g,$$
while we avoid inverting $lc(f)$ and $lc(g)$ in this formalization so that it doesn't require a
field or units () over ring.

An equality between these two versions holds: $$sPoly(f,g) = lc(f) * lc(g) * sPoly'(f,g).$$

## Implementation Notes

In , we generalize the criterion for
topological nilpotency by proving that, if the base ring is equipped with a *linear* topology, then
a power series is topologically nilpotent if and only if its constant coefficient is.
This is lemma .

Mathematically, everything proven in this file follows from that general statement. However,
formalizing this yields a few (minor) annoyances:

- we would need to push the results in this file slightly lower in the import tree
  (likely, in a new dedicated file);
- we would have to work in s rather than s (this probably does not
  matter in any way though);
- because  holds for *any* topology,
  not necessarily discrete nor linear, the proof going through the general case involves
  juggling a bit with the topologies.

Since the code duplication is rather minor (the interesting part of the proof is already extracted
as ), we just leave this as is for now.
But future contributors wishing to clean this up should feel free to give it a try!

# Renaming variables of power series

This file establishes the  operation on multivariate power series
under a map with finite fibers, which modifies the set of variables.

Unlike polynomials, renaming variables in power series requires a finiteness condition
on the map  between the index types. Specifically, we require that  has
finite fibers, which is formalized as .
To see why this is necessary, consider a map from infinitely many variables to a single
variable sending each  to . The sum  is a valid power series in
, but we cannot rename each  to  since its image
would have an infinite coefficient for .

To avoid writing this assumption everywhere, we usually work with the typeclass assumption
. Note that this holds automatically if  is injective
or if  is finite.

For an -algebra ,  and ,

It is only well defined under one of the two following conditions:
  *  is a polynomial, in which case it is the classical evaluation;
  * or the condition  holds, which means:
    - For every , the constant coefficient of  is nilpotent;
    - For every , all but finitely many of the coefficients
       vanish.

In the other cases, it is defined as 0 (dummy value).

.

invocation of the discrete uniformity ().

and similar lemmas that hold for whatever uniformity on the space as soon
as it is discrete.

# Noetherian rings and modules

The following are equivalent for a module M over a ring R:
1. Every increasing chain of submodules M₁ ⊆ M₂ ⊆ M₃ ⊆ ⋯ eventually stabilises.
2. Every submodule is finitely generated.

A module satisfying these equivalent conditions is said to be a *Noetherian* R-module.
A ring is a *Noetherian ring* if it is Noetherian as a module over itself.

(Note that we do not assume yet that our rings are commutative,
so perhaps this should be called "left-Noetherian".
To avoid cumbersome names once we specialize to the commutative case,
we don't make this explicit in the declaration names.)

## Main definitions

Let  be a ring and let  and  be -modules. Let  be an -submodule of .

*  is the proposition that  is a Noetherian -module. It is a class,
  implemented as the predicate that all -submodules of  are finitely generated.

## Main statements

*  is the theorem that an R-module M is Noetherian iff  is well-founded on
  .

Note that the Hilbert basis theorem, that if a commutative ring R is Noetherian then so is R[X],
is proved in .

## References

* M. F. Atiyah and I. G. Macdonald, *Introduction to commutative algebra*
* P. Samuel, *Algebraic Theory of Numbers*

blocks ( here), then take the determinant over the base ring.

The Chebyshev polynomials are families of polynomials indexed by ,
with integral coefficients.

## Main definitions

* : the Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind.
* : the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind.
* : the rescaled Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind (also known as the
  Vieta–Lucas polynomials), given by $C_n(2x) = 2T_n(x)$.
* : the rescaled Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind (also known as the
  Vieta–Fibonacci polynomials), given by $S_n(2x) = U_n(x)$.

## Main statements

* The formal derivative of the Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind is a scalar multiple of the
  Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind.
* , twice the product of the -th and -th Chebyshev polynomials
  of the first kind is the sum of the -th and -th Chebyshev polynomials of the first
  kind. There is a similar statement  for the  polynomials.
* , the -th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind is the
  composition of the -th and -th Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind. There is a similar
  statement  for the  polynomials.

## Implementation details

Since Chebyshev polynomials have interesting behaviour over the complex numbers and modulo ,
we define them to have coefficients in an arbitrary commutative ring, even though
technically  would suffice.
The benefit of allowing arbitrary coefficient rings, is that the statements afterwards are clean,
and do not have  interfering all the time.

## References

[Lionel Ponton, _Roots of the Chebyshev polynomials: A purely algebraic approach_]
[ponton2020chebyshev]

# Quotients of polynomial rings

For a commutative ring $R$, evaluating a polynomial at an element $x \in R$ induces an
isomorphism of $R$-algebras $R[X] / \langle X - x \rangle \cong R$.

For a commutative ring $R$, evaluating a polynomial at an element $y \in R$ induces an
isomorphism of $R$-algebras $R[X] / \langle x, X - y \rangle \cong R / \langle x \rangle$.

For a commutative ring $R$, evaluating a polynomial at elements $y(X) \in R[X]$ and $x \in R$
induces an isomorphism of $R$-algebras $R[X, Y] / \langle X - x, Y - y(X) \rangle \cong R$.

# Formal power series (in one variable)

This file defines (univariate) formal power series
and develops the basic properties of these objects.

A formal power series is to a polynomial like an infinite sum is to a finite sum.

Formal power series in one variable are defined from multivariate
power series as .

The file sets up the (semi)ring structure on univariate power series.

We provide the natural inclusion from polynomials to formal power series.

Additional results can be found in:
* , truncation of power series;
* , about inverses of power series,
  and the fact that power series over a local ring form a local ring;
* , the order of a power series at 0,
  and application to the fact that power series over an integral domain form an integral domain.

## Implementation notes

Because of its definition,
  .
a lot of proofs and properties from the multivariate case
can be ported to the single variable case.
However, it means that formal power series are indexed by ,
which is of course canonically isomorphic to .
We then build some glue to treat formal power series as if they were indexed by .
Occasionally this leads to proofs that are uglier than expected.

# Weakly Quasi-finite primes

The definition  is equivalent to the usual definition "isolated in fibers"
mathematically for algebras of finite type, but this requires Zariski's main theorem to prove.
Hence we introduce a weaker notion of being  that we shall state
Zariski's main theorem in terms of, and deduce from this that  is
equivalent to  under all relevant scenarios.

This class should only be used in stating (and proving) Zariski's main theorem and should not be
used elsewhere, and all public API shall have a  version.

## Implementation details

The definition of  as is says that the whole  is quasi-finite,
which requires not only  to be quasi-finite, but also all primes below it (i.e. all generic
points that specialize to it) to also be quasi-finite.
This is fine mathematically because the set of quasi-finite primes is open
(according to Zariski's Main theorem). But this requires the statement of Zariski's main
to be stated with an a priori weaker notion of quasi-finite.
Hence we introduce  where we mod out all the primes that lie in a
different fiber.

which turns out to be equivalent to  (for finite type algebras)
due to Zariski's main theorem.

# Simple Modules

## Main Definitions
*  indicates that a module has no proper submodules
  (the only submodules are  and ).
*  indicates that every submodule has a complement, or equivalently,
  the module is a direct sum of simple modules.
* A  structure on the endomorphism ring of a simple module.

## Main Results
* Schur's Lemma:  shows that a linear map between simple modules
  is either bijective or 0, leading to a  structure on the endomorphism ring.
* :
  a module is simple iff it's isomorphic to the quotient of the ring by a maximal left ideal.
* :
  a module is semisimple iff it is generated by its simple submodules.
* :
  the annihilator of a semisimple module over a commutative ring is a radical ideal.
* , :
  any submodule or quotient module of a semisimple module is semisimple.
* :
  a module generated by semisimple submodules is itself semisimple.
* : every module over a semisimple ring is semisimple.
* : a finite product of semisimple rings is semisimple.
* : any quotient of a semisimple ring is semisimple.

# Wedderburn–Artin Theorem

## Main results

* : a simple ring is semisimple iff it is Artinian,
  iff it has a minimal left ideal.

* : a ring is simple Artinian iff it is semisimple, isotypic,
  and nontrivial.

* : a simple Artinian algebra is
  isomorphic to a (finite-dimensional) matrix algebra over a division algebra. The division
  algebra is the opposite of the endomorphism algebra of a simple (i.e., minimal) left ideal.

* : a semisimple algebra is
  isomorphic to a finite direct product of matrix algebras over division algebras. The division
  algebras are the opposites of the endomorphism algebras of the simple (i.e., minimal)
  left ideals.

* ,
  :
  if the simple Artinian / semisimple algebra is finite as a module over a base ring, then the
  division algebra(s) are also finite over the same ring.
  If the base ring is an algebraically closed field, the only finite-dimensional division algebra
  over it is itself, and we obtain  and
   (in a later file).

A simple ring is semisimple iff it is Artinian, iff it has a minimal left ideal.

The **Wedderburn–Artin Theorem**: an Artinian simple ring is isomorphic to a matrix
ring over the opposite of the endomorphism ring of its simple module.

The **Wedderburn–Artin Theorem**: an Artinian simple ring is isomorphic to a matrix
ring over a division ring.

The **Wedderburn–Artin Theorem**, algebra form: an Artinian simple algebra is isomorphic
to a matrix algebra over the opposite of the endomorphism algebra of its simple module.

The **Wedderburn–Artin Theorem**, algebra form: an Artinian simple algebra is isomorphic
to a matrix algebra over a division algebra.

The **Wedderburn–Artin Theorem**, algebra form, finite case: a finite Artinian simple algebra is
isomorphic to a matrix algebra over a finite division algebra.

# Chevalley's theorem with complexity bound

⚠ For general usage, see .

Chevalley's theorem states that if  is a finitely presented ring hom between commutative
rings, then the image of a constructible set in  is a constructible set in .

Constructible sets in the prime spectrum of  are made of closed sets in the prime spectrum
(using unions, intersections, and complements), which are themselves made from a family of
polynomials.

We say a closed set *has complexity at most * if it can be written as the zero locus of a family
of at most  polynomials each of degree at most . We say a constructible set *has complexity
at most * if it can be written as  where ,  are closed
sets of complexity at most  and  is a closed set.

This file proves a complexity-aware version of Chevalley's theorem, namely that a constructible set
of complexity at most  in  gets mapped under
 to a constructible set of complexity  in
.

The bound  we find is of tower type.

## Sketch proof

We first show the result in the case of . We prove this by induction on the number of
components of the form , then by induction again on the number of polynomials
used to describe . See the (private) lemma .

Secondly, we prove the result in the case of  by composing the first result
with itself  times. See the (private) lemma .

Note that, if composing the first result for  and  naïvely,
the second map  won't *see* the -degree of the polynomials used to

## Main results

  a topological basis.

  range of the embedding is the  associated to the element.

  commutative semirings induces an embedding between the prime spectra.

* : a surjective ring homomorphism between
  commutative rings induces a closed embedding between the prime spectra.

  to the disjoint union of the prime spectra.

# Extension of Valuations

In this file, we define the typeclass for valuation extensions and prove basic facts about the
extension of valuations. Let  be an  algebra, equipped with valuations  and
respectively. Here, the extension of a valuation means that the pullback of valuation  to
is equivalent to the valuation  on . We only require equivalence, not equality, of
valuations here.

Note that we do not require the ring map from  to  to be injective. This holds automatically
when  is a division ring and  is nontrivial.

A motivation for choosing the more flexible  rather than strict equality here is
to allow for possible normalization. As an example, consider a finite extension  of ,
which is a discretely valued field. We may choose the valuation on  to be either:

1. the valuation where the uniformizer is mapped to one (more precisely,  in ) or

2. the valuation where  is mapped to one.

For the algebraic closure of , if we choose the valuation of  to be one, then the
restriction of this valuation to  equals the second valuation, but is only equivalent to the
first valuation. The flexibility of equivalence here allows us to develop theory for both cases
without first determining the normalizations once and for all.

## Main Definition

*  : The valuation  on  is an extension of the valuation
   on .

## Remark

The last two axioms in , namely  and , are
used to ensure that we have a well-behaved valuation taking values in a *value group* (with zero).
In principle, it should be possible to drop these two axioms and obtain a value monoid,
however, such a value monoid would not necessarily embed into an ordered abelian group with zero.
Similarly, without these axioms, the support of the valuation need not be a prime ideal.
We have thus opted to include these two axioms and obtain a  associated to
a  in order to best align with the literature about valuations on commutative rings.

Future work could refactor  by dropping the  and
axioms, opting to make these mixins instead.

# The  predicate

 is a (type-valued) predicate on functions .
It asserts that there is a family of polynomials ,
such that the th coefficient of  is equal to  evaluated on the coefficients of .
Many operations on Witt vectors satisfy this predicate (or an analogue for higher arity functions).
We say that such a function  is a *polynomial function*.

The power of satisfying this predicate comes from .
It shows that if  and  witness that  and  are polynomial functions,
then  not merely when , but in fact it suffices to prove
(in other words, when evaluating the Witt polynomials on  and , we get the same values)
which will then imply  and hence .

Even though this sufficient condition looks somewhat intimidating,
it is rather pleasant to check in practice;
more so than direct checking of .

In practice, we apply this technique to show that the composition of
and  is equal to multiplication by .

## On higher arity analogues

Ideally, there should be a predicate  for functions of higher arity,
together with  that shows how such functions compose.
Since mathlib does not have a library on composition of higher arity functions,
we have only implemented the unary and binary variants so far.
Nullary functions (a.k.a. constants) are treated
as constant functions and fall under the unary case.

# Club sets and stationary sets

A subset of a well-ordered type  is called a **club set** when it is closed in the order topology
and cofinal. If  has no maximum, then an equivalent condition is that  is closed and
unbounded; hence the name.

# A computable model of ZFA without infinity

In this file we define finite hereditary lists. This is useful for calculations in naive set theory.

We distinguish two kinds of ZFA lists:
* Atoms. Directly correspond to an element of the original type.
* Proper ZFA lists. Can be thought of (but are not implemented) as a list of ZFA lists (not
  necessarily proper).

For example,  contains stuff like , , , .

## Implementation note

As we want to be able to append both atoms and proper ZFA lists to proper ZFA lists, it's handy that
atoms and proper ZFA lists belong to the same type, even though atoms of  could be modelled as
 directly. But we don't want to be able to append anything to atoms.

This calls for a two-step definition of ZFA lists:
* First, define ZFA prelists as atoms and proper ZFA prelists. Those proper ZFA prelists are defined
  by inductive appending of (not necessarily proper) ZFA lists.
* Second, define ZFA lists by rubbing out the distinction between atoms and proper lists.

## Main declarations

* : Atoms as ZFA prelists. Basically a copy of .
* : Proper ZFA prelists. Defined inductively from the empty ZFA prelist
  () and from appending a ZFA prelist to a proper ZFA prelist ().
* : ZFA lists. Sum of the atoms and proper ZFA prelists.
* : ZFA sets. Defined as  quotiented by , the extensional
  equivalence.

Prelists, helper type to define .  are the "atoms", a copy of .
 are the "proper" ZFA prelists, inductively defined from the empty ZFA prelist and
from appending a ZFA prelist to a proper ZFA prelist. It is made so that you can't append anything
to an atom while having only one appending function for appending both atoms and proper ZFA prelists
to a proper ZFA prelist.

Hereditarily finite list, aka ZFA list. A ZFA list is either an "atom" (),
corresponding to an element of , or a "proper" ZFA list, inductively defined from the empty ZFA
list and from appending a ZFA list to a proper ZFA list.

Appending a ZFA list to a proper ZFA prelist.

Converts a ZFA prelist to a  of ZFA lists. Atoms are sent to .

Converts a  of ZFA lists to a proper ZFA prelist.

equivalent as a ZFA list to this ZFA list.

# Ordinal arithmetic

Ordinals have an addition (corresponding to the disjoint union) that turns them into an additive
monoid, and a multiplication (corresponding to the lexicographic order on the product) that turns
them into a monoid. One can also define (truncated) subtraction and division operators.

# Ordinals

Ordinals are defined as equivalences of well-ordered sets under order isomorphism. They are endowed
with a total order, where an ordinal is smaller than another one if it embeds into it as an
initial segment (or, equivalently, in any way). This total order is well founded.

# Cantor Normal Form

The Cantor normal form of an ordinal is generally defined as its base  expansion, with its
non-zero exponents in decreasing order. Here, we more generally define a base  expansion
 in this manner, which is well-behaved for any .

## Implementation notes

We implement  as an association list, where keys are exponents and values are
coefficients. This is because this structure intrinsically reflects two key properties of the Cantor
normal form:

- It is ordered.
- It has finitely many entries.

commonly refers to the values given by . Likewise, multiplicative principal ordinals

are elements in the set arbitrarily close to the ordinal from below.

# Von Neumann ordinals

This file works towards the development of von Neumann ordinals, i.e. transitive sets, well-ordered
under .

## Definitions

-  means that every element of a set is a subset.
-  means that the set is transitive and well-ordered under . We show multiple
  equivalences to this definition.
-  converts Lean's type-theoretic ordinals into ZFC ordinals. We prove that these
  two notions are order-isomorphic.

### Transitive sets

A transitive set is one where every element is a subset.

This is equivalent to being an infinite-open interval in the transitive closure of membership.

The union of a transitive set is transitive.

The union of transitive sets is transitive.

### Ordinals

A set  is a von Neumann ordinal when it's a transitive set, that's transitive under . We
prove that this further implies that  is well-ordered under  in .

The transitivity condition  can be written without assuming  and
. The lemma  shows this condition is equivalent to the usual one.

An ordinal is a transitive set.

The membership operation within an ordinal is transitive.

The simplified form of transitivity used within  yields an equivalent definition to
the standard one.

An ordinal is a transitive set of transitive sets.

An ordinal is a transitive set of ordinals.

An ordinal is a transitive set, trichotomous under membership.

An ordinal is a transitive set, well-ordered under membership.

A pre-set is inductively defined by its indexing type and its members, which are themselves
pre-sets.

 instance from it, and in  we define ZFC sets as the

with polynomials, but would be an issue when working with a number field over its ring of integers.

in the sense that either  is an -algebra or  is an -algebra.

## Further functionality

When given a composition of s, e.g. , the tactic will also try to
add the instance  if possible.

After having added suitable  and  instances, the tactic will search through
the local context for  properties that can be converted to properties of the corresponding
. For example, given  and , then  will add
the instance  and the corresponding property . The tactic knows
which  properties have a corresponding  property through the

## Algebraize attribute

The  attribute is used to tag  properties that can be converted to
properties. It assumes that the tagged declaration has a name of the form  and
that the corresponding  property has the name .

If not, the  of the corresponding algebra property can be provided as optional argument. The
specified declaration should be one of the following:

1. An inductive type (i.e. the  property itself), in this case it is assumed that the
    and the  property are definitionally the same, and the tactic will construct
   the  property by giving the  property as a term. Due to how this is performed,
   we also need to assume that the  property can be constructed only from the homomorphism,
   so it cannot have any other explicit arguments.
2. A lemma (or constructor) proving the  property from the  property. In this case
   it is assumed that the  property is the final argument, and that no other explicit
   argument is needed. The tactic then constructs the  property by applying the lemma or
   constructor.

A simp set for the  tactic.

is a simp set to prove tautologies about morphisms from some (tensor) power of
to , where  is a (commutative) monoid object in a (braided) monoidal category.

**This  set is incompatible with the standard simp set.**
If you want to use it, make sure to add the following to your simp call to disable the problematic
default simp lemmas:

The general algorithm it follows is to push the associators  and commutators  inwards until
they cancel against the right sequence of multiplications.

This approach is justified by the fact that a tautology in the language of (commutative) monoid
objects "remembers" how it was proved: Every use of a (commutative) monoid object axiom inserts a
unitor, associator or commutator, and proving a tautology simply amounts to undoing those moves as
prescribed by the presence of unitors, associators and commutators in its expression.

This simp set is opinionated about its normal form, which is why it cannot be used concurrently with
some of the simp lemmas in the standard simp set:
* It eliminates all mentions of whiskers by rewriting them to tensored homs,
  which goes against  and :
  , .
  This goes against  and  in the standard simp set.
* It collapses compositions of tensored homs to the tensored hom of the compositions,
  which goes against :
  . TODO: Isn't this direction Just Better?
* It cancels the associators against multiplications,
  which goes against :
  ,

* It unfolds non-primitive coherence isomorphisms, like the tensor strengths , .

is a simp set useful to prove tautologies on coalgebras.

The general algorithm it follows is to push the associators  and
commutators  inwards (to the right) until they cancel against
co-multiplications.

The simp set makes the following choice of normal form
* It regards , ,  as the primitive
  constructions and rewrites everything else such as ,  using them.
* It rewrites both sides into a right associated composition of linear maps.

## The  tactic

 is an  wrapper that proves inequalities by straightforward recursion on structure,
assuming that intermediate terms are nonnegative or positive as needed.  It also has some support
for guessing where it is unclear where to recurse, such as which side of a  or  to use
as the bound or whether to assume a power is less than or greater than one.

### Aesop rules

 uses threes types of aesop rules: , , and closing s.  To register a
lemma as an  rule, tag it with .  It will be automatically converted into either a
 or  rule depending on the number and type of its hypotheses:

1. Nonnegativity/positivity/nonpositivity/negativity hypotheses get score 1 (those involving ).
2. Other inequalities get score 10.
3. Disjunctions  get score 100, plus the score of  and .

Score  lemmas turn into  rules, and score  lemmas turn into
rules.  The score is roughly lexicographic ordering on the counts of the three type (guessing,
general, involving-zero), and tries to minimize the complexity of hypotheses we have to prove.
See  for the full algorithm.

To register a lemma as a  rule, tag it with .  The most important
builtin forward rule is , so that strict inequalities can be used to prove weak
inequalities.  Another example is , so that  knows that any
power series present in the context have positive radius of convergence.  Custom
rules that similarly expose inequalities inside structures are often useful.

### Guessing apply rules

There are several cases where there are two standard ways to recurse down an inequality, and it is
not obvious which is correct without more information.  For example,  is registered as
a  rule, since we always need to prove .  But if we see ,
either  or  suffices, and we don't know which.

In these cases we declare a new lemma with an  hypotheses that covers the two cases.  Tagging
it as  will add a +100 penalty to the score, so that it will be used only if necessary.
Aesop will then try both ways by splitting on the resulting  hypothesis.

Currently the two types of guessing rules are
1.  and  rules, for both  and
2.  and  monotonicity rules which branch on  or .
