# Normalization of 2-morphisms in bicategories

This file provides a function that normalizes 2-morphisms in bicategories. The function also
used to normalize morphisms in monoidal categories. This is used in the string diagram widget given
in , as well as  and  tactics.

We say that the 2-morphism  in a bicategory is in normal form if
1.  is of the form  where each  is a
  structural 2-morphism (consisting of associators and unitors),
2. each  is a non-structural 2-morphism of the form , and
3.  is of the form , and
4. each  is of the form .

Note that the horizontal composition  is not currently defined for bicategories. In the monoidal
category setting, the horizontal composition is defined as the , denoted by .

Note that the structural morphisms  are not necessarily normalized, as the main purpose
is to get a list of the non-structural morphisms out.

Currently, the primary application of the normalization tactic in mind is drawing string diagrams,
which are graphical representations of morphisms in monoidal categories, in the infoview. When
drawing string diagrams, we often ignore associators and unitors (i.e., drawing morphisms in
strict monoidal categories). On the other hand, in Lean, it is considered difficult to formalize
the concept of strict monoidal categories due to the feature of dependent type theory. The
normalization tactic can remove associators and unitors from the expression, extracting the
necessary data for drawing string diagrams.

The string diagrams widget is to use Penrose () via ProofWidgets.
However, it should be noted that the normalization procedure in this file does not rely on specific
settings, allowing for broader application. Future plans include the following. At least I (Yuma)
would like to work on these in the future, but it might not be immediate. If anyone is interested,
I would be happy to discuss.

- Currently, the string diagrams widget only do drawing. It would be better they also generate
  proofs. That is, by manipulating the string diagrams displayed in the infoview with a mouse to
  generate proofs. In ,
  the string diagram widget only uses the morphisms generated by the
  normalization tactic and does not use proof terms ensuring that the original morphism and the
  normalized morphism are equal. Proof terms will be necessary for proof generation.

- There is also the possibility of using homotopy.io (), a graphical
  proof assistant for category theory, from Lean. At this point, I have very few ideas regarding
  this approach.

#  tactic

This file provides  tactic, which solves equations in a monoidal category, where
the two sides only differ by replacing strings of monoidal structural morphisms (that is,
associators, unitors, and identities) with different strings of structural morphisms with the same
source and target. In other words,  solves equalities where both sides have the same
string diagrams.

The core function for the  tactic is provided in
. See this file for more details about the
implementation.

# Monoidal composition  (composition up to associators)

We provide , the  operation,
which automatically inserts associators and unitors as needed
to make the target of  match the source of .

## Example

Suppose we have a braiding morphism  in a monoidal category, and that we
want to define the morphism with the type  that
transposes the second and third components by . How to do this? The first guess would be
to use the whiskering operators  and , and define the morphism as .
However, this morphism has the type ,
which is not what we need. We should insert suitable associators. The desired associators can,
in principle, be defined by using the primitive three-components associator
 as a building block, but writing down actual definitions
are quite tedious, and we usually don't want to see them.

The monoidal composition  is designed to solve such a problem. In this case, we can define the
desired morphism as , where the first and the second
are completed as  and , respectively.

A typeclass carrying a choice of monoidal structural isomorphism between two objects.
Used by the  monoidal composition operator, and the  tactic.
We could likely turn this into a -valued existential if that proves useful.

out of unitors and associators.

# Point & click suggestions

This file defines , a command that enables an interactive interface that
gives lemma/tactic suggestions for any expression selected by the user.

The library search uses a (lazy)  to lookup a list of candidate rewrite lemmas.
It excludes lemmas that are automatically generated.
Each lemma is then checked one by one (in parallel) to see whether it is applicable.
For each lemma that works, the corresponding /// tactic is constructed,
so that it can be pasted into the editor when selected by the user.

The  lookup groups the results by match pattern and gives a score to each pattern.
This is used to display the results in sections. The sections are ordered by this score.
Within each section, the lemmas are sorted by
- lemmas with fewer extra goals come first
- left-to-right rewrites come before right-to-left rewrites
- shorter lemma names come first
- shorter replacement expressions come first (when taken as a string)
- alphabetically ordered by lemma name

The lemmas are optionally filtered to avoid duplicate rewrites, or trivial rewrites. This
is controlled by the filter button on the top right of the results.

When a rewrite lemma introduces new goals, these are shown after a .

# Generating a shortlist of candidate lemmas for suggestions

## Discrimination tree lookup

This file defines how to build and match with the discrimination trees, for premises that are
- imported
- from the current module
- local hypotheses

## Performance note

When importing all of mathlib, building the discrimination trees takes on the order of 10-15
seconds. This is because of two distinct performance bottlenecks:

1. Looping through the environment, and computing all of the discrimination tree entries is
  expensive, and is done in parallel to speed it up.
2. Building the final discrimination tree by inserting all of the computed entries is less
  expensive, but it cannot be done in parallel, because a single datastructure is being built.

These two bottlenecks cost about the same amount of time. Luckily, we can already start doing (2)
as soon as any of the parallel tasks from (1) have finished. So, we build the discrimination tree
(on the main thread) at the same time that the entries are being computed on various parallel
threads.

A multiseries is *trimmed* when its leading coefficient (the head of its expansion) is itself
trimmed and non-zero. For a trimmed multiseries, the leading monomial captures the main
asymptotic behavior of the approximated function.

# The  and  tactics

The  and  tactics are variants of the  tactic in Lean core,
except that
-  does not reorder goals
-  adds only non-dependent premises as new goals.

, on a goal which is an inductive type, solves it by applying the first matching
constructor, creating new goals for all arguments to the constructor in the same order.
This is like  except the goals are not reordered.

, on a goal which is an inductive type, solves it by applying the first matching
constructor, creating new goals for non-dependent arguments to the constructor in the same order.
This is like  except only non-dependent arguments are shown as new goals.

# Continuity

We define the  tactic using .

adds the tagged definition to the set of lemmas used by the  tactic.
Lemmas are used without backtracking: when the conclusion of this lemma matches the goal, the lemma
is applied unconditionally. Thus a lemma should preserve provability: if the goal can be proven,
then after applying a  lemma to it, the generated subgoals should remain provable.

solves goals of the form  by applying lemmas tagged with the attribute
. If the goal is not solved after attempting all rules,  fails.

to solve more goals.

There is a term elaborator  implementing the derivation of  instances.

This is implemented using  and , which is a term elaborator
that creates an equivalence from a "proxy type" composed of basic type constructors. If Lean

## Implementation notes

There are two kinds of  instances that we generate, depending on the inductive type.

If it is an enum (an inductive type with only 0-ary constructors), then we generate the
complete  of all constructors; see  for more
details. The proof has $O(n)$ complexity in the number of constructors.

Otherwise, the strategy we take is to generate a "proxy type", define an equivalence between
our type and the proxy type (see ), and then use  to pull a
 instance on the proxy type (if one exists) to our inductive type. For example, with
the  type above, we generate . While the proxy type is not a finite type
in general, we add  instances for every type parameter of our inductive type (and
 instances for every  parameter). Hence, in our example we get

There is a source of quadratic complexity in this  instance from the fact that an
inductive type with  constructors has a proxy type of the form ,
so mapping to and from  requires looking through  levels of  constructors.
Ignoring time spent looking through these constructors, the construction of
contributes just linear time with respect to the cardinality of the type since the instances
involved compute the underlying  for the  as  with
right associativity.

Note that an alternative design could be that instead of using  we could create a
function  with  and then use  for
the proxy type, which would save us from the nested  constructors.

This implementation takes some inspiration from the one by Mario Carneiro for Mathlib 3.
A difference is that the Mathlib 3 version does not explicitly construct the total proxy type,
and instead it opts to construct the underlying  as a disjoint union of the
for each individual constructor's proxy type.

using all the assumptions in the local context; this can be useful, for example, if one
needs an extra  instance. It works only if  is an inductive

expected type, so  works.

# A tool for finding duplicate declarations

It is easy to accidentally create multiple instances of the same theorem or instance.
This file defines a tool to automatically detect such cases.
The order of hypotheses, and their binder info and binder names are ignored.
Universe parameters are also ignored.

For theorems, it is completely redundant to have multiple of the same type.
For instances, we typically also don't want to have multiple of the same type.

To use it, simply run the following command in a file that does not use the module system:

## How does it work

The function  reorders the forall binders of a declaration type into a canonical form,
which lets us detect duplication even when the arguments are in a different order.
We also erase the binder kinds (e.g. implicit/explicit) in the type,
and we erase all universe levels, both of which help to find more duplicates.

To avoid flagging aliases as duplicate (which are most likely intentionally duplicated),
we filter out declarations that are defined as another declaration (see ).

The results are sorted by module name.

Clear all universe levels from an expression, so that they are ignored.
Note: I tried using a cache in the implementation, but that seemed to only slow things down.

Sort the hypotheses in  into a normalized order by sorting their types.
Also replace universe levels with a default value.

This is a limitation of the current approach.

If so, we assume that the declaration is intentionally duplicated.
This only works for exposed definitions.

Main definition behind  command.

displays a proof term in a line-by-line format somewhat akin to a Fitch-style
proof or the Metamath proof style.

For example, exploding the following theorem:


produces:


## Overview

The  command takes the body of the theorem and decomposes it into its parts,
displaying each expression constructor one at a time. The constructor is indicated
in some way in column 3, and its dependencies are recorded in column 2.

These are the main constructor types:

  - Lambda expressions (). The expression  is displayed as
    with  a wildcard, and there can be intervening steps between 0 and 1.
    Nested lambda expressions can be merged, and  can depend on a whole list of arguments.

  - Applications (). The expression  is displayed as
     There can be intervening steps between each of these.
     As a special case, if  is a constant it can be omitted and the display instead looks like

  - Let expressions () do not display in any special way, but they do
    ensure that in  that  is processed first and then , rather
    than first doing zeta reduction. This keeps lambda merging and application merging
    from making proofs with  confusing to interpret.

  - Everything else (constants, fvars, etc.) display  as

## In more detail

The output of  is a Fitch-style proof in a four-column diagram modeled after Metamath
proof displays like this. The headers of the columns are
"Step", "Hyp", "Ref", "Type" (or "Expression" in the case of Metamath):
* **Step**: An increasing sequence of numbers for each row in the proof, used in the Hyp fields.
* **Hyp**: The direct children of the current step. These are step numbers for the subexpressions
  for this step's expression. For theorem applications, it's the theorem arguments, and for
  foralls it is all the bound variables and the conclusion.
* **Ref**: The name of the theorem being applied. This is well-defined in Metamath, but in Lean
  there are some special steps that may have long names because the structure of proof terms doesn't
  exactly match this mold.
  * If the theorem is :
    * the Ref field will contain ,
    *  and  will be suppressed, because term construction is not interesting, and
    * the Hyp field will reference steps proving  and . This corresponds to a proof term
      like  where  and  are subproofs.
    * In the Hyp column, suppressed terms are omitted, including terms that ought to be
      suppressed but are not (in particular lambda arguments).
      TODO: implement a configuration option to enable representing suppressed terms using
      an  rather than a step number.
  * If the head of the proof term is a local constant or lambda, then in this case the Ref will
    say  for forall-elimination. This happens when you have for example  and
     and prove  by ; we reinterpret this as if it said  where  is
    (n-ary) modus ponens.
  * If the proof term is a lambda, we will also use  for forall-introduction, referencing the
    body of the lambda. The indentation level will increase, and a bracket will surround the proof
    of the body of the lambda, starting at a proof step labeled with the name of the lambda variable
    and its type, and ending with the  step. Metamath doesn't have steps like this, but the
    style is based on Fitch proofs in first-order logic.
* **Type**: This contains the type of the proof term, the theorem being proven at the current step.

Also, it is common for a Lean theorem to begin with a sequence of lambdas introducing local
constants of the theorem. In order to minimize the indentation level, the  steps at the end of
the proof will be introduced in a group and the indentation will stay fixed. (The indentation
brackets are only needed in order to delimit the scope of assumptions, and these assumptions
have global scope anyway so detailed tracking is not necessary.)

Adapted from  implementation

Have  extract the full local context.

Configuration for  for which variables from the context to include.

formats the current goal as a stand-alone theorem or definition after
cleaning up the local context of irrelevant variables.

A variable is *relevant* if (1) it occurs in the target type, (2) there is a relevant variable
that depends on it, or (3) the type of the variable is a proposition that depends on a

# Fail if no progress

This implements the  tactic, which fails if no actual progress is made by the
following tactic sequence.

"Actual progress" means that either the number of goals has changed, that the
number or presence of expressions in the context has changed, or that the type of some expression
in the context or the type of the goal is no longer definitionally equal to what it used to be at
reducible transparency.

# A tactic for proving algebraic goals in a field

This file contains the  tactic, a finishing tactic which roughly consists of running
.

solves equality goals in (semi-)fields. The goal must be an equality which is *universal*,
in the sense that it is true in any field in which the appropriate denominators don't vanish.
(That is, it is a consequence purely of the field axioms.)

The  tactic is built from the tactics  (which clears the denominators) and
(which proves equality goals universally true in commutative (semi-)rings). If  fails to
prove your goal, you may still be able to prove your goal by running the  and
normalizations in some order.

The tactic will try discharge proofs of nonzeroness of denominators, and skip steps if discharging
fails. These denominators are made out of denominators appearing in the input expression, by
repeatedly taking products or divisors. The default discharger can be non-universal, i.e. can be
specific to the field at hand (order properties, explicit  hypotheses,  if that is
known, etc). See  for full details of the default discharger
algorithm.

*  uses the tactic sequence  to discharge nonzeroness proofs.
*  provides terms , ...,  to the discharger for nonzeroness proofs.

normalizes expressions in (semi-)fields (i.e., does not require additive inverses)
by rewriting them to a common denominator, i.e. to reduce them to expressions of the form
where neither  nor  contains any division symbol. The  tactic will also clear
denominators in field *(in)equalities*, by cross-multiplying.

A very common pattern is  (clear denominators, then the resulting goal is
solvable by the axioms of a commutative ring). The finishing tactic  is a shorthand for this
pattern.

The tactic will try discharge proofs of nonzeroness of denominators, and skip steps if discharging
fails. These denominators are made out of denominators appearing in the input expression,

specific to the field at hand (order properties, explicit  hypotheses,  if that is

### Advanced

### Type of Theorems

There are four types of theorems that are used a bit differently.

- Lambda Theorems:
    These theorems are about basic lambda calculus terms like identity, constant, composition, etc.
    They are used when a bigger expression is decomposed into a sequence of function compositions.
    They are also used when, for example, we know that a function is continuous in the  and
    variables, but we want continuity only in .

    There are five of them, and they should be formulated in the following way:

    - Identity Theorem

    - Constant Theorem

    - Composition Theorem

    - Apply Theorem
      It can be either non-dependent version
      or dependent version

    - Pi Theorem

    Not all of these theorems have to be provided, but at least the identity and composition
    theorems should be.

    You should also add theorems for , , and . Technically speaking,
    they fall under the *function theorems* category, but without them,  can't function
    properly. We are mentioning them as they are used together with *lambda theorems* to break
    complicated expressions into a composition of simpler functions.

- Function Theorems:
    When  breaks complicated expression apart using *lambda theorems* it then uses
    *function theorems* to prove that each piece is, for example, continuous.

    The function theorem for  and  can be stated as:
    or as:
    The first form is called *uncurried form* and the second form is called *compositional form*.
    You can provide either form; it is mainly a matter of convenience. You can check if the form of
    a theorem has been correctly detected by turning on the option:
    If you really care that the resulting proof term is as short as possible, it is a good idea to
    provide both versions.

    One exception to this rule is the theorem for , which has to be stated in compositional
    form. This because this theorem together with *lambda theorems* is used to break expression to
    smaller pieces and   assumes it is written in compositional form.

    The reason the first form is called *uncurried* is because if we have a function of multiple
    arguments, we have to uncurry the function:
    and the *compositional form* of this theorem is:

    When dealing with functions with multiple arguments, you need to state, e.g., continuity only
    in the maximal set of arguments. Once we state that addition is jointly continuous in both
    arguments, we do not need to add new theorems that addition is also continuous only in the first
    or only in the second argument. This is automatically inferred using lambda theorems.


- Morphism Theorems:
    The  tactic can also deal with bundled morphisms. For example, we can state that every
    continuous linear function is indeed continuous:
    In this case, the head of the function body  is . This function is
    treated differently and its theorems are tracked separately.

     has two arguments: the morphism  and the argument . One difference is that
    theorems talking about the argument  have to be stated in the compositional form:
    Note that without notation and coercion, the function looks like
    .

    In fact, not only  but any function coercion is treated this way. Such function
    coercion has to be registered with  with coercion type .
    Here is an example of custom structure  that should be considered as bundled
    morphism by :

- Transition Theorems:
    Transition theorems allow  to infer one function property from another.
    For example, a theorem like:
    There are two features of these theorems: they mix different function properties and the
    conclusion is about a free variable .

    Transition theorems are the most dangerous theorems as they considerably increase the search
    space since they do not simplify the function in question. For this reason,  only
    applies transition theorems to functions that can't be written as a non-trivial composition of
    two functions (,  is considered to be a trivial composition).

    For this reason, it is recommended to state *function theorems* for every property. For example,
    if you have a theorem:
    you should also state the continuous theorem:
    even though  can already prove  from  and
    . Doing this will have a considerable impact on  speed.

    By default,  will not apply more than one transition theorem consecutively. For
    example, it won't prove  from  by using transition theorems
     and . You can enable this by running
    .
    Ideally  theorems should be transitively closed i.e. if  and
     are  theorems then  should be too.

    Transition theorems do not have to be between two completely different properties. They can be
    between the same property differing by a parameter. Consider this example:
    which is first reduced to  using lambda theorems and then the transition
    theorem:
    is used together with  to discharge the  subgoal.

# The  ("generalized congruence") tactic

The  tactic applies "generalized congruence" rules, reducing a relational goal
between an LHS and RHS matching the same pattern to relational subgoals between the differing
inputs to the pattern.  For example,
This example has the goal of proving the relation  between an LHS and RHS both of the pattern
(with inputs ,  on the left and ,  on the right); after the use of
, we have the simpler goals  and .

A depth limit, or a pattern can be provided explicitly;
this is useful if a non-maximal match is desired:

## Sourcing the generalized congruence lemmas

Relevant "generalized congruence" lemmas are declared using the attribute .  For
example, the first example constructs the proof term
using the generalized congruence lemmas  and . The term
 is automatically generated by a discharger (see below).

When a lemma is tagged , it is verified that the lemma is of "generalized congruence"
form, , that is, a relation between the application of a function to two
argument lists, in which the "varying argument" pairs (here / and /) are all free
variables. The  tactic will try a lemma only if it matches the goal in relation ,
head function  and the arity of .  It prioritizes lemmas with fewer "varying arguments". Thus,
for example, all three of the following lemmas are tagged  and are used in different
situations according to whether the goal compares constant-left-multiplications,
constant-right-multiplications, or fully varying multiplications:
The advantage of this approach is that the lemmas with fewer "varying" input pairs typically require
fewer side conditions, so the tactic becomes more useful by special-casing them.

There can also be more than one generalized congruence lemma dealing with the same relation
and head function, for example with purely notational head
functions which have different theories when different typeclass assumptions apply.  For example,
the following lemma is stored with the same  data as  above, and the two
lemmas are simply tried in succession to determine which has the typeclasses relevant to the goal:

## Resolving goals

The tactic attempts to discharge side goals to the "generalized congruence" lemmas (such as the
side goal  in the above application of ) using the tactic
, which wraps  but can also be extended. Side goals not discharged
in this way are left for the user.

The tactic also attempts to discharge "main" goals using the available hypotheses, as well as a
limited amount of forward reasoning.  Such attempts are made *before* descending further into
matching by congruence. The built-in forward-reasoning includes reasoning by symmetry and
reflexivity, and this can be extended by writing tactic extensions tagged with the
 attribute.

## Introducing variables and hypotheses

Some natural generalized congruence lemmas have "main" hypotheses which are universally quantified
or have the structure of an implication, for example
The tactic automatically introduces the variable  and hypothesis  in the
subgoal  generated by applying this lemma.  By default this is done
anonymously, so they are inaccessible in the goal state which results.  The user can name them if
needed using the syntax .

## Variants

The tactic  is a variant of , intended for teaching.  Local hypotheses are not
used automatically to resolve main goals, but must be invoked by name:
The  tactic is finishing-only: it fails if any main or side goals are not resolved.

## Implementation notes

### Patterns

When you provide a pattern, such as in , this is elaborated with a metadata
annotation at each  hole. This is then unified with the LHS of the relation in the goal.
As a result, the pattern becomes the same as the LHS, but with mdata annotations that
indicate where the original  holes were. The LHS is then replaced with this expression so that
 can tell based on the LHS how far to continue recursively. We also keep track of when
then LHS and RHS swap around, so that we know where to look for the metadata annotation.

# Custom grind-sets

In this file we declare custom grind attributes and tactics that call grind using only these grind
attributes. These grind sets are helpful because they can contain a lot of specialized ways to
prove a particular problem.

Currently, this implements the  and  grind attribute and tactic.

## Usage Notes

These tactics can be useful for various purposes:
* directly as a tactic:
* as auto-params for lemmas:
* as discharger for other tactics, e.g.
* You can also use the grind sets directly: .
  This is especially useful if you want to combine multiple grind sets.

## Implementation Notes

We define these grind sets so that we can aggressively tag lemmas in one particular topic as
grind lemmas for a particular grind set. For the default grind set we should be a lot
more careful with tagging lemmas, to avoid slowing down , but since these specialized grind
attributes don't have any tagged lemmas outside its specialized domain, it should still be
performant.

These tactics will not use the full power of grind, and could disable some of the grind engines if
these would slow down these tactics. We could have alternatively used a tactic similar to
 here, but we think that the efficient implementation of  is helpful even for
these simpler tactics. For example, we can safely tag both the following lemmas, and  will
add both pairs of hypotheses to the whiteboard without having to backtrack.

We will tag transition theorems, e.g.  should be
tagged , even if  won't contain lemmas about finite sets.
The advantages of this are that we can use local finiteness hypotheses, and this will ensure that
the different grind sets will interact well with each other. For the same reason we tag lemmas
that involve other properties, e.g.

## To do

* Implement other grind sets, e.g. , , , ...

#  tactic

Normalizes expressions in the language of groups. The basic idea is to use the simplifier
to put everything into a product of group powers ( which takes a group element and an
integer), then simplify the exponents using the  tactic. The process needs to be repeated
since  can normalize an exponent to zero, leading to a factor that can be removed
before collecting exponents again. The simplifier step also uses some extra lemmas to avoid
some  invocations.

## TODO

- Surface non-progress-related errors from .
- Allow s  behavior to be configurable.

## Tags

group theory

The next three lemmas are not general purpose lemmas, they are intended for use only by
the  tactic.

normalizes expressions in multiplicative groups that occur in the goal.  does not
assume commutativity, instead using only the group axioms without any information about which group
is manipulated. If the goal is an equality, and after normalization the two sides are equal,
closes the goal.

For additive commutative groups, use the  tactic instead.

*  normalizes at the given locations.

# Intuitionistic tautology () decision procedure

The  tactic will prove any intuitionistic tautology. It implements the well-known
 algorithm:
Dyckhoff, *Contraction-free sequent calculi for intuitionistic logic*.

All built in propositional connectives are supported: , , , , ,
, , , as well as  and  on propositions. Anything else, including definitions
and predicate logical connectives ( and ), are not supported, and will have to be
simplified or instantiated before calling this tactic.

The resulting proofs will never use any axioms except possibly , and  is only
used if the input formula contains an equality of propositions . Using , one can
enable the selective use of LEM for case splitting on specified propositions.

## Implementation notes

  It will either return the new context, or if it happens to notice a proof of false, it will
  return a function to compute a proof of any proposition in the original context.

def Proof.check : Lean.NameMap IProp → Proof → Option IProp
  | _, .sorry A => some A
  | Γ, .hyp i => Γ.find? i
  | _, triv => some .true
  | Γ, .exfalso' A p => guard (p.check Γ = some .false) *> pure A
  | Γ, .intro x A p => do let B ← p.check (Γ.insert x A); pure (.imp A B)
  | Γ, .andLeft ak p => do
    let .and' ak' A B ← p.check Γ | none
    guard (ak = ak') *> pure (ak.sides A B).1
  | Γ, .andRight ak p => do
    let .and' ak' A B ← p.check Γ | none
    guard (ak = ak') *> pure (ak.sides A B).2
  | Γ, .andIntro .and p q => do
    let A ← p.check Γ; let B ← q.check Γ
    pure (A.and B)
  | Γ, .andIntro ak p q => do
    let .imp A B ← p.check Γ | none
    let C ← q.check Γ; guard (C = .imp B A) *> pure (A.and' ak B)
  | Γ, .curry ak p => do
    let .imp (.and' ak' A B) C ← p.check Γ | none
    let (A', B') := ak.sides A B
    guard (ak = ak') *> pure (A'.imp $ B'.imp C)
  | Γ, .curry₂ ak p q => do
    let .imp (.and' ak' A B) C ← p.check Γ | none
    let A₂ ← q.check Γ
    let (A', B') := ak.sides A B
    guard (ak = ak' ∧ A₂ = A') *> pure (B'.imp C)
  | Γ, .app' p q => do
    let .imp A B ← p.check Γ | none
    let A' ← q.check Γ
    guard (A = A') *> pure B
  | Γ, .orImpL B p => do
    let .imp (.or A B') C ← p.check Γ | none
    guard (B = B') *> pure (A.imp C)
  | Γ, .orImpR A p => do
    let .imp (.or A' B) C ← p.check Γ | none
    guard (A = A') *> pure (B.imp C)
  | Γ, .orInL B p => do let A ← p.check Γ; pure (A.or B)
  | Γ, .orInR A p => do let B ← p.check Γ; pure (A.or B)
  | Γ, .orElim' p x q r => do
    let .or A B ← p.check Γ | none
    let C ← q.check (Γ.insert x A)
    let C' ← r.check (Γ.insert x B)
    guard (C = C') *> pure C
  | _, .em _ _ A => pure (A.or A.not)
  | Γ, .decidableElim _ A _ x p₂ p₃ => do
    let C ← p₂.check (Γ.insert x A)
    let C' ← p₃.check (Γ.insert x A.not)
    guard (C = C') *> pure C
  | Γ, .impImpSimp _ A p => do
    let .imp (.imp A' B) C ← p.check Γ | none
    guard (A = A') *> pure (B.imp C)

assumption), and . We decompose the double implication into two subgoals: one to
prove , which can be written  (where we used  to simplify

potentially many implications to split like this, and we have to try all of them if we want to be
complete.

we don't make any more progress, we go to the search phase.

The description of the preprocessor.

A preprocessor transforms a proof of a proposition into a proof of a different proposition.
The return type is , since some preprocessing steps may create multiple new hypotheses,
and some may remove a hypothesis from the list.
A "no-op" preprocessor should return its input as a singleton list.

Some preprocessors perform branching case splits.

# : solving linear arithmetic goals

 is a tactic for solving goals with linear arithmetic.

Suppose we have a set of hypotheses in  variables
,
where .
Our goal is to determine if the inequalities in  are jointly satisfiable, that is, if there is
an assignment of values to  such that every inequality in  is true.

Specifically, we aim to show that they are *not* satisfiable. This amounts to proving a
contradiction. If our goal is also a linear inequality, we negate it and move it to a hypothesis
before trying to prove .

When the inequalities are over a dense linear order,  is a decision procedure: it will
prove  if and only if the inequalities are unsatisfiable.  will also run on some
types like  that are not dense orders, but it will fail to prove  on some unsatisfiable
problems. It will run over concrete types like , , and , as well as abstract types that
are instances of ,  and .

## Algorithm sketch

First, the inequalities in the set  are rearranged into the form , where
 and each  is of the form .

 uses an untrusted oracle to search for a certificate of unsatisfiability.
The oracle searches for a list of natural number coefficients  such that , where for
at least one ,  and .

Given a list of such coefficients,  verifies that  using a normalization
tactic such as . It proves that  by transitivity, since each component of the sum
is either equal to, less than or equal to, or less than zero by hypothesis. This produces a
contradiction.

## Preprocessing

 does some basic preprocessing before running. Most relevantly, inequalities over natural
numbers are cast into inequalities about integers, and rational division by numerals is canceled
into multiplication. We do this so that we can guarantee the coefficients in the certificate are
natural numbers, which allows the tactic to solve goals over types that are not fields.

Preprocessors are allowed to branch, that is, to case split on disjunctions.  will succeed
overall if it succeeds in all cases. This leads to exponential blowup in the number of
calls, and should be used sparingly. The default preprocessor set does not include case splits.

## Oracles

There are two oracles that can be used in  so far.

1. **Fourier-Motzkin elimination.**
  This technique transforms a set of inequalities in  variables to an equisatisfiable set in
   variables. Once all variables have been eliminated, we conclude that the original set was
  unsatisfiable iff the comparison  is in the resulting set.
  While performing this elimination, we track the history of each derived comparison. This allows us
  to represent any comparison at any step as a positive combination of comparisons from the original
  set. In particular, if we derive , we can find our desired list of coefficients
  by counting how many copies of each original comparison appear in the history.
  This oracle was historically implemented earlier, and is sometimes faster on small states, but it
  has bugs and cannot handle
  large problems. You can use it with .

2. **Simplex Algorithm (default).**
  This oracle reduces the search for an unsatisfiability certificate to some Linear Programming
  problem. The problem is then solved by a standard Simplex Algorithm. We use
  Bland's pivot rule to guarantee that the algorithm
  terminates.
  The default version of the algorithm operates with sparse matrices as it is usually faster. You
  can invoke the dense version by .

## Implementation details

 homogenizes numerical constants: the expression  is treated as a variable .

Often  is called on goals that have comparison hypotheses over multiple types. This
creates multiple  problems, each of which is handled separately; the goal is solved as
soon as one problem is found to be contradictory.

Disequality hypotheses  do not fit in this pattern.  will attempt to prove equality
goals by splitting them into two weak inequalities and running twice. But it does not split
disequality hypotheses, since this would lead to a number of runs exponential in the number of
disequalities in the context.

The oracle is very modular. It can easily be replaced with another function of type
,
which takes a list of comparisons and the largest variable
index appearing in those comparisons, and returns a map from comparison indices to coefficients.
An alternate oracle can be specified in the  object.

A variant, , adds an extra preprocessing step to handle some basic nonlinear goals.
There is a hook in the  configuration object to add custom preprocessing routines.

The certificate checking step is *not* by reflection.  converts the certificate into a
proof term of type .

Some of the behavior of  can be inspected with the option
.
However, both oracles mainly runs outside the tactic monad, so we cannot trace intermediate
steps there.

## File structure

The components of  are spread between a number of files for the sake of organization.

*  contains proofs of some arithmetic lemmas that are used in preprocessing and in
  verification.
*  contains data structures that are used across multiple files, along with some
  useful auxiliary functions.
*  contains functions used at the beginning of the tactic to transform
  hypotheses into a shape suitable for the main routine.
*  contains functions used to compute the linear structure of an expression.
* The  folder contains files implementing the oracles that can be used to produce a
  certificate of unsatisfiability.
*  contains the certificate checking functions that produce a proof of .
*  contains the control methods and user-facing components of the tactic.

# The Fourier-Motzkin elimination procedure

The Fourier-Motzkin procedure is a variable elimination method for linear inequalities.


Given a set of linear inequalities ,
we aim to eliminate a single variable  from the set.
We partition  into , , and ,
where  contains the comparisons  in which
the coefficient of  in  is positive, and similar.

For each pair of comparisons , ,
we compute coefficients  such that  cancels out .
We collect these sums  in a set  and set ,
a new set of comparisons in which  has been eliminated.

Theorem:  and  are equisatisfiable.

We recursively eliminate all variables from the system. If we derive an empty clause ,
we conclude that the original system was unsatisfiable.

2. We solve the equation  using Gauss Elimination, splitting the set of variables into
  *free* variables, which can take any value,
  and *basic* variables which are linearly expressed through the free one.
  This gives us an initial tableau for the Simplex Algorithm.
  See .

3. We run the Simplex Algorithm until it finds a solution.
  See the file .

We introduce two auxiliary variables and one constraint:
* The variable  is interpreted as "homogenized" . We need it because dealing with a
  homogenized problem is easier, but having some "unit" is necessary.
* To bound the problem we add the constraint  introducing new variable .

# Parsing input expressions into linear form

 computes the linear form of its input expressions,
assuming (without justification) that the type of these expressions
is a commutative semiring.
It identifies atoms up to ring-equivalence: that is,  will be identified ,
where the monomial  is the linear atom.

* Variables are represented by natural numbers.
* Monomials are represented by .
  The monomial  is represented by the empty map.
* Linear combinations of monomials are represented by .

All input expressions are converted to s, preserving the map from expressions to variables.
We then discard the monomial information, mapping each distinct monomial to a natural number.
The resulting  represents the ring-normalized linear form of the expression.
This is ultimately converted into a  in the obvious way.

 is the main entry point into this file. Everything else is contained.

looks for a key in  that is defeq to  (up to transparency ),
and returns the value associated with this key if it exists.
Otherwise, it fails.

We introduce a local instance allowing addition of s,
removing any keys with value zero.
We don't need to prove anything about this addition, as it is only used in meta code.

#  Tactic

In this file, the  tactic is created.  This tactic, which
works over s, attempts to simplify the target by creating a linear combination
of a list of equalities and subtracting it from the target. A
object can also be passed into the tactic, allowing the user to specify a
normalization tactic.

Over ordered algebraic objects (such as ), taking linear combinations of
inequalities is also supported.

## Implementation Notes

This tactic works by creating a weighted sum of the given equations with the
given coefficients.  Then, it subtracts the right side of the weighted sum
from the left side so that the right side equals 0, and it does the same with
the target.  Afterwards, it sets the goal to be the equality between the
left-hand side of the new goal and the left-hand side of the new weighted sum.
Lastly, calls a normalization tactic on this target.

## References

A value, equivalently a proof of .

The handling in  of left- and right-multiplication and scalar-multiplication
and of division all five proceed according to the same logic, specified here: given a proof  of
an (in)equality and a constant ,
* if  is a proof of an equation, multiply/divide through by ;
* if  is a proof of a non-strict inequality, run  to find a proof that  is
  nonnegative, then multiply/divide through by , invoking the nonnegativity of  where needed;
* if  is a proof of a strict inequality, run  to find a proof that  is positive
  (if possible) or nonnegative (if not), then multiply/divide through by , invoking the
  positivity or nonnegativity of  where needed.

This generic logic takes as a parameter the object : the four lemmas corresponding to the four
cases.

The  tactic attempts to prove an (in)equality goal by exhibiting it as a
specified linear combination of (in)equality hypotheses, or other (in)equality proof terms, modulo
(A) moving terms between the LHS and RHS of the (in)equalities, and (B) a normalization tactic
which by default is ring-normalization.

Example usage:

The input  in  is a linear combination of proofs of (in)equalities,
given as a sum/difference of coefficients multiplied by expressions.
The coefficients may be arbitrary expressions (with nonnegativity constraints in the case of
inequalities).
The expressions can be arbitrary proof terms proving (in)equalities;
most commonly they are hypothesis names , , ....

The left and right sides of all the (in)equalities should have the same type , and the
coefficients should also have type .  For full functionality  should be a commutative ring --
strictly speaking, a commutative semiring with "cancellative" addition (in the semiring case,
negation and subtraction will be handled "formally" as if operating in the enveloping ring). If a
nonstandard normalization is used (for example  or ), the tactic will work over types
 with less algebraic structure: for equalities, the minimum is instances of
 together with instances of whatever operations are used in the tactic
call.

The variant  specifies explicitly the "normalization tactic"
 to be run on the subgoal(s) after constructing the linear combination.
* The default normalization tactic is  (for equalities) or
  (for inequalities). These are finishing tactics: they close the goal or fail.
* When working in algebraic categories other than commutative rings -- for example fields, abelian
  groups, modules -- it is sometimes useful to use normalization tactics adapted to those categories
  (, , ).
* To skip normalization entirely, use  as the normalization tactic.
* The  tactic creates a linear combination by adding the provided (in)equalities
  together from left to right, so if  is not invariant under commutation of additive
  expressions, then the order of the input hypotheses can matter.

The variant  will take the goal to the th power before
subtracting the combination . In other words, if the goal is ,
 will change the goal to  before proceeding as
above.  This variant is implemented only for linear combinations of equalities (i.e., not for
inequalities).

These names are internal implementation details generated by the Lean elaborator.
They are not stable across refactors (e.g. reordering fields in a structure can renumber

,  and  provide backward-compatible implementations of their
unprimed equivalents in Lean 3 –,  and  respectively.
They have been superseded by Lean 4 tactics:

*  and  replace . While they are similar, they handle metavariables

  completely replace another. However,  and  are more readable and (heuristically)
  tend to be more efficient on average.
* ,  and  replace . Unlike the replacement tactics,

# The "flexible" linter

The "flexible" linter makes sure that a "rigid" tactic (such as ) does not act on the
output of a "flexible" tactic (such as ).

For example, this ensures that, if you want to use  in the middle of a proof,
then you should replace  by one of
* a  line;
* the output of , so that the final code contains ;
* something else that does not involve !

Otherwise, the linter will complain.

Simplifying and appealing to a geometric intuition, you can imagine a (tactic) proof like a
directed graph, where
* each node is a local hypothesis or a goal in some metavariable and
* two hypotheses/goals are connected by an arrow if there is a tactic that modifies the source
  of the arrow into the target (this does not apply well to all tactics, but it does apply to
  a large number of them).

With this in mind, a tactic like  takes a *very specific* input and return a
*very predictable* output.
Such a tactic is "rigid". Any tactic is rigid, unless it is in  or .
Conversely, a tactic like  acts on a wide variety of inputs and returns an output that
is possibly unpredictable: if later modifications adds a -lemma or some internals of
 changes, the output of  may change as well.
Such a tactic is . Other examples are , , ,...
Let's go back to the graph picture above.
* ✅️ [ --> ]
  A sequence  is unlikely to break, since  produces the same output
  unless some *really major* change happens!
* ❌️ [ --> ]
  A sequence  is instead more likely to break, since the goal after  is
  subject to change by even a small, likely, modification of the  set.
* ✅️ [ --> ]
  A sequence  is also quite stable, since if  was able to close the
  goal with a "weaker" , it will likely still be able to close the goal with a
  that takes one further step.
* ✅️ [ --> ]
  Finally, a sequence  is stable and, moreover, the output of  is a
  "normal form", which means that it is likely to produce an unchanged result, even if the initial
  input is different from the proof in its initial form.
  A stopper can be followed by a rigid tactic, "stopping" the spread of the flexible reach.

What the linter does is keeping track of nodes that are connected by  tactics and
makes sure that only  or  follow them.
Such nodes are .
Whenever it reaches a  edge, the target node is no longer  and it is
available again to  tactics.

Currently, the only tactics that "start" the bookkeeping are most forms of non- s.
These are encoded by the  predicate.
Future modifications of the linter may increase the scope of the  predicate and
forbid a wider range of combinations.

# -command linter

The -command linter produces a warning when a command starting with  is used *and*
* either the command emits no message;
* or  is set to .

The rationale behind this is that -commands are intended to be transient:
they provide useful information in development, but are not intended to be present in final code.
Most of them are noisy and get picked up anyway by CI, but even the quiet ones are not expected to
outlive their in-development status.

The linter emits a warning on any command beginning with  that itself emits no message.
For example,  and  trigger a message.
There is a list of silent -command that are allowed.

logs a warning only for the -commands that do not already emit a message.

# The "header" linter

The "header" style linter checks that a file starts with
It emits a warning if
* the copyright statement is malformed;
*  is imported;
* any import in  is present;
* the first non- command is not a module doc-string.

The linter allows -only files and does not require a copyright statement in .

## Implementation
The strategy used by the linter is as follows.
The linter computes the end position of the first module doc-string of the file,
resorting to the end of the file, if there is no module doc-string.
Next, the linter tries to parse the file up to the position determined above.

If the parsing is successful, the linter checks the resulting  and behaves accordingly.

If the parsing is not successful, this already means there is some "problematic" command
after the imports. In particular, there is a command that is not a module doc-string
immediately following the last import: the file should be flagged by the linter.
Hence, the linter then falls back to parsing the header of the file, adding a spurious
after it.
This makes it possible for the linter to check the entire header of the file, emit warnings that
could arise from this part and also flag that the file should contain a module doc-string after
the  statements.

* the first non- command in , otherwise.

- that function does not return the Syntax corresponding to each import,
which we use to log more precise warnings.

  parseable).

or the parsing is not successful and the linter will flag a missing module doc-string!

# The  linter

The  linter incrementally computes the minimal imports needed for each file to build.
Whenever it detects that a new command requires an increase in the (transitive) imports that it
computed so far, it emits a warning mentioning the bigger minimal imports.

Unlike the related  command, the linter takes into account notation and tactic
information.
It also works incrementally, accumulating increasing import information.
This is better suited, for instance, to split files.

The "multiGoal" linter emits a warning where there is more than a single goal in scope.
There is an exception: a tactic that closes *all* remaining goals is allowed.

There are a few tactics, such as ,  or the  combinator, that are intended to work
specifically in such a situation.
Otherwise, the mathlib style guide ask that goals be focused until there is only one active goal
at a time.
If this focusing does not happen, the linter emits a warning.
Typically, the focusing is achieved by the : , but, e.g.,  or
also serve a similar purpose.

# A linter for declarations with local instances that overlap

If the same data can be obtained from two different instances, we risk having
non-defeq versions of that data. This situation is known as an "instance diamond".
This linter warns against instance diamonds in local contexts.

This is a syntax linter. It is run on partially and fully elaborated declarations.

To find diamonds, we compute the parent classes of each local instance.
For classes that aren't structures, this is just the class itself.
If any of these parent classes is duplicated, we throw a warning.

This linter also warns on redundant proposition classes, i.e. those that can be synthesized from
the other instances in the local context. (Note: we do *not* warn on proposition classes that
merely overlap.) Even though redundant proposition classes cause no meaningful issue, they are
still undesirable.

A common case where this linter may fire is if the same type class assumption is given in both a
 statement and a declaration. This kind of variable shadowing does not actually produce
declarations with duplicate type class assumptions, but it is still not desirable.

# Private module linter

This linter lints against nonempty modules that have only private declarations, and suggests adding
 to the top or selectively marking declarations as .

## Implementation notes

 contains all locally-defined constants, and accessing this waits until all
declarations are added. By linting (only) the  token, we can capture all constants defined in
the file.

Note that private declarations from the current module are exactly those which satisfy
, whether private due to an explicit  or due to not being made .

Since initializers have downstream effects regardless of whether they're  or , any
module which registers an initializer is considered non-private.

We also do not count declarations which satisfy  as public declarations *from the
current module*. While they might indeed be public, the declarations associated with reserved names
are generated automatically and lazily, sometimes in downstream modules from the one in which the
name was reserved.

For example, Lean might reserve the name  in one module, but only add a declaration with
the name  to the environment in some downstream module, when Lean attempts to
realize the name. If the original module is a  of the downstream module, then this
new declaration  will be added to the public scope, as it would be if it had been
declared in the original module.

As such, if e.g.  realized the public declaration  in some module
downstream of the module in which  was declared, but  did not add any other public
declarations, the linter should still fire on . Ignoring reserved names ensures this.

See also the type , invocations of  and
 for examples, and the module  for further insight.

Note that metaprograms should not add public declarations when run in private scopes. Doing so would
likely be a bug in the metaprogram. As such, we do not perform further checks for automatically
generated declarations such as those detected by  or .

## Style linters

This file contain linters about stylistic aspects: these are only about coding style,
but do not affect correctness nor global coherence of mathlib.
Historically, some of these were ported from the  Python script.

This file defines the following linters:
- the  linter checks for the presence of  commands activating
  options disallowed in mathlib: these are meant to be temporary, and not for polished code.
  It also checks for  options being present which are not scoped to single commands.
- the  linter checks for sections or namespaces which are not closed by the end
  of the file: enforcing this invariant makes minimising files or moving code between files easier
- the  linter checks for focusing dots  which are typed using a  instead:
  this is allowed Lean syntax, but it is nicer to be uniform
- the  linter checks for use of the dollar sign  instead of the  pipe operator:
  similarly, both symbols have the same meaning, but mathlib prefers  for the symmetry with
  the  symbol
- the  linter checks for uses of the  symbol for anonymous functions,
  instead of the  keyword: mathlib prefers the latter for reasons of readability
- the  linter checks for files which have more than 1500 lines
- the  linter checks for lines which have more than 100 characters
- the  linter checks for  statements which are not
  scoped to a single declaration
- the  linter checks for s that change the goal and should be replaced by
- the  linter checks for declarations whose names are in non-standard style, such as
  by containing a double underscore. The  environment linter checks for
  definitions whose name contains an underscore: that is also very likely to be a violation of
  mathlib's naming convention.

All of these linters are enabled in mathlib by default, but disabled globally
since they enforce conventions which are inherently subjective.

## Text-based linters

This file defines various mathlib linters which are based on reading the source code only.
In practice, all such linters check for code style issues.

Currently, this file contains linters checking
- if the string "adaptation note" is used instead of the command ,
- for lines with windows line endings,
- for lines containing trailing whitespace,
- for module names to be in upper camel case,
- for module names to be valid Windows filenames, and containing no forbidden characters such as
  ,  or spaces.
- for any code containing unicode characters not on the allowlist
- for incorrect usage of unicode variant selectors

For historic reasons, some further such checks are written in a Python script :
these are gradually being rewritten in Lean.

This linter has a file for style exceptions (to avoid false positives in the implementation),
or for downstream projects to allow a gradual adoption of this linter.

An executable running all these linters is defined in .

# The unused tactic linter

The unused linter makes sure that every tactic call actually changes *something*.

The inner workings of the linter are as follows.

The linter inspects the goals before and after each tactic execution.
If they are not identical, the linter is happy.
If they are identical, then the linter checks if the tactic is whitelisted.
Possible reason for whitelisting are
* tactics that emit messages, such as , , or ;
* tactics that are in place to assert something, such as ;
* tactics that allow to work on a specific goal, such as ;
* "flow control" tactics, such as  and related.

The only tactic that has a bespoke criterion is : the reason is that the only change that
 has is to relabel the usernames of local declarations.
Thus, to check that  was used, so we inspect the names of all the local declarations
before and after and see if there is some change.

## Notable exclusions

*  is completely ignored by the linter.

* The linter does not enter a "sequence tactic": upon finding
  the linter assumes that the tactic is doing something and does not recurse into each
  .
  This is just for lack of an implementation: it may not be hard to do this.

* The tactic does not check the discharger for ,
  but checks  itself.
  The main reason is that  is a common discharger tactic and the linter would
  then always fail whenever the user explicitly chose to pass  as a discharger tactic.

## TODO
* The linter seems to be silenced by : maybe it should enter s?

, , etc.

Drop all the unresolvable constants, otherwise  fails.

We allow depending on theorems and constructors.
  We explicitly allow constructors since  declarations are reported to depend on their
  own constructors, and we want inductives to behave the same as definitions, so place one
  warning on the inductive itself but nothing on its downstream uses.
  (There does not seem to be an easy way to determine, given  and ,
  whether the  is a constructor declared in this piece of .)

The  linter detects declarations that could be moved to a file higher up in the
import hierarchy. If this is the case, it emits a warning.

By default, this linter will not fire on definitions, nor private declarations:
see options  and .

This is intended to assist with splitting files.

If set to , the  linter will add warnings on definitions.

The linter does not place a warning on any declaration depending on a definition in the current file
(while it does place a warning on the definition itself), since we often create a new file for a
definition on purpose.

If set to , the  linter will add warnings on private declarations.

This file provides the two tactics  and .  Given a goal which is an equality
in a type  (with  an ), the  tactic parses the LHS and RHS of
the goal as linear combinations of -atoms over some semiring , and reduces the goal to
the respective equalities of the -coefficients of each atom.  The  tactic does this and
then runs the  tactic on each of these coefficient-wise equalities, failing if this does not
resolve them.

The scalar type  is not pre-determined: instead it starts as  (when each atom is initially
given a scalar ) and gets bumped up into bigger semirings when such semirings are
encountered.  However, to permit this, it is assumed that there is a "linear order" on all the
semirings which appear in the expression: for any two semirings  and  which occur, we have
either  or .

# Monotonicity tactic

The tactic  applies monotonicity rules (collected through the library by being tagged
).

The version of the tactic here is a cheap partial port of the  tactic from Lean 3, which had
many more options and features.  It is implemented as a wrapper on top of .

Temporary syntax change: Lean 3  applied a single monotonicity rule, then applied local
hypotheses and the  tactic as many times as it could.  This is hard to implement on top of
 because the counting system used in the  field of its configuration would
count these as separate steps, throwing off the count in the desired configuration
.  So instead we just implement a version of  in which monotonicity rules,
local hypotheses and  are all applied repeatedly until nothing more is applicable.  The syntax
for this in Lean 3 was . Both  and  implement this behavior for now.

applies monotonicity rules and local hypotheses repetitively.  For example,

# The  tactic

Solve goals in not necessarily commutative rings.

This tactic is rudimentary, but useful for solving simple goals in noncommutative rings. One
glaring flaw is that numeric powers are unfolded entirely with  and can easily exceed the
maximum recursion depth.

 is just a  followed by . It automatically uses
to close the goal, and if that doesn't succeed, defaults to .

simplifies expressions in not-necessarily-commutative rings in the main goal
then tries closing it by "cheap" (reducible) .
This tactic supports the operators , , ,  and  (for scalar multiplication by
natural numbers or integers).

If the ring is commutative, prefer the  tactic instead, which is more powerful and efficient.
The tactic is implemented as a combination of  and . The precise invocation
of  can be customized using the options listed below.

Limitation: numeric powers are unfolded entirely with  and can easily exceed the
maximum recursion depth.

*  adds the term  as simplification lemma, rewriting from left to right.
  Multiple arguments can be combined as .
*  adds the term  as simplification lemma, rewriting from right to left.
*  simplifies using all hypotheses in the local context.
*  uses  as configuration for the simplification step.
  See  for more details.
*  uses the tactic sequence  to discharge assumptions
  to the simplification lemmas. This only applies to user-supplied lemmas, since the default lemmas
  used by  do not require a discharger.

This plugin is noticeably less powerful than the equivalent version in Mathlib 3: the design of
 means plugins have to return numerals, rather than a generic expression.

efficiently, roughly comparable in effort with the Euclidean algorithm for the computation
of the gcd of  and . More precisely, the computation is done in the following steps.

  via  and , where the sign is determined

* Once  is odd, we use Quadratic Reciprocity (QR) in the form
  , where the sign is determined by the residue classes
  of  and  mod 4. We are then back in the previous case.

2. Collect the set of *facts*, i.e., atomic expressions in one of six forms: , ,

   set of facts.

   Note that the last two operations weaken the set of facts.

    is present in our set of facts. We call this graph a -graph.
5. **Growing the -graph with -facts**.

   graph while possible.
6. **Finding contradictions using -facts**.
   For each fact , we check if  is reachable from  in the -graph. If so, we
   derive the desired contradiction.

### Partial Order

#### Why is this a decision procedure?

### Linear Order
3. **Preprocessing**.
   We replace some facts as follows:
   * Replace  with  and .

4. **Building the -graph**: Same as for preorders.
5. **Finding contradictions using -facts**: Same as for partial orders.

Note that the algorithm for linear orders is simply the algorithm for partial orders with an
additional preprocessing step. It also skips the growing step because there is no -facts.

#### Why is this a decision procedure?
We need to slightly modify the proof for partial orders. In this case,  and  are again
equisatisfiable. Suppose the algorithm cannot find a contradiction, and construct the model of .
The carrier of the model is once again the set of strongly connected components in the -graph,
with variables interpreted as their respective components. Note that the reachability relation
(used before) on components is acyclic. Therefore, it can be
topologically ordered, meaning it forms a
linear order where  whenever  is reachable from . It is easy to see that all facts
in  are satisfied by the model.

### Lattice
The algorithm for lattices is similar to that for partial orders, with two differences:
1. During the preprocessing step, we add the facts  and  if  is present
   in the context, and similarly for .
2. In step 5, we expand the -graph using the following procedure: if a vertex  is reachable
   from both  and , and  is present in the set of atoms, we add the edge
   using , and similarly for .

One can show that this algorithm also serves as a decision procedure for the theory of lattices.

# Generating "proxy types"

This module gives tools to create an equivalence between a given inductive type and a
"proxy type" constructed from , , , , and .
It works for any non-recursive inductive type without indices.

The intended use case is for pulling typeclass instances across this equivalence. This
reduces the problem of generating typeclass instances to that of writing typeclass instances for
the above five types (and whichever additional types appear in the inductive type).

The main interface is the  elaborator, where  gives an equivalence
between the proxy type for  and . See the documentation for  for an example.

For debugging information, do .

It is possible to reconfigure the machinery to generate other types. See
and look at how it is used in .

## Implementation notes

For inductive types with  constructors, the  elaborator creates a proxy
type of the form . The equivalence then needs to handle  levels
of  constructors, which is a source of quadratic complexity.

An alternative design could be to generate a  function for the proxy types
for each constructor and then use  for the total proxy type. However,
typeclass inference is not good at finding instances for such a type even if there are instances
for each . One seems to need to add, for example, an explicit
instance given .

## Implementation notes

# -like tactics

The core normalization procedure for ring-like tactics that solve equations in commutative
(semi)rings where the exponents can also contain variables.
Based on  .

More precisely, expressions of the following form are supported:
- constants (non-negative integers)
- variables
- coefficients (living in ; for  this is a rational embedded into the semiring)
- addition of expressions
- multiplication of expressions ()
- scalar multiplication of expressions ()
- exponentiation of expressions (the exponent must have type )
- subtraction and negation of expressions (if the base is a full ring)

The extension to exponents means that something like  can be proved,
even though it is not strictly speaking an equation in the language of commutative rings.

## Implementation notes

The basic approach to prove equalities is to normalise both sides and check for equality.
The normalisation is guided by building a value in the type  at the meta level,
together with a proof (at the base level) that the original value is equal to
the normalised version.

The outline of the file:
- Define a mutual inductive family of types , , ,
  which can represent expressions with , ,  and some parametric .
  The mutual induction ensures that associativity and distributivity are applied,
  by restricting which kinds of subexpressions appear as arguments to the various operators.
- Represent addition, multiplication and exponentiation in the  type,
  thus allowing us to map expressions to  (the  function drives this).
  We apply associativity and distributivity of the operators here (helped by  types)
  and commutativity as well (by sorting the subterms; unfortunately not helped by anything).
  Any expression not of the above formats is treated as an atom (the same as a variable).

There are some details we glossed over which make the plan more complicated:
- The order on atoms is not initially obvious.
  We construct a list containing them in order of initial appearance in the expression,
  then use the index into the list as a key to order on.
- For , the exponent must be a natural number, while the base can be any semiring .
  We swap out operations for the base ring  with those for the exponent ring
  as soon as we deal with exponents. Unfortunately this has to be done with a separate inductive
  type due to universe issues outlined later in this file.

## Caveats and future work

The normalized form of an expression is the one that is useful for the tactic,
but not as nice to read. To remedy this, the user-facing normalization calls .

Subtraction cancels out identical terms, but division does not.
That is:  solves the goal,
but  doesn't.
Note that  is generally defined to be ,
so division cancelling out is not true in general.

Multiplication of powers can be simplified a little bit further:
 could be implemented
in a similar way that  already works.
This feature wasn't needed yet, so it's not implemented yet.

## Implementation notes

The automation is provided in the  monad; that is, these functions are not user-facing. It
would not be hard to provide user-facing versions (see the test file), but the scope of this
automation is rather specialized and might be confusing to users.

However, this automation serves as the discharger for the  tactic on inequality
goals, so it is available to the user indirectly as the "degenerate" case of that tactic -- that is,
by calling  without arguments.

Rather than having the metaprograms  and
 perform all type class inference at the point of use, we record in
advance, as s, a few type class deductions which will certainly be necessary.  They add no
new information (they can already be proved by ).

This helps in speeding up the metaprograms in this file substantially -- about a 50% reduction in
heartbeat count in representative test cases -- since otherwise a substantial fraction of their
runtime is devoted to type class inference.

#  command

Defines a macro for producing SAT proofs from CNF / LRAT files.
These files are commonly used in the SAT community for writing proofs.

Most SAT solvers support export to DRAT format,
but this format can be expensive to reconstruct because it requires recomputing all
unit propagation steps. The LRAT format solves this
issue by attaching a proof to the deduction of each new clause.
(The L in LRAT stands for Linear time verification.)
There are several verified checkers for the LRAT format, and the program implemented here
makes it possible to use the lean kernel as an LRAT checker as well and expose the results
as a standard propositional theorem.

The input to the  command is the name of the theorem to define,
and the statement (written in CNF format) and the proof (in LRAT format).

# SetLike Rule Set

This module defines the  and  Aesop rule sets.
Aesop rule sets only become visible once the file in which they're declared is imported,
so we must put this declaration into its own file.

The Aesop tactic () can automatically prove obvious facts about membership in structures
such as subgroups and subrings. Certain lemmas regarding membership in algebraic substructures
are given the  attribute according to the following principles:
- Rules are in the  ruleset: .
- Apply-style rules with trivial hypotheses are registered both as  rules and as
   Aesop rules. The latter is needed in case there are metavariables in the goal.
  For instance, Aesop can use the rule  to prove
  .
- Apply-style rules with nontrivial hypotheses are marked . This is because applying them
  might not be provability-preserving in the context of more complex membership rules.
  For instance,  is marked .
  - Unsafe rules are given a probability no higher than 90%. This is the same probability
    Aesop gives to safe rules when they generate metavariables. If the priority is too high, loops
    generated in the presence of metavariables will time out Aesop.
  - Rules that cause loops (even in the absence of metavariables) are given a low priority of 5%.
    These rules are placed in the  ruleset instead of the  ruleset so that
    they are not invoked by default. An example is .
  - Simplifying the left-hand side of a membership goal is prioritised over simplifying the
    right-hand side. By default, rules simplifying the LHS (e.g., ) are given
    probability 90% and rules simplifying the RHS are given probability 80%
    (e.g., ).
  - These default probabilities are for rules with simple hypotheses that fail quickly when
    not satisfied, such as . Rules with more complicated hypotheses, or rules that are
    less likely to progress the proof state towards a solution, are given a lower priority.
- To optimise performance and avoid timeouts, Aesop should not be invoking low-priority rules
  unless it can make no other progress. If common usage patterns cause Aesop to invoke such rules,
  additional lemmas are added at a higher priority to cover that pattern.
  For example,  covers a common use case of .

Some examples of membership-related goals which Aesop with this ruleset is designed to close
can be found in the file .

## Implementation Notes

There are three attributes being defined here
*  is the attribute for objects of a structure or instances of a class. It will
  automatically generate simplification lemmas for each projection of the object/instance that
  contains data. See the doc strings for  and
  for more details and configuration options.
*  (just an environment extension, not actually an attribute)
  is automatically added to structures that have been used in
  at least once. This attribute contains the data of the projections used for this structure
  by all following invocations of .
*  should be added to all classes that define notation, like  and
  . This specifies that the projections that  used are the projections from
  these notation classes instead of the projections of the superclasses.
  Example: if  is tagged with  then the projection used for
  will be  instead of .
  [this is not correctly implemented in Lean 4 yet]

* The attribute will now raise an error if it tries to generate a lemma when there already exists

*  has been replaced by
* The  configuration option has been split into  and  (for extra attributes)
* Because Lean 4 uses bundled structures, this means that  applied to anything that
  implements a notation class will almost certainly require a user-provided custom simps projection.

This command allows customisation of the lemmas generated by .

By default, tagging a definition of an element  of a structure  with
generates one  lemma  for each projection  of . There are a
few exceptions to this general rule:
* For algebraic structures, we will automatically use the notation (like )
  for the projections if such an instance is available.
* By default, the projections to parent structures are not default projections,
  but all the data-carrying fields are (including those in parent structures).

This default behavior is customisable as such:
* You can disable a projection by default by running

  This will ensure that no simp lemmas are generated for this projection,
  unless this projection is explicitly specified by the user (as in
  ).
* Conversely, you can enable a projection by default by running
  .
* You can specify custom names by writing e.g.
  .
* If you want the projection name added as a prefix in the generated lemma name, you can use
  :

  Note that this does not influence the parsing of projection names: if you have a declaration
   and you want to apply the projections ,  (which is a prefix) and , in that
  order you can run  and this will generate a lemma with the
  name .

Here are a few extra pieces of information:
* Run  (or )

  same effect if you just add  to a declaration.

are three cases
* If the declaration  has been declared, then the value
  of this declaration is used (after checking that it is definitionally equal to the actual
  projection). If you rename the projection name, the declaration should have the *new* projection
  name.
* You can also declare a custom projection that is a composite of multiple projections.
* Otherwise, for every class with the  attribute, and the structure has an
  instance of that notation class, then the projection of that notation class is used for the
  projection that is definitionally equal to it (if there is such a projection).
  This means in practice that coercions to function types and sorts will be used instead of
  a projection, if this coercion is definitionally equal to a projection. Furthermore, for
  notation classes like  and  those projections are used instead of the
  corresponding projection.
  Projections for coercions and notation classes are not automatically generated if they are
  composites of multiple projections (for example when you use  without the
   (does this exist?)).
* Otherwise, the projection of the structure is chosen.
  For example:  gives the default projections.
