# Tactic analysis framework

In this file we define a framework for analyzing sequences of tactics.
This can be used for linting (for instance: report when two  calls can be merged into one),
but it can also be run in a more batch-like mode to report larger potential refactors
(for instance: report when a sequence of three or more tactics can be replaced with ,
without taking more heartbeats than the original proof did).

## Using the framework

The framework runs, but does nothing by default (
to turn it off completely). Enable the analysis round  by enabling its corresponding
option: .

To add a round of analysis called , declare an option ,
make a definition of type  and give the  declaration the
 attribute. Don't forget to enable the option.

## Warning

The  interface doesn't feel quite intuitive and flexible yet and should be changed
in the future. Please do not rely on this interface being stable.

While in simple cases it might be possible to use  or ,
congruence quotations are more general,
since for example  could have implicit arguments, complicated dependent types,
and subsingleton instance arguments such as  or .

The implementation strategy is the following:

1. The pattern is elaborated twice, once with each hole replaced by the LHS
   and again with each hole replaced by the RHS. We do not force the hole to
   have any particular type while elaborating, but if the hole has a type
   with an obvious LHS or RHS, then we propagate this information outward.
   We use  with metadata for these replacements
   to hold onto the hole itself.
2. Once the pattern has been elaborated twice,
   we unify them against the respective LHS and RHS of the target type
   if the target has a type with an obvious LHS and RHS.
   This can fill in some metavariables and help typeclass inference make progress.
3. Then we simultaneously walk along the elaborated LHS and RHS expressions
   to generate a congruence.
   When we reach s, we make sure they elaborated in a compatible way.
   Each  type has some logic to come up with a suitable congruence.
   For applications we use a version of  that tries
   to fill in some of the equality proofs using subsingleton lemmas.

The point of elaborating the expression twice is that we let the elaborator handle
activities like synthesizing instances, etc., specialized to LHS or RHS, without trying
to derive one side from the other.

During development there was a version using  transformations, but there was
no way to inform  about the expected RHS, which could cause  to fail because
it eagerly wants to solve for instance arguments. The current version is able to use the
expected LHS and RHS to fill in arguments before solving for instance arguments.

using terms with attached metadata and a reducible wrapper.
We try to avoid doing so, but these terms can leak into the local context through unification.
This can potentially break tactics that are sensitive to metadata or reducible functions.

   and we're able to transform them into whatever is appropriate for a

(like ) have multiple relevant arguments.

we will not be able to translate declarations that (e.g.) talk about multiplication on
anyway.

A hint about the translated declaration

-  indicates that the translated form of the declaration is a pre-existing declaration.
  This is useful when the value cannot be translated, either because of a limitation in the
  translation heuristics, or because the value/proof is genuinely different.

-  indicates that the declaration translates to itself, up to some reordering of arguments.
  If no arguments are reordered then the attribute is redundant, which the
  linter will warn about.

-  indicates that the translated declaration should not get a user-facing name,
  instead being named like an auxiliary declaration. This is particularly useful for  when
  using the  attribute, because the dual of a right associated term is left associated,
  but we only want user-facing lemmas with right associated terms.

# Reordering arguments in a translation

This module defines reorders, which can be specified with  or
, to deal with definitions and theorems that need to have their
arguments and/or universe parameters reordered.

A reordering is specified using disjoint cycle notation. For example,  will
move the 1st argument to the 2nd, move the 2nd to the 3rd, and the 3rd to the 1st, and it will
swap the 4th and 5th arguments.

Instead of using numbers to refer to argument, you can also refer to them by name. For example
 will swap the arguments named  and . This is implemented in .

To specify reordering arguments of arguments, the syntax is recursive. For example,
 will reorder the first two arguments of the fourth argument.

If the declaration is translated to itself or to an existing declaration,
the heuristic in  tries to predict the argument reorder.
This is done with a syntactic comparison of which variable is moved where.

The universe reordering is always inferred automatically, using .

  Thanks to the heuristic in , it suffices to write .

## Implementation notes

The transport process generally works by taking all the names of
identifiers appearing in the name, type, and body of a declaration and
creating a new declaration by mapping those names to additive versions
using a simple string-based dictionary and also using all declarations
that have previously been labeled with . The dictionary is
and can be found in the  file. If you introduce a new name which
should be translated by  you should add the translation to this dictionary.

*  to ,

*  to .

### Heuristics

 uses heuristics to determine whether a particular identifier has to be
mapped to its additive version. The basic heuristic is

* Only map an identifier to its additive version if its first argument doesn't
  contain any unapplied identifiers.

Examples:
*  (i.e. ) will not change to , since its
  first argument is , an identifier not applied to any arguments.
*  will change to . It's first argument contains only the identifier
  , but this is applied to arguments,  and .
*  will not change to , since its first argument contains .

The reasoning behind the heuristic is that the first argument is the type which is "additivized",
and this usually doesn't make sense if this is on a fixed type.

There are some exceptions to this heuristic:

* Identifiers that have the  attribute are ignored.
  For example, multiplication in  is replaced by addition in .
  You can turn this behavior off by *also* adding the  attribute.
* If an identifier  has attribute  then the argument
   is checked for a fixed type, instead of checking the first argument.
   will automatically add the attribute  to a
  declaration when the first argument has no multiplicative type-class, but argument  does.
* If an identifier has attribute  then all the arguments in
  positions , , ... will not be checked for unapplied identifiers (start counting from 1).
  For example,  has attribute , which means
  that its 21st argument  can contain
  (usually in the form ) and still be additivized.
  So  will be additivized.

### Troubleshooting

If  fails because the additive declaration raises a type mismatch, there are
various things you can try.
The first thing to do is to figure out what  did wrong by looking at the type
mismatch error.

* Option 1: The most common case is that it didn't additivize a declaration that should be
  additivized. This happened because the heuristic applied, and the first argument contains a
  fixed type, like  or . However, the heuristic misfires on some other declarations.
  Solutions:
  * First figure out what the fixed type is in the first argument of the declaration that didn't
    get additivized. Note that this fixed type can occur in implicit arguments. If manually finding
    it is hard, you can run  and search the output for the
    fragment "contains the fixed type" to find what the fixed type is.
  * If the fixed type has an additive counterpart (like ), give it the
    attribute.
  * If the fixed type has nothing to do with algebraic operations (like ), add the attribute
     to the fixed type .
  * If the fixed type occurs inside the -th argument of a declaration , and the
    -th argument is not connected to the multiplicative structure on , consider adding
    attribute  to .
    Example:  ignores the argument
  * If none of the arguments have a multiplicative structure, then the heuristic should not apply at
    all. This can be achieved with the option .
* Option 2: It additivized a declaration  that should remain multiplicative. Solution:
  * Make sure the first argument of  is a type with a multiplicative structure. If not, can you
    reorder the (implicit) arguments of  so that the first argument becomes a type with a
    multiplicative structure (and not some indexing type)?
    The reason is that  doesn't additivize declarations if their first argument
    contains fixed types like  or . See section Heuristics.
    If the first argument is not the argument with a multiplicative type-class,
    should have automatically added the attribute  to the declaration.
    You can test this by running the following (where  is the full name of the declaration):
    The expected output is  where the -th (0-indexed) argument of  is a type (family)
    with a multiplicative structure on it.  means .
    If you get a different output (or a failure), you could add the attribute
     manually, where  is an (1-indexed) argument with a
    multiplicative structure.
* Option 3: Arguments / universe levels are incorrectly ordered in the additive version.
  This likely only happens when the multiplicative declaration involves /. Solutions:
  * Ensure that the order of arguments of all relevant declarations are the same for the
    multiplicative and additive version. This might mean that arguments have an "unnatural" order
    (e.g.  corresponds to , but it is convenient that  has this
    argument order, since it matches .
  * If this is not possible, add  argument to .

If neither of these solutions work, and  is unable to automatically generate the
additive version of a declaration, manually write and prove the additive version.
Often the proof of a lemma/theorem can just be the multiplicative version of the lemma applied to
.
Afterwards, apply the attribute manually:

- Equality casts. This is for propositions and terms,

- Explicit casting functions, both for unfolding and refolding. This is for types, where we
  cannot express their equivalence with an equality. For example .

# The  command

This defines a command like  that automatically adds all missing typeclass
arguments. For example,  is the same as
, though if any of these three instance
arguments can be inferred from previous variables then they will be omitted.

An inherent limitation with this command is that variables are recorded in the scope as
*syntax*. This means that  needs to pretty print the expressions we get
from typeclass synthesis errors, and these might fail to round trip.

Get the type out of a bracketed binder.

The  command has the same syntax as , but it will auto-insert
missing instance arguments wherever they are needed.
It does not add variables that can already be deduced from others in the current context.
By default the command checks that variables aren't implied by earlier ones, but it does *not*
check that earlier variables aren't implied by later ones.
Unlike , the  command does not support changing variable binder types.

The  command will give a suggestion to replace itself with a command of the form
.  The binders after the  are the completed
list of binders. When this  clause is present, the command verifies that the expanded
binders match the post- binders.  The purpose of this is to help keep code that uses
 resilient against changes to the typeclass hierarchy, at least in the sense
that this additional information can be used to debug issues that might arise.
One can also replace  with .

The core algorithm is to try elaborating binders one at a time, and whenever there is a
typeclass instance inference failure, it synthesizes binder syntax for it and adds it to
the list of binders and tries again, recursively. There are no guarantees that this
process gives the "correct" list of binders.

Structures tagged with the  attribute can serve as aliases for a collection
of typeclasses. For example, given
then  is
equivalent to , assuming
that there are no pre-existing instances on  and .
Note that this is not a simple replacement: it only adds instances not inferable
from others in the current scope.

A word of warning: the core algorithm depends on pretty printing, so if terms that appear
in binders do not round trip, this algorithm can fail. That said, it has some support
for quantified binders such as .

Attribute to record aliases for the  command. Aliases are structures that have no
fields, and additional typeclasses are recorded as *arguments* to the structure.

# Point & click library rewriting

This file defines , an interactive tactic that suggests rewrites for any expression selected
by the user.

 uses a (lazy)  to lookup a list of candidate rewrite lemmas.
It excludes lemmas that are automatically generated.
Each lemma is then checked one by one to see whether it is applicable.
For each lemma that works, the corresponding rewrite tactic is constructed
and converted into a  that fits inside mathlib's 100 column limit,
so that it can be pasted into the editor when selected by the user.

The  lookup groups the results by match pattern and gives a score to each pattern.
This is used to display the results in sections. The sections are ordered by this score.
Within each section, the lemmas are sorted by
- rewrites with fewer extra goals come first
- left-to-right rewrites come first
- shorter lemma names come first
- shorter replacement expressions come first (when taken as a string)
- alphabetically ordered by lemma name

The lemmas are optionally filtered to avoid duplicate rewrites, or trivial rewrites. This
is controlled by the filter button on the top right of the results.

When a rewrite lemma introduces new goals, these are shown after a .

- We could look for rewrites of partial applications of the selected expression.
  For example, when clicking on , there should still be an  suggestion.

# String Diagram Widget

This file provides meta infrastructure for displaying string diagrams for morphisms in monoidal
categories in the infoview. To enable the string diagram widget, you need to import this file and
inserting  at the beginning of the
proof. Alternatively, you can also write
to enable the string diagram widget in the current section.

We also have the  command. For example,
displays the string diagram for the exchange law of the left and right whiskerings.

String diagrams are graphical representations of morphisms in monoidal categories, which are
useful for rewriting computations. More precisely, objects in a monoidal category is represented
by strings, and morphisms between two objects is represented by nodes connecting two strings
associated with the objects. The tensor product  corresponds to putting strings associated
with  and  horizontally (from left to right), and the composition of morphisms
and  corresponds to connecting two nodes associated with  and  vertically (from
top to bottom) by strings associated with .

Currently, the string diagram widget provided in this file deals with equalities of morphisms
in monoidal categories. It displays string diagrams corresponding to the morphisms for the
left-hand and right-hand sides of the equality.

Some examples can be found in .

When drawing string diagrams, it is common to ignore associators and unitors. We follow this
convention. To do this, we need to extract non-structural morphisms that are not associators
and unitors from lean expressions. This operation is performed using the
function.

A monoidal category can be viewed as a bicategory with a single object. The program in this
file can also be used to display the string diagram for general bicategories. With this in mind we
will sometimes refer to objects and morphisms in monoidal categories as 1-morphisms and 2-morphisms
respectively, borrowing the terminology of bicategories. Note that the relation between monoidal
categories and bicategories is formalized in ,
although the string diagram widget does not use it directly.

## : generators for functions

This file defines  instances for  injective functions.

Injective functions are generated by creating a list of numbers and
a permutation of that list. The permutation insures that every input
is mapped to a unique output. When an input is not found in the list
the input itself is used as an output.

Injective functions  could be generated easily instead of
 by generating a , removing duplicates and creating a
permutation. One has to be careful when generating the domain to make
it vast enough that, when generating arguments to apply  to,
they argument should be likely to lie in the domain of . This is
the reason that injective functions  are generated by
fixing the domain to the range , with
the size parameter of the  monad.

Much of the machinery provided in this file is applicable to generate
injective functions of type  and new instances should be easy
to define.

Other classes of functions such as monotone functions can generated using
similar techniques. For monotone functions, generating two lists, sorting them
and matching them should suffice, with appropriate default values.
Some care must be taken for shrinking such functions to make sure
their defining property is invariant through shrinking. Injective
functions are an example of how complicated it can get.

This theorem exists because plausible does not have access to dlookup but
mathlib has all the theory for it and wants to use it. We probably want to
bring these two together at some point.

# Alexandrov-discrete topological spaces

This file defines Alexandrov-discrete spaces, aka finitely generated spaces.

A space is Alexandrov-discrete if the (arbitrary) intersection of open sets is open. As such,
the intersection of all neighborhoods of a set is a neighborhood itself. Hence every set has a
minimal neighborhood, which we call the *neighborhoods kernel* of the set.

## Main declarations

* : Prop-valued typeclass for a topological space to be Alexandrov-discrete

## Tags

Alexandroff, discrete, finitely generated, fg space

A topological space is **Alexandrov-discrete** or **finitely generated** if the intersection of
a family of open sets is open.

The intersection of a family of open sets is an open set. Use  in the root
 namespace instead.

# Asymptotic cone of a set

This file defines the asymptotic cone of a set in a topological affine space.

## Implementation details

The asymptotic cone of a set $A$ is usually defined as the set of points $v$ for which there exist
sequences $t_n > 0$ and $x_n \in A$ such that $t_n \to 0$ and $t_n x_n \to v$. We take a different
approach here using filters: we define the asymptotic cone of  as the set of vectors  such
that  holds.

## Main definitions

* : the filter of neighborhoods at infinity in some direction.
* : the asymptotic cone of a subset of a topological affine space.

## Main statements

* : if  is in the asymptotic cone of a
  closed convex set , then every ray of direction  starting from  is contained in .
* : if  is in the asymptotic cone of a
  convex set , then every ray of direction  starting from the interior of  is contained in
  .

In a topological affine space  over ,  is the filter of
neighborhoods at infinity in directions near . In a topological vector space, this is the filter
. To support affine spaces, the actual definition is different and should be
considered an implementation detail. Use  or
 for unfolding.

The set of directions  for which the set has points arbitrarily far in directions near .

If a closed set  is star-convex at  and  is in the asymptotic cone of , then the ray
of direction  starting from  is contained in .

If  is in the asymptotic cone of a closed convex set , then for every , the ray of
direction  starting from  is contained in .

If  is in the asymptotic cone of a convex set , then for every interior point , the ray
of direction  starting from  is contained in .

# Topological fields

A topological division ring is a topological ring whose inversion function is continuous at every
non-zero element.

Left-multiplication by a nonzero element of a topological division ring is proper, i.e.,
inverse images of compact sets are compact.

Right-multiplication by a nonzero element of a topological division ring is proper, i.e.,
inverse images of compact sets are compact.

Compact Hausdorff topological fields are finite. This is not an instance, as it would apply to
every  goal, causing slowly failing typeclass search in some cases.

A topological division ring is a division ring with a topology where all operations are
continuous, including inversion.

The (topological-space) closure of a subfield of a topological field is
itself a subfield.

In an ordered field, the units of the nonnegative elements are the positive elements.

This section is about affine homeomorphisms from a topological field  to itself.
Technically it does not require  to be a topological field, a topological ring that
happens to be a field is enough.

# Open mapping theorem for morphisms of topological groups

We prove that a continuous surjective group morphism from a sigma-compact group to a locally compact
group is automatically open, in .

We deduce this from a similar statement for the orbits of continuous actions of sigma-compact groups
on Baire spaces, given in .

Note that a sigma-compactness assumption is necessary. Indeed, let  be the real line with
the discrete topology, and  the real line with the usual topology. Both are locally compact
groups, and the identity from  to  is continuous but not open.

Consider a sigma-compact group acting continuously and transitively on a Baire space. Then
the orbit map is open around the identity. It follows in  that it
is open around any point.

Consider a sigma-compact additive group acting continuously and transitively on a
Baire space. Then the orbit map is open around zero. It follows in
 that it is open around any point.

Consider a small closed neighborhood  of the identity. Then the group is covered by
 countably many translates of , say . Let also  be a sequence of compact sets covering
 the space. Then the image of  in the orbit is compact, and their unions covers the
 space. By Baire, one of them has nonempty interior. Then  has nonempty interior, and
 so does . Its interior contains a point  with . Then  contains
 a neighborhood of , and it is included in , which is itself contained in
 if  is small enough.

Consider a sigma-compact group acting continuously and transitively on a Baire space. Then
the orbit map is open. This is a version of the open mapping theorem, valid notably for the
action of a sigma-compact locally compact group on a locally compact space.

Consider a sigma-compact additive group acting continuously and transitively on a
Baire space. Then the orbit map is open. This is a version of the open mapping theorem, valid
notably for the action of a sigma-compact locally compact group on a locally compact space.

We have already proved the theorem around the basepoint of the orbit, in
 . The general statement follows around an arbitrary
 point by changing basepoints.

A surjective morphism of topological groups is open when the source group is sigma-compact and
the target group is a Baire space (for instance a locally compact group).

# Infinite sum and product in a topological monoid

This file defines infinite products and sums for (possibly infinite) indexed families of elements
in a commutative topological monoid (resp. add monoid).

To handle convergence questions we use the formalism of *summation filters* (defined in the
file ). These are filters on the finite
subsets of a given type, and we define a function to be *summable* for a summation filter  if
its partial sums over finite subsets tend to a limit along  (and similarly for products).

This simultaneously generalizes several different kinds of summation: for instance,
*unconditional summation* (which makes sense for any index type) where we take the limit with
respect to the  filter; but also *conditional summation* for functions on , where the
limit is over the partial sums  as  (so there exist
conditionally-summable sequences which are not unconditionally summable).

## Implementation notes

We say that a function  has a product of  w.r.t. the summation filter  if the
function  converges to  w.r.t. the filter  on
.

In the most important case of unconditional summation, this translates to the following condition:
for every neighborhood  of , there exists a finite set  of indices such
that  for any finite set  which is a superset of .

This may yield some unexpected results. For example, according to this definition, the product
 unconditionally exists and is equal to . More strikingly,
the product  unconditionally exists and is equal to , because one
of its terms is  (even though the product of the remaining terms diverges). Users who would
prefer that these products be considered not to exist can carry them out in the unit group
rather than in .

## References

* Bourbaki: General Topology (1995), Chapter 3 §5 (Infinite sums in commutative groups)

# Infinite sum or product in an order

This file provides lemmas about the interaction of infinite sums and products and order operations.

For infinite sums taking values in a linearly ordered monoid, the existence of a least upper
bound for the finite sums is a criterion for summability.

This criterion is useful when applied in a linearly ordered monoid which is also a complete or
conditionally complete linear order, such as , , , because it is then easy to check
the existence of a least upper bound.

Positivity extension for infinite sums.

This extension only proves non-negativity, strict positivity is more delicate for infinite sums and
requires more assumptions.

# Cardinality of open subsets of vector spaces

Any nonempty open subset of a topological vector space over a nontrivially normed field has the same
cardinality as the whole space. This is proved in .

We deduce that a countable set in a nontrivial vector space over a complete nontrivially normed
field has dense complement, in . This follows from the previous
argument and the fact that a complete nontrivially normed field has cardinality at least
continuum, proved in .

A complete nontrivially normed field has cardinality at least continuum.

A nontrivial module over a complete nontrivially normed field has cardinality at least
continuum.

In a topological vector space over a nontrivially normed field, any neighborhood of zero has
the same cardinality as the whole space.

See also .

As  is a neighborhood of , the space is covered by the rescaled sets ,
 where  is any element of  with norm . All these sets are in bijection and have
 therefore the same cardinality. The conclusion follows.

In a topological vector space over a nontrivially normed field, any neighborhood of a point has
the same cardinality as the whole space.

In a topological vector space over a nontrivially normed field, any nonempty open set has
the same cardinality as the whole space.

In a nontrivial topological vector space over a complete nontrivially normed field, any nonempty
open set has cardinality at least continuum.

In a nontrivial topological vector space over a complete nontrivially normed field, any
countable set has dense complement.

# Topological complements of submodules

Let  be a topological -module. Two submodules  of  are said to be
*topological complements* () if they are algebraic complements and the
algebraic isomorphism  is a homeomorphism.

Not all submodules of  admit such a topological complements (even if they admit algebraic
complements). In the literature, such a submodule is called *topologically complemented*
or *direct*. One may also find the terminology *closed complemented* because,
in a Banach space, a closed algebraic complement is automatically a topological complement.
This is the terminology we use for now (), but we should eventually
change to something less misleading.

## Main definitions

  algebraic complements and the projection on  along  is continuous. This is equivalent
  to the definition given above.
* : we say that a submodule is (topologically) *complemented* if
  there exists a continuous projection .

# A linear map which is locally an embedding is an embedding

Fix  a , ,  two topological vector spaces over , and
 a -linear map. We show that, if there is a neighborhood  of
such that the restriction  is an embedding, then  itself is an embedding.

Note that this result is false for topological groups, as shown by the following counterexamples:
* first, in the group setting, there are local embeddings (even local homeomorphisms) which
  are not globally injective; an example is the quotient map ;
* even if assume that  is globally injective, the theorem still fails. Consider for example
   given by , with  irrational.  is injective, and locally
  an embedding by the inverse function theorem, yet it is not globally an embedding: any
  neighborhood of  contains infinitely many points , , since
   gets arbitrarily close to being an integer infinitely many times.

## Implementation details

The content of this file is essentially (variations of)
N. Bourbaki, *Théories Spectrales*, Chapitre III, § 5, n° 1, lemme 1, except
Bourbaki's proof is very specific to  or , since it relies crucially on balanced
sets being connected.

Nevertheless, we are able to adapt their proof to arbitrary nontrivially normed fields.
The key argument, replacing the fact that a connected set cannot be covered nontrivially by
disjoint open sets, is that a balanced set  cannot intersect nontrivially both
and , when  is a neighborhood of  and . We refer to the (highly commented!)
proof for more details.

## References

* N. Bourbaki, *Théories Spectrales*, Chapitre III, § 5, n° 1, lemme 1

# Weak topologies on modules

Given a bilinear form , the weak topology on  is the coarsest topology
such that for all  every map  is continuous; equivalently, it is the topology
on  induced by the map .

This file defines a -valued typeclass  expressing that an existing topology
on  is the weak topology. Although this could be passed around explicitly as a hypothesis
, given the ubiquity of weak topologies in functional analysis, the
numerous properties that can be deduced because the inducing map  is bilinear, the fact that
several theorems (e.g., one version of the bipolar theorem) require this hypothesis, and we can
instantiate this class for several extant types in Mathlib, we choose to make this a typeclass
instead.

Note that establishing  before proving theorems about a particular type can help
prevent abuse of definitional equalities. This because spaces equipped with a weak topology are
frequently type synonyms of some other type . For example, suppose  is a type (potentially
with some extant topology other than the weak topology) and  is a
bilinear form. To consider the weak topology on  induced by , in practice we must create a
type synonym  with an instance .

However, this statement contains an abuse of the the definitional equality  since ,
but  has domain . Moreover, one might be tempted to say that , but this is
impossible because the domain of  is , which is equipped with the incorrect topology.
Instead, what one should do is to first define a new bilinear form  by
composing  with the linear equivalence between  and , and then establish .
If then one proves theorems about  using only the  API, then one can have more
confidence that the statements are type correct.

# A "module topology" for modules over a topological ring

If  is a topological ring acting on an additive abelian group , we define the
*module topology* to be the finest topology on  making both the maps
 and  continuous (with all the products having the
product topology). Note that  is also automatically continuous as it is .

This topology was suggested by Will Sawin here.


## Mathematical details

I (buzzard) don't know of any reference for this other than Sawin's mathoverflow answer,
so I expand some of the details here.

First note that the definition makes sense in far more generality (for example  just needs to
be a topological space acting on an additive monoid).

Next note that there *is* a finest topology with this property! Indeed, topologies on a fixed
type form a complete lattice (infinite infs and sups exist). So if  is the Inf of all
the topologies on  which make  and  continuous, then the claim is that  and
are still continuous for  (note that topologies are ordered so that finer topologies
are smaller). To show  is continuous we equivalently need to show
that the pushforward of the product topology  along  is , and because  is
the greatest lower bound of the topologies making  and  continuous,
it suffices to show that it's  for any topology  on  which makes  and  continuous.
However pushforward and products are monotone, so , and the pushforward of
 is  because that's precisely the statement that  is continuous for .
The proof for  follows mutatis mutandis.

A *topological module* for a topological ring  is an -module  with a topology
making  and  continuous. The discussion so far has shown that the module topology makes
an -module  into a topological module, and moreover is the finest topology with this property.

A crucial observation is that if  is a topological -module, if  is an -module with no
topology, and if  is linear, then the pullback of 's topology to  is a topology
making  into a topological module. Let's for example check that  is continuous.
If  is open then by definition of the pullback topology,  for some open ,
and now the pullback of  under  is just the pullback along the continuous map
 of the preimage of  under the continuous map ,
so it's open. The proof for  is similar.

As a consequence of this, we see that if  is a linear map between topological -modules
modules and if  has the module topology, then  is automatically continuous.
Indeed the argument above shows that if  is linear then the module
topology on  is  the pullback of the module topology on  (because it's the inf of a set
containing this topology) which is the definition of continuity.

We also deduce that the module topology is a functor from the category of -modules
( a topological ring) to the category of topological -modules, and it is perhaps
unsurprising that this is an adjoint to the forgetful functor. Indeed, if  is an -module
and  is a topological -module, then the previous paragraph shows that
the linear maps  are precisely the continuous linear maps
from ( with its module topology) to , so the module topology is a left adjoint
to the forgetful functor.

This file develops the theory of the module topology.

# Images of (von Neumann) bounded sets under continuous multilinear maps

In this file we prove that continuous multilinear maps
send von Neumann bounded sets to von Neumann bounded sets.

We prove 2 versions of the theorem:
one assumes that the index type is nonempty,
and the other assumes that the codomain is a topological vector space.

## Implementation notes

We do not assume the index type  to be finite.
While for a nonzero continuous multilinear map
the family  has to be essentially finite
(more precisely, all but finitely many  has to be trivial),
proving theorems without a  assumption saves us some typeclass searches here and there.

The image of a von Neumann bounded set under a continuous multilinear map
is von Neumann bounded.

This version does not assume that the topologies on the domain and on the codomain
agree with the vector space structure in any way
but it assumes that  is nonempty.

The image of a von Neumann bounded set under a continuous multilinear map
is von Neumann bounded.

This version assumes that the codomain is a topological vector space.

# Continuous perfect pairings

This file defines continuous perfect pairings.

For a topological ring  and two topological modules  and , a continuous perfect pairing is
a continuous bilinear map  that is bijective in both arguments.

We require continuity in the forward direction only so that we can put several different topologies
on the continuous dual (e.g., strong, weak, weak-\*). For example, if  is weakly reflexive then
there is a continuous perfect pairing between  and , even though the map
 (where  is equipped with its strong topology) is
not in general a homeomorphism.

# Character space of a topological algebra

The character space of a topological algebra is the subset of elements of the weak dual that
are also algebra homomorphisms. This space is used in the Gelfand transform, which gives an
isomorphism between a commutative C⋆-algebra and continuous functions on the character space
of the algebra. This, in turn, is used to construct the continuous functional calculus on
C⋆-algebras.


## Implementation notes

We define  as a subset of the weak dual, which automatically puts the
correct topology on the space. We then define  which provides the
algebra homomorphism corresponding to any element. We also provide
which provides the element as a continuous linear map. (Even though  is a type copy of
, this is often more convenient.)

# Nonarchimedean Topology

In this file we set up the theory of nonarchimedean topological groups and rings.

A nonarchimedean group is a topological group whose topology admits a basis of
open neighborhoods of the identity element in the group consisting of open subgroups.
A nonarchimedean ring is a topological ring whose underlying topological (additive)
group is nonarchimedean.

## Definitions

- : nonarchimedean additive group.
- : nonarchimedean multiplicative group.
- : nonarchimedean ring.

A topological additive group is nonarchimedean if every neighborhood of 0
 contains an open subgroup.

A topological group is nonarchimedean if every neighborhood of 1 contains an open subgroup.

A topological ring is nonarchimedean if its underlying topological additive
 group is nonarchimedean.

see Note [lower instance priority]
Every nonarchimedean ring is naturally a nonarchimedean additive group.

If a topological group embeds into a nonarchimedean group, then it is nonarchimedean.

An open neighborhood of the identity in the Cartesian product of two nonarchimedean groups
contains the Cartesian product of an open neighborhood in each group.

An open neighborhood of the identity in
the Cartesian product of two nonarchimedean groups contains the Cartesian product of
an open neighborhood in each group.

An open neighborhood of the identity in the Cartesian square of a nonarchimedean group
contains the Cartesian square of an open neighborhood in the group.

An open neighborhood of the identity in
the Cartesian square of a nonarchimedean group contains the Cartesian square of
an open neighborhood in the group.

The Cartesian product of two nonarchimedean groups is nonarchimedean.

The Cartesian product of two nonarchimedean groups is nonarchimedean.

The Cartesian product of two nonarchimedean rings is nonarchimedean.

# Open subgroups of a topological group

This file builds the lattice  of open subgroups in a topological group ,
and its additive version . This lattice has a top element, the subgroup of all
elements, but no bottom element in general. The trivial subgroup which is the natural candidate
bottom has no reason to be open (this happens only in discrete groups).

Note that this notion is especially relevant in a non-archimedean context, for instance for
-adic groups.

## Main declarations

* : An open subgroup is automatically closed.
* : A subgroup containing an open subgroup is open.
                           There are also versions for additive groups, submodules and ideals.
* : Open subgroups can be pulled back by a continuous group morphism.

# Restricted products of topological spaces, topological groups and rings

We endow a restricted product of topological spaces with a natural topology,
which we describe below. We also show various compatibility results when we change
filters, and extend the construction of restricted products of algebraic structures
to the topological setting.

In particular, with the theory of adeles in mind, we show that if each  is a locally compact
topological ring with open subring , and if all but finitely many of the s are also
compact, then  is a locally compact topological ring.

## Main definitions

* : the  instance on
  the restricted product .

## Topology on the restricted product

The topology on the restricted product  is defined in the following way:
1. If  is some principal filter , recall that  is canonically
   identified with . We endow it with the product topology,
   which is also the topology induced from the full product .
2. In general, we note that  is the infimum of the principal filters coarser than . We
   then endow  with the inductive limit / final topology associated to the
   inclusion maps  where .

In particular:
* On the classical restricted product, with respect to the cofinite filter, this corresponds to
  taking the inductive limit of the  over all *cofinite* sets .
* If  is a principal filter, this second step clearly does not change the topology, since
   belongs to the indexing set of the inductive limit.

Taking advantage of that second remark, we do not actually declare an instance specific to
principal filters. Instead, we provide directly the general instance (corresponding to step 2 above)
as . We then prove that, for a principal filter, the
map to the full product is an inducing (),
and that the topology for a general  is indeed the expected inductive limit
().

## Implementation details

Outside of principal filters and the cofinite filter, the topology we define on the restricted
product does not seem well-behaved. While declaring a single instance is practical, it may conflict
with more interesting topologies in some other cases. Thus, future contributions should not
restrain from specializing these instances to principal and cofinite filters if necessary.

restricted product, adeles, ideles

### Topological facts in the case where  and all s are open

properties when each  is an open subset of . The key fact is that each

# Topological (semi)rings

A topological (semi)ring is a (semi)ring equipped with a topology such that all operations are
continuous. Besides this definition, this file proves that the topological closure of a subring
(resp. an ideal) is a subring (resp. an ideal) and defines products and quotients
of topological (semi)rings.

## Main Results

- /: the topological closure of a
  / is itself a .
- The product of two topological (semi)rings is a topological (semi)ring.
- The indexed product of topological (semi)rings is a topological (semi)ring.

A topological semiring is a semiring  where addition and multiplication are continuous.
We allow for non-unital and non-associative semirings as well.

multiplication as it is multiplication with . (See

A semitopological semiring is a semiring  where addition is jointly continuous and
multiplication is continuous in each variable separately.
We allow for non-unital and non-associative semirings as well.

 instance; if there is an instance of ,

# Compact Hausdorff Rings

## Main results
- :
  Compact Hausdorff Artinian rings are finite (and thus discrete).
- :
  Maximal ideals are open in compact Hausdorff Noetherian rings.
- :
  An ideal in a compact Hausdorff Noetherian local ring is open iff it has finite index.
- :
  An ideal in a compact Hausdorff Dedekind domain (that is not a field) is open iff it is non-zero.

# Completion of topological fields

The goal of this file is to prove the main part of Proposition 7 of Bourbaki GT III 6.8 :

The completion  of a Hausdorff topological field is a field if the image under
the mapping  of every Cauchy filter (with respect to the additive uniform structure)
which does not have a cluster point at  is a Cauchy filter
(with respect to the additive uniform structure).

Bourbaki does not give any detail here, he refers to the general discussion of extending
functions defined on a dense subset with values in a complete Hausdorff space. In particular
the subtlety about clustering at zero is totally left to readers.

Note that the separated completion of a non-separated topological field is the zero ring, hence
the separation assumption is needed. Indeed the kernel of the completion map is the closure of
zero which is an ideal. Hence it's either zero (and the field is separated) or the full field,
which implies one is sent to zero and the completion ring is trivial.

The main definition is  which packages the assumptions as a Prop-valued
type class and the main results are the instances  and
.

A topological field is completable if it is separated and the image under
the mapping x ↦ x⁻¹ of every Cauchy filter (with respect to the additive uniform structure)
which does not have a cluster point at 0 is a Cauchy filter
(with respect to the additive uniform structure). This ensures the completion is
a field.

extension of inversion to the completion of a field.

The value of  at zero is not really specified, although it's probably zero.
Here we explicitly enforce the  axiom.

The pullback of a completable topological field along a uniform inducing
ring homomorphism is a completable topological field.

# Baire spaces

A topological space is called a *Baire space*
if a countable intersection of dense open subsets is dense.
Baire theorems say that all completely metrizable spaces
and all locally compact regular spaces are Baire spaces.
We prove the theorems in
and .

In this file we prove some lemmas about Baire spaces.

The good concept underlying the theorems is that of a Gδ set, i.e., a countable intersection
of open sets. Then Baire theorem can also be formulated as the fact that a countable
intersection of dense Gδ sets is a dense Gδ set. We deduce this version from Baire property.
We also prove the important consequence that, if the space is
covered by a countable union of closed sets, then the union of their interiors is dense.

We also prove that in Baire spaces, the  sets are exactly those containing a dense Gδ set.

The intersection of finitely many open dense sets is dense.

A finite set is Baire.

A dense Gδ subset of a Baire space is Baire.

An open subset of a Baire space is Baire.

Baire theorem: a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense. Formulated here with
an index set which is a countable set in any type.

Baire theorem: a countable intersection of dense open sets is dense. Formulated here with
an index set which is a countable type.

A set is residual (comeagre) if and only if it includes a dense  set.

that is, it cannot be written as a countable union of nowhere‐dense sets.

# Bases of topologies. Countability axioms.

A topological basis on a topological space  is a collection of sets,
such that all open sets can be generated as unions of these sets, without the need to take
finite intersections of them. This file introduces a framework for dealing with these collections,
and also what more we can say under certain countability conditions on bases,
which are referred to as first- and second-countable.
We also briefly cover the theory of separable spaces, which are those with a countable, dense
subset. If a space is second-countable, and also has a countably generated uniformity filter
(for example, if  is a metric space), it will automatically be separable (and indeed, these
conditions are equivalent in this case).

  sets.

concrete basis itself. This allows us to declare these type classes as  to use them as mixins.

# Basic theory of bornology

We develop the basic theory of bornologies. Instead of axiomatizing bounded sets and defining
bornologies in terms of those, we recognize that the cobounded sets form a filter and define a
bornology as a filter of cobounded sets which contains the cofinite filter.  This allows us to make
use of the extensive library for filters, but we also provide the relevant connecting results for
bounded sets.

The specification of a bornology in terms of the cobounded filter is equivalent to the standard
one (e.g., see Bourbaki, *Topological Vector Spaces*, **covering bornology**, now
often called simply **bornology**) in terms of bounded sets (see ,
, ), except that we do not allow the empty bornology (that is,
we require that *some* set must be bounded; equivalently,  is bounded). In the literature the
cobounded filter is generally referred to as the *filter at infinity*.

## Main definitions

- : a class consisting of  and a proof that this filter
  contains the  filter.
- : the predicate that a set is a member of the  filter. For
  , one should prefer  over .
- : the predicate that states a set is bounded (i.e., the complement of a
  cobounded set). One should prefer  over .
- : a class extending  with the condition


Although use of  is discouraged for indicating the (co)boundedness of individual sets,
it is intended for regular use as a filter on .

A **bornology** on a type  is a filter of cobounded sets which contains the cofinite filter.
Such spaces are equivalently specified by their bounded sets, see
and

The filter of cobounded sets in a bornology.

The cobounded filter in a bornology is smaller than the cofinite filter.

and showing that they satisfy the appropriate conditions.

# Bounded operations

This file introduces type classes for bornologically bounded operations.

In particular, when combined with type classes which guarantee continuity of the same operations,

## Main definitions

* : A relative CW-complex is the colimit of an expanding sequence of subspaces
   (called the $(i-1)$-skeleton) for , where  (i.e., the $(-1)$-skeleton) is an
  arbitrary topological space, and each  (i.e., the $n$-skeleton) is obtained from
   (i.e., the $(n-1)$-skeleton) by attaching -disks.

* : A CW-complex is a relative CW-complex whose  (i.e., $(-1)$-skeleton) is empty.

## Implementation Notes

This file provides a categorical approach to CW complexes,
defining them via colimits and transfinite compositions.
For a classical approach that defines CW complexes via explicit cells and attaching maps,
see .
The two approaches are equivalent but serve different purposes:
* This approach is more suitable for categorical arguments and generalizations
* The classical approach is more convenient for concrete geometric arguments

# CW complexes

This file defines (relative) CW complexes and proves basic properties about them using the classical
approach of Whitehead.

A CW complex is a topological space that is made by gluing closed disks of different dimensions
together.

## Main definitions
* : the class of CW structures on a subspace  relative to a base set
   of a topological space .
* : an abbreviation for . The class of CW structures on a
  subspace  of the topological space .
* : indexed family of all open cells of dimension .
* : indexed family of all closed cells of dimension .
* : indexed family of the boundaries of cells of dimension .
* : the -skeleton of the (relative) CW complex .

## Main statements
* : the skeletons can also be seen as a union of open cells.
* : the edge of a cell is contained in a finite union of
  open cells of a lower dimension.

## Implementation notes
* We use the historical definition of CW complexes, due to Whitehead: a CW complex is a collection
  of cells with attaching maps - all cells are subspaces of one ambient topological space.
  This way, we avoid having to work with a lot of different topological spaces.
  On the other hand, it requires the union of all cells to be closed.
  If that is not the case, you need to consider that union as a subspace of itself.
* For a categorical approach that defines CW complexes via colimits and transfinite compositions,
  see .
  The two approaches are equivalent but serve different purposes:
  * This approach is more convenient for concrete geometric arguments
  * The categorical approach is more suitable for abstract arguments and generalizations
* The definition  does not require  to be a Hausdorff space.
  A lot of the lemmas will however require this property.
* This definition is a class to ease working with different constructions and their properties.
  Overall this means that being a CW complex is treated more like a property than data.
* The natural number is explicit in ,  and  because  and
   might be the same type in an explicit CW complex even when  and  are different.
*  is a separate class from . This not only gives absolute CW complexes a
  better constructor but also aids typeclass inference: a construction on relative CW complexes may
  yield a base that for the special case of CW complexes is provably equal to the empty set but not
  definitionally so. In that case we define an instance specifically for absolute CW complexes and
  want this to be inferred over the relative version. Since the base is an  this is
  especially necessary since you cannot provide typeclass inference with a specified base.
  But having the type  be separate from  makes this specification possible.
* For a similar reason to the previous bullet point we make the instance
   have high priority. For example, when talking about the type of
  cells  of an absolute CW complex , this actually refers to
  through this instance. Again, we want typeclass inference to first consider absolute CW
  structures.
* The namespaces  and  generally should not be opened at the same time
  as they contain many declarations with identical names. Still, we want working with absolute
  CW complexes to be  as convenient as possible. Thus every declaration about relative CW complexes
  that doesn't have a modified version for absolute CW complexes should receive an alias in the
   namespace. It is recommended to use the  attribute for this here. See
  below for a restriction on when we want to create aliases.
* For types and definitions relevant to CW complexes like , , ,
  ,  and similar, we want there to exist only one actually used version,
  namely the version in the  namespace (and thus no separate definition in the
   namespace.) This is to avoid unnecessary duplication of lemmas. To achieve this,
  definitions from the  namespace should be added to the  namespace with
   instead of /. These will then apply to the absolute CW complex through
  the instance .
* For statements, the auxiliary construction  is preferred over  as it makes
  the base case of inductions easier. The statement about  should then be derived from the
  one about .

## References
* A. Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*

spaces was defined as follows:

of the motivation for introducing .

definitions. Using the new definitions, this becomes a matter of identifying what common property
of  and  is used in the proof in question, and then proving the theorem for

# Cofiltered limits of profinite sets.

This file contains some theorems about cofiltered limits of profinite sets.

## Main Results

-  shows that any clopen set in a cofiltered limit of profinite
  sets is the pullback of a clopen set from one of the factors in the limit.
-  shows that any locally constant function from a cofiltered limit
  of profinite sets factors through one of the components.

If  is a cofiltered limit of profinite sets, then any clopen subset of  arises from
a clopen set in one of the terms in the limit.

First, we have the topological basis of the cofiltered limit obtained by pulling back
  clopen sets from the factors in the limit. By continuity, all such sets are again clopen.

Using this, since  is open, we can write  as a union of clopen sets all of which
  are preimages of clopens from the factors in the limit.

Since  is also closed, hence compact, it is covered by finitely many of the
  clopens constructed in the previous step.

We thus obtain a finite set  and a clopen set of  for each
  such that  is the union of the preimages of these clopen sets.

Since  is cofiltered, we can find a single  dominating all the .
  Pulling back all of the sets from the previous step to  and taking a union,
  we obtain a clopen set in  which works.

Conclude, using the  and the clopen set of  obtained above.

Any locally constant function from a cofiltered limit of profinite sets factors through
one of the components.

# Topological Kőnig's lemma

A topological version of Kőnig's lemma is that the inverse limit of nonempty compact Hausdorff
spaces is nonempty.  (Note: this can be generalized further to inverse limits of nonempty compact
T0 spaces, where all the maps are closed maps; see [Stone1979] --- however there is an erratum
for Theorem 4 that the element in the inverse limit can have cofinally many components that are
not closed points.)

We give this in a more general form, which is that cofiltered limits
of nonempty compact Hausdorff spaces are nonempty
().

# Clopen subsets in Cartesian products

In general, a clopen subset in a Cartesian product of topological spaces
cannot be written as a union of "clopen boxes",
i.e. products of clopen subsets of the components (see [buzyakovaClopenBox] for counterexamples).

However, when one of the factors is compact, a clopen subset can be written as such a union.
Our argument in
follows the one given in [buzyakovaClopenBox].

We deduce that in a product of compact spaces, a clopen subset is a finite union of clopen boxes,
and use that to prove that the property of having countably many clopens is preserved by taking
Cartesian products of compact spaces (this is relevant to the theory of light profinite sets).

## References

- [buzyakovaClopenBox]: *On clopen sets in Cartesian products*, 2001.
- [engelking1989]: *General Topology*, 1989.

Every clopen set in a product of two compact spaces
is a union of finitely many clopen boxes.

## Implementation notes

Parts of the formalization are based on “Ultrafilters and Topology”
by Marius Stekelenburg, particularly section 5. However the construction in the general
case is different because the equivalence relation on spaces of ultrafilters described
by Stekelenburg causes issues with universes since it involves a condition
on all compact Hausdorff spaces. We replace it by a two steps construction.
The first step called  guarantees the expected universal property but
not the Hausdorff condition. We then define  as .

In this file we will define compactly coherent spaces and the compact coherentification and prove
basic properties about them. This is a weaker version of .
These notions agree on Hausdorff spaces. They are both referred to as compactly generated spaces in
the literature while the compact coherentification is often called the k-ification.

## Main definitions
* : A compactly coherent space is a topological space in which a set  is
  open iff for every compact set , the intersection  is open in .
* : For a topological space  one can define

* : every weakly locally compact space is a
  compactly coherent space.
* : every sequential space is a compactly coherent space.
* : The compact sets of
  a topological space and its compact coherentification agree.
* : The compact
  coherentification makes any space into a compactly coherent space.

   preserves the topology on .

   to .

# Countably compact sets

A set  in a topological space is **countably compact** if every countably generated proper
filter contained in  has a cluster point in . Equivalently, every sequence in  has a
cluster point in , and every countable open cover of  admits a finite subcover.

## Main definitions

* :  is countably compact (every countably generated proper filter
  contained in  has a cluster point in ).
* : the whole space  is countably compact.

## Main results

* : for every countable open directed cover of a
  countably compact set, some single element of the cover contains the set.
* : a countably compact set has a finite subcover for
  any countable open cover.
* : countable compactness is equivalent to the
  finite subcover property for countable covers.
* : compact sets are countably compact.
* : sequentially compact sets are countably compact.
* : in a first-countable space, countable compactness implies
  sequential compactness.
* : every infinite subset of a countably compact
  set has an accumulation point in the set.
* : in a T₁ space, countable compactness is
  equivalent to the Bolzano–Weierstrass property (every infinite subset has an accumulation point).
* : a countably compact Lindelöf set is compact.
* : the continuous image of a countably compact set is countably compact.

# Delta-generated topological spaces

This file defines delta-generated spaces, as topological spaces whose topology is coinduced by all
maps from Euclidean spaces into them. This is the strongest topological property that holds for
all CW-complexes and is closed under quotients and disjoint unions; every delta-generated space is
locally path-connected, sequential and in particular compactly generated.

See .

The notions defined in this file (see also the file
 for the category )
are a particular case of the notion of -generated topological spaces where
 is a family of topological spaces (see the file
.)

by the continuous maps from topological spaces of the form .

# Connected subsets of topological spaces

In this file we define connected subsets of a topological spaces and various other properties and
classes related to connectivity.

## Main definitions

We define the following properties for sets in a topological space:

* : a nonempty set that has no non-trivial open partition.
  See also the section below in the module doc.
*  is the connected component of an element in the space.

We also have a class stating that the whole space satisfies that property:

## On the definition of connected sets/spaces

In informal mathematics, connected spaces are assumed to be nonempty.
We formalise the predicate without that assumption as .
In other words, the only difference is whether the empty space counts as connected.
There are good reasons to consider the empty space to be “too simple to be simple”
See also ,
and in particular
.

A preconnected set is one where there is no non-trivial open partition.

A connected set is one that is nonempty and where there is no non-trivial open partition.

If any point of a set is joined to a fixed point by a preconnected subset,
then the original set is preconnected as well.

then the original set is preconnected as well.

whether two sets intersect is preconnected.

whether two sets intersect is preconnected.

indexed by the vertices of a preconnected graph,
where two vertices are joined when the corresponding sets intersect.

# Locally connected topological spaces

A topological space is **locally connected** if each neighborhood filter admits a basis
of connected *open* sets. Local connectivity is equivalent to each point having a basis
of connected (not necessarily open) sets --- but in a non-trivial way, so we choose this definition
and prove the equivalence later in .

A topological space is **locally connected** if each neighborhood filter admits a basis
of connected *open* sets. Note that it is equivalent to each point having a basis of connected
(not necessarily open) sets but in a non-trivial way, so we choose this definition and prove the
equivalence later in .

Open connected neighborhoods form a basis of the neighborhoods filter.

A space with discrete topology is a locally connected space.

If a space is locally connected, the topology of its connected components is discrete.

A locally connected compact space has finitely many connected components.

# Constructible sets

This file defines constructible sets, which are morally sets in a topological space which we can
make out of finite unions and intersections of open and closed sets.

Precisely, constructible sets are the Boolean subalgebra generated by open retrocompact sets,
where a set is retrocompact if its intersection with every compact open set is compact.
In a locally Noetherian space, all sets are retrocompact, in which case this Boolean subalgebra is
simply the one generated by the open sets.

Constructible sets are useful because the image of a constructible set under a finitely presented
morphism of schemes is a constructible set (and this is *not* true at the level of varieties).

## Main declarations

* : Predicate for a set to be retrocompact, namely to have its intersection with
  every compact open be compact.
* : Predicate for a set to be constructible, namely to belong to the Boolean
  subalgebra generated by open retrocompact sets.
* : Predicate for a set to be locally constructible, namely to be
  partitionable along an open cover such that each of its parts is constructible in the
  respective open subspace.

### retrocompact sets

A retrocompact set is a set whose intersection with every compact open is compact.

### Constructible sets

A constructible set is a set that can be written as the
finite union/finite intersection/complement of open retrocompact sets.

In other words, constructible sets form the Boolean subalgebra generated by open retrocompact sets.

An induction principle for constructible sets. If  holds for all open retrocompact
sets, and is preserved under union and complement, then  holds for all constructible sets.

If  is continuous and is such that preimages of open retrocompact sets are retrocompact,
then preimages of constructible sets are constructible.

### Locally constructible sets

A set in a topological space is locally constructible, if every point has a neighborhood on
which the set is constructible.

A variant that requires constructible in the ambient space.
This is as strong as the unprimed version only when the open cover consists of retrocompact sets.

The library contains many lemmas stating that functions/operations are continuous. There are many
ways to formulate the continuity of operations. Some are more convenient than others.
Note: for the most part this note also applies to other properties
(, , , ...).

### The traditional way
As an example, let's look at addition . We can state that this is continuous
in different definitionally equal ways (omitting some typing information)
* ;
* ;
* . ( is notation for recursively uncurrying a function)

However, lemmas with this conclusion are not nice to use in practice because
1. They confuse the elaborator. The following example fails, because of limitations in the
  elaboration process.

2. If the operation has more than 2 arguments, they are impractical to use, because in your
  application the arguments in the domain might be in a different order or associated differently.

### The convenient way

A much more convenient way to write continuity lemmas is like :
The conclusion can be , which is definitionally equal.
This has the following advantages
* It supports projection notation, so is shorter to write.
*  is recognized correctly by the elaborator and gives useful new goals.
* It works generally, since the domain is a variable.
  (Having a domain  would be less convenient in general.)

As an example for a unary operation, we have .
For unary functions, the elaborator is not confused when applying the traditional lemma
(like ), but it's still convenient to have the short version available (compare
 with ).

As a harder example, consider an operation of the following type:
The precise definition is not important, only its type.

argument  that arises since  has a coercion to . The paths  and  (which
are unary functions from ) become binary functions in the continuity lemma.

### Summary
* Make sure that your continuity lemmas are stated in the most general way, and in a convenient
  form. That means that:
  - The conclusion has a variable  as domain (not something like );
  - Wherever possible, all point arguments  are replaced by functions ;
  - All -ary function arguments are replaced by -ary functions
    ( becomes );
  - All (relevant) arguments have continuity assumptions, and perhaps there are additional
    assumptions needed to make the operation continuous;
  - The function in the conclusion is fully applied.
* These remarks are mostly about the format of the *conclusion* of a continuity lemma.
  In assumptions it's fine to state that a function with more than 1 argument is continuous using
   or .

still continuous. For example, consider the fractional part of a number, .

A set of continuous maps "separates points strongly"
if for each pair of distinct points there is a function with specified values on them.

We give a slightly unusual formulation, where the specified values are given by some
function , and we ask . This avoids needing a hypothesis .

(This may need to change if we do Stone-Weierstrass on non-compact spaces,
where the functions would be continuous functions vanishing at infinity.)

# The Arzelà–Ascoli theorem for bounded continuous functions

Arzelà–Ascoli asserts that, on a compact space, a set of functions sharing a common modulus of
continuity and taking values in a compact set forms a compact subset for the topology of
uniform convergence. This file proves the theorem and several useful variations around it.

First version, with pointwise equicontinuity and range in a compact space.

We have to find a finite discretization of , i.e., finite information
   that is sufficient to reconstruct  up to . This information will be
   provided by the values of  on a sufficiently dense set ,
   slightly translated to fit in a finite -dense set  in the image. Such
   sets exist by compactness of the source and range. Then, to check that these
   data determine the function up to , one uses the control on the modulus of
   continuity to extend the closeness on tα to closeness everywhere.

For all , the set  is an open set containing  on which the elements of
   fluctuate by at most .
   We extract finitely many of these sets that cover the whole space, by compactness.

Associate to every point  in the space a nearby point  in

,
  Associate to every function a discrete approximation, mapping each point in
   to a point in  close to its true image by the function.

If two functions have the same approximation, then they are within distance

Second version, with pointwise equicontinuity and range in a compact subset.

This version is deduced from the previous one by restricting to the compact type in the target,
 using compactness there and then lifting everything to the original space.

Third (main) version, with pointwise equicontinuity and range in a compact subset, but
without closedness. The closure is then compact.

This version is deduced from the previous one by checking that the closure of , in
 addition to being closed, still satisfies the properties of compact range and equicontinuity.

# Cocompact continuous maps

The type of *cocompact continuous maps* are those which tend to the cocompact filter on the
codomain along the cocompact filter on the domain. When the domain and codomain are Hausdorff, this
is equivalent to many other conditions, including that preimages of compact sets are compact.

### Cocompact continuous maps


A *cocompact continuous map* is a continuous function between topological spaces which
tends to the cocompact filter along the cocompact filter. Functions for which preimages of compact
sets are compact always satisfy this property, and the converse holds for cocompact continuous maps
when the codomain is Hausdorff (see  and
).

Cocompact maps thus generalise proper maps, with which they correspond when the codomain is
Hausdorff.

The cocompact filter on  tends to the cocompact filter on  under the function

### Local normal convergence

A sum of continuous functions (on a locally compact space) is "locally normally convergent" if the
sum of its sup-norms on any compact subset is summable. This implies convergence in the topology
of  (i.e. locally uniform convergence).

# Equivalence between  and

If  is a connected topological space, then for every continuous map  from  to the disjoint
union of a collection of topological spaces  there exists a unique index  and a continuous
map from  to  such that  is the composition of the natural embedding
 with .

This defines an equivalence between  and . In fact, this equivalence
is a homeomorphism if the spaces of continuous maps are equipped with the compact-open topology.

## Implementation notes

There are two natural ways to talk about this result: one is to say that for each  there exist
unique  and ; another one is to define a noncomputable equivalence. We choose the second way
because it is easier to use an equivalence in applications.

  For each , we pick a function  so  and .

  We use compactness to identify a certain finitely indexed infimum of finitely indexed supremums

# Covering maps to quotients by free and properly discontinuous group actions

A function from a topological space  with an action by a discrete group to another
topological space  is a quotient covering map if it is a quotient map, the action is
continuous and transitive on fibers, and every point of  has a neighborhood whose translates
by the group elements are pairwise disjoint.

A function from a topological space  with an action by a discrete group to another
topological space  is a quotient covering map if it is a quotient map, the action is
continuous and transitive on fibers, and every point of  has a neighborhood whose translates
by the group elements are pairwise disjoint.

The group action on the domain of a quotient covering map is free.

## Main definitions

  the induced topology on  is the collection of sets
  that are preimages of some open set in .
  This is the coarsest topology that makes  continuous.

* : given  and a topology on ,
  the coinduced topology on  is defined such that
   is open if the preimage of  is open.
  This is the finest topology that makes  continuous.

* : a map  is called *inducing*,
  if the topology on the domain is equal to the induced topology.

* : a map  is called *coinducing*,
  if the topology on the codomain is equal to the coinduced topology.

* : a map  is an *embedding*,
  if it is a topology inducing map and it is injective.

* : a map  is an *open embedding*,
  if it is an embedding and its range is open.
  An open embedding is an open map.

* : a map  is an *open embedding*,
  if it is an embedding and its range is open.
  An open embedding is an open map.

* : a map  is a *quotient map*,
  if it is surjective
  and the topology on the codomain is equal to the coinduced topology.

# Sequences in topological spaces

In this file we define sequential closure, continuity, compactness etc.

## Main definitions

### Set operation
* : sequential closure of a set, the set of limits of sequences of points of ;

### Predicates

* : predicate saying that a set is sequentially closed, i.e., ;
* : predicate saying that a function is sequentially continuous, i.e.,
  for any sequence  that converges to a point , the sequence  converges to
  ;
* : predicate saying that a set is sequentially compact, i.e., every sequence
  taking values in  has a converging subsequence.

### Type classes

* : a typeclass saying that a topological space is a *Fréchet-Urysohn
  space*, i.e., the sequential closure of any set is equal to its closure.
* : a typeclass saying that a topological space is a *sequential space*, i.e.,
  any sequentially closed set in this space is closed. This condition is weaker than being a
  Fréchet-Urysohn space.
* : a typeclass saying that a topological space is sequentially compact, i.e.,
  every sequence in  has a converging subsequence.

## Tags

sequentially closed, sequentially compact, sequential space

The sequential closure of a set  in a topological space  is the set of all
which arise as limit of sequences in . Note that the sequential closure of a set is not
guaranteed to be sequentially closed.

A set  is sequentially closed if for any converging sequence  of elements of , the
limit belongs to  as well. Note that the sequential closure of a set is not guaranteed to be
sequentially closed.

A function between topological spaces is sequentially continuous if it commutes with limit of
convergent sequences.

A set  is sequentially compact if every sequence taking values in  has a
converging subsequence.

A space  is sequentially compact if every sequence in  has a
converging subsequence.

A topological space is called a *Fréchet-Urysohn space*, if the sequential closure of any set
is equal to its closure. Since one of the inclusions is trivial, we require only the non-trivial one
in the definition.

A topological space is said to be a *sequential space* if any sequentially closed set in this
space is closed. This condition is weaker than being a Fréchet-Urysohn space.

In a sequential space, a sequentially closed set is closed.

## Discreteness and compact sets

Given a topological space  together with a subset , there are two distinct concepts of
"discreteness" which may hold. These are:
  (i) Every point of  is isolated (i.e., the subset topology induced on  is the discrete
      topology).
 (ii) Every compact subset of  meets  only finitely often (i.e., the inclusion map
      tends to the cocompact filter along the cofinite filter on ).

When  is closed, the two conditions are equivalent provided  is locally compact and T1,
see .

# Functions of bounded variation

We study functions of bounded variation. In particular, we show that a bounded variation function
is a difference of monotone functions, and differentiable almost everywhere. This implies that
Lipschitz functions from the real line into finite-dimensional vector space are also differentiable
almost everywhere.

## Main definitions and results

*  is the total variation of the function  on the set , in .
*  registers that the variation of  on  is finite.
*  registers that  has finite variation on any compact
  subinterval of .
*  is the signed variation of  on , converted to .

*  states that the variation of  on  is the sum of its
  variations on  and .
*  proves that a function
  with locally bounded variation is the difference of two monotone functions.
*  shows that a Lipschitz function has locally
  bounded variation.

We also give several variations around these results.

## Implementation

We define the variation as an extended nonnegative real, to allow for infinite variation. This makes
it possible to use the complete linear order structure of . The proofs would be much
more tedious with an -valued or -valued variation, since one would always need to check
that the sets one uses are nonempty and bounded above as these are only conditionally complete.

The (extended-real-valued) variation of a function  on a set  inside a linear order is
the supremum of the sum of  over all finite increasing
sequences  in .

A function has bounded variation on a set  if its total variation there is finite.

A function has locally bounded variation on a set  if, given any interval  with
endpoints in , then the function has finite variation on .

### Basic computations of variation

The variation can be expressed using strictly monotone functions. This formulation is
often less convenient than the one with monotone functions as it involves dependent types, but
it is sometimes handy.
